citation: Professional Football Athletic Trainers Society. NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update - January 2023. Sports Science Research Update. 2023.
abstract: The January 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update is a practitioner-facing research digest covering 18 recent papers and commentaries relevant to professional football medicine, performance, and athlete care. Topics include adolescent/team-sport sleep timing, adductor and hamstring prevention, sport-related concussion biomarkers, hamstring return-to-sport testing, mindfulness and mental health, compression recovery, repeated-sprint fatigue mechanics, neurological readiness monitoring, genetic associations with muscle injury, hamstring injury epidemiology, sprint force profiling, COVID-19 cardiac return-to-play screening, NFL retiree neurocognitive outcomes, placebo/media effects in cannabis pain trials, late-night competition sleep architecture, anti-doping peptide detection, and vibration therapy. For football staff, the issue clusters around hamstring/adductor injury risk, sprint exposure and mechanics, sleep/recovery decision-making, concussion assessment, and cautious interpretation of emerging diagnostics.
tldr: January's digest reinforces that hamstring and groin management need more than isolated strength scores: sprint mechanics, fatigue response, exposure history, sleep, recovery tools, and concussion/medical context all shape availability decisions.
methods: Secondary monthly evidence digest rather than an original experimental study. The PDF compiles titles, citations, abstracts, study designs, results, conclusions, strengths, limitations, and commentary from recently published sport science and sports medicine papers. Included designs span crossover sleep studies, surveys, prospective and cross-sectional cohorts, systematic reviews/meta-analyses, laboratory sprint testing, case series, clinical commentaries, and diagnostic biomarker studies.
findings:
- A delayed evening meal 1.5 hours before bedtime improved total sleep time and sleep efficiency in young rugby players compared with dinner 3.5 hours before bed.
- Norwegian professional soccer teams widely adopted the Adductor Strengthening Program, but most modified the original protocol, highlighting the gap between evidence-based programming and real-world delivery.
- CARE Consortium proteomics suggested EPB41 and alpha-synuclein may help discriminate sport-related concussion after 6 hours, but this remains an emerging diagnostic area.
- In 60 NCAA Division I athletes returning from hamstring strain, NordBord eccentric strength and asymmetry at RTS did not distinguish those who reinjured within 1 or 3 months.
- Repeated sprint fatigue reduced horizontal power and changed trunk, hip, and knee mechanics differently by athlete; some patterns implied higher hamstring strain while others did not.
- A systematic review/meta-analysis of field team sports reported hamstring injuries at 0.81 per 1000 exposure hours, about 10% of all injuries, with higher incidence in matches than training.
- COVID-19 RTP screening in competitive athletes found low myocarditis prevalence but a notable rate of uncommon PVCs, supporting targeted cardiac follow-up when indicated.
- The digest also flags mindfulness, compression, vibration, sleep architecture, placebo effects, and anti-doping analytics as adjunct areas that require disciplined interpretation before operational use.
limitations: This is a curated digest and does not report a single search strategy, inclusion criteria, risk-of-bias framework, or pooled analysis across all included papers. The evidence base mixes sports, ages, competitive levels, and study designs, so translation to Power Five American football requires judgment. Many included studies are small, observational, or from soccer/rugby rather than American football. The digest summarizes published abstracts and selected details, so staff should consult original papers before changing policy.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the strongest operational themes are to combine hamstring/adductor strength testing with sprint exposure history, individual fatigue mechanics, and field progression; avoid over-relying on a single NordBord or asymmetry cutoff at RTP; treat sleep timing and late competition routines as modifiable recovery levers; and keep emerging concussion biomarkers or recovery modalities as research-informed adjuncts rather than stand-alone clearance tools.
athleteDev: Build athlete development around robust posterior-chain capacity, progressive high-speed running, groin strength adherence, individualized sprint mechanics under fatigue, and consistent sleep/recovery habits. DB, WR, RB, LB, and specialists should receive regular sprint-force and hamstring monitoring, while larger positions still need posterior-chain resilience and recovery education matched to their role demands.
rtp: The issue supports criteria-based RTP for hamstring and concussion cases. Hamstring RTP should include pain-free function, eccentric and rapid-force testing, sprint mechanics, repeated-sprint tolerance, and position-specific exposure rather than isolated strength symmetry. Concussion RTP should remain protocol-driven, with biomarkers viewed as investigational and cardiac/COVID-19 screening targeted to symptoms, history, and abnormal findings.

citation: Professional Football Athletic Trainers Society. NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update - July 2023. Sports Science Research Update. 2023.
abstract: The July 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update summarizes 17 recent papers relevant to football performance, injury risk, and clinical decision-making. Major topics include eccentric-only and accentuated eccentric training technology, turf versus grass injury risk, return-to-play timing analysis, load management definitions, NFL lower extremity strains, MRI findings in NFL ACL tears, American football injury bibliometrics, NFL Combine predictive validity, CARE Consortium concussion symptom clusters, ramping isometrics after hamstring tendon repair, upper-extremity injury risk after concussion, rugby safety systems, repeated-sprint training demands, mental fatigue effects, open science for prediction models, topical cannabidiol tolerability, and the limitations of publicly obtained sports medicine data. The issue is especially useful for football staffs because it combines NFL-specific epidemiology with applied rehab, monitoring, and research-quality cautions.
tldr: July's digest is a football operations-heavy issue: lower-extremity strain burden, special teams risk, ACL surface questions, concussion symptom profiling, Combine interpretation, and better load-management language all matter for availability planning.
methods: Secondary evidence digest summarizing recent peer-reviewed studies, consensus/commentary pieces, systematic reviews, epidemiology studies, and case reports. The update does not perform its own meta-analysis; it reproduces and condenses methods and conclusions from the included publications. Notable included methods include NFL electronic health record epidemiology, systematic reviews, CARE Consortium cross-sectional concussion analysis, Delphi consensus/commentary, and an elite rugby hamstring tendon repair case study.
findings:
- NFL lower extremity strain data from 2015-2019 identified 5780 strains among 2769 players; 69% caused time loss, hamstrings made up 54.7%, and the estimated burden was 16,748 missed participation days per year.
- Defensive secondary players accounted for the largest share of time-loss lower extremity strains, and punt plays showed the highest game strain rate in the NFL strain study.
- The football-surface systematic review and NFL ACL/MRI papers keep surface, mechanism, and tissue presentation on the agenda, but the digest emphasizes interpretation rather than simple grass-versus-turf conclusions.
- A systematic review of NFL Combine validity found 68 eligible articles with mixed evidence that Combine tests, medical findings, draft position, and performance measures predict long-term success.
- CARE Consortium concussion work identified vestibular-cognitive, migrainous, cognitive fatigue, and affective acute symptom clusters; delayed reporting, less sleep, female sex, practice/training injury, depression, amnesia, and migraine history related to symptom patterns.
- A hamstring tendon repair case study reported return to team training at 10 weeks and RTP at 12 weeks after early low-jerk ramping isometrics, without reinjury across the remaining two seasons.
- Repeated-sprint training, mental fatigue, and load-management papers point toward clearer session intent, better monitoring language, and avoiding vague 'load' explanations.
- Open science and public-data reviews warn that prediction models and publicly sourced injury studies can mislead when methods, missingness, and definitions are not transparent.
limitations: As a digest, this PDF is not a formal systematic review of all July-relevant evidence and does not grade certainty across included papers. Some included work uses NFL data, while other papers come from rugby, collegiate athletes, military cohorts, or general team-sport samples. Case reports and commentaries are hypothesis-generating. Publicly obtained NFL studies may undercapture injuries compared with league medical databases. Findings should be integrated with Baylor's own injury surveillance, exposure data, and medical governance.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, this issue supports a sharper availability dashboard: track lower-extremity strains by position, period, drill type, and special teams exposure; treat punts and high-speed transition roles as specific risk contexts; define load management in terms of planned exposure, recovery, and performance goals; use concussion symptom clusters to guide referral and rehab emphasis; and be cautious about over-weighting Combine scores or public-injury datasets in personnel or medical decisions.
athleteDev: The athlete development message is to prepare players for the real high-risk actions of football: repeated sprinting, eccentric braking, special teams coverage, defensive back transition work, and contact-related ACL scenarios. CARE/eccentric technologies and ramping isometrics may be useful tools, but they should sit inside a broader progression that includes strength, tissue tolerance, sprint exposure, deceleration quality, sleep, and cognitive freshness.
rtp: RTP decisions should be criteria-based and role-specific. Hamstring tendon and strain cases may benefit from carefully progressed ramping isometrics, then sprint and position exposure. Concussion RTP should account for symptom cluster, sleep, prior history, and subsequent musculoskeletal risk. For ACL and lower-extremity injuries, staff should verify that players tolerate football-specific deceleration, contact, and special teams demands before full clearance.

citation: Professional Football Athletic Trainers Society. NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update - March 2023. Sports Science Research Update. 2023.
abstract: The March 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update is a 22-article digest focused on player availability, injury mechanisms, rehabilitation evidence, readiness monitoring, sleep, workload, and NFL-specific injury trends. Included topics cover availability as a team performance determinant, acute adductor injury, athlete suicide risk, COVID-era NFL injuries, biceps femoris architecture after repeated sprints, NFL ACL injury surface risk, conservative hamstring rehab evidence, contact/collision sport gait, hamstring active stiffness under fatigue, Achilles rupture epidemiology, Lisfranc snap counts, neuromechanics of rate of force development, nutrition and sleep, sleep-tracking technology, NFL injury rates after the shortened 2020 preseason, repeated sprint/jump/thermography relationships, concurrent training timing after simulated match play, CMJ strategy after injury, NFL ACL video mechanisms, biologics consensus among NFL physicians, acute:chronic workload ratio windows, and weekly external load effects.
tldr: March's digest centers on availability: build systems that reduce preventable soft-tissue and ACL risk, respect fatigue and recovery timing, use workload metrics carefully, and avoid treating biologics or wearables as magic answers.
methods: Secondary monthly research update summarizing individual papers and commentaries. Included evidence ranges from systematic reviews, living reviews, consensus statements, epidemiology and video-analysis studies, laboratory neuromechanics papers, observational workload analyses, and applied sleep/readiness technology discussions. The PDF itself does not pool results or apply an independent risk-of-bias rating across all papers.
findings:
- The player availability commentary frames team success as the product of health, tactical/technical capacity, neuromuscular readiness, cognition, emotion, and long-term preparation rather than isolated fitness traits.
- NFL ACL surface data from 2017-2021 found a trend toward higher ACL injury rate on non-natural surfaces versus grass, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
- A living systematic review of conservative acute hamstring interventions included 14 studies and found an evidence base limited by high or critical risk of bias in many trials.
- NFL ACL video review found deceleration in 60% of available injury videos, contact in 58%, valgus collapse in 53%, and DB/WR as frequently represented positions.
- The biologics Delphi consensus among NFL team physicians reached 47 statements, supporting PRP for patellar tendinopathy and early osteoarthritis symptoms while warning against unproven cell therapies marketed as stem cells.
- The shortened/COVID-era NFL preseason, Achilles rupture, Lisfranc, and workload papers keep the focus on how preparation, exposure progression, and schedule disruption can influence injury surveillance.
- Rate-of-force-development neuromechanics, fatigue-related hamstring stiffness, CMJ strategy, and repeated-sprint data reinforce that force quality and movement strategy can change before gross performance markers fail.
- Sleep nutrition and wearable sleep-tracking papers support practical sleep intervention while warning that consumer technology needs context and validation.
limitations: This is a broad digest, not a single controlled study. Evidence quality varies widely across included papers. Several findings come from soccer, rugby, or mixed athlete samples, while NFL-specific papers often rely on public reports, retrospective data, or limited available video. Workload metrics and surface comparisons are vulnerable to exposure definition, confounding, and missing context. Baylor staff should treat the issue as a scanning tool and verify original studies before changing protocols.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the issue supports integrated availability meetings where medical, performance, nutrition, and coaching staff review exposure progression, high-risk positions/actions, sleep/recovery status, and tissue-specific rehab criteria. It also argues for precise language around workload, cautious biologics governance, structured sprint and deceleration progressions, and a local injury database that can answer Baylor-specific questions better than public NFL data.
athleteDev: Development should emphasize rate of force development, eccentric hamstring/adductor strength, deceleration and contact mechanics, progressive sprint exposure, sleep routines, and individualized readiness monitoring. DBs, WRs, RBs, and LBs need repeated exposure to shallow-flexion deceleration and transition tasks under fatigue; linemen and larger athletes still need tissue-specific progressions after schedule disruptions or altered preseason loads.
rtp: RTP themes include criteria-based hamstring rehab, careful ACL mechanism replication before clearance, workload ramping after disrupted preparation, and skepticism toward passive modalities or biologics as substitutes for function. Objective testing should include strength, RFD or explosive capacity when relevant, CMJ/movement strategy, sprint/COD exposure, sleep/recovery context, and position-specific contact demands.

citation: Professional Football Athletic Trainers Society. NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update - May 2023. Sports Science Research Update. 2023.
abstract: The May 2023 NFL-PFATS Sports Science Research Update summarizes 18 papers and letters spanning emergency response, recovery modalities, hamstring prevention, speed exposure, gluteal loading, rugby hamstring mechanics, nutrition during musculoskeletal rehabilitation, wearable heat-injury prediction, Damar Hamlin-related public interest, NFL Lisfranc RTP and economic impact, distal biceps repair, beta-alanine safety, media effects on CTE research, the Deceleration Index, hip cam/pincer morphology and hamstring injury, COVID-19 effects on NFL performance, consumer sleep technology, and validity concerns with publicly obtained NFL concussion data. The issue is especially relevant to football staffs managing heat, hamstring exposure, return-to-play economics, emergency preparedness, and the quality of data used for medical decisions.
tldr: May's digest links emergency readiness with day-to-day availability work: near-max speed exposure, heat-risk prediction, rehab nutrition, deceleration metrics, and public-data caution all have practical football consequences.
methods: Secondary monthly digest summarizing abstracts and key details from recent research articles, reviews, letters, and commentaries. Designs represented include observational cohort studies, systematic/integrative reviews, chamber validation of wearable prediction, public-data analyses, biomechanical modeling, current concepts reviews, and expert commentary. The update itself does not run a new statistical analysis.
findings:
- The Damar Hamlin cardiac arrest article highlights Chain of Survival execution, neurologic prognostication, and neurorehabilitation as core emergency-care lessons.
- Elite football/soccer data from 36 team-seasons suggested that programming greater than 95% maximal sprint speed exposures at D-2 was associated with no match hamstring injuries in observed turnarounds, while injuries still occurred when athletes had no or lower speed exposure.
- The 2B-Cool wearable/predictive system showed good agreement with measured core temperature, 98% sensitivity, 81% specificity, and about a 35-minute warning horizon for a 38.5 C threshold in a heat chamber study.
- The nutrition rehabilitation review supports adequate energy, protein, creatine, omega-3, vitamin D/calcium when indicated, and targeted anti-inflammatory strategies during musculoskeletal injury recovery.
- NFL Lisfranc and distal biceps papers keep surgical RTP, performance, and economic burden visible for football medical planning.
- The Deceleration Index commentary promotes measuring braking demands as a missing link between rehab and field sport performance.
- The public-data concussion review found publicly obtained NFL concussion studies captured about 70% of medically reported concussions on average and misrepresented some play and position distributions.
- Consumer sleep tech, CTE media analysis, beta-alanine safety, and CBD/recovery-related items reinforce the need for evidence hierarchy and clear communication with athletes.
limitations: The digest combines different sports, populations, and evidence levels. Some hamstring speed-exposure findings are observational and from soccer, not American football. Wearable heat prediction was validated in a controlled chamber with young adults, so field, equipment, and practice-condition generalizability require local validation. Public NFL data can miss injuries and distort distributions. The PDF is best used as a curated alerting document rather than a protocol by itself.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, this issue supports rehearsed emergency action plans, individualized heat monitoring during camp, planned near-max speed exposures rather than accidental sprint deprivation, nutrition support embedded in rehab, and deceleration metrics for bridging weight room, rehab, and field work. It also warns staff not to base concussion or injury policy solely on public reporting when internal medical data are available.
athleteDev: Athlete development should include routine exposure to high-speed running, braking, hip/glute strength, hamstring length-tension demands, hydration/heat education, and nutrition habits that preserve lean mass during rehab. Players should be familiar with emergency and recovery routines before crises or injuries occur, making compliance and communication easier under pressure.
rtp: RTP implications are strongest for hamstring, heat illness, Lisfranc, distal biceps, and post-emergency care. Hamstring RTP should include near-max speed progression and deceleration tolerance; heat-risk RTP should use symptoms, environmental load, physiologic response, and gradual re-acclimatization; post-surgical foot/upper-extremity RTP should include role-specific contact and performance benchmarks; and concussion decisions should rely on validated internal medical assessment rather than incomplete public data.

citation: Okonkwo DO, Mares A, Wasserman EB, Shrestha R, Terry DP, Solomon G, Sills A, Eagle SR. No Association Between Fencing Response After Concussion and Recovery Time, Concussion Severity, or Clinical Outcomes in Professional American Football Players. Neurosurgery. 2025;00:1-8.
abstract: This case-control study tested whether tonic posturing/fencing response after concussion was associated with recovery time, concussion severity, or clinical outcomes in professional American football players. NFL in-game concussions from the 2018-2023 preseasons and regular seasons were reviewed. Fifty-seven players with documented fencing response were matched 1:2 to 112 players without documented fencing response by age, position, and concussion history. Primary outcome was days until return to full football participation; secondary outcomes included day-of-injury SAC and mBESS scores and SCAT-5 symptom scores through postinjury day 10. Median return to full participation was 10 days with fencing response and 9 days without fencing response (P=.16), with no hazard difference for return time (P=.34). SAC, mBESS, and symptom recovery trajectories also did not differ. Wide receivers and defensive backs represented more than 60% of documented fencing-response cases.
tldr: In NFL players, a visible fencing response after concussion looked dramatic but did not predict slower return, worse day-of-injury SAC/mBESS scores, or higher symptom burden compared with matched concussions without fencing response.
methods: Case-control study using the NFL injury analytics database and electronic medical records for in-game preseason and regular-season concussions from 2018-2023. Unaffiliated neurotrauma consultant reports identified documented fencing response; questionable/probable cases were excluded. Each fencing-response concussion was matched to two non-fencing concussions by age, position, and prior NFL concussion history when possible. Outcomes were days to full participation, SAC, mBESS, and SCAT-5 symptom scores. Analyses used nonparametric independent-samples median tests, Kaplan-Meier/log-rank survival analysis for return time, and linear mixed-effects modeling of log-transformed SCAT-5 symptom scores.
findings:
- 983 preseason/regular-season game concussions occurred during the observation period; 57 (5.8%) had documented fencing response.
- Final sample included 57 fencing-response cases and 112 matched non-fencing controls.
- Nearly two-thirds of fencing-response cases were defensive backs or wide receivers.
- Median days to full participation were 10.0 (IQR 5.5-16.0) with fencing response and 9.0 (IQR 5.3-16.0) without fencing response; the between-group difference was not significant (P=.16).
- Kaplan-Meier analysis found no significant change in return-to-participation hazard associated with fencing response (chi-square=0.91; P=.34).
- Day-of-injury SAC subscores and total score did not differ significantly between groups (reported P range .18-.99), and mBESS medians were both 4 (P=.87).
- SCAT-5 total symptom scores over day of injury through postinjury day 10 did not differ by group (P=.92).
- The authors concluded that fencing response was not associated with symptom recovery, concussion severity, or short-term recovery in professional American football.
limitations: Return time may be affected by team schedule or bye weeks, which were not controlled. Additional clinical measures such as serial formal neurocognitive testing and vestibular/ocular motor testing were unavailable. SAC and mBESS are screening tools with known limitations. Practice concussions were not included. Fencing response classification depended on observed, video-reviewed, and documented medical reports, so some non-documented responses may have been missed. Mechanism, head impact forces, prior history of fencing response, and long-term outcomes were unavailable. Generalizability is limited to NFL players under a highly resourced concussion protocol.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, a fencing response should still trigger immediate concussion recognition, removal, emergency assessment, and protocol-driven care, but staff should avoid assuming the sign alone means a longer recovery or worse short-term outcome. Communication with coaches, players, and families can be calmer and evidence-based: the presentation is serious because it is a concussion sign, not because it independently predicts poor recovery in this NFL dataset.
athleteDev: The position distribution suggests high-speed collision roles such as WR and DB deserve continued emphasis on technique, spatial awareness, neck/trunk strength, and concussion education. Athlete development staff should reinforce early symptom reporting and sleep/recovery behaviors after head impacts, while avoiding stigma that a dramatic acute sign automatically means the athlete is fragile or permanently impaired.
rtp: RTP should follow the established concussion protocol and individualized clinical progression, not the presence or absence of fencing response alone. Clearance should require symptom resolution, neurologic exam normalization, cognitive/balance recovery, exertional progression, medical review, and sport-specific reintegration. The study supports using fencing response as an acute recognition sign, not as an independent timeline-setting criterion.

citation: Lolli L, Bahr R, Weston M, Whiteley R, Tabben M, Bonanno D, Gregson W, Chamari K, Di Salvo V, van Dyk N. No association between perceived exertion and session duration with hamstring injury occurrence in professional football. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;00:1-8. doi:10.1111/sms.13591
abstract: This exploratory study examined whether perceived exertion and session duration were associated with acute hamstring injury occurrence in professional football. Thirty outfield Qatar Stars League players with valid load and injury data across three seasons were included. The authors calculated average RPE, average session-RPE, cumulative minutes, cumulative session-RPE, and week-to-week changes across 7-, 14-, 21-, and 28-day windows, then used conditional logistic regression to compare each injured player's load before injury with that player's own non-injury periods. Corrected odds ratios for all candidate load variables were not practically important, with confidence intervals generally near null values. The authors concluded that perceived exertion and session duration remain useful for load management, but these measures alone were not empirically supported as hamstring injury risk determinants.
tldr: In pro soccer, RPE, session duration, and session-RPE over common weekly windows did not meaningfully distinguish hamstring injury periods from normal periods within the same player.
methods: Retrospective analysis of prospectively collected Qatar Stars League injury surveillance and load-monitoring data from May 2015 to February 2018. Acute traumatic hamstring injuries causing more than 3 days lost were clinically confirmed; recurrent injuries were excluded from primary analysis. Session duration and Borg CR-10 RPE were collected after training and matches, with session-RPE calculated as duration x RPE. Exposure variables were summarized across 7-, 14-, 21-, and 28-day windows plus week-to-week changes. Conditional fixed-effects logistic regression modeled injury odds per 2 within-player SD increase, using each injured player as his own control.
findings:
- Thirty outfield players met inclusion criteria; median hamstring time loss was 18 days.
- Corrected odds ratios for average RPE, cumulative duration, average session-RPE, cumulative session-RPE, and week-to-week changes were not practically important across 7-, 14-, 21-, or 28-day windows.
- The 95% confidence intervals were close to null and did not support a clinically useful load-hamstring injury relationship for these internal-load measures.
- The study challenged broad load-injury claims when injury type, within-athlete comparison, and continuous modeling are handled more carefully.
- The authors still emphasized that load monitoring is valuable for player management, just not sufficient for type-specific hamstring risk prediction.
limitations: Small effective sample after large data loss; no formal a priori sample size was possible; RPE is a global perceptual measure and may miss local hamstring-specific stress; differential RPE and external-load variables such as sprinting were not primary exposures; match and training demands may need clearer separation; the cohort was mainly Middle-East professional soccer players, limiting transfer to NCAA American football.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, do not treat high session-RPE, total minutes, or week-to-week RPE changes as stand-alone hamstring injury alarms. Keep using RPE to manage total stress, communication, and recovery, but pair it with sprint exposure, high-speed running, position demands, eccentric strength, prior injury history, soreness reports, and technical/mechanical review when making hamstring-risk decisions.
athleteDev: The paper supports building robust hamstring preparation rather than simply chasing load thresholds. For skill players and specialists, athlete development should combine progressive sprint exposure, eccentric hamstring strength, high-speed mechanics, tissue capacity, and individualized recovery patterns while using RPE as one context marker.
rtp: Not an RTP study. Its RTP relevance is cautionary: session duration and RPE should not be used alone to decide return to high-speed running or full practice after hamstring injury. RTP decisions should include symptoms, strength, sprint mechanics, high-speed progression, prior injury context, and on-field tolerance.

citation: van Dyk N, Bahr R, Burnett AF, Verhagen E, von Tiggelen D, Witvrouw E. No association between rate of torque development and onset of muscle activity with increased risk of hamstring injury in elite football. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018;00:1-11. doi:10.1111/sms.13224
abstract: This prospective cohort study tested whether hamstring rate of torque development and timing of muscle activity onset during isokinetic testing predicted future hamstring injury in elite male football players. Players from 18 Qatar Stars League teams completed annual periodic health evaluations across two seasons, including isokinetic knee flexion/extension testing with synchronized surface EMG of the biceps femoris and medial hamstrings. A total of 367 unique players contributed 514 player-seasons and sustained 65 hamstring injuries. There were no significant differences in muscle activity onset or rate of torque development between injured and uninjured limbs or between injured and uninjured players, and Cox models showed no meaningful association with future injury. The authors concluded that these measures are unsupported as screening tools for hamstring injury risk.
tldr: One-off isokinetic RTD and hamstring EMG onset testing did not identify elite soccer players who later sustained hamstring injuries.
methods: Prospective cohort across two Qatar Stars League seasons. Eligible adult players completed preseason or periodic health evaluation testing on a Biodex dynamometer with surface EMG over medial hamstrings and biceps femoris. Testing included concentric knee flexion/extension at 60 and 300 degrees/s and eccentric knee extension at 60 degrees/s. RTD was calculated over 30, 50, and 100 ms from contraction onset; EMG onset was detected relative to torque onset. Team medical staff prospectively recorded training/match exposure and clinically confirmed acute hamstring injuries. Analyses compared injured and uninjured limbs and used Cox regression for injury risk.
findings:
- The cohort included 367 unique players and 65 hamstring injuries.
- No significant differences were found in onset of muscle activity between injured and uninjured players for biceps femoris or medial hamstrings.
- No significant differences were found for RTD across contraction modes or early time windows; effect sizes were small, generally below d=0.3.
- Cox regression did not support EMG onset or RTD as future hamstring injury predictors.
- The authors interpreted prior retrospective deficits as more likely consequences of hamstring injury than pre-injury causes.
- Once-off periodic testing during the season was not valuable for identifying players at risk.
limitations: Although large for this topic, 65 injuries may still be underpowered for small associations; isokinetic seated testing does not replicate sprinting, cutting, or football-specific hamstring loading; dynamometer lag limits precision for EMG onset; fatigue and language/comprehension differences may have affected maximal efforts; repeated measures across a season may not reflect player status at injury time; results are from elite male soccer in Qatar and may not generalize to American football, female athletes, or youth players.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, do not invest in hamstring RTD plus surface EMG onset as a primary preseason screen for who will pull a hamstring. These tests may still help profile neuromuscular recovery or identify deficits after injury, but injury-risk decisions should prioritize a broader model: previous injury, sprint exposure, strength, fascicle/tendon qualities where available, fatigue, mechanics, and football workload.
athleteDev: Rapid force and coordinated hamstring activation still matter for sprinting and deceleration development, but this paper argues against using one lab snapshot as a risk label. Build RTD through progressive sprinting, resisted sprinting, eccentric work, hip extension strength, and high-speed skill exposures, then evaluate whether athletes can express those qualities in football-specific tasks.
rtp: Directly relevant to hamstring rehabilitation. Deficits in RTD and activation may be post-injury consequences, so restoring rapid torque production and biceps femoris function can be useful during RTP. However, passing a once-off RTD or EMG test should not be treated as proof of low recurrence risk without sprint progression and field-based criteria.

citation: Bellinger PM, Ferguson C, Newans T, Minahan CL. No Influence of Prematch Subjective Wellness Ratings on External Load During Elite Australian Football Match Play. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020;(Ahead of Print):1-7. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2019-0395
abstract: This retrospective observational study examined whether prematch subjective wellness influenced external match load in elite Australian football. Thirty-four elite male AFL players from one team completed wellness questionnaires before, on, and after matches across two seasons, producing 460 match observations and 1840 wellness entries. Wellness items included mood, energy, stress, leg heaviness, muscle soreness, sleep quality, hours slept, and total wellness, expressed as within-player z scores. GPS and accelerometer data quantified relative distance, high-speed distance, PlayerLoad, and directional PlayerLoad metrics. Linear mixed models showed trivial effects of match-day wellness on subsequent external match load. Match result and PlayerLoad in the anteroposterior vector were associated with next-day wellness, suggesting match context and movement demands affected perceived recovery more than prematch wellness affected match output.
tldr: In AFL match play, players' prematch wellness scores did not meaningfully predict how much external load they produced, likely because normal 6- to 8-day match cycles restored wellness by game day.
methods: Retrospective two-season AFL study in 34 elite male players with at least 20 AFL matches and at least 75% match time in included games. Players completed mobile wellness questionnaires at -3, -2, -1, match day, and +1 to +3 days around matches. GPS at 10 Hz and accelerometers at 100 Hz measured relative distance, high-speed distance, total PlayerLoad, PlayerLoadSLOW, 2D PlayerLoad, and anteroposterior, mediolateral, and vertical PlayerLoad per minute. Linear mixed models evaluated wellness, match result, location, and between-match recovery duration, with player and match as random effects.
findings:
- Match-day total wellness and individual wellness items had trivial effects on all external match-load metrics.
- Wellness was lowest on the day after matches and generally improved toward match day across 6-, 7-, and 8-day microcycles.
- A win was associated with a 0.30 z-score increase in next-day subjective wellness.
- Each 1-unit increase in PlayerLoadAP per minute was associated with a 0.15 z-score reduction in next-day wellness.
- Higher high-speed distance was associated with higher next-day wellness, possibly reflecting less contested or less physically damaging matches.
- The authors still recommended wellness monitoring using individual-relative changes rather than raw group thresholds.
limitations: Single elite AFL team; retrospective design; the wellness questionnaire was practical but not rigorously validated for reliability and validity; training load prescription was not controlled; AFL match cycles and substitution rules differ from college American football; wellness had little variation by match day, so findings may not apply to short turnarounds, travel stress, heat, illness, or congested schedules.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, a low or high wellness score should not automatically imply an athlete will produce less game load. Wellness is still useful for identifying recovery problems and guiding the practice week, but game-day role, competitive context, position rotation, and tactical demands may override self-reported readiness. Use individual z-score changes and follow up with conversation rather than rigid cutoffs.
athleteDev: Daily wellness can help teach athletes to connect sleep, soreness, stress, and recovery behaviors to the training week. It is most actionable when paired with GPS, practice intensity, lift outputs, and staff notes, especially for developing players learning how to recover between high-contact or high-speed exposures.
rtp: Wellness should support, not replace, RTP decision-making. A returning athlete who reports good match-day wellness may still need objective exposure progression, strength testing, position-specific movement, and contact tolerance. Conversely, poor wellness after a game or practice can flag the need to slow the next progression.

citation: Smith NA, Bourne MN, Franettovich Smith MM, Barrett RS, Hides JA. Nordic strength and history of hamstring injury in Australian Football League players. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2022;57:11-16. doi:10.1016/j.ptsp.2022.06.006
abstract: This cross-sectional retrospective study compared Nordic hamstring strength in AFL players with and without a history of hamstring injury. One hundred twenty-four players from three clubs were recruited, with exclusions for other lower-limb or lumbopelvic injuries. Players completed a self-reported hamstring injury history questionnaire and bilateral Nordic Hamstring Exercise strength testing on a Nordbord. After grouping, 43 players with complete data had no prior hamstring injury and 15 had complete data with prior hamstring injury. Nineteen hamstring injuries were reported overall. Nordic strength, relative strength, and between-limb asymmetry did not differ significantly between previously injured and uninjured players. Injury number, recency, and severity also did not significantly influence strength. The authors concluded that these elite AFL players did not show residual Nordic strength deficits after prior hamstring injury.
tldr: In modern AFL players, prior hamstring injury did not automatically mean lower Nordic strength or meaningful asymmetry, possibly reflecting stronger rehabilitation and prevention practices.
methods: Cross-sectional retrospective study in AFL players from three clubs. Players completed self-reported injury history, including injured leg, time since injury, return-to-play time, and matches missed. Prior hamstring injury was defined as an acute non-contact hamstring injury during AFL training or play, diagnosed by club medical staff, causing at least one missed match. Nordic strength was assessed bilaterally during three maximal Nordic Hamstring Exercise repetitions on a Nordbord. Analyses compared no-injury and hamstring-injury groups, then injury subgroups by single versus multiple injuries, less than or equal to 1 year versus more than 1 year since injury, and less than or equal to 3 versus more than 3 matches missed.
findings:
- No significant Nordic strength differences were found between uninjured players and players with prior hamstring injury in absolute or body-mass-relative terms.
- No significant asymmetry differences were found between groups.
- Previously injured limbs were not significantly weaker than contralateral uninjured limbs.
- Number of prior injuries, recency of injury, and severity based on matches missed did not significantly affect Nordic strength or asymmetry.
- Previously injured players were older, but age adjustment did not change the strength findings.
- The authors suggested improved hamstring strengthening and rehabilitation practices in AFL may explain higher strength values and lack of residual deficits.
limitations: Small number of players with complete prior-injury data and very small subgroup sizes, increasing type II error risk; hamstring injury history relied on self-report and recall; training and rehabilitation history were not controlled; data came from elite AFL players and may not transfer to lower-level athletes; testing occurred across four sites with different assessors and devices, although Nordbord reliability is generally high.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, do not assume an athlete with prior hamstring injury is currently weak on Nordic testing. Measure it. If Nordic strength and asymmetry are normal, the remaining risk may sit elsewhere: sprint exposure history, tissue architecture, fatigue, mechanics, position demands, prior injury recency, or incomplete football-specific reconditioning.
athleteDev: This supports keeping Nordic strength as a standing development quality for speed-position athletes, not only as a rehab tool. Strong team norms and regular exposure may reduce persistent deficits after injury, but Nordics should be one part of a broader posterior-chain and sprint-development plan.
rtp: Useful for RTP benchmarking after hamstring injury. Athletes should restore Nordic strength and symmetry toward individual or position norms, but normal Nordbord values do not guarantee readiness for maximal sprinting, reactive cuts, or return to contact. Field progression remains essential.

citation: Havira P, Brewer BW, Van Raalte JL, Jennison D, France TJ III. Not much I in Team: Content analysis of pregame speeches in American football. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2023;1-8. doi:10.1177/17479541231165135
abstract: This descriptive content-analysis study examined the content, delivery, and context of American football pregame speeches. Researchers identified 127 complete, audible, visually clear speeches on YouTube, including 77 high school, 37 intercollegiate, and 13 cinematic speeches. Speeches were transcribed, coded with a custom descriptive/verbal content system, and analyzed with LIWC2015 software. Actual speeches typically lasted about two minutes, were usually delivered by coaches in locker rooms, and commonly included repeated words, questioning, game instructions, references to opponents, team past, and the physical environment. Compared with natural speech, football pregame speeches used more analytical, confident, collective, motivational, emotional, and future-oriented language, with relatively less first-person singular language. The authors concluded that pregame speeches are a distinct communication form tailored to the moment before competition.
tldr: Real football pregame speeches are short, collective, confident, emotionally charged, and instruction-linked, with more 'we/you/team' language than ordinary speech.
methods: Video clips of American football pregame speeches were identified on YouTube using the search term 'football pregame speech' on January 1, 2018. Complete, audible, visually available speeches were downloaded and transcribed; incomplete, inaudible, or visually unclear clips were excluded. A custom coding system captured 16 descriptive and verbal content variables such as speaker, setting, opponent references, game instructions, questioning, repeated phrases, metaphor, and anecdote. LIWC2015 quantified analytical thinking, clout, authenticity, emotional tone, pronouns, emotion, drives, time focus, and swear words. Chi-square tests, MANOVAs, and one-sample t-tests compared actual speeches with cinematic speeches, high school with intercollegiate speeches, and actual speeches with natural speech norms.
findings:
- Actual pregame speeches averaged about 123 seconds and were most often delivered by coaches in locker rooms.
- Common actual-speech features included repeated words, game instructions, questioning, opponent references, team-past references, and environmental references.
- Actual speeches differed from natural speech on 14 of 17 LIWC variables, indicating a distinct communication style.
- Compared with natural speech, actual speeches showed higher analytical thinking, clout, we, you, they, negative emotion, drives, and future focus, and lower I, he/she, compare, positive emotion, and emotional tone.
- High school and intercollegiate speeches were broadly similar, though intercollegiate speeches used more we, positive emotion, negative emotion, present focus, and swear words.
- Actual and cinematic speeches were similar on LIWC variables, but actual speeches included more football- and team-specific references and fewer metaphors.
limitations: Speeches were limited to public YouTube clips and may not represent all team environments; the presence of cameras may have changed speaker behavior; findings may not generalize to professional, youth, female, or non-football teams; the study was descriptive and did not measure athlete motivation, physiology, execution, or performance outcomes; no causal claim can be made about what speech style improves play.
practicalImplications: For Baylor football, the study supports pregame communication that is brief, collective, confident, and connected to the opponent and game plan. The useful takeaway is not theatrical hype, but a clear blend of emotional activation, tactical reminders, shared identity, and concrete behavioral cues. Sport science staff can align readiness language with coaching messages so athletes hear one coherent theme before competition.
athleteDev: Developing athletes may benefit from consistent, team-oriented language that links preparation, identity, and immediate execution. Captains and position leaders can be coached to use short collective cues, repeat key behaviors, and avoid overlong or unfocused messages that dilute attention before play.
rtp: Not an RTP study. Indirectly, the communication findings can help staff frame return-to-play messaging so returning athletes feel integrated into the team without being overloaded. RTP communication should be specific, calm, and role-linked rather than purely emotional.

citation: Wollin M, Thorborg K, Welvaert M, Pizzari T. In-season monitoring of hip and groin strength, health and function in elite youth soccer: Implementing an early detection and management strategy over two consecutive seasons. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2018;21(10):988-993.
abstract: This longitudinal cohort study described an in-season hip and groin surveillance strategy in 27 elite male youth soccer players. Monthly adductor strength, adductor-to-abductor strength ratio, and HAGOS scores were compared with predefined alert thresholds to prompt further assessment.
tldr: Monthly hip and groin monitoring generated frequent alerts and showed that group strength and self-reported function improved early in the season. The study demonstrates a workable surveillance process, but it does not validate the thresholds as injury-prediction or prevention rules.
methods: Twenty-seven elite male youth players were followed across two seasons. Testing included adductor strength, adductor-to-abductor strength ratio, and six HAGOS subscales; alerts were triggered by greater than 15% strength loss, a ratio below 0.90, or a HAGOS subscale below 75.
findings: The system generated 105 alerts involving 70% of players; 40% were strength related and 60% came from HAGOS. Adductor strength and strength ratio increased by month two, most HAGOS subscales improved at the first in-season time point, and 87% of time-loss events were minimal or mild.
limitations: This was a small, single-program male youth cohort without a control group. Alert thresholds were operational choices rather than validated diagnostic or prognostic cut points, so the design cannot establish that monitoring prevented injury.
practicalImplications: A repeatable monthly battery can help identify meaningful within-athlete changes and prompt targeted follow-up. Staff should evaluate trends alongside symptoms, exposure, clinical findings, and the athlete's own baseline rather than treating one threshold breach as a diagnosis.
athleteDev: Use serial adductor strength and hip/groin function measures to guide individualized supplemental strength or load-management conversations. Preserve preseason and early-season baselines because rapid group improvement can make a single preseason value a poor long-term comparator.
rtp: During groin reconditioning, serial strength ratios and HAGOS domains can document progress and flag setbacks. They should complement—not replace—clinical examination, sport-specific loading, and shared return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Kramer A, Sinclair J, Sharpe L, Sarris J. Chronic cannabis consumption and physical exercise performance in healthy adults: A systematic review. Journal of Cannabis Research. 2020;2(1):34.
abstract: This systematic review examined chronic cannabis use and exercise-performance outcomes in healthy adults. Eight databases and forward searching produced four eligible studies assessing measures such as maximal oxygen uptake, physical work capacity, resting heart rate, blood pressure, and pulmonary function.
tldr: Four small cross-sectional studies found no consistent difference in VO2max or physical work capacity between chronic cannabis users and non-users. That thin evidence base does not establish safety, recovery benefit, or absence of impairment with current products, doses, or acute use.
methods: The authors searched eight databases through January 2020 for cross-sectional, longitudinal, or intervention studies relating chronic cannabis consumption to sports-performance outcomes. Four studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized qualitatively.
findings: Resting heart rate differed between groups in one study, while VO2max and physical work capacity did not differ consistently. The included studies did not directly evaluate recovery or endurance effects, and no ergogenic or ergolytic conclusion could be established.
limitations: Only four studies were eligible, all with cross-sectional limitations and several with small samples or older, lower-potency exposure patterns. Exposure definitions varied, confounding was substantial, and causal effects cannot be inferred.
practicalImplications: Do not interpret null group differences as evidence that cannabis improves recovery or is performance-neutral for an individual athlete. Decisions should account for acute impairment, health, policy, product composition, dose, and timing beyond the narrow chronic-use outcomes reviewed here.
athleteDev: This review provides no basis for recommending cannabis as an ergogenic or recovery strategy. Education should distinguish unsupported performance claims from medical, behavioral, legal, and anti-doping considerations.
rtp: No return-to-sport protocol or clearance evidence was studied. Cannabis use should not be used to infer readiness, symptom resolution, or safe participation.

citation: Rico-González M, González Fernández FT, Oliveira R, Clemente FM. Acute:chronic workload ratio and training monotony variations over the season in professional soccer: A systematic review. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part P: Journal of Sports Engineering and Technology. 2023;238(4):401-416.
abstract: This systematic review summarized seasonal variation in acute:chronic workload ratio and training monotony among professional soccer players. PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and FECYT searches identified 27 studies with heterogeneous workload measures, calculation methods, periods, and outcomes.
tldr: ACWR and training monotony vary substantially across the professional soccer season, but the literature does not support a universal injury-risk threshold. These measures are most defensible as descriptive workload context when their calculation and limitations are explicit.
methods: The review followed PRISMA procedures and screened 225 records, retaining 27 studies. Extracted outcomes included different internal and external workload variables, ACWR calculations, monotony estimates, seasonal phases, and injury comparisons.
findings: Reported ACWR and monotony values varied across preseason, competitive congestion, and lower-load weeks. Methodological differences were large, and the reviewed data did not conclusively distinguish injured from non-injured players.
limitations: Workload definitions, sensors, aggregation windows, mathematical models, durations, and injury outcomes differed markedly. Most evidence was observational, limiting causal interpretation and preventing a defensible universal cut point.
practicalImplications: If ACWR or monotony is displayed, show the underlying load variable, calculation method, time window, and athlete context. Use the measures to support longitudinal discussion, not as autonomous injury alarms or proof that a workload caused an injury.
athleteDev: Use workload ratios as one view of progression alongside absolute exposure, intensity distribution, availability, and athlete response. Programming decisions should remain anchored to the actual work completed and the adaptation being targeted.
rtp: ACWR should not serve as a return-to-sport clearance threshold. Reconditioning progression requires tissue-specific capacity, symptoms, clinical findings, sport demands, and exposure tolerance in addition to workload history.

citation: Draper G, Wright MD, Ishida A, Chesterton P, Portas MD, Atkinson G. Do environmental temperatures and altitudes affect physical outputs of elite football athletes in match conditions? A systematic review of the 'real world' studies. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022;7(1):81-92.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated real-world studies of temperature, heat, cold, and altitude effects on elite football match-running outputs. Twelve observational studies were included, using varied tracking systems, exposure definitions, competitions, and physical-performance measures.
tldr: Environmental temperature and altitude can influence selected match outputs, but the direction and size of effects were inconsistent across 12 real-world studies. Treat weather and altitude as planning context rather than deterministic performance penalties.
methods: The authors systematically searched for observational match studies in elite football codes that reported environmental exposure and physical outputs. Study quality and the direction of findings were reviewed narratively because measurement and outcome heterogeneity limited pooling.
findings: Some studies reported lower high-intensity or total running output in hotter conditions or at altitude, while others found minimal or different effects. Match context, tactics, opposition, pacing, acclimatization, and measurement choices likely contributed to the inconsistency.
limitations: Only 12 heterogeneous real-world studies were available. Environmental categories, tracking technology, competitions, and outcomes differed, and uncontrolled match factors prevent strong causal estimates.
practicalImplications: Use forecast temperature, humidity, and altitude to inform travel, acclimatization, hydration, warm-up, recovery, and substitution planning. Avoid forecasting an exact performance decrement from a single environmental threshold.
athleteDev: Build environmental tolerance progressively when competition conditions warrant it and monitor individual responses. Preserve technical and tactical objectives while adjusting exposure and recovery support to the actual setting.
rtp: Environmental load may change the cost of a return-to-participation session, especially after illness or deconditioning. Adjust exposure conservatively, but do not use this review as a standalone clearance or acclimatization protocol.

citation: Moore BP, Hackl CM, Kneedler SC, Weiss WM. Return to play and performance after patellar fracture in American professional sports: A case-control cohort analysis. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2025;53(1):86-96.
abstract: This retrospective case-control cohort study identified patellar fractures in NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL athletes from public reports and archives spanning 1965-2021. Return, playing volume, and sport-specific performance were assessed against preinjury levels and matched controls for two seasons after return.
tldr: Twenty-nine of 41 professional athletes returned after patellar fracture, averaging 217 days. Playing volume commonly fell in the first season and approached baseline in the second, but the public-record design and missing fracture details make individual prognosis and treatment comparisons uncertain.
methods: Forty-one professional athletes with an isolated patellar fracture were identified from public sources. Performance scores, playing time, and games were compared across the preinjury season and two post-return seasons, including matched-control analyses and operative versus nonoperative descriptions.
findings: The return-to-play rate was 71% with a mean 217-day absence. Overall playing volume declined in year one and recovered toward baseline in year two; operative cases recovered performance by year two in this cohort, while year-one performance remained below matched controls.
limitations: The study relied on retrospective public records, included a small multi-league sample, and used non-equivalent sport performance metrics. Fracture pattern, operative technique, rehabilitation details, and clinical decision criteria were unavailable, so treatment superiority cannot be inferred.
practicalImplications: Set expectations around a potentially prolonged return and a staged restoration of playing volume after return. Use the cohort as a broad benchmark, not an athlete-specific timeline or evidence that one treatment strategy is better.
athleteDev: Plan beyond the clearance date: the first season back may require deliberate exposure management, while performance volume may continue recovering into a second season. Coordinate strength, skill, and competition-load progression across disciplines.
rtp: Return decisions should be individualized to healing, knee function, strength and power, sport-specific capacity, symptoms, and risk tolerance. The 217-day average and 71% return rate are descriptive professional-sport benchmarks, not clearance criteria.

citation: Dridi N, Souissi MA, Dridi R, et al. Evening smartphone exposure impairs sleep quality and next-day performance in elite soccer players: A randomized controlled trial. Biology of Sport. 2026;43:227-242.
abstract: This randomized crossover trial compared five nights of two-hour pre-bed smartphone use with magazine reading in 16 elite male soccer players. Sleep measures and morning and afternoon cognitive and physical performance tests were collected, separated by a one-week washout.
tldr: Five nights of extended pre-bed smartphone use worsened sleep and selected next-day cognitive and physical outcomes in 16 elite male soccer players. A device-free wind-down period is reasonable, but the unusually large effects and very small, short study require replication.
methods: Sixteen elite male players completed smartphone and control conditions in randomized crossover order. The smartphone condition involved two hours of use before bedtime; sleep duration, latency, efficiency, sleepiness, reaction time, jumping, and reactive agility were assessed across the intervention.
findings: Smartphone exposure reduced total sleep time and efficiency, increased sleep latency and sleepiness, and worsened selected reaction-time, jumping, and reactive-agility outcomes, with several afternoon effects after five nights.
limitations: The sample was very small, male, and limited to elite soccer; exposure lasted only five nights and participant blinding was impossible. Several reported effect sizes were unusually large, and behavior, content, light exposure, and expectancy may not be separable.
practicalImplications: A consistent device-free period before bed is a low-cost sleep-support option, especially during demanding schedules. Monitor whether the strategy improves the individual athlete's sleep and daytime function rather than enforcing the study's exact duration as a universal rule.
athleteDev: Include evening screen habits in sleep education and travel or competition routines. Focus on repeatable behavior change and athlete-specific response rather than framing all smartphone use as equally harmful.
rtp: Sleep hygiene can support recovery and decision-making during rehabilitation, but smartphone restriction is not a return-to-sport criterion and cannot substitute for clinical or performance readiness measures.

citation: Curzi D, Amatori S, Silvestri F, et al. Professional football training and recovery: A longitudinal study on the effects of weekly conditioning session and workload variables. PLOS ONE. 2024;19(9):e0310036.
abstract: This longitudinal study examined salivary testosterone and cortisol responses in 24 professional soccer players during comparable microcycles in the first and second halves of a season. Seven- and 28-day GPS workloads were related to hormonal measures collected before, after, and 24 hours after an MD-5 conditioning session.
tldr: Later-season hormonal profiles were less favorable, and higher chronic workload was associated with a lower testosterone-to-cortisol ratio in one professional club. The findings are contextual correlations, not evidence that salivary hormones diagnose readiness or that workload caused the changes.
methods: Twenty-four professional players were sampled at two seasonal time points. Salivary cortisol and testosterone were collected around an MD-5 session, while GPS total and high-intensity distance over the previous 7 and 28 days represented acute and chronic external workload.
findings: Pretraining testosterone decreased and cortisol increased at the second time point. Chronic load correlated with cortisol and the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio more than acute load, suggesting accumulated seasonal context was related to the measured hormonal response.
limitations: The cohort came from one club, attrition reduced available observations, and only two comparable microcycles were sampled. Hormonal measures are variable, the analyses were correlational, and ratio-based workload descriptors carry known limitations.
practicalImplications: Interpret hormonal data, if collected, as one contextual trend alongside workload, sleep, wellness, performance, and clinical information. Avoid individual readiness labels or program changes from a single salivary value or testosterone-to-cortisol ratio.
athleteDev: Review accumulated load and recovery response across the season, not just the most recent week. Adjust programming through converging evidence from exposure, athlete response, and performance rather than a hormone-only decision rule.
rtp: Neither salivary hormones nor acute:chronic workload ratios should determine clearance. They may add context during reconditioning but require clinical, functional, and sport-specific readiness evidence.

citation: Fownes-Walpole M, Heyward O, Till K, et al. Combining evidence and practice to optimise neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport: A systematic review and Delphi-consensus study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;59(15):1027-1042.
abstract: This two-part consensus statement combined a systematic review of 21 neck-training studies with a three-round Delphi process involving 18 international experts. The work produced 57 consensus statements across assessment, programming, implementation, and monitoring topics intended to guide neck training for head-acceleration mitigation.
tldr: The paper offers a practical expert-informed framework for neck training in collision, combat, and motor sport, but intervention evidence was too heterogeneous for quantitative efficacy estimates. Consensus on programming is not proof that a protocol reduces head acceleration or injury.
methods: Four databases were searched through September 2024, with study quality assessed using modified Downs and Black and GRADE approaches. Findings informed three Delphi rounds with 18 experts, and statements meeting the prespecified agreement threshold were retained.
findings: Twenty-one heterogeneous intervention studies were reviewed and 57 statements reached consensus. The resulting guidance emphasized individualized assessment, progressive multi-directional neck training, sport integration, technique, monitoring, and practitioner collaboration.
limitations: Interventions, participants, outcomes, and measurement methods were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis, and much of the evidence was low certainty. Delphi agreement reflects expert judgment and does not establish causal reduction in head acceleration, concussion, or long-term brain-health risk.
practicalImplications: Use the consensus as a structured implementation checklist while monitoring athlete tolerance, neck capacity, technique, and sport exposure. Keep claims proportional: the framework guides programming but does not guarantee fewer head impacts or injuries.
athleteDev: Develop neck strength and control progressively across relevant directions and contraction types, integrated with whole-body collision or contact preparation. Individualize loading by training age, sport demands, symptoms, and technical competence.
rtp: This is primarily preventive programming evidence, not a concussion return-to-sport protocol. Neck training should only be introduced within appropriate clinical guidance and cannot replace symptom, neurological, exertional, and sport-specific progression criteria.

citation: Sukan-Karaçağıl B, Akbulut G, Açar Y, Demirkoparan M. A little pepper-upper? Systematic review of randomized controlled studies on capsaicinoids, capsinoids, and exercise performance. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2023;33(5):291-301.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated randomized placebo-controlled human studies of capsaicinoid or capsinoid supplementation and exercise performance. Five databases were searched, risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool, and 19 trials were synthesized qualitatively.
tldr: Ten of 19 randomized trials reported a positive performance outcome, with more apparent signal in resistance exercise than endurance exercise. Heterogeneous compounds, doses, outcomes, and incomplete safety reporting do not support a blanket supplement recommendation.
methods: The review followed PRISMA procedures and searched PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library. Nineteen randomized placebo-controlled trials met inclusion criteria and were evaluated qualitatively because protocols and outcomes varied.
findings: Ten studies reported positive performance effects, with the pattern appearing more frequently in resistance exercise. Findings were inconsistent across endurance and other exercise modes, and a pooled effect estimate was not produced.
limitations: Compounds, doses, timing, participant training status, exercise tests, and outcomes were heterogeneous. Adverse effects were inconsistently reported, no meta-analysis was performed, and long-term effectiveness and safety remain uncertain.
practicalImplications: Treat capsaicinoids and capsinoids as an unresolved, protocol-dependent supplement question. Any consideration requires dietitian and medical review of product quality, dose, gastrointestinal tolerance, interactions, and applicable sport rules.
athleteDev: The evidence is not strong enough to build routine performance programming around these supplements. Prioritize established nutrition, training, and recovery practices before considering an individualized monitored trial.
rtp: No return-to-sport benefit or rehabilitation protocol was established. Supplement use should not influence clearance or substitute for recovery milestones.

citation: Luo WT, Lee CJ, Tam KW, Huang TW. Effects of low-level laser therapy on muscular performance and soreness recovery in athletes: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Sports Health. 2022;14(5):687-693.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined low-level laser therapy before exercise in physically active athletes. PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library searches through December 2020 identified 24 randomized or crossover studies reporting muscular performance, soreness, or recovery biomarkers.
tldr: Low-level laser therapy improved selected lower-limb strength follow-ups and some soreness or biomarker outcomes across 24 studies. Protocol heterogeneity and study limitations mean the therapy remains promising rather than an established standard recovery intervention.
methods: Randomized controlled and crossover studies were pooled where outcomes and follow-up periods allowed. Risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane methods, and analyses examined strength, repetitions, oxygen kinetics, soreness, creatine kinase, interleukin-6, and oxidative-stress markers.
findings: Preexercise therapy was associated with improved lower-limb strength at several follow-ups and reductions in selected soreness and biomarker outcomes. Trends were also reported for repetition performance and oxygen kinetics, but effects varied by outcome and protocol.
limitations: Laser wavelength, dose, application site, timing, muscle group, exercise task, follow-up, and study quality varied. The authors noted that a definite therapeutic effect was not established and called for larger, more robust trials.
practicalImplications: If used, document the exact device, wavelength, dose, site, and timing and evaluate whether the athlete experiences a meaningful benefit. Do not assume that findings from one protocol transfer to another device or recovery problem.
athleteDev: Low-level laser therapy may be considered an adjunct around demanding training, but it should not displace load planning, sleep, nutrition, or progressive physical preparation with stronger foundations.
rtp: The evidence does not establish low-level laser therapy as a return-to-sport milestone. It may be an adjunct within rehabilitation when clinically appropriate, while readiness remains based on tissue, symptoms, function, exposure, and sport demands.

citation: Celorrio San Miguel AM, Roche E, Herranz-López M, Celorrio San Miguel M, Mielgo-Ayuso J, Fernández-Lázaro D. Impact of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and circulating biomarkers in highly trained athletes: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Nutrients. 2024;16(7):1011.
abstract: This systematic review examined controlled trials of melatonin supplementation in highly trained athletes, focusing on performance and circulating health biomarkers. Searches of Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus through February 2024 yielded 21 studies using doses from 5 to 100 mg.
tldr: Melatonin was associated with improvements in selected oxidative-stress, inflammatory, muscle-damage, and metabolic biomarkers across 21 controlled trials. Direct performance benefit remains unresolved, and the wide 5-100 mg dosing range prevents a simple athlete recommendation.
methods: The review followed PRISMA procedures and applied modified McMaster, PEDro, and Cochrane appraisal tools. Twenty-one controlled trials in highly trained athletes were synthesized across varied exercise protocols, timing strategies, doses, and biomarker panels.
findings: Selected antioxidant, inflammatory, liver, muscle-damage, glycemic, lipid, creatinine, hematological, and hormonal outcomes improved in some trials. The authors concluded that direct performance-enhancing efficiency still requires assessment and that any benefit may be indirect through health biomarkers.
limitations: Dose, timing, exercise protocol, participant samples, biomarker selection, and study quality were heterogeneous. Biomarker changes do not necessarily represent meaningful performance or recovery improvement, and the review does not establish an optimal or universally safe dose.
practicalImplications: Do not translate biomarker findings into routine high-dose supplementation. Melatonin decisions should be individualized with medical and nutrition oversight, attention to timing, side effects, product quality, sleep goals, and applicable regulations.
athleteDev: Melatonin is not established as a direct performance enhancer. Address schedule, light exposure, sleep opportunity, and behavioral sleep practices before treating supplementation as the primary solution.
rtp: No return-to-sport criterion or rehabilitation benefit was established. Melatonin may be considered for a specific sleep-related indication under appropriate oversight, but not as evidence of readiness.

citation: Wolf M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Roberts MD, et al. Does longer-muscle length resistance training cause greater longitudinal growth in humans? A systematic review. Sports Medicine and Health Science. 2026;8(1):34-42.
abstract: This systematic review compared resistance training at longer versus shorter muscle lengths in healthy adults when studies measured both muscle size and fascicle length. Eight interventions totaling 120 participants met the criteria and were narratively synthesized.
tldr: Training at longer muscle lengths generally favored muscle hypertrophy and may favor fascicle-length change, but the evidence is mixed. No included study directly measured serial sarcomere number, so sarcomerogenesis remains a proposed mechanism rather than a demonstrated human adaptation.
methods: Google Scholar, PubMed/MEDLINE, and Scopus were searched in February 2024, supplemented by citation searching and author knowledge. Eligible studies lasted at least four weeks, compared longer- with shorter-muscle-length training, and measured muscle size and fascicle length.
findings: Across eight studies and 120 participants, longer-muscle-length training generally produced greater overall hypertrophy and sometimes greater estimated fascicle-length change. Results were mixed, and the structural basis of the observed changes remains unresolved.
limitations: No study directly estimated serial sarcomere number, and all but one used questionable linear-extrapolation methods for fascicle length. Samples and exercises were limited, results were narratively synthesized, and applicability to highly trained athletes is uncertain.
practicalImplications: Include well-tolerated loading at longer muscle lengths when hypertrophy is a goal, but progress range and load to the athlete and exercise. Avoid promising a unique sarcomerogenesis effect that current human measurements cannot confirm.
athleteDev: Longer-muscle-length resistance exercise can be one programming option for hypertrophy rather than a replacement for sound volume, effort, progression, and exercise selection. Monitor tolerance because the review did not establish one universal protocol.
rtp: The review studied healthy-adult hypertrophy, not injured-athlete return. Longer-length loading may be introduced during later rehabilitation when tissue tolerance and clinical goals support it, but it is not a clearance standard.

citation: Ascenzi G, Filetti C, Di Salvo V, et al. Inter-limb asymmetry in youth elite soccer players: Effect of loading conditions. PLOS ONE. 2022;17(6):e0269695.
abstract: This experimental study examined whether inter-limb strength asymmetry changes with test and load conditions. Fifteen elite youth soccer players performed rear-foot-elevated split squats under three external loads plus isokinetic knee-flexor and knee-extensor assessments.
tldr: The size and favored side of inter-limb asymmetry changed across loads and test modes in 15 elite youth players. An asymmetry score is specific to how it was measured; one percentage should not become a stable athlete label or universal injury threshold.
methods: Players completed split-squat tests with body mass, an additional 25% of body mass, and an additional 50% of body mass, along with concentric and eccentric isokinetic tests. Agreement statistics compared the magnitude and direction of asymmetry between conditions.
findings: Agreement was moderate only between the body-mass and body-mass-plus-25% split-squat conditions and was fair or absent for most other comparisons. Both asymmetry magnitude and the limb identified as lower performing were inconsistent across loads and assessments.
limitations: The sample was small, male, and drawn from one academy; testing was cross-sectional and no injury or future-performance outcomes were tracked. The findings do not validate a diagnostic threshold or show that reducing asymmetry improves outcomes.
practicalImplications: Standardize the task, load, range, and metric when monitoring asymmetry and interpret change within that exact test. Confirm an unusual result across repeated sessions and relevant tasks before changing a program.
athleteDev: Select unilateral tests that match the physical quality and loading context of interest. Use asymmetry as descriptive information alongside bilateral capacity and sport performance, not as the sole target of training.
