rtp: During rehabilitation, reproduce the same test conditions when tracking side-to-side recovery. Clearance should not depend on one asymmetry percentage or on a side designation that may change with task and load.

citation: Quintana-Cepedal M, Vicente-Rodríguez G, Crespo I, Olmedillas H. Is hip adductor or abductor strength in healthy athletes associated with future groin pain? A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;59(7):501-509.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined prospective associations between preseason hip adductor or abductor strength and later groin pain or time-loss injury in healthy athletes. Thirteen cohort studies were included and evidence certainty was assessed with GRADE.
tldr: Lower hip-adductor strength had a moderate, low-certainty association with future groin pain across 13 cohorts. Abductor strength and the adductor-to-abductor ratio were not associated, and the review does not establish a predictive cut point.
methods: Six databases were searched for prospective studies that measured hip strength before follow-up and separately reported athletes who remained healthy or developed groin pain. Risk of bias used QUIPS and pooled standardized effects were evaluated with evidence-certainty grading.
findings: Athletes who remained uninjured had greater baseline adductor strength than those who later developed groin pain. Pooled findings did not support associations for abductor strength or the adductor-to-abductor ratio, and diagnostic criteria were not a significant moderator.
limitations: Strength tests, diagnostic criteria, follow-up periods, sports, and reporting varied, the adductor finding was low certainty, and female athletes made up only about 3% of the sample. Association does not establish prevention or an individual risk probability.
practicalImplications: Adductor strength is reasonable to include in a broader groin-health assessment, particularly as a repeatable within-athlete measure. Avoid categorical high-risk labels or decisions based on the strength ratio alone.
athleteDev: Develop adequate adductor capacity as part of comprehensive lower-body preparation, but do not chase a universal ratio. Interpret strength alongside prior symptoms, exposure, training history, and movement demands.
rtp: Adductor strength can document recovery from groin problems, but this review does not provide a clearance threshold. Combine it with pain, clinical examination, change-of-direction and kicking exposure, and full training tolerance.

citation: Julian R, Page RM, Harper LD. The effect of fixture congestion on performance during professional male soccer match-play: A systematic critical review with meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(2):255-273.
abstract: This systematic critical review evaluated physical, technical, and tactical performance during congested professional male soccer schedules, defined as successive matches separated by less than 96 hours. Sixteen studies were reviewed and five contributed total-distance data to meta-analysis.
tldr: Fixture congestion did not meaningfully reduce total match distance in the pooled analysis, but other physical outcomes were inconsistent and tactical evidence was sparse. Stable distance does not prove complete recovery or unchanged individual performance.
methods: Three databases were searched under a preregistered PRISMA process. Eligible studies involved professional male players, at least two matches within 96 hours, and physical, technical, or tactical match outcomes; total distance was the only consistently pooled variable.
findings: The pooled standardized effect for total distance was not significant and heterogeneity was moderate. Physical findings outside total distance were equivocal, technical performance was generally maintained, and one available tactical study suggested possible impairment.
limitations: Few outcomes were measured consistently, several studies had weak designs, and player rotation, opposition, match importance, travel, position, and substitution could confound results. The review included only professional men.
practicalImplications: Plan congested periods with individual exposure, high-intensity actions, travel, wellness, and tactical demands in view rather than relying on total distance alone. Rotation and recovery support remain contextual decisions.
athleteDev: Prepare players for repeated-match demands while preserving training quality between fixtures. Use position- and athlete-specific response to determine whether maintenance, recovery, or top-up work is appropriate.
rtp: A returning athlete may have lower congestion tolerance than a fully available player even when match distance appears normal. Progress repeated exposures deliberately and use symptoms, function, and recovery response rather than schedule alone.

citation: Booth M, Orr R, Cobley S. The effect of training loads on performance measures and injury characteristics in rugby league players: A systematic review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2018;13(10):1259-1272.
abstract: This systematic review examined training-load relationships with physical performance and injury characteristics in rugby league. Five databases were searched through December 2016 and 12 studies with quantified load and performance or injury outcomes were included.
tldr: Higher rugby-league training loads were associated with both selected fitness improvements and more injury in a heterogeneous 12-study literature. The evidence does not identify one optimal or harmful workload threshold.
methods: The PRISMA-guided search included studies using measures such as session rating of perceived exertion with physical-performance tests or injury surveillance. Results were synthesized across preseason and in-season contexts.
findings: The highest loads generally occurred in preseason. Higher loads accompanied improvements in aerobic power, jump, and agility outcomes but were also associated with strains, sprains, lower-limb injuries, and overuse or overexertion problems.
limitations: Definitions, load metrics, age and competitive levels, performance tests, injury surveillance, and study designs varied. The primarily observational evidence cannot isolate causality or establish a universal dose-response curve.
practicalImplications: Evaluate load as both an adaptation stimulus and an exposure cost. Make decisions from absolute work, progression, recent history, athlete response, and available recovery rather than a single ratio or threshold.
athleteDev: Progress collision, running, and conditioning demands with the target adaptation explicit. Fitness development and injury exposure can rise together, so greater workload is neither automatically good nor automatically unsafe.
rtp: Reconditioning should rebuild rugby-specific load progressively without using population associations as clearance rules. Track symptoms, contact tolerance, physical capacity, and repeated training exposure.

citation: Clemente FM, Ramirez-Campillo R, Sarmento H. Detrimental effects of the off-season in soccer players: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(4):795-814.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated at least two weeks of training cessation or off-season training in healthy male soccer players. Twelve studies reported body composition, aerobic fitness, intermittent-running, jumping, sprinting, or repeated-sprint outcomes.
tldr: Complete off-season cessation produced meaningful losses across several fitness qualities, while off-season programs attenuated declines in VO2max and repeated-sprint ability. Even trained groups lost some qualities, so maintenance programs reduce rather than eliminate detraining.
methods: Controlled trials and cohorts with pre-post off-season measures were pooled by outcome. Comparisons examined training cessation and off-season programs for body fat, VO2max, Yo-Yo performance, jumping, sprint time, and repeated-sprint ability.
findings: Training cessation worsened body fat, VO2max, Yo-Yo performance, vertical jump, and repeated-sprint ability. Off-season programs also showed some losses but produced smaller declines than cessation for VO2max and repeated-sprint ability.
limitations: Studies involved males, used varied program content and durations, and included different ages and competition levels with small samples and inconsistent control. The review cannot prescribe one ideal off-season dose.
practicalImplications: Use a low-burden off-season plan that maintains key aerobic, sprint, and strength exposures while allowing psychological and physical recovery. Select the minimum effective work for the athlete's next reporting date and needs.
athleteDev: Avoid both extremes of uninterrupted high load and complete inactivity. Maintain important qualities with flexible, individualized exposures and plan a progressive return into preseason.
rtp: Athletes returning from injury need individualized off-season work rather than the healthy-player template. Preserve rehabilitation continuity and account for detraining before resuming team preseason loads.

citation: Stensø J, Andersen TE, Harøy J. Adductor Strengthening Programme is successfully adopted but frequently modified in Norwegian male professional football teams: A cross-sectional study. BMJ Open. 2022;12(9):e060611.
abstract: This cross-sectional RE-AIM survey examined adoption and real-world use of the Adductor Strengthening Programme among delivery agents in the top two Norwegian male professional football divisions. Twenty-nine of 32 invited practitioners responded.
tldr: Practitioners widely knew and adopted the Adductor Strengthening Programme, but only 10% delivered the original protocol. Implementation success should include fidelity and active dose, not just whether a team says it uses the program.
methods: A questionnaire mapped awareness, adoption, implementation, effectiveness beliefs, and maintenance intentions across the five RE-AIM dimensions. Respondents also described common protocol changes and one professional-team application was documented.
findings: All respondents were aware of and had adopted the program, 97% intended to continue, and the injury-prevention evidence and lack of equipment were valued. Only 10% used the original protocol, with common changes to frequency, progression, and delivery.
limitations: The survey was self-reported, cross-sectional, and limited to one country's male professional system. Fidelity was not directly observed and player exposure or injury outcomes were not linked to the modified versions.
practicalImplications: When implementing an evidence-based program, record what was actually completed and why it changed. Audit frequency, progression, intensity, reach, and maintenance rather than counting program adoption alone.
athleteDev: Adaptations may be necessary in a team setting, but preserve the mechanism and sufficient dose. Review modifications with performance and medical staff so convenience does not silently remove the active ingredients.
rtp: This study addressed primary prevention implementation, not return-to-sport treatment. A modified program should not be assumed to reproduce either the trial's prevention effect or an individualized rehabilitation plan.

citation: Bowman EN, Elshaar R, Milligan H, et al. Proximal, distal, and contralateral effects of blood flow restriction training on the lower extremities: A randomized controlled trial. Sports Health. 2019;11(2):149-156.
abstract: This randomized controlled trial evaluated six weeks of unilateral low-load blood-flow-restriction training in healthy adults. Sixteen BFR and 10 control participants completed strength testing and limb-circumference measurements before and after training.
tldr: Low-load BFR increased strength and limb circumference around the trained limb, with smaller gains in the noncuffed limb and no reported adverse events in 26 screened healthy adults. The small healthy sample does not establish safety or effectiveness in injured athletes.
methods: Participants were randomized to unilateral BFR training or control and completed a standardized six-week protocol. Isokinetic torque, work, power, and thigh and leg circumference were compared within and between the cuffed, contralateral, and control limbs.
findings: The BFR group improved knee-extension torque, work, power, and limb circumference more than controls. Proximal, distal, and smaller contralateral improvements were observed, and no adverse events were reported during the study.
limitations: Only 26 healthy young adults completed the trial, medical-risk groups and previously operated limbs were excluded, and follow-up was short. Circumference is an imprecise hypertrophy measure and adverse-event absence in this sample is not broad safety proof.
practicalImplications: BFR can provide a low-load strengthening option when high loads are not desirable, but requires appropriate screening, individualized cuff pressure, supervision, and documentation of symptoms and response.
athleteDev: Use BFR as an adjunct for a specific loading constraint, not a default replacement for progressive high-load training. Transition toward task-relevant loading as tolerance and goals allow.
rtp: BFR may support capacity during rehabilitation, but this healthy-adult study does not supply postoperative protocols or clearance criteria. Clinical risk screening and tissue-specific progression remain essential.

citation: Harøy J, Clarsen B, Wiger EG, et al. The Adductor Strengthening Programme prevents groin problems among male football players: A cluster-randomised controlled trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(3):150-157.
abstract: This cluster-randomized trial tested a single-exercise progressive Copenhagen-adduction program in 35 Norwegian semiprofessional male football teams. The intervention included three weekly preseason sessions for six to eight weeks and one weekly in-season session for 28 weeks.
tldr: The studied adductor program reduced average weekly groin-problem prevalence from 21.3% to 13.5%, a 41% relative reduction. The effect belongs to this progressive protocol and male semiprofessional setting, not every modified Copenhagen routine.
methods: Eighteen teams with 339 players were assigned to the program and 17 teams with 313 players continued normal training. Weekly groin problems were measured during the competitive season with the Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center Overuse Injury Questionnaire.
findings: Average weekly groin-problem prevalence was 13.5% in the intervention group and 21.3% in controls. The relative risk of reporting any groin problem was 41% lower, while the reduction in substantial groin problems was smaller and not statistically significant.
limitations: Teams and athletes could not be blinded, adherence varied, outcomes were self-reported, and the setting was male semiprofessional football. The trial does not establish equal effects in women, youth, other sports, or altered protocols.
practicalImplications: Use the simple progressive program as a team-level groin-prevention option and protect the studied frequency and progression. Monitor adherence, soreness, and actual weekly exposure.
athleteDev: Build adductor strength before and throughout the competitive season with progressive Copenhagen-adduction exposure. Integrate it with the rest of the lower-body program so dosage is sustainable.
rtp: The protocol was preventive, not a treatment or clearance pathway for current groin pain. Symptomatic athletes require individualized assessment and graded rehabilitation before joining the team dose.

citation: McCartney D, Irwin C, Bawa Z, et al. The effect of cannabidiol on subjective responses to endurance exercise: A randomised controlled trial. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10(1):61.
abstract: This randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial examined whether 150 mg oral cannabidiol changed subjective experience or performance during a self-paced 10 km track run. Fifty-one recreationally active adults completed the analysis.
tldr: A single 150 mg CBD dose did not improve affect, enjoyment, motivation, runner's-high features, perceived exertion, pain, or 10 km time. The trial provides no acute endurance-experience benefit and does not address other doses, chronic use, recovery, or treatment.
methods: Participants took CBD or placebo 90 minutes before each 10 km trial in randomized crossover order. Repeated measures assessed affective valence, positive and negative affect, enjoyment, motivation, self-efficacy, euphoria, pain, anxiety, sedation, perceived effort, and run time.
findings: Exercise produced expected changes in affect and pain, but CBD did not significantly affect any measured subjective outcome or running performance compared with placebo.
limitations: The sample was young and recreational, the study tested one acute dose and product, and several outcomes were self-reported. Results do not establish long-term safety, recovery effects, clinical benefit, or responses in elite athletes.
practicalImplications: Do not recommend CBD to improve the immediate subjective endurance experience or performance based on this trial. Product quality, health, medication interactions, policy, and anti-doping risk remain separate considerations.
athleteDev: CBD should not displace established endurance preparation, pacing, fueling, recovery, or psychological strategies. A null result is not evidence of broader safety or effectiveness.
rtp: The trial studied healthy recreational exercise and offers no return-to-sport evidence. CBD use should not influence clearance or symptom-readiness decisions.

citation: Simmons R, Doma K, Sinclair W, Connor J, Leicht A. Acute effects of training loads on muscle damage markers and performance in semi-elite and elite athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(10):2181-2207.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated acute muscle-damage markers and performance responses to periodized training in semi-elite and elite athletes. Thirty-two studies compared preseason with off-season, similar seasonal loads, or acute increases and decreases in load.
tldr: Creatine kinase generally rose early in preseason and moved with acute training-load changes, while other inflammatory and performance responses were inconsistent. CK is a context-sensitive group signal, not an individual readiness diagnosis.
methods: Five databases were searched for studies of acute response to training in periodized semi-elite or elite programs. Kmet quality appraisal was used and compatible data were pooled for creatine kinase and related outcomes with heterogeneity assessment.
findings: CK and indirect damage signals were higher in early preseason than off-season, did not differ consistently at two comparable-load time points, and rose or fell alongside acute load changes. Other inflammatory and performance results were inconclusive.
limitations: Age, sex, sport, competition level, training load, biomarker timing, and outcomes varied, and several pooled analyses had substantial heterogeneity. Group averages cannot define individual damage, recovery, or a safe load threshold.
practicalImplications: If CK is used, standardize collection and interpret within-athlete change alongside recent load, soreness, performance, illness, and baseline variability. Do not make readiness decisions from CK alone.
athleteDev: Expect a larger response when load is reintroduced or increased and progress preseason work accordingly. Use performance and athlete response to decide whether adaptation is occurring as intended.
rtp: A biomarker response during reconditioning may add context but cannot determine tissue healing or clearance. Progression still depends on symptoms, function, sport exposure, and clinical judgment.

citation: Johns W, Walley KC, Seedat R, Thordarson DB, Jackson B, Gonzalez T. Career outlook and performance of professional athletes after Achilles tendon rupture: A systematic review. Foot & Ankle International. 2021;42(4):495-509.
abstract: This systematic review examined return, performance, participation, and career outcomes after Achilles tendon rupture in professional NFL, NBA, MLB, and soccer athletes. Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria.
tldr: About 76% of professional athletes returned after Achilles rupture at an average of 11 months, and returning players often had reduced performance or durability. These league-level averages set expectations but are not individual timelines or clearance criteria.
methods: MEDLINE, Google Scholar, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library were searched for professional-sport studies reporting time and rate of return, durability, participation, or postrupture performance.
findings: Professional athletes returned 76% of the time after a mean 11 months. Efficiency, power, and sport- or position-specific metrics often declined compared with preinjury values or noninjured controls, and return rates were lower than for several other orthopedic injuries.
limitations: The evidence was retrospective and heterogeneous across leagues, eras, treatments, rehabilitation, and performance metrics. Public-data selection, survivor bias, and limited female professional evidence restrict individualized prognosis.
practicalImplications: Discuss both probability and quality of return: clearance may precede full restoration of workload, performance, and career durability. Plan progression and support beyond the initial return date.
athleteDev: Rebuild plantar-flexor capacity, elastic qualities, high-speed exposure, and sport-specific actions over a long horizon. Expect performance restoration to continue after return to participation.
rtp: The 76% return rate and 11-month mean are expectation-setting benchmarks only. Individual decisions require healing, calf and tendon function, strength and power, running and change-of-direction exposure, confidence, and full training tolerance.

citation: Roberts SSH, Teo WP, Warmington SA. Effects of training and competition on the sleep of elite athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(8):513-522.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis characterized objectively measured sleep in elite athletes and training or competition factors associated with poorer sleep. Fifty-four observational studies reported total sleep time or sleep efficiency.
tldr: Elite athletes frequently obtained less sleep than common recommendations, especially around competition. Early training, abrupt load increases, late or early travel, eastward travel, and altitude were recurring schedule-level risks that staff can modify.
methods: PubMed, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus were searched through February 2018 for observational elite-athlete studies with objective total-sleep-time or sleep-efficiency data. Competition nights and identified training or travel factors were compared with preceding conditions.
findings: Many studies reported inadequate sleep time or efficiency during training and competition. Competition nights averaged about 60 fewer minutes of sleep, night competitions about 80 fewer minutes, and early training, load increases above 25%, difficult travel timing, eastward travel, and altitude were associated with impairment.
limitations: Studies were predominantly observational and heterogeneous in sport, device, schedule, and sleep criteria, with limited control of individual chronotype and environment. Group recommendation thresholds do not define each athlete's sleep requirement.
practicalImplications: Protect sleep opportunity through schedule design: reconsider very early sessions, build load progressively, and plan postcompetition and travel timing. Combine objective trends with athlete report and daytime function.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to anticipate high-risk nights and use consistent routines, light timing, naps, and recovery planning where appropriate. Focus on sustainable opportunity and response rather than one universal target.
rtp: Sleep supports recovery but is not a standalone clearance criterion. During rehabilitation, address schedule barriers and interpret sleep alongside symptoms, function, mood, and training tolerance.

citation: Steinl GK, Padaki AS, Irvine JN, et al. The prevalence of high school multi-sport participation in elite National Football League athletes. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2021;49(4):476-479.
abstract: This retrospective cohort study described high-school sport participation among 318 NFL first-round draft selections from 2008 through 2017 and compared subsequent availability and career outcomes between multi-sport and football-only athletes.
tldr: Most NFL first-round picks in this cohort played multiple high-school sports, but multi-sport and football-only groups did not differ significantly in games missed because of injury, games played, career length, or Pro Bowl selection. This is descriptive association evidence, not proof that specialization or diversification causes an NFL outcome.
methods: Publicly available high-school participation histories and NFL career data were assembled for 318 first-round picks. Athletes were classified as multi-sport or football-only, then compared on injury-related games missed, total games, career longevity, and Pro Bowl selection.
findings: Two hundred eighty athletes (88%) were classified as multi-sport and 38 (12%) as football-only. The authors found no statistically significant between-group differences in the measured NFL injury, availability, longevity, or achievement outcomes.
limitations: Only 38 athletes were football-only, participation histories could be misclassified from public sources, injury reports lacked clinical detail, off-season injuries were not captured, and first-round picks are a highly selected population. Causality cannot be inferred.
practicalImplications: Do not use early sport specialization as a prerequisite for identifying football talent. Support broad youth sport participation when it fits the athlete, while recognizing that this study did not establish an injury-prevention or career-performance advantage.
athleteDev: Multi-sport backgrounds were common among elite draft selections and can coexist with high football attainment. Preserve opportunities to develop varied movement, competition, and learning experiences without promising that participation pattern alone improves professional outcomes.
rtp: The study does not test rehabilitation or return-to-sport decisions. Do not use prior multi-sport status to estimate recovery time, reinjury risk, or readiness after injury.

citation: Warrier AA, Azua EN, Kasson LB, et al. Performance-enhancing drugs in healthy athletes: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Sports Health. 2024;16(5):695-705.
abstract: This umbrella review synthesized 27 systematic reviews and meta-analyses on creatine, anabolic-androgenic steroids, growth hormone, recombinant human erythropoietin, and cannabis in healthy athletes, considering both performance effects and adverse outcomes.
tldr: Effects and harms differed sharply by agent. Creatine had the clearest support for strength and repeated high-intensity performance; anabolic steroids could increase strength and lean mass but carried health harms; growth hormone and cannabis lacked clear performance benefit; and erythropoietin evidence was limited alongside serious cardiovascular risk.
methods: The authors searched PubMed and Scopus for systematic reviews and meta-analyses involving healthy athletes and five performance-related agents. Twenty-seven reviews were included, with findings summarized by agent and graded as level-4 evidence.
findings: Creatine supported strength and repeated high-intensity performance. Anabolic-steroid reviews reported strength gains ranging from 5% to 52% and a lean-mass standardized mean difference of 0.62, alongside adverse lipid effects. Growth hormone improved body composition without clear performance benefit; recombinant erythropoietin evidence was sparse with serious cardiovascular risk; cannabis did not improve performance and could impair it.
limitations: Only two databases were searched; included reviews were heterogeneous and often based on limited primary evidence. The umbrella review found no eligible review evidence for selective androgen receptor modulators or angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, and its broad agent-level summaries cannot define individual risk.
practicalImplications: Separate permitted, evidence-supported supplementation from prohibited or high-risk drug use. Direct medication, supplement, and anti-doping questions to qualified medical and nutrition staff; never treat a performance effect as evidence of safety or eligibility.
athleteDev: Build performance through training, recovery, nutrition, and transparent supplement governance. Creatine may be considered within individualized, independently tested protocols, while illicit or medically inappropriate agents require clear education on health, eligibility, and ethical consequences.
rtp: This review does not establish return-to-sport protocols. Drug exposure, adverse effects, or suspected misuse requires medical assessment, and clearance should address organ-system risk and anti-doping status rather than perceived performance benefit.

citation: Murray IR, McAdams TR, Hammond KE, et al. The use of biologics in NFL athletes: An expert consensus of NFL team physicians. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(2):23259671221143778.
abstract: This expert-consensus project used a three-round Delphi process to develop 47 statements about biologic treatments in NFL athletes, including platelet-rich plasma, bone-marrow-derived products, and other cell-based interventions.
tldr: NFL team physicians reached consensus supporting selected platelet-rich-plasma uses, including patellar tendinopathy and symptom management in early osteoarthritis, while emphasizing that many cell products are marketed beyond the evidence. Consensus describes expert practice and judgment; it does not prove comparative efficacy.
methods: A six-member working group developed statements that were rated through three Delphi rounds by physicians representing 26 NFL teams plus NFL London. Agreement thresholds were used to identify 47 final consensus statements.
findings: The panel supported platelet-rich plasma for selected conditions such as patellar tendinopathy and symptomatic early osteoarthritis. It also highlighted inconsistent biologic preparation and reporting and cautioned that uncharacterized cell-based products are commonly promoted beyond the supporting evidence.
limitations: Delphi agreement is expert opinion rather than a treatment trial, and participant selection can introduce bias. The recommendations reflect NFL physician experience and may not generalize to college athletes, other sports, different products, or different regulatory environments.
practicalImplications: Require a condition-specific medical rationale, transparent product characterization, informed consent, and realistic discussion of uncertainty before using a biologic. Avoid broad claims that a product regenerates tissue or accelerates recovery when comparative evidence is absent.
athleteDev: Biologics should not replace progressive loading, rehabilitation, sleep, nutrition, or workload management. When considered, integrate the intervention into a coordinated medical and performance plan with explicit outcome measures.
rtp: A biologic injection is not a clearance criterion or a fixed recovery shortcut. Return-to-sport progression should remain based on tissue status, symptoms, function, sport demands, and response to graded loading.

citation: Sarmento H, Clemente FM, Araújo D, et al. What performance analysts need to know about research trends in association football (2012–2016): A systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(4):799-836.
abstract: This systematic review mapped performance-analysis research on adult male association football published from 2012 through 2016, organizing 77 studies by tactical, technical, physical, contextual, and methodological themes.
tldr: The literature concentrated on set pieces, collective behavior, match statistics and outcomes, activity profiles, fatigue and substitutions, plus environmental and situational constraints. The review helps analysts locate relevant evidence but does not validate a universal metric, model, or workflow.
methods: Following PRISMA procedures, the authors screened 483 records and included 77 studies of adult male football match performance. Studies were categorized by research focus and their methods and findings were synthesized narratively.
findings: Recurring themes included set-piece effectiveness, collective tactical behavior, associations between match statistics and outcomes, physical activity profiles, fatigue and substitution patterns, and effects of score line, venue, opposition, and environmental context.
limitations: The search was limited to Web of Science and a five-year publication window. Included studies were heterogeneous, predominantly observational, and restricted to adult male football; mapping research activity is not the same as validating practical decision tools.
practicalImplications: Frame match analysis around a specific decision and account for opponent, match state, venue, competition, and role. Combine tactical, technical, and physical information instead of treating a context-free count as a performance explanation.
athleteDev: Use longitudinal, role-specific analysis to connect player behavior with team principles and development goals. A metric is most useful when its definition, context, and coaching response are consistent.
rtp: The review does not validate return-to-sport thresholds. Match-analysis variables can help describe reintegration demands, but medical and functional readiness require separate evidence and individualized progression.

citation: Askling CM, Tengvar M, Saartok T, Thorstensson A. Acute first-time hamstring strains during high-speed running. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(2):197-206.
abstract: This longitudinal case series followed 18 elite sprinters after acute first-time hamstring strains sustained during high-speed running, combining serial clinical examination, magnetic resonance imaging, time to return, and two-year follow-up.
tldr: All injuries involved the biceps femoris long head, and return to preinjury training ranged widely from 6 to 50 weeks, with a median of 16 weeks. Greater injury extent and involvement near the proximal free tendon were associated with longer recovery, but the small case series cannot supply a universal MRI-based timeline.
methods: Athletes were assessed clinically and with magnetic resonance imaging approximately 2–4 days after injury and again around days 10, 21, and 42. Injury location and extent were compared with time to resume preinjury training, and athletes were followed for two years.
findings: Every injury involved the long head of biceps femoris. Median time to return to preinjury training was 16 weeks, with a 6–50-week range. More extensive injury and proximity to or involvement of the proximal free tendon were associated with longer recovery.
limitations: The study included only 18 elite sprinters, had no comparison group, and allowed rehabilitation to vary after the initial six weeks. Associations between MRI features and recovery do not create deterministic individual timelines or directly generalize to field-sport athletes.
practicalImplications: Expect substantial variation after high-speed-running hamstring injury and integrate mechanism, clinical function, loading response, and imaging when available. Communicate a range and update the forecast as running exposure progresses.
athleteDev: Prepare athletes for progressive exposure to high-speed running and the specific force demands that precede sprinting. Prioritize capacity and graded exposure rather than assuming symptom resolution alone restores readiness.
rtp: Proximal free-tendon involvement and greater injury extent may justify a more conservative forecast, but MRI should not determine clearance by itself. Progress running speed, volume, sprint mechanics, strength, symptoms, and sport-specific demands before unrestricted return.

citation: Bonello C, King MG, Crossley KM, et al. The association between hip/groin pain and hip strength in football players: An exploratory analysis of the FORCe cohort. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2023;26(9):471-475.
abstract: This exploratory cross-sectional analysis compared hip-strength measures in football players with and without hip or groin pain and examined whether associations differed between soccer and Australian football participants.
tldr: Symptomatic football players showed lower hip adduction, internal-rotation, and external-rotation strength than pain-free controls. Hip-abduction findings differed by sport, reinforcing that cross-sectional group differences are context dependent and cannot serve as causal, diagnostic, or prospective injury thresholds.
methods: The analysis included 190 symptomatic players and 64 controls, representing 291 symptomatic limbs and 128 control limbs. Standardized hip-strength tests were compared by pain status, with exploratory evaluation of soccer and Australian-football subgroups.
findings: Hip adduction, internal-rotation, and external-rotation strength were lower in limbs from players with hip or groin pain. Lower abduction strength was evident in Australian-football participants but not in soccer participants, suggesting a sport-specific association.
limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot determine whether weakness preceded or resulted from pain. Participants were subelite, pain presentations were mixed, limbs were analyzed within players, and observed group differences do not establish a diagnostic cutoff or future-injury prediction rule.
practicalImplications: Assess hip strength as one part of a broader pain evaluation and compare athletes with their own repeated results and sport demands. A low value may identify a rehabilitation target, but it should not be interpreted as the cause of symptoms in isolation.
athleteDev: Develop multi-planar hip capacity appropriate to the athlete's sport and position, while monitoring symptoms and movement tolerance. Avoid applying one sport's group reference or one isolated strength ratio to every football code.
rtp: Track adduction and rotational strength alongside pain, function, running, cutting, kicking, and training tolerance. Clearance should reflect restored sport capacity rather than crossing an unvalidated single-test threshold.

citation: Fitzgerald D, Beckmans C, Joyce D, Mills K. The influence of sleep and training load on illness in nationally competitive male Australian Football athletes: A cohort study over one season. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019;22(2):130-134.
abstract: This prospective cohort study followed 44 nationally competitive male Australian-football athletes across a 46-week season to examine associations among self-reported sleep, external training load, and subsequent illness.
tldr: Across 67 recorded illnesses, shorter acute sleep quantity was the only independent factor associated with illness after the multivariable analysis; higher sleep was associated with lower odds. The finding supports routine sleep monitoring but does not prove that a sleep prescription will prevent illness.
methods: Athletes reported sleep while external training load was monitored across 46 weeks. Acute and longer-window sleep and load variables were related to illness occurrence using multivariable statistical models.
findings: The cohort recorded 67 illnesses. Acute sleep quantity remained independently associated with illness after adjustment, with an odds ratio of 0.49 (95% confidence interval 0.25–0.94); external-load measures were not independently associated when sleep was included.
limitations: The sample was small, male, and limited to one sport and competitive level. Sleep was self-reported, illness and exposure relationships were observational, and residual confounding or reverse effects are possible. The odds ratio does not define an individual sleep cutoff.
practicalImplications: Monitor recent sleep alongside load, symptoms, travel, and schedule pressure. When sleep falls below an athlete's normal pattern, investigate modifiable causes and coordinate recovery support rather than automatically reducing training from one value.
athleteDev: Build consistent sleep routines and the skills to manage travel, late competition, academics, and stress. Use trends and athlete conversation to guide support instead of enforcing a universal number without context.
rtp: During illness or injury, recent sleep can inform recovery planning but is not a clearance measure. Combine it with symptoms, medical status, functional progression, and tolerance of training exposure.

citation: Oxford SW, Clarke ND, Tallis J. Between-session reliability of field-based assessments of isometric neck strength. Sensors. 2024;24(15):5015.
abstract: This methodological study evaluated between-session reliability of quadruped isometric neck-strength testing with VALD ForceFrame and DynaMo devices in 27 recreationally active men, including peak force and early force-development measures.
tldr: Field-based quadruped neck-strength measures showed generally good between-session reliability, particularly for peak force, but early force-development metrics were more variable and the two devices should not be treated as interchangeable. Reliability supports repeat measurement; it does not establish injury prediction or a clearance threshold.
methods: Twenty-seven recreationally active men completed repeated isometric neck-strength sessions using ForceFrame and DynaMo systems. Intraclass correlation coefficients, coefficients of variation, and agreement statistics quantified reliability across directions and force-time variables.
findings: ForceFrame intraclass correlations exceeded 0.80 and DynaMo values exceeded 0.76, while coefficients of variation were below 13.8%. Peak-force measures were more stable than early force-development measures, and agreement did not support interchanging devices.
limitations: Participants were healthy recreationally active men rather than contact-sport athletes or patients. The study evaluated reliability, not diagnostic validity, responsiveness, concussion risk, injury prevention, or return-to-play criteria; device-specific error must be respected.
practicalImplications: Use the same device, setup, direction, instructions, and warm-up across sessions. Interpret changes against the measure's typical error and be more cautious with early force-development metrics than with peak force.
athleteDev: If neck strength is monitored, establish an individual baseline and prioritize technically consistent, progressive training. Do not convert a reliable field test into an unsupported universal target or injury-risk label.
rtp: Repeatable neck-strength testing may contribute to a broader cervical or contact-readiness assessment, but this study supplies no clearance cutoff. Use device-consistent trends with symptoms, examination, function, and graded contact exposure.

citation: Harper DJ, Carling C, Kiely J. High-intensity acceleration and deceleration demands in elite team sports competitive match play: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. Sports Medicine. 2019;49(12):1923-1947.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 19 observational studies involving 469 elite male athletes across seven team sports to characterize high-intensity acceleration and deceleration demands during competition.
tldr: High-intensity decelerations were generally more frequent than accelerations, except in American football, and soccer showed the largest imbalance. Large differences in thresholds, tracking systems, roles, and exposure definitions prevent a universal acceleration or deceleration dose from being transferred across sports or teams.
methods: The authors pooled match-play observations from 19 studies across seven elite team sports. They compared frequencies and temporal patterns of high-intensity acceleration and deceleration while evaluating methodological differences among global-positioning and tracking approaches.
findings: Decelerations occurred more often than accelerations in most included sports, with American football as an exception and soccer showing the largest acceleration-deceleration imbalance. Pooled data also suggested small declines in high-intensity actions during the second half.
limitations: Definitions, thresholds, sampling and processing methods, exposure units, playing positions, and sport demands varied substantially. Evidence was limited to elite adult men and observational match data, so pooled values do not prescribe an optimal training dose or individual readiness target.
practicalImplications: Create sport-, position-, and system-specific reference distributions with stable processing rules. Prepare athletes for both propulsive and braking demands and track how exposure is accumulated, not merely the total number of events.
athleteDev: Progress acceleration and deceleration exposure through technique, strength, tissue capacity, and representative movement tasks. Use match demands to frame preparation while individualizing for role, training age, and current tolerance.
rtp: Reintroduce acceleration and especially deceleration demands progressively, using the athlete's sport and position as context. Avoid declaring readiness from a generic event count or threshold derived from another tracking system.

citation: Fiorini S, Guglielmetti M, Neri LCL, et al. Mediterranean diet and athletic performance in elite and competitive athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutrition, Metabolism and Cardiovascular Diseases. 2025;35(11):104165.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated Mediterranean-diet adherence and performance in elite and competitive athletes. Nine small, predominantly male studies were included, with five cross-sectional studies examining diet-performance relationships.
tldr: Four of the nine included studies reported a positive effect of Mediterranean-diet adherence on some performance outcomes, but the pooled performance effect was null: standardized mean difference 0.00 (95% confidence interval -0.26 to 0.25). The evidence supports a healthful food pattern more strongly than a guaranteed direct performance gain.
methods: Nine studies involving 192 athletes were reviewed, and eligible performance outcomes were pooled. Study designs, adherence measures, sports, and performance tests varied, with five studies using cross-sectional association designs.
findings: Five of the nine studies reported an impact of Mediterranean-diet adherence on athletic performance, four of them positive; the remaining studies found no effect. The meta-analysis found no pooled performance difference, with a standardized mean difference of 0.00 and a 95% confidence interval from -0.26 to 0.25.
limitations: The evidence base was small, mostly male, heterogeneous, and low to moderate in quality; many studies were cross-sectional. Dietary assessment and performance outcomes differed, and supplement use was often not adequately measured. Causality and sport-specific effects remain uncertain.
practicalImplications: A Mediterranean-style pattern can guide food quality and variety, but performance nutrition still requires adequate total energy, carbohydrate availability, protein distribution, hydration, and sport-specific timing. Do not promise a direct performance boost from adherence alone.
athleteDev: Use the pattern as a flexible foundation built around vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, olive oil, fish, and minimally processed foods, then individualize portions and timing to training demands, preferences, access, and tolerance.
rtp: During rehabilitation, the dietary pattern may support general health, but it is not a treatment or clearance tool. Ensure adequate energy and protein for healing and coordinate individualized needs with qualified sports-nutrition and medical staff.

citation: Chen Z, Wang J, Zhao K, He G. Adherence to strength training and lower rates of sports injury in contact sports: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(5):23259671251331134.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 16 randomized controlled trials of strength-training interventions intended to reduce injuries in contact-sport participants, including single-component and multicomponent programs.
tldr: Strength-training interventions were associated with a 30% lower pooled injury rate, but programs, sports, adherence, and outcome definitions varied. The result supports consistently delivered strength exposure as part of prevention; it does not identify one universally superior exercise, dose, or program.
methods: Sixteen randomized controlled trials were included and injury risk ratios were pooled. Analyses examined overall effects and subgroups based on single-component or multicomponent programs and injury location.
findings: The pooled injury risk ratio was 0.70 (95% confidence interval 0.60–0.82). Single-component analyses reported lower groin-injury risk (0.69) and hamstring-injury risk (0.37), while multicomponent analyses reported lower knee-injury risk (0.71) and ankle-injury risk (0.68).
limitations: Sports, participant characteristics, program content, dose, adherence, exposure, and injury definitions varied. Subgroup findings do not directly compare components or prove superiority, and the review provides insufficient detail for one universal prescription.
practicalImplications: Protect regular, progressive strength-training exposure and track completion, quality, and tolerance. Select exercises and doses for the sport's injury patterns and the athlete's needs, then adapt without losing the program's essential loading stimulus.
athleteDev: Embed strength development across the year instead of relying on short prevention blocks. Sustainable adherence, progressive overload, and technically sound execution are more defensible targets than copying a single pooled protocol.
rtp: Rebuild relevant strength capacity progressively and transition from rehabilitation exercises to representative contact-sport loading. The pooled prevention effect does not define a clearance threshold or replace functional and sport-specific testing.

citation: İnce İ, Tortu E. Association between intra and inter-limb strength asymmetry with sprint kinematics and force-velocity profile in youth team athletes. The Knee. 2025;52:99-107.
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined relationships among isokinetic knee-strength asymmetry, sprint kinematics, and sprint force-velocity characteristics in 74 youth athletes from football, volleyball, and handball.
tldr: Strength-asymmetry measures showed only weak-to-moderate, metric-dependent relationships with sprint variables. Most athletes were below 15% asymmetry, but some reached 42%; neither value creates a universal performance, injury-risk, or training threshold.
methods: Athletes completed two sessions 48 hours apart, including anthropometry, sprint testing, Optojump kinematic analysis, Samozino force-velocity profiling, and isokinetic knee-flexor and knee-extensor testing at 60 and 180 degrees per second. Standard percentage-difference equations quantified asymmetry.
findings: Associations between intra- and inter-limb strength asymmetry and sprint measures ranged from weak to moderate and changed with the strength and sprint variable examined. Group asymmetry was usually below 15%, but individual values were highly variable and reached 42%.
limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot show whether asymmetry causes performance or injury outcomes. A mixed-sport youth sample, multiple test speeds and definitions, and no prospective injury or intervention follow-up prevent causal interpretation or a universal cutoff.
practicalImplications: Standardize the muscle action, speed, limb comparison, and sprint metric before monitoring change. Investigate large or changing values in the context of the athlete's own strength, sprint mechanics, symptoms, and training history.
athleteDev: Develop bilateral and unilateral strength and sprint skill while judging progress from multiple performance measures. Do not devote training to reducing an asymmetry percentage unless the underlying limb capacity or sport function also warrants attention.
rtp: During rehabilitation, reproduce the same test conditions and examine absolute limb capacity alongside symmetry, symptoms, sprint progression, and sport tasks. A 15% boundary is not a validated clearance rule.

citation: Ahmed M, Zaki S, Alam MF, et al. The impact of intrinsic foot muscle strengthening exercises in asymptomatic athletes with normal foot structure: A systematic review. Clinical Epidemiology and Global Health. 2024;27:101597.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated intrinsic-foot-muscle strengthening in asymptomatic athletes with normal foot structure. Four heterogeneous studies were included, preventing meta-analysis.
tldr: The small evidence base suggested improvements in intrinsic-foot strength and some morphological, motor, and propulsive-force outcomes, but running economy did not improve and one study found no change in arch stiffness. Results are promising but too heterogeneous and bias-prone for a guaranteed performance or prevention claim.
methods: Six databases were searched for eligible athlete studies, and the Cochrane tool was used to assess risk of bias. Four studies were synthesized qualitatively because protocols, measurement units, and outcomes could not be pooled.
findings: All four studies reported improved intrinsic-foot strength, with some favorable changes in foot morphology, clinician-rated motor performance, subjective function, and vertical running propulsive force. Running economy was unchanged, and one eight-week intervention did not alter medial-longitudinal-arch stiffness.
limitations: Only four heterogeneous studies were available, interventions were only roughly comparable, outcome units differed, and risk of bias was present. Healthy athletes with normal feet do not establish treatment efficacy for painful or pathological feet or injury prevention.
practicalImplications: Intrinsic-foot work can be a low-cost accessory when foot capacity is relevant, but select outcomes deliberately and reassess them. Do not promise improved running economy, arch stiffness, or fewer injuries from short-foot exercises alone.
athleteDev: Progress foot-muscle control and loading within a broader program that includes calf strength, balance, jumping, running, footwear, and sport exposure. Keep the dosage tolerable and judge value by the athlete's targeted function.
rtp: For foot or lower-limb rehabilitation, these healthy-athlete findings provide a possible exercise option rather than a clinical protocol. Progress symptoms, tissue loading, whole-limb capacity, running, and sport tasks before clearance.

citation: Ackerman DR, Ptasinski AM, Edmond T, et al. Prophylactic knee bracing in offensive linemen of the National Football League: A retrospective analysis of usage trends, player performance, and major knee injury. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2023;11(8):23259671231191767.
abstract: This retrospective cohort analysis compared major knee injury and Pro Football Focus performance grades in NFL offensive-lineman seasons with and without observed bilateral prophylactic knee-brace use from 2014 through 2020.
tldr: Brace use was associated with fewer major knee injuries (0.013 versus 0.049 per player; P=.04) and no cumulative performance-grade difference, even as use declined from 16.3% to 5.6%. Nonrandom brace choice, unequal groups, unknown prior injury, and public-data classification prevent a causal conclusion.
methods: Offensive linemen with at least 200 regular-season snaps were classified as bracers or nonbracers using public images and game video. Public injury reports identified knee injuries causing missed games, and season-level Pro Football Focus grades represented performance.
findings: Bracers had a lower cumulative rate of major knee injury than nonbracers, and isolated medial-collateral-ligament injury was the most common event among nonbracers. Cumulative and most season-specific performance grades did not differ significantly, while brace use declined across the seven seasons.
limitations: Brace exposure was self-selected and groups were imbalanced. Prior injury, baseline knee risk, player skill, brace type, fit, and compliance could not be fully controlled, while brace and injury identification depended on public sources and performance grades may miss relevant task effects.
practicalImplications: Consider prophylactic bracing through shared medical, equipment, performance, and player decision-making for offensive linemen. Discuss fit, comfort, role demands, prior injury, and uncertainty instead of presenting the observed association as guaranteed protection.
athleteDev: If bracing is used, integrate it during practice so stance, footwork, leverage, and conditioning adapt to the equipment. Maintain strength, mobility, technique, and exposure management rather than treating the brace as the sole prevention strategy.
rtp: This study concerns prophylaxis, not postinjury clearance. A brace may be one risk-management component after knee injury, but readiness still requires medical stability, strength, function, football movement, contact tolerance, and position-specific work.

citation: Fereday K, Hills SP, Russell M, et al. A comparison of rolling averages versus discrete time epochs for assessing the worst-case scenario locomotor demands of professional soccer match-play. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2020;23(8):764-769.
abstract: This descriptive observational study compared fixed epochs with rolling averages for estimating peak total-distance and high-speed-running demands in 25 professional outfield soccer players across 28 matches.
tldr: Fixed epochs underestimated rolling-average peak demand by roughly 7-10% for total distance and 12-25% for high-speed distance. Peak values also changed substantially with window length, position, starting status, and match context, so the calculation method must travel with the number.
methods: Players from one English Championship club wore 10-Hz tracking systems. Relative total and high-speed distance were calculated with fixed and rolling windows from 60 to 600 seconds, and mixed models examined epoch, position, starting status, result, location, formation, and time of day.
findings: Rolling 60-second peaks averaged 190.1 m/min for total distance and 59.5 m/min for high-speed distance, falling to 120.9 and 14.2 m/min at 600 seconds. Fixed windows consistently returned lower values, and several positional and match-context effects were present.
limitations: One club and 28 matches limit generalization, while estimates depend on the device, speed threshold, processing, window, and tactical context. Peak locomotor values omit technical, tactical, collision, acceleration, and individual physiological demands and do not identify an optimal training dose.
practicalImplications: Use rolling averages when the goal is to capture true peak passages, and report the window, threshold, device, and processing rules. Build club- and position-specific distributions instead of copying a published number into practice design.
athleteDev: Expose athletes progressively to short intense passages and longer sustained demands that reflect their role. Use peak-demand data as a planning reference while preserving technical and tactical representativeness.
rtp: Compare reintegration exposure with the athlete's own role-specific rolling-window demands. Progress both intensity and duration, but do not use one peak running value as a standalone clearance criterion.

citation: Casamichana D, Martín-García A, Gómez Díaz A, et al. Accumulative weekly load in a professional football team: With special reference to match playing time and game position. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(1):115-124.
abstract: This observational study compared GPS-derived weekly external load in 24 professional reserve-squad soccer players according to match-minute group and playing position.
tldr: Players completing more match minutes generally accumulated greater weekly total, high-speed, sprint, and high-metabolic-load distance. Match participation can create predictable exposure gaps, but this one-team study did not test a universal compensatory top-up dose or show that top-ups improve outcomes.
methods: Training and official-match GPS data were accumulated for total distance, high-speed and sprint distance, high-metabolic-load distance, and high-intensity accelerations and decelerations. Weeks were compared across 90-minute, more-than-60, less-than-60, and zero-minute match groups and by position.
findings: Greater match participation produced higher weekly exposure for most variables, particularly total and high-metabolic-load distance and, for full-match players, high-speed and sprint distance. Position-specific patterns were evident, although relative-to-match comparisons showed less positional variation.
limitations: The sample came from one professional reserve squad. Indoor work and internal-load measures were absent, and broad match-minute groups masked exposure differences such as 61 versus 89 minutes. No injury, adaptation, or performance response to compensatory training was tested.
practicalImplications: Use match minutes and position as an early flag for underexposure, then quantify the athlete's actual week and deliver individualized top-up work that targets the missing qualities without compromising recovery.
athleteDev: Protect adequate high-speed, sprint, and total-volume exposure for nonstarters across the season. Build these opportunities into a consistent development plan rather than waiting for match selection to supply all conditioning.
rtp: Match-minute groups can contextualize the demands an athlete is missing during reintegration. Progress external load and internal response toward individual role demands while accounting for tissue status and next-day recovery.

citation: Ekstrand J, Spreco A, Windt J, Khan KM. Are elite soccer teams' preseason training sessions associated with fewer in-season injuries? A 15-year analysis from the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;48(3):723-729.
abstract: This team-level epidemiological study examined whether the number of preseason training sessions was associated with competitive-season injury outcomes across 244 team-seasons from 44 elite European soccer clubs.
tldr: Every 10 additional preseason sessions was associated with lower injury burden and severe-injury incidence plus slightly better training attendance and match availability. Model fit was only 1.3-3.2%, so session count explained little of the variation and should not be interpreted as a causal dose.
methods: UEFA Elite Club Injury Study data spanning up to 15 seasons were analyzed with separate linear regressions. Preseason session count was related to in-season injury burden, severe-injury incidence, overall injury incidence, training attendance, and match availability.
findings: Ten additional sessions corresponded to 22 fewer layoff days per 1000 hours, 0.18 fewer severe injuries per 1000 hours, 1.4 percentage points greater training attendance, and 1.0 point greater match availability. Four of five outcomes favored more sessions.
limitations: The team-level observational design cannot separate session count from player availability, roster quality, medical systems, travel, coaching, content, or resilience. Low adjusted R-squared values show that most injury variation was unexplained, and the association does not establish an optimal number or intensity.
practicalImplications: Protect enough preseason time for progressive preparation and reduce avoidable travel or scheduling erosion. Judge preseason quality through participation, content, progression, and response rather than chasing a session total.
athleteDev: Use preseason to rebuild exposure systematically across strength, running, football, and recovery demands. Preserve individual modification while avoiding unnecessary underpreparation for athletes who can train.
rtp: Athletes returning during preseason need an individualized progression, not automatic completion of the team session count. Track the relevant loading content, function, symptoms, and football exposure before full availability.

citation: West MA, Compton HR, Dascombe BJ, Secomb JL. Introducing the novel deceleration threshold method: Comparative reliability to previous sprint deceleration analysis methods in team-sport athletes. European Journal of Sport Science. 2025;25(4):e12278.
abstract: This methodological study compared three analysis methods for preplanned sprint deceleration testing in 20 team-sport participants using motorized linear-encoder data collected across two days.
tldr: A threshold-based start point combined with the average of the best two trials produced excellent interday reliability for time to stop, distance to stop, and average deceleration. That reliability is protocol specific and does not establish criterion validity, injury prediction, or transfer to multidirectional play.
methods: Ten women and 10 men performed three maximal 30-m sprint-to-stop trials on two testing days. Set-distance, peak-velocity, and novel deceleration-threshold analyses produced time-to-stop, distance-to-stop, and average-deceleration metrics, with reliability tested using ICC, CV, and standard error.
findings: The threshold method using the average of the best two trials returned interday ICC and CV values of .93 and 6.4% for time to stop, .97 and 5.3% for distance to stop, and .92 and 7.1% for average deceleration.
limitations: The small mixed sample, one linear task, motorized encoder, customized processing, and two-day design constrain generalization. The study did not compare against a criterion measure or test responsiveness, multidirectional deceleration, sport performance, or injury outcomes.
practicalImplications: If adopting the test, reproduce the threshold definition, equipment, filtering, 30-m protocol, and average-of-best-two rule. Interpret change against device- and metric-specific error.
athleteDev: Use reliable linear testing to profile stopping strategy alongside strength, sprinting, multidirectional movement, and sport practice. Train braking capacity progressively without treating one laboratory metric as the whole quality.
rtp: The protocol may document recovery of repeatable linear deceleration performance, but clearance also requires symptoms, tissue capacity, directional variety, unplanned tasks, fatigue tolerance, and representative sport exposure.

citation: Pérez-Castilla A, García-Ramos A, Janicijevic D, et al. Unilateral or bilateral standing broad jumps: Which jump type provides inter-limb asymmetries with a higher reliability? Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2021;20:317-327.
abstract: This methodological study compared between-session reliability of force-platform performance and inter-limb-asymmetry variables from unilateral and bilateral standing broad jumps in 24 amateur basketball players.
tldr: Most raw single-limb performance variables were acceptably reliable in both jump variants, but derived asymmetry values were not: ICCs ranged from -.40 to .58 and the favored limb was usually inconsistent. Reliable limb measurements do not automatically create a reliable asymmetry score.
methods: Twelve women and 12 men completed two identical sessions of four unilateral and two bilateral standing broad jumps. Dual force platforms measured limb-specific force, velocity, power, and impulse; percentage-difference and bilateral-asymmetry equations generated asymmetry metrics.
findings: Most performance-variable CVs were 3.65-9.81%, with some force and power variables reaching 10.00-15.46%. Asymmetry reliability was unacceptable and direction agreement was mostly slight to fair, with only isolated metrics showing moderate agreement.
limitations: The sample was small, amateur, and limited to basketball and two sessions. Results depend on the jump variant, metric, and asymmetry equation, while no injury, performance, intervention, or clinical outcome was evaluated.
practicalImplications: Track absolute performance for each limb and its measurement error before calculating asymmetry. Confirm an unusual result across repeated sessions and relevant tasks rather than reacting to one percentage.
athleteDev: Use unilateral and bilateral broad jumps to describe horizontal-jump qualities, not to impose a stable weak-side identity. Base training priorities on repeatable capacity deficits and sport needs.
rtp: A broad-jump asymmetry percentage should not determine clearance. Use repeated absolute limb performance alongside symptoms, strength, landing and propulsion skill, running, and sport-specific tolerance.

citation: Dos'Santos T, Evans DT, Read DB. Validity of the Hawkin Dynamics wireless dual force platform system against a piezoelectric laboratory grade system for vertical countermovement jump variables. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):1144-1148.
abstract: This criterion-comparison study placed Hawkin Dynamics wireless dual force platforms directly over Kistler laboratory platforms while two recreational male soccer players performed 25 countermovement jumps each.
tldr: Across 16 countermovement-jump variables, system differences were no more than 3.4% and 15 variables correlated .977-1.000, but fixed bias affected six variables and proportional bias affected 10. The platforms appear suitable for the tested uses, yet values should not be assumed interchangeable.
methods: Vertical ground-reaction force was collected simultaneously from stacked Hawkin Dynamics and Kistler systems during 50 jumps. Sixteen outcome and strategy variables were compared for fixed and proportional bias, percentage difference, and correlation.
findings: Near-perfect to perfect correlations were observed for 15 variables. Fixed bias affected braking power, mean propulsion force, time to takeoff, flight time, and body weight measures; proportional bias affected multiple propulsion, braking, timing, power, and body-weight variables despite small overall percentage differences.
limitations: Only two participants generated the 50 repeated observations in one session, limiting independence and generalization. High correlation does not prove agreement, and the design did not assess between-session reliability, longitudinal sensitivity, broader populations, or device interchangeability.
practicalImplications: Use the Hawkin system consistently and establish its own baselines, error, and change rules for each variable. Avoid mixing historical Kistler values or assuming small changes are biological when bias or noise could explain them.
athleteDev: Force-platform data can clarify jump outcome and strategy when testing is standardized. Use it to support, not replace, strength, power, movement, and sport-performance assessment.
rtp: Device-consistent jump trends may contribute to rehabilitation monitoring, but this validation study supplies no return-to-sport cutoff. Combine results with symptoms, strength, function, and graded sport exposure.

citation: Winter IP, Burdin J, Wilson PB. Associations between skeletal muscle mass, fat-free mass, and saliva osmolality: A cross-sectional study. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2026;36(4):508-513.
abstract: This cross-sectional study evaluated whether skeletal muscle mass or fat-free mass was associated with portable-device saliva osmolality in 72 adults.
tldr: Neither skeletal muscle mass nor fat-free mass was meaningfully associated with saliva osmolality before or after adjustment; correlations were only .10 and .08. This reduces concern about one potential body-composition confounder but does not validate a single saliva value as a complete hydration assessment.
methods: Forty-two men and 30 women completed bioelectrical-impedance body-composition measurement and provided two saliva samples three to five minutes apart for MX3 osmolality testing. Models adjusted for age, sex, four-hour fluid intake, and sampling time.
findings: Unadjusted associations for muscle mass and fat-free mass were nonsignificant, as were adjusted models. Spearman correlations with saliva osmolality were small and nonsignificant at .10 and .08, respectively.
limitations: This convenience sample was not an athlete validation cohort, body composition was estimated by bioelectrical impedance, and paired saliva samples were collected within minutes. Cross-sectional null associations do not establish diagnostic validity, responsiveness, or decision thresholds across hydration states.
practicalImplications: Do not automatically correct saliva osmolality for muscle mass in similar adults, but interpret it with recent intake, environment, symptoms, body-mass change, urine measures, and individual trends.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that hydration assessment is contextual and that one portable reading is not a verdict. Build individualized drinking routines around training demand, climate, access, and observed fluid loss.
rtp: Saliva osmolality may supplement monitoring during illness, heat exposure, or rehabilitation, but it is not a clearance test. Resolve clinical hydration concerns with medical assessment and corroborating evidence.

citation: Jiang T, Zhang M, Wang Z, Wang P. The effects of integrative neuromuscular training on injury risk and athletic performance in athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2026;18(1):115.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 25 randomized trials involving 10,124 participants to evaluate integrative neuromuscular training for injury risk and jump, sprint, change-of-direction, and dynamic-balance performance.
tldr: Multicomponent neuromuscular training was associated with 27% lower injury risk and moderate-to-large performance improvements, but most outcomes were heterogeneous and most trials had some risk-of-bias concerns. Favorable subgroup and dose patterns are hypotheses, not proof of one best program.
methods: Nine databases were searched through August 31, 2025. Randomized trials were pooled using risk ratios and standardized mean differences, with ROB2, GRADE, publication-bias checks, and subgroup analyses by athlete and intervention characteristics.
findings: Pooled injury risk was .73 (95% CI .58-.91). Standardized mean differences favored training for jump .88, sprint .75, change of direction .97, and dynamic balance .91; subgroup analyses suggested larger effects in some adult, female, football, higher-frequency, and longer-session categories.
limitations: Intervention content, populations, sports, outcomes, and follow-up varied, significant heterogeneity affected most analyses, and most trials had some risk-of-bias concerns. Subgroups cannot establish causal superiority, and the reviewed local source is an unedited early-access manuscript.
practicalImplications: Use structured multicomponent training that combines strength, landing, balance, plyometric, agility, and movement exposure appropriate to the sport. Protect adherence and progression while monitoring whether the chosen program changes its intended outcomes.
athleteDev: Embed neuromuscular development consistently rather than as a brief warm-up campaign. Progress complexity and load with training age and preserve enough high-quality exposure for adaptation.
rtp: Components can support restoration of strength, landing, balance, and change-of-direction capacity, but pooled prevention effects do not define clearance. Rebuild individual deficits and representative sport tolerance before unrestricted return.

citation: Eckard TG, Padua DA, Hearn DW, Pexa BS, Frank BS. The relationship between training load and injury in athletes: A systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(8):1929-1961.
abstract: This systematic review examined prospective relationships between training load and musculoskeletal injury across athlete, military, and first-responder populations, including 57 studies published before July 2017.
tldr: Forty-seven studies reported at least partly significant load–injury relationships, with the most consistent evidence for subjective internal load. Direction depended on the metric and timeframe; the review supports thoughtful load monitoring but not a universal safe ratio, cutoff, or individual injury prediction.
methods: Five databases were searched for prospective studies. Fifty-seven articles underwent Newcastle-Ottawa quality assessment and Oxford evidence grading, followed by narrative synthesis because populations, exposures, timeframes, outcomes, and analyses were heterogeneous.
findings: Forty-seven studies found at least some significant relationship between load and injury. Thirty-six studies were rated good, six fair, and 15 poor; subjective internal-load measures showed the strongest overall support, while both high and low loads could be associated with risk depending on timing and context.
limitations: Most evidence was observational and vulnerable to confounding, reverse causation, exposure misclassification, and inconsistent injury definitions. Heterogeneity prevented a pooled threshold, and statistical associations at group level cannot reliably predict which athlete will be injured.
practicalImplications: Use load data to improve conversations and planning: monitor external exposure, internal response, rapid changes, chronic preparation, schedule, and athlete context together. Avoid automated red-light decisions from one ratio or threshold.
athleteDev: Build durable capacity through progressive, consistent exposure and use monitoring to identify unusual change or underpreparation. The aim is informed adjustment, not keeping every athlete below a single workload number.
rtp: Track rehabilitation and team exposure as context for graded reintegration, but do not infer reinjury probability from one load metric. Combine response to loading with symptoms, function, tissue status, and sport-specific demands.

citation: Benoy R, Ramirez C, Hitchcock M, Reardon C. Cannabis use in adolescent and young adult athletes: A clinical review. Sports Health. 2024;16(2):279-284.
abstract: This clinical review examined cannabis prevalence, performance effects, health risks, and regulatory considerations for adolescent and young adult athletes using literature published from 2010 through 2022.
tldr: Survey evidence suggested up to one in four athletes used cannabis in the prior year, while the literature did not support performance enhancement and described objective impairment plus cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, mental-health, and substance-use risks. Product, dose, route, and athlete context vary, so broad claims remain inappropriate.
methods: The authors searched PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and SportDiscus for literature published between January 2010 and December 2022 and added relevant references. The clinical review was classified as level-4 evidence.
