citation: Domroes T, Weidlich K, Bohm S, Mersmann F, Arampatzis A. Personalized Tendon Loading Reduces Muscle-Tendon Imbalances in Male Adolescent Elite Athletes. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2024;34:e14555.
abstract: This seasonal cohort study examined whether tendon-strain-targeted exercise changed muscle-tendon mechanical balance in adolescent elite handball athletes.
tldr: Personalized tendon loading improved strength and tendon stiffness in a small adolescent handball cohort, but it did not measure fewer tendon injuries. Use it as a measured training approach, not a universal prevention prescription.
methods: Thirteen male adolescent elite handball athletes added patellar-tendon exercises three times weekly for about 31 weeks, while 13 controls continued usual training. Dynamometry, ultrasonography, tendon strain, and ultrasound structural-integrity measures were assessed four times during the season.
findings: Only the intervention group increased knee-extensor strength and normalized patellar-tendon stiffness. It had lower seasonal fluctuation in maximal tendon strain and descriptively fewer athletes with strain at or above 9%, while structural integrity and between-group strain changes were not significant.
limitations: The small, nonrandomized male handball sample limits causal inference and transfer. Mechanical surrogate outcomes, rather than injury incidence, were measured, and the specialized imaging and strain prescription may not be routinely feasible.
practicalImplications: If measurement capability is valid, individualize tendon loading and track response rather than prescribing the same relative load to every athlete. Combine training decisions with symptoms, clinical assessment, exposure, and progression tolerance.
athleteDev: Explain that tendon capacity develops over time and that the same gym load can create different tissue demand across athletes. Encourage early reporting of persistent tendon symptoms rather than chasing a target strain.
rtp: Use tendon loading as one part of graded capacity restoration. Return decisions still require symptoms, clinical findings, sport-specific force and speed exposure, confidence, and progression through practice.

citation: Jiang Z, Hao Y, Jin N, Li Y. A Systematic Review of the Relationship Between Workload and Injury Risk of Professional Male Soccer Players. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19:13237.
abstract: This PRISMA review assessed workload and injury-risk evidence in professional male soccer through 2021.
tldr: No GPS metric or ACWR threshold reliably identified a minimum injury-risk level. Workload is useful context, but availability decisions require more than one load number.
methods: Two reviewers searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus through December 2021 for original English-language studies of professional male soccer players reporting load parameters and injury outcomes.
findings: Short-term fixture congestion appeared to increase match-injury incidence, whereas longer congestion had no consistent overall or match-injury effect. GPS total distance, high-speed running, and acceleration had inconclusive associations; s-RPE ACWR related to non-contact injury in some studies, but no minimum-risk threshold emerged.
limitations: Included studies varied in injury definitions, GPS devices, speed thresholds, analyses, and exposure windows. The evidence was observational and male professional soccer-specific, so it cannot establish causation or individual prediction.
practicalImplications: Use internal and external load trends with symptoms, availability, recovery, exposure history, and schedule context. Investigate abrupt or unusual changes rather than setting one universal threshold.
athleteDev: Help athletes understand why a workload score is a conversation starter, not a pass-fail injury forecast. Pair monitoring with honest reporting of recovery and emerging symptoms.
rtp: Rebuild load progressively across total running, high-speed work, and sport tasks while tracking response. Avoid using ACWR or a GPS value as a standalone clearance criterion.

citation: Page RM, Field A, Langley B, Harper LD, Julian R. The Effects of Fixture Congestion on Injury in Professional Male Soccer: A Systematic Review. Sports Medicine. 2023.
abstract: This systematic review examined injury findings when professional male soccer schedules contained at least two matches separated by four days or less.
tldr: Congested schedules were usually linked with higher match-injury incidence, but the evidence cannot isolate fixture density from rotation, recovery, and other club decisions.
methods: Following a preregistered PRISMA approach, the review searched four databases through February 2022 and included eight studies reporting time-loss injury data during congested professional male soccer schedules.
findings: Five studies found higher match-injury incidence in congested periods. Findings for training and overall injury incidence varied, and layoff duration was typically lower during congestion.
limitations: The evidence base was small and observational, with varying injury and congestion definitions. Scheduling effects could not be separated from rotation, training modification, travel, and recovery practices.
practicalImplications: Plan congested weeks collaboratively: adjust exposure, recovery, rotation, and symptom surveillance while preserving the sport-specific work athletes need. Review team patterns locally.
athleteDev: Frame schedule management as preparation and communication, not an assumption that every short turnaround is unsafe. Encourage prompt reporting of recovery problems during dense periods.
rtp: Match return progression to current capacity and the actual fixture sequence. A short interval should increase review and coordination, not automatically determine participation.

citation: Flore Z, Hambly K, De Coninck K, Welsch G. Time-Loss and Recurrence of Lateral Ligament Ankle Sprains in Male Elite Football: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized time-loss and recurrence after lateral ligament ankle sprain in male elite soccer.
tldr: Lateral ankle sprain recurrence was about 17%, while a typical absence was about 15 days but varied too much to define a reliable timeline. Time alone is a weak return guide.
methods: Six databases were searched through April 2021 for English-language cohort, case, case-control, and randomized studies reporting recurrence or time-loss in male professional soccer players; 13 recurrence and 12 time-loss studies were included.
findings: Among 16,442 players in the recurrence meta-analysis, recurrence was 17.11% (95% CI 13.31%-20.92%). Time-loss data were highly heterogeneous and therefore descriptive: weighted mean 15.92 days and median 14.95 days.
limitations: Time-loss heterogeneity was considerable, and injury definitions, recurrence windows, severity reporting, and designs differed. Results are population estimates in male elite soccer, not individual healing or readiness criteria.
practicalImplications: Use a criteria-based lateral-ankle-sprain process that includes symptoms, examination, function, sport exposure, and athlete confidence. Audit local recurrence and timelines rather than adopting the mean absence as a target.
athleteDev: Clarify that early symptom improvement does not guarantee restored ankle capacity. Build confidence through progressive balance, strength, running, cutting, and ball-work exposure.
rtp: Do not clear by days missed. Progress clinical, functional, and soccer-specific criteria together and monitor the response to repeated practice and match-demand tasks.

citation: Flore Z, Hambly K, De Coninck K, Welsch G. A Rehabilitation Algorithm After Lateral Ankle Sprains in Professional Football (Soccer): An Approach Based on Clinical Practice Guidelines. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;19(7):910-922.
abstract: This clinical commentary presents a guideline-informed, criteria-based lateral-ankle-sprain rehabilitation algorithm for professional soccer.
tldr: The four-level algorithm organizes symptom, clinical, functional, and kicking progression so return is not time-only. Its effectiveness and thresholds still need testing.
methods: The authors integrated clinical-practice-guideline assessments, professional-soccer experience, an ankle-function score, standardized examination, functional performance tests, and interval kicking into a four-level progression model.
findings: Advancement requires passing a level-dependent ankle-function score, clinical examination, and performance tests. The proposed approach links each level to expected next-stage demands and includes progressive return to ball work.
limitations: This is a Level 5 clinical commentary, not an effectiveness trial. Phase-specific tests and thresholds have not been validated for sensitivity, specificity, or reinjury reduction and may not translate outside professional soccer.
practicalImplications: Use the model as a transparent multidisciplinary checklist and adapt the tests to available equipment and the athlete's presentation. Record criteria and response at each progression step.
athleteDev: Give athletes visible targets across symptoms, function, and soccer tasks so return is understood as rebuilding capability rather than waiting for a date.
rtp: Combine algorithm steps with medical judgment, tissue healing, sport role, training response, and full-practice progression. Passing a proposed threshold alone does not prove safe return.

citation: Ribeiro-Alvares JB, Cetolin T, Haupenthal A, Baroni BM. Acute-Chronic Workload Ratio of Professional Soccer Players Preceding Hamstring Muscle Injuries: A 2-Season Retrospective Study. Sport Sciences for Health. 2023.
abstract: This retrospective one-team study described GPS acute:chronic workload ratios before professional male soccer hamstring injuries.
tldr: Three quarters of hamstring injuries occurred without any GPS ACWR above 1.5. A danger-zone cutoff should not be the main availability decision.
methods: Forty-eight professional male soccer players were reviewed across two seasons; 28 days of GPS total distance, high-speed distance, very-high-speed distance, and actions above 19 km/h were calculated before each hamstring injury.
findings: Twenty players sustained hamstring injuries. Fifteen injuries had ACWR below 1.5 in all four metrics before the injurious exposure; five exceeded 1.5 for very-high-speed distance, with fewer also exceeding it for the other metrics.
limitations: Only injury cases from one team were examined, without uninjured exposure controls or prospective prediction testing. Gym load was omitted, and the selected cutoff and windows may not represent total individual load.
practicalImplications: Use external-load data to prompt context review, not as a binary clearance filter. Include prior injury, symptoms, sprint tolerance, clinical information, and the rest of training when planning availability.
athleteDev: Avoid labeling one ratio as dangerous or safe. Teach athletes to report hamstring symptoms and recovery changes while staff progress high-speed exposure deliberately.
rtp: Reintroduce high-speed running and match actions through a graded plan; do not clear or withhold an athlete solely because of an ACWR threshold.

citation: Lievens E, Van Vossel K, Van de Casteele F, Wezenbeek E, Deprez D, Matthys S, et al. Muscle Fibre Typology as a Novel Risk Factor for Hamstring Strain Injuries in Professional Football (Soccer): A Prospective Cohort Study. Sports Medicine. 2021.
abstract: This prospective cohort study tested whether noninvasively estimated muscle-fibre typology was associated with hamstring-strain injury in professional soccer.
tldr: Fast fibre typology was associated with higher hamstring-injury risk in this cohort, but it is not a deterministic, directly modifiable, or standalone screening result.
methods: Professional Belgian and English soccer players were followed over three seasons. Soleus carnosine measured with proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy classified typology, and multivariable Cox models evaluated 27 index hamstring strains.
findings: Fast typology was associated with 5.3-fold higher index hamstring-strain risk than slow typology in the combined cohort (95% CI 1.92-14.8). The association was reported independently in both leagues.
limitations: There were relatively few injuries and the cohort was male professional soccer only. Soleus spectroscopy is a proxy for broader muscle typology, and observational association does not show that modifying training from this result prevents injury.
practicalImplications: If specialist measurement is valid and feasible, consider typology as one risk-context variable alongside modifiable strength, capacity, exposure, and clinical information. Do not use it as a label or exclusion criterion.
athleteDev: Communicate that biological traits are not destiny. Focus athletes on controllable preparation, recovery, honest symptom reporting, and progressive sprint exposure.
rtp: Return decisions should emphasize current capacity and sport-specific tolerance. Fibre typology cannot substitute for clinical assessment, strength, high-speed exposure, and practice progression.

citation: Edouard P, Lahti J, Fleres L, Ahtiainen J, Ulvila JJ, Lehtinen T, et al. A Musculoskeletal Multifactorial Individualised Programme for Hamstring Muscle Injury Risk Reduction in Professional Football: Results of a Prospective Cohort Study. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2024;10:e001866.
abstract: This prospective cohort study evaluated a multifactorial, individualized hamstring-risk program in Finnish professional soccer.
tldr: The program was feasible, but its primary time-to-injury comparison was not significant. Favorable secondary results should be tested locally rather than treated as proof.
methods: Finnish premier-league teams used 2019 as a control season and implemented the individualized program in 2021. Screening informed lumbopelvic, range-of-motion, posterior-chain, sprint, and related training targets; Cox regression assessed hamstring injury.
findings: There were 20 hamstring injuries among 90 control-season players and 16 among 87 intervention-season players. The primary hazard ratio was not significant (0.77, 95% CI 0.39-1.51); among 31 players in both seasons, secondary analysis found lower injury burden (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.85).
limitations: The prior-season nonrandomized control assumes comparable seasons; COVID disruption, club implementation differences, small samples, and possible underpowering limit inference. Secondary and compliance associations cannot establish primary efficacy.
practicalImplications: A multifactorial approach can organize individualized strength, sprint exposure, range of motion, lumbopelvic work, and monitoring. Define local adherence and outcome measures before assuming it reduces injuries.
athleteDev: Show athletes how screening informs a flexible plan rather than a deficit label. Consistent completion and progression of relevant work may matter more than any one exercise.
rtp: Use progressive capacity restoration across posterior-chain strength, sprint mechanics, running exposure, and sport practice. A program checklist does not replace tissue, symptom, and performance criteria.

citation: Balboni JM, Semelsberger SD, Boggiano VJ, Webber K, Moran J, Mast P, et al. Jones Fractures in Elite Athletes—2025 International Foot and Ankle Sports Consensus and Systematic Review. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2025.
abstract: This modified-Delphi consensus and systematic review addressed diagnosis and management of Jones fractures in elite athletes.
tldr: Treatment and return varied by stress versus traumatic aetiology and fracture features. Imaging and specialist decision-making matter more than a fixed return-to-sport average.
methods: Thirty-seven international experts completed two modified-Delphi rounds to develop 37 statements. A systematic review of 27 studies including 1,056 patients compared operative and nonoperative management in athletes.
findings: Stress-aetiology fractures were treated with open reduction internal fixation in 86.4% of cases, with mean return at 13.3 plus or minus 4.5 weeks and 8.4% complications. Traumatic fractures returned at 11.6 plus or minus 2.2 weeks regardless of modality; treatment failure was highest for conservatively managed traumatic fractures (16.1%).
limitations: This is Level V consensus supported largely by nonrandomized studies with varying treatment selection, chronicity, athlete level, and return criteria. Some statements lacked clinical data, and expert consensus cannot eliminate bias.
practicalImplications: Differentiate stress and traumatic presentation, use appropriate imaging, and coordinate orthopedic, rehabilitation, and performance decisions. Discuss timelines as ranges tied to healing and sport demand.
athleteDev: Explain why a Jones fracture needs individualized imaging and progression rather than comparison with another athlete's timeline. Emphasize adherence to loading and healing restrictions.
rtp: Confirm healing and functional sport demands before return. Surgical status or an average return time alone cannot establish readiness for practice or competition.

citation: Rudisill SS, Varady NH, Kucharik MP, Eberlin CT, Martin SD. Evidence-Based Hamstring Injury Prevention and Risk Factor Management: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized randomized trials of hamstring-injury prevention and modifiable risk-factor interventions in adult sport participants.
tldr: Eccentric training reduced hamstring-injury incidence and improved several related capacities, but the evidence does not specify one optimal exercise, dose, or individual solution.
methods: MEDLINE, CINAHL, Cochrane Central, and SPORTDiscus were searched in October 2020. One hundred eight parallel-group randomized trials in noninjured adult recreational, semiprofessional, or professional athletes were included.
findings: Eccentric training reduced injury incidence by 56.8%-70.0% and improved concentric strength, eccentric strength, fascicle length, functional hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, and strength asymmetry. Static stretching produced the largest flexibility gains but with more transient effects than other approaches.
limitations: Nineteen trials had some risk-of-bias concerns and seven were high risk, often from randomization or missing data; blinding was usually impossible. English-only searching and heterogeneous interventions, outcomes, and populations limited pooling and protocol certainty.
practicalImplications: Include progressive eccentric hamstring loading within a broader preparation plan, then select flexibility, strength, sprint, and sport-specific work according to the athlete's needs and response.
athleteDev: Teach athletes that prevention is repeated capacity building, not a one-time exercise. Progress effort and range carefully, and communicate soreness or symptoms that change normal training response.
rtp: Use eccentric work to rebuild capacity when appropriate, then demonstrate transfer through high-speed running, acceleration, deceleration, and sport-specific exposure. No isolated strength or flexibility result is return clearance.

citation: Ross BJ, Savage-Elliott I, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK. Return to Play and Performance After Primary ACL Reconstruction in American Football Players: A Systematic Review. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;8(10):2325967120959654.
abstract: This systematic review synthesized return-to-play and performance outcomes after primary ACL reconstruction in American football players.
tldr: About two-thirds of included American football players returned after ACL reconstruction, with a mean return time of 11.6 months and generally worse postinjury performance than controls. Use this for expectation setting, not an individual timeline or clearance rule.
methods: The authors searched five databases for English-language studies since 2000 reporting return, performance, or career length after primary ACL reconstruction in American football. Seventeen studies met inclusion criteria.
findings: Return to play was 67.2% (1249/1859), and mean return time was 11.6 months (range 35.8-55.8 weeks). Across heterogeneous comparisons, most players had greater postinjury performance declines than controls over the same period.
limitations: Studies varied in players, outcomes, controls, and definitions; many did not separate isolated reconstruction from concomitant procedures. Evidence was predominantly observational and professional-football focused.
practicalImplications: Use sport- and position-specific expectations alongside individual clinical and performance progress. Plan a graded route from rehabilitation to football exposure rather than promising return from a pooled rate or calendar milestone.
athleteDev: Explain that return and return to previous performance are different outcomes. Build confidence through transparent progression targets while acknowledging that role, prior performance, and recovery course affect the path.
rtp: Combine symptoms, examination, strength, power, movement quality, psychological readiness, conditioning, position demands, and progressive practice exposure. The review does not support a single time point or test for clearance.

citation: Hsieh CC, Nosaka K, Chou TY, Hsu ST, Chen TC. Effects of Far-Infrared Radiation-Lamp Therapy on Recovery From Simulated Soccer Match Running Activities in Elite Soccer Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022;17(9):1432-1438.
abstract: This randomized trial examined far-infrared lamp therapy during recovery from repeated simulated soccer-match running in elite female players.
tldr: In 24 elite female soccer players completing six daily simulated matches, far-infrared lamp therapy produced smaller performance decrements and lower soreness and creatine kinase than sham. It is promising but remains a small, simulated-load study.
methods: Twenty-four elite female soccer players were assigned to far-infrared or sham therapy while completing a daily 90-minute Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test for six days. Strength, soreness, creatine kinase, jump, sprint, and Yo-Yo outcomes were monitored through 120 hours after the final test.
findings: Compared with sham, the far-infrared group had smaller peak decrements in knee-extensor torque, countermovement jump, and Yo-Yo performance, smaller soreness and creatine kinase responses, and earlier recovery toward baseline.
limitations: The parallel study was small, used simulated running and an unusually demanding six-day protocol, and involved only young elite women. Longer-term, clinical, and competition-transfer effects are unknown.
practicalImplications: If considering far-infrared therapy, trial it as one monitored recovery option alongside sleep, nutrition, hydration, load planning, and athlete preference. Verify meaningful response rather than assuming a device benefit.
athleteDev: Keep recovery habits centered on the basics athletes can execute consistently. Explain that a favorable marker response in one study does not make a modality mandatory or a replacement for workload management.
rtp: Do not use far-infrared treatment as a tissue-healing or readiness criterion. During return, prioritize symptoms, tissue capacity, progressive soccer loading, and the athlete's response to each exposure.

citation: Picinini F, Della Villa F, Tallent J, et al. High Return to Competition Rate After On-Field Rehabilitation in Competitive Male Soccer Players After ACL Reconstruction: GPS Tracking in 100 Consecutive Cases. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;13(3):23259671251320093.
abstract: This case series described field-based rehabilitation workloads and return outcomes for male competitive soccer players after ACL reconstruction.
tldr: A five-stage field programme was followed by 84% return to competition among 97 players with follow-up. Final-stage loads approached team training but stayed below match demands, reinforcing the need to progress beyond controlled field work.
methods: One hundred male 11-a-side soccer players completed a criteria-based indoor-to-field ACL rehabilitation process. GPS, heart-rate, and activity data across five field stages were analyzed, and return outcomes were obtained by follow-up questionnaire and mixed models.
findings: At least nine-month follow-up was available for 97 players; 84% returned to competition, including 100% of professionals and 80% of amateurs, and 10% sustained ACL reinjury. Final-stage workload aligned with team-training demand for several metrics but was lower than match-play demand.
limitations: There was no comparator pathway, outcomes relied partly on questionnaire follow-up, and professionals and amateurs differed in workload and context. One specialist male-soccer cohort cannot establish that the programme or GPS targets caused return outcomes.
practicalImplications: Use field GPS to document staged exposure and plan the remaining gap to team training and match play. Interpret workload with skill, movement quality, symptoms, strength, confidence, and football context.
athleteDev: Show players how controlled speed, high-intensity running, acceleration, and deceleration build toward team demands. Completing a stage demonstrates progress, not immunity from reinjury.
rtp: Progress from field rehabilitation to full team training and representative match demands. GPS supports exposure accounting but cannot replace clinical criteria, psychological readiness, or observed football performance.

citation: Arner JW, Bradley JP. Practice Patterns and Return-to-Sports Timing of National Football League Head Team Physicians for ACL Reconstruction. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024;12(10):23259671241274139.
abstract: This cross-sectional survey described ACL reconstruction and return-to-sport practices reported by NFL head team orthopaedic surgeons.
tldr: All 32 NFL head team physicians responded: mean return timing was nine months, none allowed return before seven months, and nearly all used functional testing. These are practice patterns, not outcome-validated clearance criteria.
methods: All 32 NFL head team orthopaedic surgeons were surveyed about graft preferences, augmentation procedures, return timing, functional testing, and experience.
findings: Thirty-one respondents used ipsilateral bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft for primary reconstruction. Mean return-to-sport timing was nine months, none allowed return before seven months, and all but one used functional testing in decisions.
limitations: A physician survey does not measure athlete outcomes, actual care delivery, reinjury, or performance and cannot compare grafts or tests. It represents a highly resourced elite professional setting.
practicalImplications: Use the findings to inform discussion of how NFL surgeons report approaching ACL care, while maintaining a locally accountable, individualized decision process.
athleteDev: Distinguish a reported average practice timeline from a personal clearance date. Encourage athletes to focus on progressive capacity and decision criteria they can influence.
rtp: Time and functional testing can contribute to a decision, but neither the survey's seven-month floor nor a test result alone establishes readiness for American football.

citation: Vopat BG, Vopat ML, van Dijk PAD, et al. Return to Sport after Surgical Treatment of Lisfranc Injuries in Athletes: A Retrospective Case Series. Kansas Journal of Medicine. 2019;12(4):141-145.
abstract: This retrospective case series reported return-to-sport outcomes after open reduction and internal fixation of ligamentous Lisfranc injuries in athletes.
tldr: Eight of 10 followed athletes returned after surgical fixation at a mean 29.4 weeks and reported 87% of prior function, but occasional sport pain was common. The small uncontrolled series cannot set a universal Lisfranc timeline.
methods: Athletes aged 18 to 40 who received single-surgeon open reduction and screw fixation for ligamentous Lisfranc injury were identified retrospectively. Follow-up questionnaires captured return, timing, function, pain, and complications.
findings: Ten athletes had follow-up; eight returned to sport at a mean 29.4 weeks (range 22-52) and reported 87% of prior function. Six of nine reported occasional sport pain, and two complications were reported.
limitations: This was a very small retrospective single-surgeon series with selected recreational or competitive athletes and no nonoperative or alternative-procedure comparator. Self-reported outcomes do not establish readiness or long-term joint health.
practicalImplications: Use the series to counsel that return can occur after fixation but residual symptoms may persist. Progress foot function, strength, loading tolerance, and sport tasks against the individual surgical and clinical course.
athleteDev: Frame return as rebuilding confidence and function despite a variable timeline. Encourage early reporting of pain or difficulty as loading and sport tasks advance.
rtp: Use tissue healing, symptoms, foot and ankle capacity, running and cutting progression, sport demands, and clinician assessment. A mean return week is not a release criterion.

citation: Jo J, Davidar AD, Hersh AM, Theodore N, Zuckerman SL. Cervical and Lumbar Disk Replacement in Athletes: Is It Safe to Return to Play? A Systematic Review of the Scientific Literature and Lay Press. Neurosurgery. 2023.
abstract: This systematic review summarized reported return to play after cervical or lumbar total disk replacement in athletes and supplemented sparse scientific reports with lay-press cases.
tldr: Reported athletes generally returned after disk replacement, but evidence for contact sport rests on very few, selected cases. It cannot establish broad safety or a standard return pathway.
methods: The authors used PRISMA-guided searches of five scientific databases for athlete total-disk-replacement reports and separately searched lay press; sports were classified by contact level.
findings: Ten scientific studies described 53 cervical and 51 lumbar disk-replacement athletes. Reported professional and semiprofessional athletes generally returned without complication; across scientific literature and lay press, 14 professional contact-sport athletes were identified.
limitations: Evidence was sparse and composed mainly of case reports and small retrospective cohorts, with selected athletes, variable procedures and follow-up, few contact-sport cases, and potential publication bias from successful reports.
practicalImplications: Use specialist spine consultation and shared risk discussion when considering sport after disk replacement. Build decisions from procedure details, neurological status, imaging, sport contact exposure, and athlete goals.
athleteDev: Communicate uncertainty honestly: a reported successful return in another athlete is not a prediction of safety or performance for an individual.
rtp: Return after spine surgery requires injury- and procedure-specific specialist clearance, neurological and functional assessment, graduated sport exposure, and an explicit discussion of contact risk.

citation: Ramazzina I, Bernazzoli B, Braghieri V, Costantino C. Groin Pain in Athletes and Non-Interventional Rehabilitative Treatment: A Systematic Review. Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2019;59(6):1001-1010.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated non-interventional rehabilitation approaches for athletes with groin pain.
tldr: Low-certainty evidence favored active over passive treatment for clinical signs, and multimodal treatment was associated with faster return than active treatment alone. The review could not provide a best-practice algorithm.
methods: Six electronic sources were searched from January 1997 through March 2017. Included studies were reviewed for participants, interventions, outcomes, retention, adverse effects, and methodological quality.
findings: Randomized trials indicated active treatment outperformed passive treatment for clinical signs. Compared with active treatment, multimodal treatment allowed faster return to sport; the authors described integrating pain assessment, running progression, and sport-specific exercise.
limitations: Evidence was poor and heterogeneous in diagnosis, intervention, dose, outcome, and quality, preventing practice guidelines or identification of one optimal algorithm.
practicalImplications: First classify the athlete's groin presentation and rule out relevant pathology, then tailor progressive active loading, running, sport exposure, and selected adjuncts to response.
athleteDev: Help athletes track symptoms and loading response while gradually restoring running and sport tasks. Avoid labeling all groin pain as the same problem or expecting one standard programme to fit every case.
rtp: Return should reflect symptom behavior, capacity, running and change-of-direction tolerance, sport-specific demands, and diagnostic context—not completion of a generic multimodal programme.

citation: Smiley T, Dallman J, Long R, et al. Lower Extremity Return to Sport Testing: A Systematic Review. The Knee. 2024;50:115-146.
abstract: This systematic review mapped joint-specific and global lower-extremity testing used before return to sport after injury.
tldr: Across 114 studies, return testing was overwhelmingly knee and ACL focused, with isokinetic dynamometry most common and no uniform clearance criterion. Hip and ankle evidence was notably limited.
methods: PRISMA-guided searches of five databases through May 2024 identified 114 eligible studies from 19,189 records; ROBINS-I was used for risk-of-bias assessment.
findings: Eighty-five percent of studies addressed knee pathology and 82% ACL reconstruction. Isokinetic dynamometry appeared in 73% of studies, whereas only 6.2% addressed hip pathology and two studies addressed ankle injury; no standardized return criterion was identified.
limitations: Injury, sport, test, threshold, and outcome heterogeneity was substantial, and the literature was dominated by ACL/knee evidence. The review does not validate a universal battery's ability to reduce reinjury.
practicalImplications: Select a joint- and sport-relevant battery that includes strength, functional performance, movement, symptoms, and patient-reported readiness, then interpret results in the athlete's exposure context.
athleteDev: Explain why multiple measures may be needed and why a symmetric score or one successful test is progress rather than a universal pass-fail answer.
rtp: Use testing to identify remaining deficits and guide progression to practice and competition. Clearance requires integrated clinical, performance, psychological, and sport-demand judgment.

citation: Herring SA, Putukian M, Kibler WB, et al. Team Physician Consensus Statement: Return to Sport/Return to Play and the Team Physician: A Team Physician Consensus Statement-2023 Update. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024.
abstract: This consensus statement updates the team physician's role in return-to-sport decision-making across injuries, illnesses, sports, and athlete populations.
tldr: Return is a context-dependent continuum from participation to sport to performance. The consensus favors an athlete-centered shared decision process led by the team physician and attentive to health, risk, goals, and coercion.
methods: A multidisciplinary team-physician group produced an updated consensus statement addressing the return-to-sport process and decision responsibilities.
findings: The statement characterizes return as ongoing and responsive to evolving information and risk. It recommends shared decision-making that incorporates diagnosis, individual risk, evidence-based options, athlete goals, sport context, and protection from coercion.
limitations: This is consensus guidance, not an injury-specific comparative outcome study. It offers no validated universal thresholds, timelines, or probabilities, and implementation varies by setting.
practicalImplications: Create a documented, athlete-centered process that names decision roles, considers health and sport risk, and revisits the plan as new information emerges.
athleteDev: Invite athletes to express goals, questions, and concerns while clarifying that shared decision-making does not transfer medical responsibility or turn return into a simple vote.
rtp: Use the continuum to stage participation, sport, and performance exposure. Pair it with injury-specific assessment and resist pressure to translate consensus principles into automatic clearance.

citation: Challoumas D, Kirwan PD, Borysov D, et al. Topical Glyceryl Trinitrate for the Treatment of Tendinopathies: A Systematic Review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(4):251-262.
abstract: This systematic review synthesized randomized trials of topical glyceryl trinitrate for tendinopathy.
tldr: Ten randomized trials suggested some midterm benefits of topical glyceryl trinitrate versus placebo, but evidence varied by outcome and headaches were more common. It is an adjunct consideration, not a replacement for progressive loading.
methods: MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and CINAHL were searched through January 2018 for randomized trials comparing topical glyceryl trinitrate with placebo or other treatment. The authors assessed validity, external validity, precision, and evidence level.
findings: Ten trials covered rotator cuff, wrist extensor, Achilles, and patellar tendinopathy. Short-term pain improvement had poor evidence; midterm satisfaction and asymptomatic daily activity had strong evidence, range and strength moderate evidence, and headaches were more frequent.
limitations: Trials were few and heterogeneous in tendon, dose, comparator, cointervention, chronicity, quality, and outcome. The evidence was not return-to-sport-specific and does not define optimal dose, safety, or superiority to loading.
practicalImplications: If a qualified clinician considers topical glyceryl trinitrate, use it as a monitored adjunct to diagnosis and progressive loading while screening contraindications, interactions, and headache tolerance.
athleteDev: Set expectations that symptom change and tendon adaptation require time and progressive work. Athletes should report headaches or other adverse effects rather than altering medication use independently.
rtp: Do not use a topical adjunct as evidence of tissue readiness. Advance sport exposure from tendon symptoms, capacity, function, load tolerance, and task-specific performance.

citation: Marigi EM, Davies MR, Marx RG, Rodeo SA, Williams RJ III. Meniscus Tears in Elite Athletes: Treatment Considerations, Clinical Outcomes, and Return to Play. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine. 2024;17:313-320.
abstract: This narrative review summarizes treatment considerations, clinical outcomes, and return-to-play issues for meniscus tears in elite athletes.
tldr: Partial meniscectomy may allow faster return, while repair is preferred for anatomically repairable tears to preserve meniscus and protect long-term joint health. Treatment and timeline must be individualized.
methods: The authors narratively reviewed contemporary literature on meniscus injury epidemiology, nonoperative and surgical treatment, and return-to-play outcomes in elite athletes.
findings: The review reports a shift toward preservation because of concern for cartilage degeneration. Partial meniscectomy can provide quicker return, while repair has similar reported return rates and return to preinjury level in some literature; allograft transplantation is a salvage option with variable outcomes.
limitations: This narrative review draws on heterogeneous, largely observational reports with different tears, procedures, sports, return definitions, and follow-up. It cannot identify a universally superior treatment or timeline.
practicalImplications: Match treatment and rehabilitation to tear pattern, location, repairability, concomitant injury, knee stability, season demands, and the athlete's long-term joint goals.
athleteDev: Help athletes understand the tradeoff between speed of return and meniscal preservation. Keep the discussion focused on their tear, role, goals, and long-term knee health rather than another athlete's timeline.
rtp: Progress from symptoms and knee function to strength, movement, conditioning, and representative sport demands. A procedure label or early return rate does not establish individual readiness.

citation: Effects of multiple cold-water immersion during pre-season on recovery performance in under-20 male soccer players: A randomized controlled trial. Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies. 2024;40:563-568.
abstract: A randomized controlled trial tested whether repeated cold-water immersion during a nine-day preseason period improved recovery in 23 under-20 male soccer players.
tldr: Daily cold-water immersion lowered creatine kinase but did not improve jump, strength, or perceived recovery versus control.
methods: Twenty-three under-20 male soccer players completed a nine-day preseason period and were randomized to 10 minutes of 10 C cold-water immersion after training or control recovery. Creatine kinase, vertical-jump performance, strength, and perceived recovery were tracked.
findings: Creatine kinase was approximately 280 U/L lower with cold-water immersion, while vertical jump, strength, and perceived recovery did not differ meaningfully between groups.
limitations: The sample was small, male, under-20, and observed over a short preseason period. The biomarker change did not translate into demonstrated functional or perceptual benefit.
practicalImplications: Cold-water immersion may reduce a muscle-damage biomarker during dense preseason training, but practitioners should not assume it improves performance recovery or how athletes feel.
athleteDev: Use selectively when short-term biomarker reduction is a priority, while preserving active recovery, sleep, nutrition, and training-design strategies that have broader developmental value.
rtp: The study did not examine injured athletes or return-to-play decisions; creatine kinase alone should not be used as a clearance marker.

citation: Wake up call for collegiate athlete sleep: narrative review and consensus recommendations from the NCAA Interassociation Task Force on Sleep and Wellness. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(12):731-736.
abstract: An NCAA interassociation task force synthesized evidence and expert consensus into recommendations for supporting sleep and wellness in collegiate athletes.
tldr: Collegiate programs should monitor time demands, screen sleep at preparticipation, educate athletes and staff, and provide referral pathways.
methods: A multidisciplinary task force used a narrative evidence review and consensus process to formulate collegiate-athlete sleep recommendations.
findings: The group recommended annual assessment of time demands, routine sleep screening during preparticipation evaluation, sleep education, and access to qualified clinical referral when concerns are identified.
limitations: This is a narrative consensus statement rather than a systematic review or intervention trial, so recommendations are not comparative-effectiveness estimates.
practicalImplications: Build sleep support into program operations: identify schedule pressures, screen consistently, teach practical sleep behaviors, and define escalation routes for clinical concerns.
athleteDev: Treat sleep as a trainable health and performance behavior supported by the environment, not solely as an athlete-compliance issue.
rtp: Sleep screening can identify barriers that affect rehabilitation and recovery, but the statement does not provide injury-specific return-to-play thresholds.

citation: Real world fatigue testing in professional rugby union: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2023;54(4):855-874.
abstract: A systematic review examined fatigue-monitoring responses after professional men's rugby-union match play and meta-analyzed outcomes with sufficient comparable data.
tldr: Post-match soreness rises reliably, but most other commonly used fatigue markers have uncertain or inconsistent responses.
methods: Thirty-seven professional male rugby-union studies were included and 14 contributed to meta-analysis of post-match fatigue and recovery markers across the first 96 hours.
findings: Muscle soreness increased during the 96 hours after match play. Pooled effects for many other subjective, neuromuscular, biochemical, and endocrine markers were non-significant or too heterogeneous for confident interpretation.
limitations: Protocols, match contexts, sampling times, and outcome definitions varied substantially. Evidence was concentrated in professional male rugby union.
practicalImplications: Use a small, repeatable monitoring battery and interpret athlete trends in context rather than expecting one universal fatigue test to dictate recovery decisions.
athleteDev: Longitudinal individual baselines and consistent testing conditions are more useful than isolated post-match values.
rtp: These post-match fatigue measures were not validated as injury rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Effect of the length of the microcycle on the daily external load, fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and muscle soreness of professional soccer players: A full-season study. Sports Health. 2022;15(5):695-699.
abstract: A full-season observational study evaluated how professional soccer microcycle length related to daily external training load and athlete-reported wellness.
tldr: Microcycle length changed how training load was distributed, but reported fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness were largely unchanged.
methods: Professional soccer players were monitored across a competitive season, with external load and daily wellness outcomes compared across microcycles of different lengths.
findings: External load distribution varied by the number of days between matches, whereas fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and muscle soreness showed little corresponding difference. Match-day loads were generally similar.
limitations: The observational single-team context limits causal inference and may not transfer to other leagues, schedules, or athlete populations.
practicalImplications: Adjust the placement of training load when match spacing changes, but continue monitoring individual wellness because group averages may appear stable.
athleteDev: Microcycle planning should balance exposure opportunities with schedule constraints instead of assuming shorter cycles automatically worsen perceived recovery.
rtp: The study informs team scheduling but does not establish rehabilitation load progressions or return-to-play criteria.

citation: Effects of consecutive domestic and international tournaments on heart rate variability in an elite rugby sevens team. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019;22(5):616-621.
abstract: An elite rugby-sevens team was monitored across consecutive domestic and international tournaments to compare heart-rate variability and subjective recovery responses.
tldr: Athletes felt worse after both tournaments, while the clearest heart-rate-variability decline occurred after international travel and competition.
methods: Ten Olympic-level rugby-sevens players completed heart-rate-variability and self-report monitoring around domestic and international tournaments with similar match-load exposure.
findings: Self-reported recovery worsened following both tournaments. Heart-rate variability declined more clearly after the international tournament despite broadly similar match load, suggesting contextual effects such as travel.
limitations: The sample was only ten athletes from one elite team, and tournament context cannot be separated cleanly from travel and other environmental factors.
practicalImplications: Interpret autonomic and self-report monitoring together and account for travel, time zones, and tournament logistics when planning recovery.
athleteDev: Build individualized travel routines and use repeated within-athlete measures rather than population cut points.
rtp: Heart-rate variability changes after competition are not an injury-clearance test and should not independently determine return to play.

citation: A Strategy to Inform Athlete Sleep Support From Questionnaire Data and Its Application in an Elite Athlete Cohort. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2022;17(10):1532-1536.
abstract: Questionnaire responses from a large elite-athlete cohort were clustered to identify recurring sleep-problem profiles that could help target support.
tldr: Combining sleep quality and behavior questionnaires produced three practical support profiles, but they are exploratory rather than diagnostic.
methods: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Athlete Sleep Behavior Questionnaire data from 412 elite athletes in 27 sports were analyzed with k-means clustering.
findings: Three distinct profiles emerged, separating athletes with broadly favorable sleep, sleep-quality concerns, and behavior-related support needs.
limitations: The analysis was cross-sectional, self-reported, and dependent on the selected clustering method. Profiles do not diagnose sleep disorders.
practicalImplications: Use questionnaires to triage education and follow-up, then confirm concerns through conversation or clinical assessment when indicated.
athleteDev: Profile-based support can make sleep education more relevant than delivering the same advice to every athlete.
rtp: The profiles may identify recovery barriers during rehabilitation but are not return-to-play thresholds.

citation: Professional athletes have poorer sleep quality and sleep hygiene compared with an age-matched cohort. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2020;31(6):488-493.
abstract: A cross-sectional cohort study compared sleep duration, quality, regularity, environment, and hygiene in professional athletes and age-matched non-athletes.
tldr: Professional athletes reported longer sleep but poorer quality, regularity, and sleep environments, with more napping than comparators.
methods: Questionnaire-based sleep characteristics were compared between 184 professional athletes and 101 age-matched clinic comparators.
findings: Athletes reported longer sleep duration but more disturbance, less regular schedules, poorer sleep environments, and more napping than the comparison cohort.
limitations: Cross-sectional self-report data cannot establish causation, and the clinic comparison group may not represent the general population.
practicalImplications: Do not equate time in bed with good sleep. Review schedule consistency, environment, disturbances, and nap practices with athletes.
athleteDev: Sleep coaching should target routines and context as well as duration.
rtp: Poor sleep may complicate recovery, but this study does not provide injury-specific prognostic or clearance criteria.

citation: Sleep quality in elite athletes: Normative values, reliability and understanding contributors to poor sleep. Sports Medicine. 2021;52(2):417-426.
abstract: A large elite-athlete study described Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index values, test-retest reliability, and questionnaire components associated with poor sleep scores.
tldr: About half of elite athletes screened as poor sleepers; sleep latency and perceived quality were important contributors, and changes under three points may be noise.
methods: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index responses from 479 elite athletes were analyzed for normative patterns, contributors, and repeatability, including estimation of a minimum detectable change.
findings: Fifty-two percent scored at least five on the PSQI. Sleep latency and subjective quality were prominent contributors, and the estimated minimum detectable change was three points.
limitations: The PSQI is a screening questionnaire rather than a clinical diagnosis, and group normative values may obscure individual or sport-specific context.
practicalImplications: Use repeated scores and component-level discussion; avoid treating small score fluctuations as meaningful change.
athleteDev: Focus support on the specific behaviors or barriers driving an athlete's score instead of labeling the athlete from a total score alone.
rtp: PSQI results can flag a recovery concern but should not be used as a standalone return-to-play test.

citation: Sleep interventions in elite sport: A systematic review. South African Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;37(1).
abstract: A systematic review synthesized intervention studies intended to improve sleep outcomes in elite athletes.
tldr: Sleep education most consistently increased sleep quantity; other interventions showed promise but the evidence was heterogeneous.
methods: Thirty-two elite-sport intervention studies covering education, light exposure, supplements, cold exposure, mindfulness, and related approaches were reviewed.
findings: Sleep-education interventions most consistently improved sleep quantity. Positive findings were also reported for several other approaches, but effects varied across methods and outcomes.
limitations: Study designs, sports, interventions, and sleep measures were heterogeneous, with many small samples and limited replication.
practicalImplications: Start with individualized sleep education and environmental or scheduling changes; treat specialized interventions as context-dependent trials that require monitoring.
athleteDev: Use behaviorally specific, athlete-centered sleep plans and evaluate whether the chosen intervention changes the intended outcome.
rtp: Sleep interventions may support rehabilitation recovery, but no universal intervention or sleep threshold was validated for return to play.

citation: The effect of alcohol on subsequent sleep in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sleep Medicine Reviews. 2025;80:102030.
abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated how alcohol consumed before sleep affects objective and subjective sleep outcomes in healthy adults.
tldr: Alcohol disrupted REM sleep even at low doses; higher doses shortened sleep latency, but many other outcomes remained uncertain.
methods: Twenty-seven controlled studies of alcohol exposure and subsequent sleep in healthy adults were synthesized, with meta-analysis where outcomes were comparable.
findings: Rapid-eye-movement sleep was disrupted even at doses approximating two standard drinks. Higher doses shortened sleep latency, while evidence for several other sleep outcomes was inconsistent or uncertain.
limitations: Participants were healthy adults rather than athlete-specific cohorts, and alcohol dose, timing, and sleep measurement varied between studies.
practicalImplications: A faster onset of sleep after alcohol should not be interpreted as better recovery; discuss the likely REM-sleep cost even at relatively low intake.
athleteDev: Include alcohol timing and dose in recovery education, especially around travel, evening competition, and dense training periods.
rtp: The evidence concerns sleep physiology, not injury clearance; alcohol use may be a modifiable recovery factor during rehabilitation.

citation: Antioxidants for preventing and reducing muscle soreness after exercise: a Cochrane systematic review. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;54(2):74-78.
abstract: A Cochrane systematic review evaluated antioxidant supplementation for preventing or reducing delayed-onset muscle soreness after exercise.
tldr: Antioxidants produced, at most, a very small soreness reduction below the review's threshold for practical importance.
methods: Fifty studies involving 1,089 participants compared antioxidant supplements with placebo or control for post-exercise muscle soreness and adverse effects.
findings: Pooled reductions in soreness were smaller than the prespecified minimal important difference. Forty-seven studies were judged at high risk of bias, and adverse-event reporting was sparse.
limitations: Most trials had high risk of bias, interventions and exercise models varied, and the evidence base provided limited safety information.
practicalImplications: Routine antioxidant supplementation should not be expected to create a meaningful reduction in post-exercise soreness.
athleteDev: Prioritize training progression, sleep, and adequate nutrition over supplements with trivial average benefit and uncertain long-term adaptation effects.
rtp: The review did not evaluate injury healing or return-to-play outcomes; soreness reduction is not evidence of tissue readiness.

citation: Compression Garments and Recovery from Exercise: A Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2017;47(11):2245-2267.
abstract: A meta-analysis assessed whether wearing compression garments after exercise improved subsequent performance and perceptual or physiological recovery outcomes.
tldr: Compression garments provided small average recovery benefits, with larger effects in some strength and next-day endurance contexts.
methods: Twenty-three studies were synthesized across resistance, running, cycling, and other exercise models, with standardized effects calculated for performance and recovery outcomes.
findings: The overall recovery effect was small. Larger effects appeared for strength recovery more than 24 hours after resistance exercise and for next-day cycling performance, but estimates varied by context.
limitations: Studies were generally small and heterogeneous, and garment pressure, participant training status, and blinding were often unclear.
practicalImplications: Compression garments are a low-burden optional recovery aid, not a substitute for sleep, nutrition, or appropriate load management.
athleteDev: Trial garments with individual athletes and retain them only when comfort, adherence, and the desired next-day outcome justify use.
rtp: The meta-analysis did not validate compression garments as a treatment or clearance criterion for injured athletes.

citation: Wageh M, Fortino SA, Pontello R, Maklad A, McGlory C, Kumbhare D, et al. The Effect of Multi-Ingredient Protein versus Collagen Supplementation on Satellite Cell Properties in Males and Females. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024;56(11):2125-2134.
abstract: This randomized trial compared a multi-ingredient supplement with collagen during resistance training.
tldr: The multi-ingredient group gained more type-II fiber area, but satellite-cell responses were mostly similar. This does not prove protein alone is responsible or required.
methods: Twenty-six adults completed 10 weeks of linear resistance training while taking twice-daily whey, creatine, leucine, calcium, and vitamin-D supplement or collagen; vastus-lateralis biopsies assessed satellite cells, myonuclei, and fiber area.
findings: The multi-ingredient group had greater type-II fiber cross-sectional-area gain. Satellite-cell content, myonuclear accretion, and most acute satellite-cell responses were similar between groups.
limitations: The sample was small, the supplement included several active ingredients, many differences were not statistically robust, and biopsies do not establish sport performance or recovery benefit.
practicalImplications: Prioritize adequate food and total protein intake, then assess whether any supplement fits a specific nutrition plan. Avoid attributing this result to a single ingredient.
athleteDev: Explain that training remains the main anabolic stimulus and supplement response varies. Report gastrointestinal issues and avoid stacking products without a clear purpose.
rtp: Do not use this study to prescribe a muscle-repair supplement after injury. Nutrition should support adequate intake alongside progressive rehabilitation.

citation: Rockwell MS, Kostelnik SB, McMillan RP, Lancaster M, Larson-Meyer DE, Hulver MW. An Association between Bioavailable 25-Hydroxyvitamin D and Bone Mineral Density in a Diverse Cohort of Collegiate Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2022;54(3):371-376.
abstract: This cross-sectional study compared total and bioavailable vitamin-D measures with bone density in collegiate basketball and swimming athletes.
tldr: Bioavailable vitamin D correlated with bone density in this small cohort, whereas total vitamin D did not. It is an association, not a supplementation trial.
methods: Fifty-three Division-I basketball and swimming athletes underwent DXA, blood testing, and diet/lifestyle questionnaires; total and bioavailable 25-hydroxyvitamin D were compared with total bone mineral density.
findings: Total and bioavailable vitamin-D classification disagreed for 53% of participants and 77% of Black participants. Bioavailable vitamin D correlated with total bone mineral density (r=0.618), while total vitamin D did not.
limitations: The small two-sport, cross-sectional cohort cannot establish cause, fracture prevention, or supplementation need. Calculated bioavailability and cutoffs need clinical interpretation.
practicalImplications: Evaluate bone health and vitamin-D status with qualified clinical and nutrition staff, especially where risk factors exist. Interpret results with diet, sun exposure, skin pigmentation, menstrual or endocrine status, and medical history.
athleteDev: Avoid self-prescribing high-dose vitamin D from one result. Help athletes understand why testing and follow-up are individualized.
rtp: Bone-health decisions during rehabilitation require diagnosis and medical oversight; this association does not supply a return-to-sport supplement protocol.

citation: Kelly VG, Oliver LS, Bowtell J, Jenkins DG. Inside the Belly of a Beast: Individualizing Nutrition for Young, Professional Male Rugby League Players: A Review. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2020.
abstract: This narrative review considers energy, macronutrient, recovery, and supplement strategies for young professional male rugby-league players.
tldr: Rugby-league nutrition should be individualized around high energy demand, contact, and season phase. The suggested targets are practical starting ranges, not sport-specific certainty.
methods: The review synthesized literature on rugby-league physiological demands, nutrition requirements, recovery, and potential ergogenic supplements across preparatory and competitive phases.
findings: It proposes approximately 6-8 g/kg/day carbohydrate, 1.6-2.6 g/kg/day protein, and 0.7-2.2 g/kg/day fat, with phase-specific pre- and postexercise carbohydrate and protein strategies. It identifies insufficient rugby-league-specific energy-expenditure data.
limitations: It is a narrative review with substantial extrapolation beyond rugby league; female athletes and individual seasonal energy needs are underrepresented.
practicalImplications: Start with food-first, periodized intake matched to training, body-composition goal, and recovery demand. Monitor body mass, appetite, availability, gastrointestinal tolerance, and health.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to adjust intake as training and match demands change rather than follow one fixed daily menu.
rtp: During injury, adjust energy and protein to changing activity and healing needs with a nutrition professional; do not automatically retain match-day targets.

citation: Collins J, Maughan RJ, Gleeson M, Bilsborough J, Jeukendrup A, Morton JP, et al. UEFA Expert Group Statement on Nutrition in Elite Football: Current Evidence to Inform Practical Recommendations and Guide Future Research. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55:416-442.
abstract: This UEFA expert statement provides a food-first, individualized nutrition framework for elite soccer.
tldr: Periodize food, fluid, and carefully selected supplements around player demands, health, and practical constraints. A consensus statement is a framework, not a rigid prescription.
methods: An international expert group synthesized current sports-nutrition evidence and its practical application to elite football training, match play, travel, recovery, body composition, and supplements.
findings: The statement emphasizes matching food and fluid intake to training and match demands, protecting health and energy availability, and using only evidence-based supplements within a food-first strategy and antidoping-aware process.
limitations: This is consensus rather than one controlled trial, and evidence quality differs by topic. Elite-soccer recommendations may require substantial adaptation for other populations and settings.
practicalImplications: Build individualized, periodized plans with food access, travel, culture, body-composition goals, medical needs, and competition schedule in view. Use supplements only with a clear rationale and quality assurance.
athleteDev: Make nutrition decisions understandable and practical: what to eat, drink, and prepare before, during, and after the actual demands of the week.
rtp: Nutrition can support rehabilitation energy needs and recovery, but it cannot replace medical criteria, progressive loading, or return-to-play decision-making.

citation: Doherty CS, Fortington LV, Barley OR. Blood, Sweat, and Tears: Implications for Hydration Testing in Combat Sports—Investigating Body Mass Loss and Biomarker Changes. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2024.
abstract: This repeated-trial study tested hydration biomarkers after passive dehydration in combat-sport athletes.
tldr: Common hydration cutoffs misclassified many athletes after dehydration, and biomarker reliability varied. One test should not determine safety or eligibility.
methods: Fifteen male and female combat athletes completed two sauna protocols 5-28 days apart targeting 4% body-mass loss; serum and urine osmolality, tear osmolarity, hematocrit, and urine-specific gravity were measured.
findings: Average body-mass loss was 3.0%. Body-mass loss explained hematocrit change but not most other marker changes; post-dehydration hematocrit showed highest reliability, while urine-specific-gravity cutoff 1.020 misclassified 42%.
limitations: The sample was small, passive sauna dehydration may not represent competition weight cutting, and the intended dehydration target was not reached. Cutoff performance depends on timing and cohort.
practicalImplications: Use validated, context-specific hydration protocols and multiple clinical signals. Prioritize safe weight-management policy over a single biomarker result.
athleteDev: Explain why an apparently normal urine measure does not prove safe hydration after a cut. Encourage early reporting of symptoms and honest weight-management planning.
rtp: Hydration status should be managed medically and operationally, especially after rapid loss; no one biomarker establishes readiness to train or compete.

citation: Rebolledo BJ, Bernard JA, Werner BC, Finlay AK, Nwachukwu BU, Dare DM, et al. The Association of Vitamin D Status in Lower Extremity Muscle Strains and Core Muscle Injuries at the National Football League Combine. Arthroscopy. 2018.
abstract: This retrospective NFL Combine study examined vitamin-D status and prior muscle-injury history.
tldr: Low vitamin D was common and linked with injury history in unadjusted analyses, but not independently after adjustment. It does not prove vitamin D caused strains.
methods: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and retrospective lower-extremity strain or core-injury histories were reviewed in 214 2015 NFL Combine athletes; regression models adjusted for recorded baseline factors.
findings: Fifty-nine percent had inadequate vitamin D. Unadjusted inadequate status was associated with lower-extremity strain/core-injury and hamstring history, but multivariable low vitamin D was not independently associated with injury history.
limitations: Retrospective history and a selected male combine cohort preclude temporality or causation. The study does not evaluate supplementation or future injury risk.
practicalImplications: Use vitamin-D testing as one clinical data point when risk factors justify it. Correct deficiencies under medical and nutrition supervision rather than promising strain prevention.
athleteDev: Avoid interpreting a result as proof of why an injury happened. Support consistent food, safe sun exposure, and follow-up when clinicians identify a need.
rtp: Muscle return decisions need current symptoms, strength, function, and sport exposure; vitamin-D status alone cannot clear return.

citation: Mertz KH, Sorensen HH, Lorentz C, Johansen E, Fredskild NU, Wulff MW, et al. Effects of Protein Supplementation During Early Rehabilitation on Muscle Volume and Function After Acute Muscle Strain Injuries: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025.
abstract: This double-blind trial tested whey protein during early rehabilitation after acute hamstring or calf strain injury.
tldr: Twice-daily whey did not preserve muscle volume, improve strength, or shorten return after strain injury in recreational athletes. Adequate diet still matters, but this protocol was not a shortcut.
methods: Fifty recreational athletes with acute hamstring or calf strains received twice-daily whey protein or isocaloric placebo during three months of early rehabilitation; MRI, strength, return time, and aponeurosis volume were followed to 12 months.
findings: Injured-muscle volume decreased 9.4% during intervention and remained lower at 12 months. Protein did not change muscle volume, strength, return-to-sport time, or aponeurosis volume.
limitations: The study involved recreational athletes and mixed injury sites. It tests one supplementation protocol, not adequacy of total dietary protein or other nutrition interventions in elite sport.
practicalImplications: Meet overall energy and protein needs through a rehabilitation nutrition plan, but do not expect supplemental whey alone to preserve muscle or accelerate return.
athleteDev: Set expectations that rehabilitation progress comes from appropriate loading, recovery, and adequate intake—not one product.
rtp: Return depends on tissue status, strength, performance, and sport exposure. This trial does not support using whey response as a return marker.

citation: Sandkühler JF, Kersting X, Faust A, Königs EK, Altman G, Ettinger U, et al. The Effects of Creatine Supplementation on Cognitive Performance—A Randomised Controlled Study. BMC Medicine. 2023;21:440.
abstract: This double-blind crossover trial evaluated six-week creatine supplementation and cognitive performance.
tldr: Creatine showed at most a small cognitive benefit in non-athlete participants and caused more reported side effects. It is not evidence for a sport-cognition or concussion protocol.
methods: One hundred twenty-three vegetarians and omnivores completed randomized double-blind six-week periods of 5 g/day creatine and placebo, with Raven matrices, backward digit span, and exploratory cognitive tasks.
findings: Bayesian analysis supported a small benefit; backward digit span bordered significance, Raven matrices and exploratory tests did not. Vegetarians did not benefit more, and side effects were more frequent with creatine.
limitations: Participants were not an athlete-performance sample, effects were small and task-specific, and the study does not establish benefit for sport decisions or head injury.
practicalImplications: Do not add creatine for cognitive performance solely from this result. When creatine is considered for another objective, review individual tolerance, goals, and product quality.
athleteDev: Separate potential training benefits from unproven promises about focus or brain protection. Report side effects and avoid unplanned supplement stacking.
rtp: Creatine is not a concussion treatment or readiness marker. Follow established medical and staged return protocols.

citation: Bodur M, Barkell J, Li X, Sajadi Hezaveh Z. Does Caffeine Supplementation Affect Sleep in Athletes? A Systematic Review of Nine Randomized Controlled Trials. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN. 2024.
abstract: This systematic review examined randomized athlete trials of caffeine supplementation and sleep.
tldr: Caffeine can impair sleep, with response shaped by dose, timing, and individual sensitivity. Performance planning should protect recovery rather than assume standard use is harmless.
methods: The authors systematically reviewed nine randomized controlled trials assessing caffeine supplementation and athlete sleep outcomes.
findings: Across heterogeneous trials, caffeine was associated with impaired sleep measures, and the review highlights dose, timing, and individual sensitivity as practical considerations.
limitations: Only nine heterogeneous trials were available and the source is an accepted pre-proof. Protocols, athlete samples, sleep measures, and study quality do not establish a universally safe dose or timing.
practicalImplications: Trial caffeine in training and schedule it around both performance and upcoming sleep opportunity. Use the lowest effective dose and account for individual sensitivity.
athleteDev: Teach athletes to notice delayed sleep onset, reduced sleep quality, and next-day recovery effects rather than focusing only on the immediate lift from caffeine.
rtp: Protect sleep during rehabilitation and return progression; stimulant use should not mask fatigue or substitute for recovery.

citation: Feinberg C, Dickerson Mayes K, Jarvis RC III, Carr C, Mannix R. Nutritional Supplement and Dietary Interventions as a Prophylaxis or Treatment of Sub-Concussive Repetitive Head Impact and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2023.
abstract: This systematic review evaluated nutrition and dietary interventions for repetitive head impact and mild traumatic brain injury.
tldr: Some studies reported benefit, especially for omega-3 approaches, but the evidence is too heterogeneous and biased to make a concussion supplement protocol.
methods: PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched without a specified time period. Fifteen studies from 12 populations, totaling 1,139 participants, met eligibility criteria.
findings: Eleven studies reported benefit across eight interventions. Omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, and Pinus radiata had multiple studies; the authors identify omega-3 as the strongest prevention evidence while calling for larger multicenter studies.
limitations: Interventions, timing, populations, and outcomes varied. Over half of studies had some bias concern and all industry-sponsored studies reported supportive findings, preventing firm efficacy conclusions.
practicalImplications: Maintain a food-first approach and do not market supplements as head-injury prevention or treatment. Any use should be medically supervised and secondary to established safety and clinical care.
athleteDev: Clarify that no supplement makes repetitive head impacts safe or replaces reporting symptoms and following medical guidance.
rtp: Nutrition may support general recovery but cannot alter concussion clearance requirements or replace staged return-to-learn and return-to-sport care.

citation: Carvalho A, Marticorena FM, Grecco BH, Barreto G, Saunders B. Can I Have My Coffee and Drink It? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Determine Whether Habitual Caffeine Consumption Affects the Ergogenic Effect of Caffeine. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis tested whether habitual caffeine intake changes the acute ergogenic response to caffeine.
tldr: Habitual caffeine use did not appear to erase acute performance benefit in pooled studies. Individual sleep, side effects, dose, and timing still determine whether caffeine is useful.
methods: Three databases were searched; 60 caffeine studies reporting habitual intake entered three-level meta-analyses and meta-regressions across exercise types, sex, training status, dose, and withdrawal periods.
findings: Caffeine improved performance versus placebo overall (SMD 0.25), with no habitual-intake moderation. Benefits appeared below 3 and at 3-6 mg/kg but not above 6 mg/kg in subgroup analysis.
limitations: Habitual intake and body mass commonly used group means, few studies directly tested habituation, caffeine estimates were imprecise, and no included study was low risk of bias.
practicalImplications: Individualize caffeine trialing around a performance target and sleep schedule. Avoid assuming high doses, habitual use, or abstinence guarantees a better response.
athleteDev: Have athletes track dose, timing, perceived benefit, anxiety, gastrointestinal response, and sleep so decisions reflect their response rather than group averages.
rtp: Caffeine should not be used to conceal fatigue during return progression. Protect sleep and use clinical and performance criteria to guide load.

citation: Blumert PA, Crum AJ, Ernsting M, Volek JS, Hollander DB, Haff EE, Haff GG. The Acute Effects of Twenty-Four Hours of Sleep Loss on the Performance of National-Caliber Male Collegiate Weightlifters. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2007;21(4):1146-1154.
abstract: A randomized counterbalanced crossover compared one maximal Olympic-weightlifting session after 24 hours of sleep loss with one after normal sleep in nine national-caliber male collegiate lifters.
tldr: Measured lifting volume and intensity were not significantly different after one night awake, but mood and sleepiness worsened. This small acute test does not show that sleep loss is harmless.
methods: Nine men completed snatch, clean-and-jerk, and front-squat sessions in two sleep conditions seven days apart. Investigators recorded exercise volume, intensity, maximum lifts, mood, sleepiness, and peri-exercise hormones.
findings: No significant differences were found in the reported weightlifting performance measures. Vigor, fatigue, confusion, total mood disturbance, and sleepiness changed significantly after sleep loss; postexercise cortisol was lower in the sleep-loss condition.
limitations: The nine-person male sample, one 24-hour total-sleep-loss exposure, and one weightlifting protocol cannot establish equivalent performance, longer-term safety, or transfer to complex sport tasks.
practicalImplications: Protect sleep opportunity and ask about alertness, mood, and task demands when a lifter reports acute sleep loss. A preserved lifting result in this study is not a reason to ignore sleep deprivation.
athleteDev: Explain that a single workout can look normal while sleepiness and mood are affected. Encourage early reporting and a practical recovery plan.
rtp: Do not use this study to clear an injured or sleep-deprived athlete for return. Rehabilitation decisions require separate clinical and task-specific assessment.

citation: Modric T, Carling C, Lago-Peñas C, Versic S, Morgans R, Sekulic D. To Train or Not to Train (on Match Day)? Influence of a Priming Session on Match Performance in Competitive Elite-Level Soccer. Journal of Sports Sciences. Published online December 19, 2023.
abstract: An observational match analysis compared competitive elite-soccer performances with and without a club's short morning priming session.
tldr: Matches preceded by priming showed more running distance at several intensities, with generally similar technical measures. One-club observational data cannot prove the routine caused the difference.
