athleteDev: For performance and coaching leaders, the review argues that coaches and entourage are well placed to notice changes in athletes' mental state and encourage help-seeking, and that staff workload and recovery deserve attention. It gives no evidence that staff mental health changes athlete performance or outcomes.
rtp: The paper does not address return to sport or athlete rehabilitation. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or guide the mental health of injured athletes.

citation: Frost J, Walton CC, Purcell R, Fisher K, Gwyther K, Kocherginsky M, et al. The Mental Health of Elite-Level Coaches: A Systematic Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. 2024;10:16.
abstract: This PRISMA-ScR systematic scoping review mapped evidence on the mental health of elite-level coaches, their risk and protective factors, and links to coaching effectiveness. From 12,376 screened records, 42 studies were included. Wellbeing and mental ill-health were both studied, with burnout the main focus, while clinical symptoms such as anxiety and depression were rarely examined. Risk and protective factors operated at individual, interpersonal, organisational and societal levels, and preliminary evidence suggested poorer mental health may reduce coaching effectiveness.
tldr: Elite coaches face stressors that can affect their mental health, but most research has looked at burnout and wellbeing rather than diagnosable disorders. Support for coaches should cover workload, recovery, social support and organisational environment, though the evidence base is small and of mixed quality.
methods: Systematic scoping review following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidance, with a protocol registered on OSF. Five electronic databases plus Google Scholar were searched, with a September 2022 update and backward snowballing, and records were screened by title, abstract and full text. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language, published after 2000 and reported on elite-level (Olympic, Paralympic, national, international, professional or NCAA Division I) coaches. Quality was assessed with the MMAT and findings were synthesised narratively.
findings: Of 42 included studies, 17 explored wellbeing, with coaches generally reporting moderate to high wellbeing. For mental ill-health, burnout was studied in 21 studies (50%) and anxiety and depression in 10 and 8 studies; anxiety and depression symptom rates were 39.5% (Dutch and Flemish, n = 119) and 43.6% probable caseness (Australia, n = 78), while 14.1% of a New Zealand sample (n = 69) had at least moderate depressive symptoms. Psychological distress ranged from 10.3% to 19.3%, burnout results were heterogeneous, social and organisational support were protective, and high workload and lack of recovery were risk factors; links to coaching effectiveness were preliminary and came from 14% of studies.
limitations: The review was descriptive, so it did not pool prevalence estimates and could not evaluate which risk factors matter most. Prevalence studies were mostly cross-sectional and small, samples were about 73% male, measures were inconsistent, quality appraisal was done by a single reviewer, and five included items were professional abstracts or an editorial letter. Searches were limited to English-language papers published after 2000 and to coaches meeting a specific elite definition.
practicalImplications: Organisations can include coaches and staff in wellbeing support by monitoring workload, recovery time and social support, and by offering early-intervention pathways before symptoms escalate. Psychological skills and emotional regulation training are reasonable options given their links to wellbeing in the included studies, but the review does not show which programmes work.
athleteDev: For performance and coaching leaders, the review suggests coach workload, recovery and organisational support may affect coaching behaviour and team functioning. It cannot establish a causal link between coach mental health and athlete performance.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport or athlete rehabilitation. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport criteria or guide athlete mental health after injury.

citation: Salloum SA, Aljanada RA, Alhumaid K, Alomari KM, Alfaisal AM, Elnekiti A, et al. Statistical Analysis and Machine Learning in College Football: Insights from Offensive Efficiency, Yards Per Play, and Clustering of Play Styles. In: Al-Marzouqi A, et al., eds. Generative AI in Creative Industries. Studies in Computational Intelligence 1208. Springer; 2025. p. 433-446.
abstract: This study used team-level college football statistics from 2013 to 2023 to examine which offensive and defensive metrics relate to wins and score margins, and to cluster teams by play style. The authors report that offensive efficiency and yards per play were the strongest predictors of wins, that three play-style clusters emerged, and that a Random Forest model predicted score margins with an RMSE of 6.82.
tldr: Team-level data suggest that offensive efficiency and yards per play are associated with winning in college football. The clusters and score-margin model are descriptive, and the predictors overlap, so they do not show which tactics would improve a specific team.
methods: Secondary dataset of college football team statistics (2013 to 2023) was cleaned, aggregated and standardised. Offensive efficiency (total yards divided by plays) and turnover margin were derived. The analysis used descriptive rankings, a correlation matrix with wins, OLS regression on wins, K-Means clustering with three clusters on standardised offensive efficiency and yards per play, and Random Forest regression for score margin with feature importance.
findings: The top-ranked team by offensive efficiency was Oklahoma (6.85 yards per play), and efficiency showed a rising trend over the decade. Correlations with wins were highest for total points (0.83) and losses (-0.82, negative). In OLS, offensive efficiency and yards per play each had a coefficient of 1.310 (p < 0.001), R-squared was 0.381, and turnover margin was not significant (p = 0.956). The Random Forest model had RMSE 6.82, with offensive efficiency (0.405) and yards per play (0.373) ranked highest. Note: Table 3 and Table 4 show identical values for offensive efficiency and yards per play, which the authors do not explain.
limitations: Offensive efficiency and yards per play are calculated the same way in this paper, so the regression and clustering double-count one measure. The number of team-seasons and out-of-sample validation of the regression are not reported, missing values were filled with means, and total points is partly determined by winning. The authors note the absence of player, weather, opponent and coaching data, and that K-Means assumes clusters of similar shape and size.
practicalImplications: Football performance and analytics staff can use team-level efficiency benchmarks as a broad reference point when reviewing season data. Any change in play style should be tested against the team's own data and opponent context, because this study does not establish cause and effect.
athleteDev: Performance staff may find the team-level efficiency framing useful for reviewing offensive output across a season. The paper does not measure individual athletes, so it cannot support player development decisions.
rtp: This paper does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport and cannot be used for return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Gervasi SF, Pengue L, Damato L, Monti R, Pradella S, Pirronti T, et al. Is extensive cardiopulmonary screening useful in athletes with previous asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection? Br J Sports Med. 2020;0:1-8.
abstract: This cohort study screened professional soccer players who had asymptomatic or mild SARS-CoV-2 infection with a comprehensive protocol including blood tests, spirometry, resting and stress ECG, and echocardiogram. The authors compared findings with pre-infection data and with uninfected players. None of the infected players had significant cardiovascular abnormalities after recovery, although spirometry values fell significantly in the infected group. The authors conclude that extensive cardiorespiratory and haematological screening appears unnecessary in athletes with asymptomatic or mild infection.
tldr: In a small group of professional soccer players with asymptomatic or mild COVID-19, a full cardiorespiratory screen found no significant heart abnormalities after recovery. Routine extended screening appears unnecessary in this group, though a raised troponin should prompt cardiac MRI and a return to training only after normalisation.
methods: Cohort study of 30 male professional soccer players at one centre, screened with the Italian FIGC protocol for resuming training. Players were grouped by serology and swab results into COVID-19 positive (IgG positive, n = 18, mild or asymptomatic) and negative (n = 12). Assessments included personal history, blood tests, spirometry, resting and stress ECG with oxygen saturation, echocardiogram, 24-hour Holter, and chest CT in the positive group. Comparisons used Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests, with pre-infection data available for a subset (15 positive and 9 negative players).
findings: After recovery, no significant differences were found between infected and uninfected players in spirometry, stress ECG or echocardiogram. Within the infected group (n = 15 with prior data), absolute FVC, FEV1, PEF and MVV and the percent-predicted values for FEV1, PEF and MVV fell significantly (p < 0.05; FVC percent predicted p = 0.18), and resting HR rose from 53 to 65 bpm; uninfected players showed non-significant falls. Values stayed in the normal range except two players with mildly reduced PEF, and one player with raised troponin I had normal ECG, echocardiogram, Holter, CT and cardiac MRI, with troponin normalising after 4 weeks.
limitations: The study had a small, single-centre sample of male professional soccer players, no longitudinal follow-up, and no pre-infection troponin or Holter data. Cardiac MRI was performed in only one player, and the authors attribute the spirometry fall to detraining rather than infection, a hypothesis supported only by a later retest. Pre-infection comparisons were available for only 24 of 30 players.
practicalImplications: For athletes with asymptomatic or mild COVID-19, the authors suggest that history, swab and antibody testing followed by routine preparticipation screening may be sufficient in most cases, with a more cautious approach for raised troponin or abnormal echocardiogram or stress ECG. Chest CT was judged unnecessary for screening, and Holter was not needed routinely when resting and stress ECGs were normal. Raised troponin should prompt contrast cardiac MRI and a pause in training until levels normalise.
athleteDev: Performance staff should expect some drop in spirometry and a higher resting heart rate after a training interruption, which the authors attribute to detraining. Retesting after a month of retraining is one practical check, since most measures improved in this cohort.
rtp: The paper gives a return-to-training approach for athletes after mild or asymptomatic COVID-19: a standard screen is enough unless troponin or cardiac findings are abnormal. Abnormal troponin should be followed by cardiac MRI and training should resume only after troponin normalises, with clinical follow-up. Findings come from one cohort, so they should be applied with a physician's clinical judgement.

citation: Rishis E, Johnston K, Baker J. On the predictive validity of the National Football League combine: does it forecast future success? J Sports Sci. 2023.
abstract: This PRISMA systematic review synthesised peer-reviewed studies on whether NFL Combine measures predict future success. Of 1,954 records, 68 studies were retained, covering medical testing, combine tests, draft position, career longevity, salary and playing performance. The authors found mixed results across combine measures, and concluded that more research is needed on long-term performance.
tldr: NFL combine results, particularly the 40-yard dash, are consistently associated with draft position, but evidence that they predict later NFL performance is mixed. Prior injuries such as ACL reconstruction were linked to worse draft position and fewer games, but evidence on career length is limited and inconsistent.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA. Five databases (EconLit, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Sports Medicine and Education Index, Web of Science) were searched with 'combine' combined with 'sport' or 'NFL', with reference-list searching. Full-text peer-reviewed articles that examined NFL combine measures against at least one future outcome were included, and studies were coded by outcome, sample size and position. Coding reliability was checked on 103 articles (100% agreement).
findings: Medical testing and future performance was the largest group (25 studies), followed by combine tests (12), draft position (10) and draft plus future performance (8). All 10 draft-position studies reported that a faster 40-yard dash was associated with better draft selection. ACL injury and reconstruction were associated with worse draft pick, fewer games and lower snap percentage, but one career-length study found isolated ACL reconstruction did not shorten mean career length while meniscectomy and combined ACL and meniscal surgery did; results for jumps, the 20-yard shuttle, the 3-cone drill and the Wonderlic test were mixed.
limitations: The review included only peer-reviewed articles, so information shared through websites, media and other non-peer-reviewed sources was excluded. Different measures of success across studies prevented statistical comparison, and the authors note far more studies on offensive than defensive positions. No pooled estimates or study quality appraisal are reported.
practicalImplications: Scouts and performance staff can treat the 40-yard dash and its split times as the best-supported combine measure for draft-related decisions, while recognising that its link to later performance is uncertain. Injury history such as ACL reconstruction, Lisfranc injury or rotator cuff repair was linked to worse draft and early-career outcomes, but the review does not support using combine results alone as a predictor of NFL success.
athleteDev: For performance staff working with college prospects, the review suggests that the 40-yard dash and split times relate to draft outcomes, but combine scores should not be read as a reliable forecast of long-term NFL playing performance.
rtp: The review gives limited guidance on return to sport. It reports conflicting evidence after ACL reconstruction: one study found no loss of functional athletic performance in fully recovered players, while another found lower snap percentage, and career-length data exist only for linemen. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Tarzi G, Tarzi C, Saha A, Cusimano MD. Predicting Severity of Head Collision Events in Elite Soccer Using Preinjury Data: A Machine Learning Approach. Clin J Sport Med. 2023;33(2):165-171.
abstract: This study built machine learning models to predict the severity of head collision events in elite soccer from 23 preinjury variables. Data came from 263 events across four elite international tournaments. Models reached an average AUC of 0.73 for men's tournaments and 0.70 for combined men's and women's tournaments. Injury mechanism and the event before injury were the most important predictors.
tldr: In elite international soccer, head collisions after corner kicks and throw-ins were more often severe, and head-to-head plus knee-to-head contact was linked to severity in men's matches only. A random forest model using pre-injury factors classified severity with modest cross-validated accuracy (AUC 0.70 to 0.73).
methods: Head collision events (direct head contact with the player unable to resume play within 5 seconds) were previously coded by 12 trained reviewers, with two reviewers independently analyzing each of 231 matches; an event was severe when the player showed more than 2 visible concussion signs. Random forest classification with nested cross-validation (100 iterations of 4-fold outer CV) was run on a male dataset (23 predictors) and a mixed male and female dataset (20 predictors), and Fisher exact tests assessed associations with severity.
findings: The male dataset (215 HCEs) had a mean AUC of 0.73 and the mixed dataset (263 HCEs) a mean AUC of 0.70. Head-to-head plus knee-to-head mechanisms were associated with severity in the male dataset (P=0.0244) but not the mixed dataset (P=0.1113). Corner kicks plus throw-ins were associated with severity in both datasets (male P=0.0001; mixed P=0.0004).
limitations: Severity reflects signs seen on video, not a medical diagnosis. Only 6 severe events occurred in women's matches, so no separate women's model was built. Performance was estimated by internal cross-validation only, with no external validation. The mechanism association disagreed between the male and mixed datasets. Camera angles could limit coding, and elite international data may not generalize.
practicalImplications: Medical staff and officials could give closer attention to players involved in head-to-head or knee-to-head contact, and to head collisions after corner kicks and throw-ins, which were more often severe in this dataset. Use this as a prompt for assessment, not as a validated screening tool.
athleteDev: This study does not inform athlete development or performance training. Its findings concern the severity of head collision events in elite soccer.
rtp: It can support a cautious decision to assess players promptly after head-to-head or knee-to-head contact, or after a head collision from a corner kick or throw-in. It cannot determine whether an individual athlete can return to play, because severity was coded from video and the model was not validated for individual prediction.

citation: Enaganti A, Pappas G. Optimizing NFL Draft Selections with Machine Learning Classification. AI. 2025;6:221.
abstract: This study used machine learning, mainly random forest models, to predict NFL draft selections and simulate drafts under best-player-available and need-based strategies. Need-based drafting produced a lower mean absolute error and higher Top-3 accuracy against the real 2017 first round. The authors present the simulator as a decision-support tool for teams.
tldr: A random forest model can predict where draft prospects are picked and, in a simulation of the 2017 first round, a need-based strategy matched real picks more closely than a best-player-available strategy. These results describe agreement with actual draft outcomes, not proof of better long-term player performance.
methods: Public ESPN draft prospect data were merged and drafts from 1967 to 2010 removed. A random forest regressor used four inputs (position, draft grade, position rank, overall rank) to predict pick number, trained on 2016 to 2019 drafts and tested on the 2020 class, and was compared with a decision tree and a linear support vector machine. Draft simulations applied best-player-available and need-based rules to the 2017 first round, scored by mean absolute error and a partial-credit Top-3 score against the real picks.
findings: The four-input random forest reached a Pearson correlation of 0.94 and RMSPE of 0.41 on the 2020 test set, better than the decision tree and support vector machine. Adding height and weight lowered the correlation, and a text-derived grade also performed worse. For the simulated 2017 first round, need-based drafting had MAE 6.7 and a Top-3 score of 77.5, compared with MAE 8.8 and 71.9 for best-player-available, which matched the exact slot and team for 12.5% of picks.
limitations: Validation uses one draft year, and the need-based weighting parameter was tuned on the same comparison. The paper does not state which training years fed the 2017 simulation, so overlap between training data and the simulated draft cannot be ruled out. Trades were not modeled, and the authors note that real draft outcomes may not reflect optimal picks; later NFL performance was not measured. The abstract's claims about beating conventional methods and judging which picks were more impactful are not tested in the results. Top-3 is reported as 77.4 in one place and 77.5 in another, and Tables 7 and 10 report identical values for different models.
practicalImplications: Front offices could use a simulator like this to anticipate which prospects are likely to be available at their pick. Its value for evaluating prospects is unproven, so it should sit alongside scouting and not replace it.
athleteDev: The study is about draft selection modeling rather than training or athlete development. It offers a possible way to forecast draft positions, which may inform recruitment and roster planning rather than how athletes develop.
rtp: This study does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

citation: Laxminarayan S, Hornby S, Belval LN, Giersch GEW, Morrissey MC, Casa DJ, et al. Prospective Validation of 2B-Cool: Integrating Wearables and Individualized Predictive Analytics to Reduce Heat Injuries. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2023;55(4):751-764.
abstract: The authors prospectively tested 2B-Cool, a wearable and smartphone system that estimates core body temperature and predicts it 20 minutes ahead to warn of rising heat strain. In a controlled chamber study of 22 young adults across four heat and clothing conditions, core temperature estimates tracked rectal measurements closely, and the early-warning system gave useful lead time before a 38.50 C threshold.
tldr: A smartwatch and smartphone system estimated core temperature within about 0.45 C of rectal measurements during 7.5-hour heat stress trials in a chamber. Its early warning for 38.50 C gave roughly 35 minutes of lead time, but this has only been shown in a laboratory.
methods: Randomized crossover chamber study in which 22 healthy young adults (11 men, 11 women) completed up to four 7.5-hour trials, varying clothing (T-shirt and shorts or combat uniform) and environment (30 C at 60% humidity or 36 C at 30% humidity), with three treadmill work bouts per trial. Core temperature was measured by rectal probe; 82 of 88 trials were analyzed. Agreement was assessed with bias, MAE, RMSE, MAPE, correlation, and Bland-Altman limits, and early-warning performance with sensitivity, specificity, prediction horizon and false alarm rate.
findings: Across 82 trials, core temperature estimates had mean bias 0.16 C (SD 0.34), MAE 0.39 C, RMSE 0.45 C, and Pearson r 0.89, meeting the authors' bias criterion of less than 0.27 C. The 20-minute predictions had RMSE 0.56 C, with 73% (SD 19%) of measurements inside the 95% prediction interval. For a 38.50 C threshold the early warning had sensitivity 98%, specificity 81%, a 36-minute effective horizon and 0.12 false alarms per hour; for 39.20 C, sensitivity was 87%, specificity 77% and 0.35 false alarms per hour, so specificity at both thresholds and sensitivity at 39.20 C fell short of the authors' preset 90% criterion. No sex differences were found in measured or estimated peak temperature or in warning performance.
limitations: Testing was limited to 22 healthy young adults in a controlled chamber with one treadmill protocol, and field validation is still needed. The smoothing step means the system cannot follow temperature changes faster than about 10 minutes, so performance in stop-and-go sports such as American football is unknown, and it cannot detect hypothermia or non-exertional temperature rises. Figures differ between sections: nearly 75% versus 73% within the prediction interval, a 35 versus 36 minute horizon, and 81% versus 80% specificity. Two authors (S. L. and J. R.) receive royalties for licensing 2B-Cool.
practicalImplications: A wrist wearable with individualized modeling tracked rectal temperature to within about 0.4 C on average and flagged most rises above 38.50 C roughly 35 minutes ahead in steady chamber exercise. Expect false alerts given the 77% to 81% specificity, and do not treat an alert or its absence as a substitute for rectal temperature when exertional heat illness is suspected.
athleteDev: The study does not measure training adaptation or performance. It shows only that core temperature during long, steady exercise in the heat can be estimated from wrist-worn heart rate, skin temperature and activity data.
rtp: The study does not address return to sport after heat illness or any injury, so it cannot be used to decide when an athlete can return to activity.

citation: Collings TJ, Lima YL, Dutaillis B, Bourne MN. Concurrent validity and test-retest reliability of VALD ForceDecks strength, balance, and movement assessment tests. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
abstract: The authors compared portable uniaxial VALD ForceDecks plates with laboratory force plates for common strength, balance and movement tests in 16 healthy adults tested twice. Vertical force and centre of pressure agreed closely, and most discrete metrics showed good or excellent validity and reliability. Reliability was similar between the two systems.
tldr: Portable ForceDecks plates recorded vertical force and centre of pressure very close to laboratory plates during strength, balance and jump tests. Most metrics were reliable between days, but this depended on the specific test and metric and on strict testing procedures.
methods: Repeated-measures study with 16 healthy physically active adults (10 men, 6 women) tested on two sessions about 7 days apart. Twelve standard ForceDecks tests were recorded simultaneously on stacked portable and laboratory force plates. Raw time series were compared using RMSE and Bland-Altman analysis, discrete metrics by percentage difference, and test-retest reliability by ICC, SEM and minimal detectable change over 3 trials.
findings: Median RMSE for vertical force ranged from 2.5 to 25.2 N, and mean bias was -2 to -1 N, with limits of agreement from -6 to 3 N. Centre of pressure bias was -0.1 to 0.0 mm. Of 674 validity metrics, about 79% had good or excellent validity (abstract figure 530/674), and about 79% of 773 metrics had good or excellent reliability (ICC above 0.75). Shoulder isometric I, T and Y metrics had the weakest agreement, and quiet-stand COP metrics had poor reliability (ICC 0.21 to 0.43). ForceDecks reliability was similar to the laboratory plates, with median ICC differences below 0.07.
limitations: The sample was small and included healthy active adults, not elite athletes. Stacking the plates may have affected the laboratory readings, and time-window alignment was imperfect. The results apply to ForceDecks' own analysis methods. Reliability was based on two sessions. The abstract reports 611 of 773 reliable metrics, while the results report 385 excellent plus 228 good, which is 613. The study was funded by VALD, and several authors have relationships with VALD, which is disclosed.
practicalImplications: Practitioners can use ForceDecks for vertical force and centre of pressure measurement when protocols are strictly standardized. Check each test and metric's validity and reliability before using it to detect change, since COP balance metrics and shoulder isometric rate of force development were weaker. Repeat a test if protocol errors are suspected.
athleteDev: The study supports using portable force plates to track jump, strength and balance performance over time. Judge change against each metric's minimal detectable change in Table 1 rather than treating any between-session difference as real.
rtp: The tests may help monitor strength, balance and jump metrics during rehabilitation, but the study used healthy adults and did not assess injured participants or return-to-sport criteria. Use the reliability values only as a guide to detectable change and do not use the study to set clearance thresholds.

citation: Barbosa GM, Calixtre LB, Fialho HRF, Locks Neto F, Kamonseki DH. Measurement properties of upper extremity physical performance tests in athletes: a systematic review. Braz J Phys Ther. 2023:100575.
abstract: This systematic review summarized the reliability, measurement error and validity of upper extremity physical performance tests used with athletes. Fifteen studies with 684 athletes covered 13 tests, and the authors graded the quality of evidence for each property. The CKCUEST and the seated single-arm shot-put test showed sufficient reliability, while most other tests had insufficient or unclear evidence.
tldr: The CKCUEST and the seated single-arm shot-put test have the strongest reliability evidence for athletes (moderate to high quality for the CKCUEST, moderate for the shot-put). Validity, measurement error and responsiveness evidence is thin or missing for nearly all upper extremity tests.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, with a prospective registration (CRD42021241883). Medline, EMBASE, CINAHL, CENTRAL, SCOPUS, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science were searched to July 2022. Two reviewers rated study quality with the COSMIN checklist, and evidence was graded by measurement property using adapted Terwee criteria. Included studies assessed upper extremity tests in athletes of any sport and level.
findings: The CKCUEST had sufficient inter-session reliability (ICC 0.79 to 0.93, moderate quality of evidence) and sufficient intra-session reliability (ICC 0.86 to 0.95, high quality), but insufficient validity against isokinetic rotator strength (r 0.55 to 0.59, low quality). The seated single-arm shot-put test had sufficient inter-session reliability (ICC 0.92 to 0.94, moderate quality) and sufficient validity in one study (r 0.73 to 0.83, low quality). The seated medicine ball throw showed insufficient validity against Wingate peak power (r 0.40 to 0.54, moderate quality). Most other tests had low quality evidence, and measurement error could not be rated because minimal important change has not been defined.
limitations: Primary studies were small, often rated doubtful in methodological quality, and none reported responsiveness or minimal important change. About 70% of participants were men, and technology-dependent instruments such as dynamometers and motion analysis were excluded. The paper is internally inconsistent: the Conclusion says the CKCUEST and repetition to failure assessment showed sufficient validity, but the results rate both insufficient (r 0.55 to 0.59 and 0.20 to 0.40), and the Implications for Practice call the seated medicine ball throw valid although the results rate its validity insufficient. The abstract gives the search date as March 2021, but the Methods say searches ran to July 2022.
practicalImplications: The CKCUEST and the seated single-arm shot-put test appear reproducible enough for clinical use with athletes, based on reliability evidence. Use the seated medicine ball throw for upper body power only with caution, given the insufficient validity evidence. Treat other upper extremity tests as unproven, and when re-testing, keep the interval, setting and instructions consistent across sessions.
athleteDev: The CKCUEST and the seated shot-put test may be used to track upper body stability and power over time, but changes should be compared against each test's measurement error, which is often missing. The review does not address how these tests relate to training outcomes.
rtp: The review notes that PPTs are used to guide rehabilitation progress and return to play, but it finds too little evidence on responsiveness, measurement error and validity to support clearance decisions. Use the CKCUEST and seated shot-put tests as reliable measures only, and do not rely on the other tests to decide when an athlete can return.

citation: Weakley J, Morrison M, García-Ramos A, Johnston R, James L, Cole MH. The Validity and Reliability of Commercially Available Resistance Training Monitoring Devices: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2021.
abstract: This systematic review examined the validity and reliability of commercial portable devices that measure force, velocity and power during resistance training. Forty-four studies were included, and the authors found that linear transducers were generally the most accurate, while accelerometers, smartphone apps and optic devices showed more variable error. Most validity studies lacked a gold-standard criterion measure, and many reliability studies did not separate device error from human variability.
tldr: Linear position transducers gave the most accurate and reproducible velocity data in this review. Accelerometers, smartphone apps and optic devices showed more error, particularly with heavy loads, and much of the evidence lacks a gold-standard comparison.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching SPORTDiscus, Web of Science and Medline in August 2020, with reference-list screening. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed, English-language original research on the validity or reliability of portable commercial devices during resistance training. Reporting quality was rated with a nine-item modified Downs and Black checklist. Acceptable validity was defined as r above 0.70, CV below 10% and effect size below 0.60, and acceptable reliability as ICC at least 0.90, CV below 10% and standardized bias below 0.60.
findings: Of 44 studies, 36 assessed validity and 28 assessed reliability. Linear transducers had the highest accuracy, but most accelerometer validity studies compared devices against other devices rather than gold-standard motion capture. Accelerometer CVs typically ranged from 10% to 20%, and mean velocity at loads above 90% of 1RM had CVs of about 27% to 35%. Smartphone and tablet apps showed substantial bias and error across devices and users. The Flex optic laser showed acceptable validity for mean velocity across 20% to 100% of 1RM, with typical error around 0.02 m/s from 40% to 100% of 1RM. Mean study reporting quality was 8.0 of 9 (SD 1.3).
limitations: The search used three databases and English-language studies only, with reference-list searches added. Most included studies were small and focused on the squat and bench press, in free-weight or Smith machine form, and few tested Olympic weightlifting. Many validity studies lacked a gold-standard criterion, and most reliability studies did not separate technological from biological variation. Statistical reporting was often incomplete, which limited the comparison of devices.
practicalImplications: Where accurate barbell velocity matters, linear transducers have the strongest evidence in this review. The authors suggest accelerometers are best kept for motivational feedback during ballistic, high-velocity exercises and should not be used to track performance changes or to set loads or set volume with velocity loss thresholds. Smartphone apps need thorough user familiarisation and standardised protocols because bias and error vary across devices and users.
athleteDev: Validated velocity monitoring can support load prescription and feedback during resistance training, which may help plan athlete development. The review advises against using accelerometers to track changes in performance or to set loads and volume, so the choice of device should match the purpose.
rtp: The review covers healthy resistance training devices and does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions. It does not support using these devices to make return-to-play clearance decisions.

citation: Loenneke JP, Wilson GJ, Wilson JM. A mechanistic approach to blood flow occlusion. Int J Sports Med 2010;31:1-4.
abstract: This narrative review describes the proposed mechanisms by which low-intensity blood flow occlusion training may increase skeletal muscle hypertrophy. The mechanisms covered are metabolite accumulation and growth hormone, fast-twitch fibre recruitment, mTOR signalling, heat shock proteins, nitric oxide synthase-1 and myostatin. The authors conclude that the supporting research is incomplete.
tldr: Low-load occlusion training (as low as 20% 1RM with moderate occlusion) is proposed to build muscle through several mechanisms. The authors describe the evidence for each as incomplete, so treat them as hypotheses rather than established causes.
methods: Narrative review of the literature on blood flow occlusion and muscle growth, organised by proposed mechanism. The article does not describe a systematic search or appraisal of study quality.
findings: The review reports that occlusion raises blood, plasma and muscle lactate and growth hormone, with one study showing a growth hormone rise about 290 times baseline. It also cites a threefold rise in S6K1 phosphorylation immediately after occlusion exercise. The authors state that the link between lactate and growth hormone is unclear and that the mechanisms remain unproven.
limitations: The review has no search strategy and no quality appraisal. Several key mechanistic findings come from animal studies, and the authors call for human studies to confirm the heat shock protein findings of Kawada and Ishii. The review does not compare occlusion training directly with heavy resistance training.
practicalImplications: Low-load occlusion training (about 20% 1RM with moderate occlusion, around 100 mmHg) is presented as an option for people who cannot tolerate heavy loading. Staff should not use any single proposed pathway, such as growth hormone, to predict hypertrophy outcomes.
athleteDev: The review describes low-load occlusion training as a hypertrophy option and states it may benefit athletes. Because the mechanisms are unproven, it does not show that occlusion training is superior to conventional heavy resistance training for athletes.
rtp: The review mentions possible benefits in ACL rehabilitation, cardiac rehabilitation and post-operative patients but calls for more research. It contains no return-to-sport criteria and no data on re-injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Esh CJ, Carter S, Galan-Lopez N, Garrandes F, Bermon S, Adami PE, et al. A review of elite athlete evidence-based knowledge and preparation for competing in the heat. Journal of Science in Sport and Exercise. 2024.
abstract: Review of how elite athletes prepare for competition in heat, covering heat acclimation or acclimatisation, pre-cooling, mid-competition cooling and hydration, and the knowledge behind these choices. The authors report that adoption of heat acclimation has increased since 2015 but is not universal, that cost and access are the main barriers, and that most research covers small samples of elite endurance athletes. They call for regularly updated, multilingual guidance and more research across sports.
tldr: Heat acclimation adoption among elite athletes rose from 15% in 2015 to around 57% to 63% in later championships but is not universal. Cooling and hydration are widely used, so athletes should complete acclimation where possible and use cooling and hydration as complements, not substitutes.
methods: Narrative review of elite athlete heat preparation research, including survey data from five championship events (532 of 9,001 athletes surveyed) and one knowledge survey of athletes and practitioners. The recommendations were drafted by the authors, refined through three rounds of author revision and checked against cited guidelines. No systematic search or formal quality appraisal is described.
findings: Dedicated heat acclimation adoption among surveyed athletes was 15% at Beijing 2015, 63% at Doha 2019 and 57% at Muscat 2022, and barriers included cost and access to hot environments. At Doha 2019, acclimated athletes finished higher (mean position 18th vs 28th, P = 0.009), but their percentage of personal best time was similar (112.6% vs 113.3%), and heat-related medical events were 19% vs 32%, not statistically significant. Pre-planned cooling was used by 50% to 80% of athletes and pre-planned fluid intake by 80% or more, while in one survey 75% to 91% of respondents had never measured core temperature.
limitations: Survey samples are small and self-reported, and they cover only about 6% of competing athletes, mostly endurance athletes at major events. The authors note that competition factors such as pacing and non-heat illness may confound the performance and medical-event comparisons, and that the surveys lack standardisation. The IAAF Beijing 2015 sample is listed as 207 surveyed athletes in Table 1 but n = 307 in Tables 2 and 5.
practicalImplications: Where time allows, plan 10 to 14 consecutive days of active heat exposure (core temperature of 38.5 C or higher, sweating for at least 60 minutes) in conditions similar to or hotter than the competition. If that is not possible, the authors suggest post-exercise sauna (80 C or higher) or hot water immersion (40 C or higher) for 20 to 40 minutes, or extra clothing in training, with supervision and temperature monitoring. Use pre-cooling to complement acclimation rather than replace it, and begin hydration planning days before competition.
athleteDev: The performance evidence is observational: acclimated athletes at Doha 2019 finished higher but did not differ on percentage of personal best time, so the data support planning for heat acclimation rather than predicting race outcome. Plan pre-cooling and fluid strategies in training so they are tested before competition.
rtp: The review covers competition preparation in heat and heat-illness risk, not return to sport after injury or illness. Its exertional heat illness data should not be used to judge when an athlete who has had heat illness can safely return to training or competition.

citation: Pearson SJ, Hussain SR. A review on the mechanisms of blood-flow restriction resistance training-induced muscle hypertrophy. Sports Medicine. 2014.
abstract: Review of how low-intensity resistance training with blood flow restriction (BFR) produces muscle growth, comparing the roles of mechanical tension and metabolic stress. The authors argue that metabolic stress probably plays the dominant role, with mechanical tension and the downstream mechanisms it triggers contributing, but that the relative contribution of each mechanism is still unclear.
tldr: The authors argue that low-load BFR training builds muscle mainly through metabolic stress, with mechanical tension likely adding to the effect. The mechanisms are not settled, so treat the model as a working hypothesis.
methods: Narrative review of the mechanisms of BFR-induced hypertrophy, with a PubMed search from January 2000 to June 2014 using terms on occlusion, hypertrophy, metabolic stress and mechanical loading, plus reference-list checks. The review groups mechanisms into primary (mechanical tension, metabolic stress) and secondary (fibre recruitment, damage, hormones, cell swelling, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, heat shock proteins) and then autocrine and paracrine actions. No formal quality appraisal is described.
findings: The authors report that low-intensity training (about 30 to 50% of 1RM) with BFR at about 110 to 200 mmHg increased muscle size more than the same training without restriction in several cited studies. They argue that metabolic stress is the dominant primary driver, citing a conventional (non-BFR) study at 75% of 1RM in which a no-rest protocol increased muscle size where a with-rest protocol did not, and links between metabolite levels and hypertrophy. They also note that tension-linked mechanisms such as fast-twitch recruitment and reactive oxygen species appear less activated at low loads, so their role under BFR is uncertain.
limitations: The authors state that the relative contribution of each mechanism under BFR is largely unknown, and that mechanical tension and metabolic stress occur together, which makes causal attribution hard. Much of the proposed pathway evidence comes from acute, animal or in vitro studies, and the proposed role of moderate-intensity training is speculative. The search was limited to PubMed and ends in 2014.
practicalImplications: Low-load BFR training is a reasonable option for muscle growth when heavy loads are not suitable, as the cited studies show growth at around 20 to 50% of 1RM with restriction. The authors speculate that moderate loads may combine metabolic stress and mechanical tension best, but this is a hypothesis from their model rather than a tested comparison. Cuff pressure and load should be matched to the study protocols the authors cite rather than to general rules.
athleteDev: Low-load BFR can increase muscle size in the cited studies, but the review does not compare it with heavy training for strength, power or sport performance. Do not use it to predict strength or power gains.
rtp: The review covers hypertrophy mechanisms in healthy training, not rehabilitation after injury or return to sport. Its brief mentions of clinical and rehabilitation settings do not establish load, cuff pressure or safety for injured athletes.

citation: Seitz LB, Mina MA, Haff GG. A sled push stimulus potentiates subsequent 20-m sprint performance. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017;20:781-785.
abstract: Twenty rugby league players completed a randomized crossover study in which one sled push, loaded at 75% or 125% body mass, preceded unresisted 20 m sprints at 15 s, 4, 8 and 12 min. After the 75% push, sprints were faster at 4, 8 and 12 min (significant at 8 and 12 min); after the 125% push, sprints were slower at every time point (significant at 15 s and 4 min).
tldr: A single sled push at 75% body mass may speed a 20 m sprint 4 to 12 minutes later, but the effect was small and not every player responded. A push at 125% body mass slowed sprints in this group.
methods: Twenty rugby league players completed one familiarization session and two randomized testing sessions a week apart. Each session had baseline 20 m sprints, a sled push at 75% or 125% body mass, and 20 m sprints at 15 s, 4, 8 and 12 min after the push, compared against each player's fastest baseline sprint.
findings: After the 75% push, sprint time was 0.26 +/- 1.03% slower at 15 s (p = 0.91) and 0.95 +/- 2.00%, 1.80 +/- 1.43% and 1.55 +/- 1.54% faster at 4, 8 and 12 min (ES -0.22, -0.42 and -0.36); only the 8 min (p = 0.001) and 12 min (p = 0.003) changes were significant, and the 4 min change was rated only possibly beneficial. After the 125% push, sprints were slower at all time points (ES 0.34 to 0.64), with Table 1 marking 15 s and 4 min as significantly slower than baseline. The between-condition differences were significant at every time point, large at 15 s (d = -1.07) and very large at 4, 8 and 12 min.
limitations: No control session without a sled push was included (the authors note a fourth session was not feasible), and the sample was 20 players. The authors report that 35% to 70% of players improved after the 75% push, depending on time point. Values differ slightly between sections: the abstract gives -1.54% at 12 min while the results give -1.55%, and the Discussion gives the 125% range as 1.36 to 2.57% (ES 0.38 to 0.67) while the abstract and Table 1 give up to 2.59% (ES 0.34 to 0.64).
practicalImplications: Coaches who use a sled push to prime sprint speed should pay attention to load: in this study 75% body mass was followed by faster sprints and 125% body mass by slower sprints. The faster sprints were seen 4 to 12 minutes after the push, and some players did not respond.
athleteDev: Coaches could try a sled push at about 75% body mass followed by 4 to 12 minutes of rest before maximal 20 m sprints, but the gains were small and not every player responded. Avoid the 125% load before speed work, because sprints were slower after it in this group.
rtp: This study tested sprint times in players after sled pushes and did not include injured players or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Charron J, Carey V, Marcotte L'Heureux V, Roy P, Comtois AS, Ferland PM. Acute Effects of Cannabis Consumption on Exercise Performance - A Systematic and Umbrella Review. The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2020.
abstract: A systematic and umbrella review of acute cannabis use and exercise performance, covering 8 original studies and 10 reviews. The authors conclude that cannabis before exercise has an ergolytic effect, reducing the ability to maintain effort and work capacity, raising heart and breathing rate and myocardial oxygen demand, and increasing sway in balance tests.
tldr: Acute cannabis use before exercise is reported to reduce work capacity, raise heart rate and worsen balance. The direct evidence is small, dated and heterogeneous, so it should not be treated as settled athlete-specific evidence.
methods: PRISMA-based search of PubMed, Scopus and SPORTDiscus (September 2019) with a manual reference search, selection repeated by a second author, a modified Downs and Black quality rating, and a random-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis of heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure in RevMan 5.4.
findings: In the included studies, cannabis before exercise was associated with lower effort tolerance and maximal and physical work capacity, higher heart rate and rate-pressure product, and more sway in balance tests; individual studies were mixed on blood pressure (3 increased, 2 decreased, 1 no effect). The authors describe the pooled analysis as higher heart rate and blood pressure after cannabis, and 4 of the 10 reviews concluded cannabis is ergolytic, conclusions the authors judge to rest on limited data.
limitations: The authors note heterogeneity in THC dose (7.5 to 50.6 mg), timing (10 to 210 minutes) and participant type, and that most included studies used lower historical THC doses than current products. The Downs and Black power domain scored 1 of 8 and external validity 0 of 16, and the search was run in September 2019, so newer studies are not covered.
practicalImplications: The authors conclude that cannabis should be avoided before exercise to maximise performance. They also state that future studies should use modern THC doses (150 mg) and examine chronic effects, since current evidence does not cover those conditions.
athleteDev: The review supports education that acute cannabis use before training or competition is a performance risk, through effects on effort tolerance, work capacity, heart rate and balance. It does not quantify the effect in trained athletes at current THC doses.
rtp: The review cannot inform return to sport, since it addresses acute performance effects in volunteers, cannabis users and cardiac patients and does not study injured athletes or rehabilitation.

citation: Alonso-Fernandez D, Lopez-Barreiro J, Garganta R, Taboada-Iglesias Y. Acute impact of Nordic hamstring exercise on sprint performance after 24, 48 and 72 hours. Sports Biomechanics. 2021.
abstract: Twenty-four men were randomly allocated to a Nordic hamstring exercise session group or a no-session control, and 30 m sprint variables were measured at baseline and 24, 48 and 72 h later. The authors report a short-lived fall in high-speed force and maximum speed in the exercise group.
tldr: One session of Nordic hamstring exercise temporarily reduced high-speed sprint force and top speed for up to 48 h in previously unexposed men, with recovery by 72 h. The control group did not change and no between-group difference was significant, so the window is a within-group finding.
methods: Participants were randomised to an experimental group (4 sets of 10 partner-assisted eccentric NHE repetitions) or a control group. A manual radar measured 30 m sprints (mean of three) and derived F0, V0, Pmax, RFmax, Drf and maximum speed by linear regression; analysis used mixed repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc tests, and soreness and recovery were rated on a 1 to 10 scale.
findings: In the experimental group, V0 fell 3.4% at 48 h (P = 0.0001), maximum speed fell 2.0% at 24 h and 3.2% at 48 h, and Pmax fell 5.0% at 24 h (P = 0.027), with no change for these outcomes at 72 h. F0, RFmax and Drf did not change, soreness and perceived recovery were unaffected, and no between-group difference was significant at any time point.
limitations: The sample was 24 men with no eccentric NHE experience, studied across a single session, so findings may not apply to conditioned athletes or weekly programmes. Soreness was self-reported in one group only, no damage markers were taken, and the authors note that lower-volume NHE protocols, now common, may give different results.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest leaving about 72 h between a high-volume NHE session and high-speed sprint or competition sessions, at least until athletes are conditioned to the exercise. This rests on within-group changes that returned to baseline by 72 h rather than on a significant between-group effect.
athleteDev: In unconditioned men, sprint force at high speed and top speed were reduced for up to 48 h after one NHE session, so NHE sessions may be best scheduled away from high-speed training or competition until athletes are conditioned. Effects on F0 and soreness were absent.
rtp: The study cannot set a return-to-sport timeline, since it tested healthy unexposed men rather than injured players. The authors' link between reduced sprint performance and hamstring injury risk is drawn from the literature and was not tested here.

citation: Weidlich K, Domroes T, Bohm S, Arampatzis A, Mersmann F. Addressing muscle-tendon imbalances in adult male athletes with personalized exercise prescription based on tendon strain. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2024.
abstract: A season-long controlled study of adult male volleyball players compared a personalised tendon-strain loading program with usual training. Knee extensor strength, patellar tendon stiffness and strain, and tendon micromorphology were measured at four time points.
tldr: Individually calibrated isometric loading kept patellar tendon strain stable over a volleyball season, while strain rose in control players on usual training. Strength gains were similar in both groups, and injuries were not measured.
methods: Two teams from one division. The intervention team trained three times a week with isometric knee-extension loads set to 4.5 to 6.5% tendon strain, adjusted every 2 weeks from maximal voluntary contraction tests. Knee extensor moment, tendon force, stiffness, maximum strain and ultrasound peak spatial frequency were measured at four time points and analysed with linear mixed-effects models.
findings: Control players' maximum tendon strain rose, and the share at 9% or more went from 18% at baseline to 80% at M3 and 64% at M4, while in the intervention group it stayed around 38% and strain fluctuations fell. In the intervention group, players with higher baseline strain showed larger strain reductions (r = -0.80) and larger stiffness gains (r = 0.72). Knee extensor strength rose about 8.2% in controls and 6.8% in the intervention group with no interaction, normalised stiffness showed only a trend in the intervention group (P = 0.051), and tendon micromorphology did not change in either group.
limitations: Allocation was by team, not random, measurement intervals differed between groups, and other training content could not be controlled. Dropout was higher than planned, the authors say power may be too low for some interactions, and Table 1 lists 11 control players at M2 although the text reports missing control data only at M1, M3 and M4. No injury outcomes were recorded, and the authors note the added benefit over non-personalised loading is not established.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest individualised loading can limit increases in tendon strain across a season, which may matter for overuse risk in players with high strain. This is a plausible prevention target rather than a demonstrated injury reduction, and the added benefit over non-personalised loading is not yet established.
athleteDev: Staff could use maximal-contraction tendon strain testing to flag players whose strain is rising and consider individualised isometric loads to hold it within 4.5 to 6.5%. The study shows this kept strain stable in the intervention team, but strength gains were not larger than with usual training.
rtp: The study does not establish return-to-sport criteria or rehabilitation progression, since it followed in-season players, a few of whom were symptomatic (VISA-P 87 or below), rather than injured athletes in rehabilitation. Symptom counts did not change systematically in either group.

citation: Bender JM, Popkin CA. Ammonia Inhalants: Use, Misuse, and Role in Sports Performance. Sports Health. 2023.
abstract: This narrative clinical review covers the use, misuse and physiology of ammonia inhalants (smelling salts) in sport. The authors searched MEDLINE and Google Scholar and report that acute inhalation raises heart rate and cerebral blood flow velocity without changing blood pressure. They conclude that ergogenic evidence is limited and inconsistent, and that ammonia inhalants have no role in medical management of head injury.
tldr: Ammonia inhalants have no role in managing a suspected head injury, and their performance benefit is unproven. The only positive signal the review highlights is one small study of repeated Wingate efforts; across single maximal efforts the results were mixed, with one study showing higher rate of force development and others showing no change.
methods: Narrative review of MEDLINE and Google Scholar records using terms including smelling salts, ammonia inhalants, strength, performance, head injury and concussion. The paper summarizes six performance studies in tables and text, along with physiology, historical use and adverse-effect reports. It does not describe a systematic selection process or appraisal of study quality.
findings: Perry et al (15 resistance-trained men) found higher heart rate and middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity after inhalation, with mean arterial pressure unchanged and no change in maximal mid-thigh pull force. Bartolomei et al (20 men) reported higher peak rate of force development, but not countermovement jump power or maximal force. Rogers et al (12 active women) found higher mean and peak power over three repeated Wingate tests, with no change in heart rate or fatigue index. Richmond et al, Vigil et al and Campbell et al found no gain in repetitions, deadlift one-repetition maximum or most functional markers, although Campbell et al found higher heart rate, alertness and perceived performance.
limitations: The review is narrative and does not report how many studies were screened. Most cited studies are small (12 to 25 participants) and mostly male, and the authors note that their results conflict. Safety conclusions rest on case reports, mechanistic reasoning and historical exposure data rather than controlled trials.
practicalImplications: Do not use ammonia inhalants to assess or manage a suspected concussion or head injury, because they can mask symptoms and the withdrawal reflex may worsen a head or neck injury. Do not present them as a proven performance aid, since benefits are small or unconfirmed. Staff should be aware that a severe allergic reaction has been reported in one case report, and the authors theorize a possible syncope risk during heavy upright lifting.
athleteDev: The performance evidence is limited and inconsistent, so ammonia inhalants should not be relied on to improve strength or power. The most consistent possible effect is on repeated high-intensity efforts, shown in one study of women, while single maximal efforts showed no benefit for most measures.
rtp: Ammonia inhalants have no role in return-to-play decisions or in managing a head injury. They can mask concussion symptoms and may encourage continued participation, so this paper cannot support any use of inhalants in return-to-sport clearance.

citation: Crotty ED, Furlong LAM, Harrison AJ. Ankle and Plantar Flexor Muscle-Tendon Unit Function in Sprinters: A Narrative Review. Sports Med. 2023.
abstract: Narrative review of ankle joint and plantar flexor muscle-tendon unit (MTU) function across the sprint start, acceleration and maximum velocity phases, and of the musculotendinous properties linked to plantar flexor performance. The authors describe the ankle as most critical during acceleration and as a net energy dissipater at maximum velocity, and they state that an optimal plantar flexor MTU profile potentially exists.
tldr: The ankle and plantar flexor MTU matter most at the sprint start and during acceleration, when rear-leg ankle function and push-off force are key. At top speed the ankle mainly absorbs energy and transfers it up the chain, and the muscle and tendon traits that make a faster sprinter are still unclear.
methods: Narrative review. One author screened titles and abstracts from PubMed and Google Scholar searches (212 records; 84 full texts; 31 excluded, mainly because participants were not sprinters). In total 53 articles were included, plus 12 from reference lists, for 65 studies. No formal quality appraisal is reported.
findings: Sprint start: the rear-leg ankle is an important contributor, and in one cited comparison elite Jamaican sprinters had a higher rate of force development than national-level sprinters (259 vs 175 N/kg/s). Acceleration: the ankle contributes about 15% of positive work in the first stance and 38-48% in the second stance, per the cited studies. Maximum velocity: the ankle is a net energy dissipater, with peak plantar flexor power larger in the negative work phase (-4930 W) than in the positive work phase (3954 W) in one cited study. Muscle roles: based on simulation, the soleus acts mainly as a supporter and the gastrocnemius as both an accelerator and a supporter. Longer gastrocnemius fascicles correlated with faster 100 m personal bests (r about -0.29 to -0.57 with PB time in cited studies), while results for muscle size and tendon stiffness are inconsistent.
limitations: Most included studies have small samples and single-subject, cross-sectional or simulation designs, and the sprinters studied are mainly male. The authors flag a lack of research on female athletes and truly world-class sprinters, and note that model-derived fascicle and tendon values depend on model assumptions.
practicalImplications: The review links rear-leg ankle and plantar flexor force production to block power and early acceleration, so these qualities are a reasonable focus for sprint-start work. Block inclination above about 65 degrees may place the plantar flexor MTU at an unfavorable part of its length-tension curve, according to the cited studies. Do not set a single muscle size or tendon stiffness value as a target, because the review says the optimal profile is not yet defined.
athleteDev: Use the review's phase framework to decide where ankle and plantar flexor work fits: sprint start and early acceleration first. Track fascicle or tendon measures only where they can be tied to sprint outcomes, since the review finds those links inconsistent.
rtp: The review covers healthy sprint mechanics and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It offers no tendon or muscle criteria for clearing an athlete to sprint.

citation: Weakley J, McLaren S, Ramirez-Lopez C, García-Ramos A, Dalton-Barron N, Banyard H, et al. Application of velocity loss thresholds during free-weight resistance training: Responses and reproducibility of perceptual, metabolic, and neuromuscular outcomes. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2020;38(5):477-485.
abstract: Twelve male team-sport athletes completed five sets of barbell back squats at about 0.70 m/s, with sets stopped at 10%, 20% or 30% velocity loss on separate days. Post-set dRPE and blood lactate rose with the threshold, and CMJ variables fell, and the four-week variability of each response is reported as an SD.
tldr: In 12 male university rugby players, higher velocity loss thresholds in the back squat produced greater perceived effort, lactate and post-set jump losses within a session. The authors report small four-week variability in these responses, though some variability estimates were imprecise.
methods: Repeated, counterbalanced crossover design. Twelve male rugby athletes performed five sets of barbell back squats at a starting mean concentric velocity of 0.70 +/- 0.01 m/s, with sets ended at 10%, 20% or 30% velocity loss. Each protocol was completed twice, four weeks apart, and dRPE, blood lactate and CMJ were measured after each set and analysed with linear mixed models.
findings: Between protocols, dRPE and blood lactate increased with the threshold (30% > 20% > 10%); lactate was 1.7 mmol/L higher for 20% vs 10% and 3.6 mmol/L higher for 30% vs 10%. CMJ height was lower at greater thresholds by small amounts (-1.9 cm for 20% vs 10%, -3.4 cm for 30% vs 10%), but impulse differences for 20% vs 10% and 30% vs 20% were likely trivial and the PPO difference for 30% vs 20% was possibly trivial. The four-week SDs were dRPE 8-11 au, B[La] 0.8-1.0 mmol/L, CMJ height 1.6-2.0 cm, CMJ peak relative power 1.0-1.8 W/kg, CMJ peak velocity 0.04-0.06 m/s and CMJ impulse at 100 ms 5.7-11.9 N s.
limitations: The sample was 12 male rugby players performing one exercise at a fixed starting velocity of 0.70 m/s, so results may not transfer to other athletes, lifts or starting velocities. Responses at 24 hours were not measured, training and lifestyle were not controlled between test occasions, and inferences used magnitude-based decisions. Several four-week SD confidence intervals for the 10% condition cross zero (for example B[La] 0.8, 90% CI -0.2 to 1.2), and one Table 1 interval is misprinted (RPE-B 30 vs 10%: 27; 23).
practicalImplications: Velocity loss thresholds give staff a way to set the internal response to a set: 30% produced more perceived effort and lactate, and larger jump losses, than 10%. The authors suggest 10% during congested periods or close to competition, and 30% for hypertrophy and strength endurance blocks. Staff should record the starting velocity in the warm-up and the first repetition of each set, since the protocol depends on it.
athleteDev: Velocity loss thresholds can set the within-session effort and fatigue for a squat session, with 30% giving more perceived exertion, lactate and CMJ loss than 10%. Choose the threshold to match the training goal, such as 10% for lower-fatigue blocks and 30% for hypertrophy or strength endurance work. The findings were from a single exercise with a fixed starting velocity of 0.70 m/s.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tested healthy male athletes in the off-season and did not include injured athletes, rehabilitation or readiness to return.

citation: Lutz C, Mancino F, Parker DA. 12-Months MRI after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Can Identify Risk Factors for Subsequent Graft Rupture and Used to Guide the Return to Sport. Results From a High-Volume Institution. Journal of ISAKOS. 2025.
abstract: Retrospective matched comparison of 13 patients with early hamstring-autograft ACL re-rupture and 50 matched controls, drawn from 430 primary ACL reconstructions (2017 to 2022) at one high-volume institution. Mean follow-up was 23.6 months. Re-rupture patients had higher graft signal on 12-month MRI (SNQ 2.93 vs 2.02, p=0.029). Tunnel position and widening, patient-reported outcomes and return-to-sport tests did not differ significantly between groups.
tldr: In this small single-centre matched comparison, a higher signal on 12-month MRI after hamstring ACL reconstruction was seen in patients who later re-tore their graft. Return-to-sport tests did not separate the groups, and the multivariable model did not confirm graft signal, so this is a hypothesis to test rather than a clearance rule.
methods: Retrospective analysis of 430 consecutive skeletally mature patients with primary hamstring-autograft ACLR. Of 346 meeting criteria, 19 ruptured and 13 with complete 12-month MRI formed the re-tear group, matched 1:4 to 50 controls. Graft signal (signal-to-noise quotient), tunnel widening and tunnel position were measured on 3.0-T MRI, with side-to-side laxity (GnRB) and return-to-sport tests at 9 to 12 months.
findings: Re-tear patients had a higher mean 12-month SNQ (2.93 vs 2.02, p=0.029; Cohen's d 0.44), and 69.2% had SNQ above 2 vs 38% of controls (p=0.044). Anterior laxity above 2 mm was more frequent in the re-tear group (83.3% vs 38.8%, p=0.058), but mean laxity did not differ significantly (2.5 vs 1.3 mm, p=0.189). Femoral tunnel widening above 50% was actually more common in controls (36% vs 7.7%, p=0.155), and logistic regression did not identify graft signal, tunnel widening or laxity as significant risk factors (R2N=0.28).
limitations: Only 13 re-tears were analysed, and 6 of 19 ruptures were excluded for missing 12-month MRI, which the authors flag as a possible detection bias. The design is retrospective, different assessors measured clinical, laxity and return-to-sport outcomes, and the cohort used one graft and fixation type in adults not described as athletes. The regression did not confirm graft signal (p=0.244), and the discussion gives 38.8% for control SNQ above 2 where Table 2 gives 38%.
practicalImplications: A high 12-month graft signal was more common in patients who re-tore, so it may justify closer follow-up or repeat imaging before a full return to sport for higher-risk patients. The study does not establish a cut-off that should delay clearance, and the multivariable model did not confirm graft signal as an independent risk factor.
athleteDev: This study does not measure training or performance outcomes. Its performance-relevant result is that hop, leg-length and ACL-RSI results at 9 to 12 months did not differ between re-tear and non-re-tear patients, so test scores in this cohort did not identify who would re-tear.
rtp: The study can inform the monitoring discussion but not a clearance threshold. High 12-month graft signal was associated with early re-tear in a small matched comparison, and the authors suggest repeat MRI may inform return-to-sport decisions. It should not set a return-to-sport date, because return-to-sport tests did not predict re-rupture and the multivariable model did not confirm graft signal.

citation: Zago M, Esposito F, Stillavato S, Zaffagnini S, Frigo CA, Della Villa F. 3-Dimensional Biomechanics of Noncontact Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Male Professional Soccer Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2024:1-10.
abstract: Video analysis of 33 male professional soccer ACL injuries (24 noncontact, 9 indirect contact) from the 2020-2021 to 2022-2023 seasons, with 3D whole-body kinematics reconstructed by model-based image matching. At the injury frame, the knee was moderately flexed with a valgus trend and external rotation, and the hip was flexed, abducted and slightly internally rotated. Knee kinematics were consistent across situational patterns, while ankle, hip and trunk differed. The authors conclude that injury biomechanics vary with the game situation.
tldr: Reconstructed 3D video analysis of 33 professional male soccer ACL injuries shows a moderately flexed knee with a valgus trend and rapid rotation changes before the injury frame. Ankle, hip and trunk postures differed by game situation, but the study does not test any prevention intervention.
methods: Cross-sectional video analysis of ACL injuries in 6 national and 2 international competitions, using publicly available broadcast footage. Of 47 identified injuries, 33 had suitable multi-view video. Model-based image matching reconstructed 3D joint angles from 400 ms before to 200 ms after the injury frame, and situational patterns were compared with one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping ANOVA.
findings: Across 33 injuries, mean knee flexion at the injury frame was 45.9 ± 21.7 degrees, with 4.3 ± 5.1 degrees of abduction and 3.0 ± 6.4 degrees of external rotation, while the hip was flexed 32.0 ± 18.7 degrees, abducted 31.1 ± 12.0 degrees and slightly internally rotated (Table 1). A dynamic knee valgus pattern was seen in 22 of 33 cases (67%), and the knee rotated externally by up to 5 degrees and then internally before the injury frame. The knee time course did not differ between pressing, offensive change-of-direction and regaining-balance patterns before 0.1 s after initial contact, whereas ankle, hip and trunk differences were significant.
limitations: Only 33 of 47 identified injuries had video suitable for analysis, and the abstract's description of 33 consecutive cases should be read with that subset in mind. Injury timing was estimated from video, the model fixes tibiofemoral translations, and the method gives estimates rather than measurements. There was no uninjured control group, and the unequal situational groups (pressing 54% of noncontact cases) limit statistical power.
practicalImplications: Because the knee pattern was similar across situations but hip, trunk and ankle postures differed, drills for pressing, change of direction and landing could be built to resemble those game situations. The authors' proposal to shift from general strengthening toward discipline-specific training is their recommendation and was not tested in this study.
athleteDev: The study suggests that sidestepping, pressing and landing work should be representative of game situations, because the postures at injury varied with the situation. It does not test any training programme or show that changing these postures reduces injury.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes how noncontact ACL injuries occurred and does not assess rehabilitation progress, readiness tests or clearance criteria.

citation: Kim S, Kleimeyer JP, Ahmed MA, Avins AL, Fredericson M, Dragoo JL, et al. A Genetic Marker Associated with Shoulder Dislocation. Int J Sports Med. 2017;38:508-514.
abstract: Genome-wide association screen for shoulder dislocation using genotype and electronic health record data from the GERA cohort of Kaiser Permanente Northern California, including 662 cases and 82,602 controls of European ancestry. rs12913965, in an intron of the TICRR gene and associated with expression of ISG20, was associated with shoulder dislocation at genome-wide significance (p = 9.7 × 10^-9, OR 1.6). Carriers of one risk allele had a 69% higher risk of shoulder dislocation in this cohort, and the authors call for replication.
tldr: In a large general-population genetic cohort, one variant (rs12913965) was associated with a higher rate of coded shoulder dislocation or stabilisation surgery. It has not been replicated or tested in athletes, so it is not ready for athlete screening.
methods: Case-control genome-wide association study in the GERA cohort (n = 102,979), with the European-ancestry group (83,264 people) as the primary analysis. Cases were defined by ICD-9 codes for closed anterior, posterior or inferior shoulder dislocation or by CPT codes for capsulorrhaphy, and about 8 million genotyped and imputed SNPs were tested with logistic regression adjusted for sex, age at enrolment, ancestry principal components and genotyping variables. Genome-wide significance was set at p < 5 × 10^-8, with sex-specific analyses and fixed-effects meta-analyses with Latino and East Asian groups.
findings: rs12913965 was the only genome-wide significant variant (additive OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.88; dominant OR 1.72, p = 3.6 × 10^-9; recessive model not significant, p = 0.146). Heterozygous carriers had a relative risk of 1.69 (95% CI 1.41 to 2.03) compared with non-carriers, while the 10 homozygous cases gave a non-significant relative risk of 1.61. The sex-specific odds ratios did not differ significantly, and the variant was not associated in the Latino (p = 0.9) or East Asian (p = 0.64) groups, so the EUR plus Latino meta-analysis (p = 5.5 × 10^-8) was driven by the European data.
limitations: Phenotypes came from electronic health record codes, which the authors note may be inaccurate, and recurrent dislocations and multidirectional instability were excluded. The cohort was not selected for sport, and the association has not been replicated. The text gives 626 European cases in the methods but 662 elsewhere, and gives a risk allele frequency of 13% in the text but 0.10 in controls in Table 3.
practicalImplications: This variant should not be used to screen or counsel athletes about shoulder dislocation risk, because it comes from one unreplicated general-population association. The authors' suggestion that it might one day identify athletes at higher risk is a hypothesis for future athlete studies.
athleteDev: The study does not measure training or performance and does not include athlete data. It cannot inform training decisions.
rtp: The study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after shoulder dislocation. It does not examine treatment, recurrence after return, or readiness criteria, and recurrent dislocations were excluded from the case definition.

citation: Lamplot JD, Rodeo SA, Brophy RH. A practical guide for the current use of biologic therapies in sports medicine. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019:1-15.
abstract: This Current Concepts review gives sports medicine clinicians a practical guide to biologic therapies, mainly PRP and BMAC. It covers FDA regulation, cost and insurance coverage, direct-to-consumer marketing, preparation variability, and clinical evidence for tendon, rotator cuff, ligament, cartilage and osteoarthritis indications. The authors conclude that these therapies remain at a proof-of-concept stage and need better-reported preparations and trials.
tldr: Biologic injections such as PRP and BMAC are widely used in sports medicine, but this review finds their efficacy, cost-effectiveness and preparation are not well established. Clinicians should check the evidence for each indication and what the patient will pay.
methods: Narrative review of FDA regulatory guidance, cost and insurance reports, direct-to-consumer marketing studies, and clinical studies and systematic reviews for each indication. A September 2018 ClinicalTrials.gov search was used to estimate the number of trials per indication. No formal systematic search or risk-of-bias method is described.
findings: The FDA does not regulate point-of-care PRP or BMAC, but clinicians must register their use, and most insurers treat these therapies as experimental. Reported patient prices were a mean of $714 per same-day unilateral PRP knee injection (153 clinics) and $5156 per stem-cell knee injection (65 centers). The authors conclude there is a lack of evidence to support PRP augmentation of rotator cuff repair; for knee osteoarthritis several RCTs favored leukocyte-poor PRP over placebo or hyaluronic acid, although AAOS and NICE guidance calls the evidence inconclusive; and for ACL reconstruction, 6 of 11 RCTs reported faster graft maturation with PRP but only 1 reported better clinical outcomes.
limitations: The authors note that most published studies lack enough detail on preparation to be reproduced, and that only 10% of PRP trials in orthopaedics gave a full protocol. The cartilage evidence rests on case series and small cohorts, and BMAC preparations vary widely in cell content, so dose and timing cannot be compared across studies.
