citation: Alt T, Knicker AJ, Nodler YT, Strüder HK. Assisted or unassisted Nordic Hamstring Exercise? Resistance exercise determinants at a glance. Sports Biomechanics. 2021.
abstract: This secondary analysis compared assisted and unassisted Nordic Hamstring Exercise in 16 male sprinters using kinetic and kinematic measures across three sets of three repetitions. Assisted repetitions met the authors' execution criteria more consistently and varied less between athletes, and three sets of three unassisted repetitions produced clear within-session fatigue.
tldr: In sprinters, rope-assisted Nordic hamstring repetitions gave a more controlled, full-range movement with less variation between athletes, while unassisted repetitions showed clear fatigue within three sets of three. The study measured execution quality and fatigue, not strength gains or injury reduction.
methods: Secondary analysis of a published cohort: after six familiarisation sessions, 16 male sprinters performed assisted and unassisted sessions (in alternating order) of 3 sets of 3 eccentric-only Nordic hamstring repetitions on an IsoMed2000 dynamometer, aiming for a knee extension velocity of about 15 degrees per second. Assisted repetitions were controlled by an examiner through a rope attached to a climbing harness, and 3D motion was captured with two high-speed cameras and Vicon Peak Motus. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested mode and repetition effects, with Bonferroni post hoc tests and Levene's test for between-participant variability.
findings: Mode differed significantly for every parameter (p <= 0.003): compared with unassisted reps, assisted reps had 17 to 21% lower peak moment, 21 to 82% higher impulse, 45 to 93% longer time under tension, 23 to 47% greater range to downward acceleration and 7 to 9 degrees less maximal hip flexion. Between-participant variability was lower for assisted reps on all parameters except angle of peak moment and maximal hip flexion. From repetition 1 to 9, unassisted reps lost 41% of impulse and 29% of time under tension and gained 79% in fractional angular velocity, whereas assisted reps changed by -11% (impulse) and -5% (time under tension), with peak moment falling at repetitions 6 and 9.
limitations: The abstract's phrase 'except for peak moments and maximal hip flexion' refers to which parameters favoured assisted execution, not to significance; Table 1 shows significant mode effects for both, with peak moment favouring unassisted reps and hip flexion rated a draw. The sample was 16 sprinters heterogeneous in training history and level, a minimum knee flexion of 28 degrees remained even when assisted, and the study did not measure strength, fascicle length or injury outcomes.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest assisted NHEs for unfamiliar, weaker or early-stage athletes, so they can complete controlled full-range reps, and reserve unassisted full-range work for athletes whose level allows it. Because fatigue appeared within three sets of three, they suggest considering muscular failure, rather than a fixed repetition count, as the set endpoint.
athleteDev: Impulse, time under tension and fractional angular velocity can be used to check repetition quality and within-session fatigue in sprinters, and assisted reps gave more consistent execution across athletes. The study does not show that either mode produces greater strength, sprint performance or fascicle change.
rtp: Only partly relevant to return to sport. Healthy sprinters were tested, and the authors suggest assisted NHEs may suit patients at early rehabilitation stages, but no injured athletes were studied and no return-to-sport criteria or injury outcomes were tested.

citation: Ginevičienė, V.; Urnikytė, A. Association of COL12A1 rs970547 Polymorphism with Elite Athlete Status. Biomedicines. 2022;10:2495.
abstract: A case-control study of the COL12A1 rs970547 polymorphism in 293 Lithuanian elite athletes from running, throwing, jumping and football, compared with 287 non-athlete controls. The T allele and TT genotype were significantly more common in athletes overall, and the C allele was less frequent in sprint/power athletes and footballers than in controls. The authors also report signals of positive selection at this variant in the Lithuanian population.
tldr: In this Lithuanian case-control study, the COL12A1 rs970547 T allele was more common in elite athletes than in controls, most clearly in sprint/power athletes and footballers. The result is a candidate association from one population and does not establish a performance effect.
methods: Genotyping of rs970547 by TaqMan allelic discrimination in 293 elite athletes (66 endurance, 80 sprint/power, 147 footballers) and 287 non-athlete controls, with chi-square and exact tests, odds ratios and sex-adjusted analyses. Positive selection was assessed with XP-EHH and Tajima's D using whole-genome data from 50 Lithuanian individuals.
findings: The T allele and TT genotype were over-represented in the total athlete group compared with controls (C allele 20.0% vs 33.3%, p < 0.05). Sprint/power athletes (C allele 16.9%) and footballers (19.4%) differed from controls, while the endurance group did not reach significance (C allele 25.0%, p = 0.082). Controls departed from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and the authors report that the derived T allele shows positive selection in the Lithuanian population.
limitations: The sample is small and limited to Caucasian Lithuanians, so results may not generalise to other ancestries or countries. No phenotype, injury or training data were collected, and only one SNP was tested. The control group deviates from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p = 0.00005). The text gives genotype percentages for male athletes (TT/TC/CC 65.2/29.5/5.4%) that differ from Table 1 (65.6/28.7/5.7%); the table values are reported here.
practicalImplications: This genetic association does not support using rs970547 to identify, select or develop athletes. Coaches and clinicians should not change training, selection or injury screening on the basis of this genotype.
athleteDev: The paper does not show that rs970547 affects athletic performance or development. Its only use for staff is as a research signal about the genetics of elite status in one population, and it should not guide athlete identification or programming.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It reports no injury, rehabilitation or return data, and the variant should not be used to estimate injury risk or recovery for an individual athlete.

citation: Greig, L., Hemingway, B.H.S., Aspe, R.R., Cooper, K., Comfort, P., Swinton, P.A. Autoregulation in Resistance Training: Addressing the Inconsistencies. Sports Medicine. 2020.
abstract: Narrative review of autoregulation of resistance training, which adjusts training based on measured or perceived performance. The authors propose a conceptual framework built on the fitness-fatigue model that separates training-driven fitness and fatigue from non-training readiness, and apply it to within-session, meta-session and program-level methods.
tldr: Autoregulation is a flexible way to adjust resistance training to day-to-day performance, but its terms have been used inconsistently. The authors offer a framework that separates fitness, fatigue and readiness, so staff can define and apply methods more consistently.
methods: Narrative review that traces the development of autoregulation from the 1940s to current practice, identifies inconsistent terminology, and builds a conceptual framework from the fitness-fatigue model. The authors then map common within-session, meta-session and program-level methods onto that framework using examples from the literature. No systematic search or pooled analysis is reported.
findings: The authors report that a growing evidence base suggests autoregulation may outperform some predetermined loading approaches for strength and lean mass gains. They report that velocity-based training produced greater strength and countermovement jump gains than percentage-based programs in some studies, and that a flexible nonlinear periodization approach showed no significant differences from a matched program in well-trained individuals. The authors conclude that autoregulation is context-specific and should be viewed as an adjunct to existing practice.
limitations: The review reports no new data and does not apply a systematic method to the cited studies. The authors note that measurement error can cause poorly calibrated autoregulation to be less effective than standard practice, and that the evidence for stopping-velocity thresholds is mostly cross-sectional.
practicalImplications: Practitioners should define terms such as readiness, fatigue and adaptation before selecting an autoregulation method, because the terms have been used interchangeably. Measurement devices should be consistent across sessions and have suitable validity and reliability, and velocity ranges should be wide enough to allow for typical error. The authors present methods such as repetitions in reserve and velocity-based training as adjuncts to existing programming rather than replacements.
athleteDev: The framework separates changes driven by training (fitness and fatigue) from day-to-day non-training changes (readiness), which can help staff decide whether a performance change warrants adjusting load or volume. The authors state that the framework's effectiveness and feasibility in practice still require testing.
rtp: The review focuses on resistance training prescription and does not evaluate return to sport after injury. It mentions autoregulated rehabilitation protocols for the knee, but it reports no outcome data for rehabilitation and cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Clemente, F.M., Pillitteri, G., Palucci Vieira, L.H., Rabbani, A., Zmijewski, P., Beato, M. Balancing the load: A narrative review with methodological implications of compensatory training strategies for non-starting soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(4):173-185.
abstract: Narrative review of external and internal load differences between starting and non-starting soccer players and of studies on compensatory (top-up) training for non-starters. Per-minute running and sprint values were often higher in non-starters, while total values were lower, and the authors conclude that the effects of compensatory training on fitness and injury risk remain uncertain.
tldr: Non-starters play fewer minutes, so their total running is lower, but their per-minute running is often higher. Top-up training is widely used, yet its effects on fitness and injury risk have not been tested experimentally.
methods: Narrative review of soccer studies on starter and non-starter load and fitness, and on compensatory training, drawing on literature searches the authors describe as of 2023 and 2024. The review also presents illustrative session scenarios drawn from practice. No systematic protocol, risk-of-bias appraisal or pooled analysis is reported.
findings: Adjusted for playing time, male youth and senior non-starters often covered higher standardized distances and high-speed running, while absolute totals were generally higher for starters. Perceived exertion and heart rate were generally higher in starters, and studies of physical fitness show mixed or no differences by playing status. In English professional players, post-match top-up sessions averaged about 17 minutes with about 0.4 km of high-speed running, and in a Spanish study of day-after-match top-up training, substitutes recorded 0.49 km (5 to 15 minutes played) to 1.3 km (30 to 45 minutes played) of high-speed running, which the authors judge still short of full-match exposure.
limitations: The review uses no systematic search, quality appraisal or pooled analysis, so its conclusions are interpretive. The authors note that most studies are descriptive, small and drawn from few teams, and that speed thresholds and playing-time standardization differ across studies. The practical scenarios are illustrative examples from the authors' practice rather than tested protocols.
practicalImplications: Staff planning top-up sessions for non-starters should first review the match schedule, the number of available players and the manager's game model, because these shape the dose. Running-based high-intensity interval training and small-sided games can be combined, because small-sided games alone fall short of match high-speed running and sprint distances. Staff should track sessions against match load per minute as well as totals, and use individualized speed thresholds where possible.
athleteDev: The review suggests that non-starters may receive less high-speed running and sprint exposure than starters, which could matter for maintaining match fitness. The authors state that the effect of playing status on physical fitness is unclear, so top-up training should not be assumed to improve fitness.
rtp: The review addresses training load in non-starters and does not study return to play after injury. One illustrative scenario modifies the session for a player in his first match back from a grade 2 hamstring injury, but this is the authors' example, not tested guidance, and the review gives no evidence that compensatory training changes return-to-play timing.

citation: Owen A, Weston M, Clancy C. Between-microcycle variability of external soccer training loads through the evaluation of a contemporary periodisation training model 'CUPs'. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024.
abstract: This observational study examined week-to-week variation in external training load for the same matchday-classified sessions across an eight-week in-season mesocycle in 37 professional soccer players. GPS-measured total distance, high-intensity distance, high-intensity accelerations and percentage of maximum speed varied substantially between microcycles. Within-player variation on the same weekday was smaller, which the authors interpret as a more consistent stimulus under the CUPs model.
tldr: In 37 professional soccer players, the same matchday-labelled training session varied substantially in GPS load from one week to the next, even though the planned content stayed consistent. Within-player variation on the same day was smaller, but the study had no comparison group.
methods: Observational study of GPS-tracked (10 Hz) training sessions from 37 male players at one professional club during microcycles 6 to 13 of the 2022/23 season, with 564 sessions in total. Mixed linear models (lme4) with player as a random effect compared each matchday-classified session (MD-4 to MD-1) with microcycle 6, and results were reported as the lower to upper limits of fixed-effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals.
findings: Between-microcycle differences were large for total distance (lower to upper limits spanning 1244, 1503, 1916 and 2248 m for MD-1 to MD-4) and for high-intensity distance (80, 86, 375 and 197 m for MD-1 to MD-4). High-intensity accelerations spanned 11 to 25 across the four session types, and percentage of maximum speed spanned 10.2 to 15.4 percentage points. Within-player standard deviations were smaller on most measures, and the authors describe MD-1 as the lowest-load day.
limitations: The study had no control group or comparison periodisation model, so it cannot attribute the observed patterns to the CUPs model, although the authors state the model 'can mediate large fluctuations'. The authors acknowledge a small sample from one club, sessions per player were unbalanced (median 14, range 1 to 31), and positional differences and personnel changes, which the authors suggest may explain the variation, were not analysed. The abstract gives a high-intensity distance range of 80 to 197 m, but the results report 375 m for MD-3.
practicalImplications: The same matchday-labelled session can differ substantially in distance and high-intensity load from week to week, so a single week's values should be read with the wider microcycle in mind. The authors suggest setting daily targets for key metrics, such as high-intensity accelerations on MD-4 and more than 90% of maximum speed on MD-3, alongside recovery monitoring.
athleteDev: The study describes how much the same weekday session varied across an in-season mesocycle and proposes daily targets for key external load metrics. It supports using MD-1 as a low-load day before matchday, but it does not show that the targets improve performance.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It measures squad training loads and reports no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Harper DJ, McBurnie AJ, Dos'Santos T, Eriksrud O, Evans M, Cohen DD, et al. Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports. Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: This review examines the biomechanical and neuromuscular demands of horizontal deceleration in random intermittent multi-directional sports. It highlights high, rapid braking forces and identifies braking force control and braking force attenuation as the key qualities, with eccentric, reactive, concentric and isometric strength, and braking technique, as possible contributors.
tldr: Braking steps produce sharper, higher peak forces than the first steps of a sprint, so the ability to brake and absorb force is a separate quality to train. Eccentric strength, reactive strength and braking technique are the main candidate qualities, though most of the supporting evidence is cross-sectional.
methods: Narrative review. Searches of PubMed, MEDLINE, Google Scholar and reference lists covered records to November 2021. Eligible studies measured deceleration kinetics or kinematics during straight-line acceleration-to-deceleration tasks or severe change-of-direction tasks with 90 degree or greater turns, in physically active participants of any age.
findings: Braking ground reaction forces peak in the first 10-40% of stance and within the first 50 ms, and total ground reaction force exposure can be up to 2.7 times that of the first steps of a maximal acceleration. In professional soccer, players performed 80-104% more high-intensity decelerations than accelerations (cited from one match-play study). Cross-sectional studies report moderate to very large associations between isokinetic eccentric quadriceps strength and deceleration measures, with a weaker association for hamstring eccentric strength, and link rapid eccentric torque and reactive strength to braking performance.
limitations: The review is narrative rather than systematic, and the determinants come mainly from cross-sectional observational studies, so causality cannot be assumed. Most determinant studies used pre-planned deceleration tasks and whole-body outcomes, and the authors say the link to unanticipated match decelerations is untested.
practicalImplications: Test and train deceleration as its own quality, not only as part of acceleration or change of direction. Include eccentric strength work, reactive strength and braking technique in the plan, and monitor braking loads and side-to-side differences. The authors suggest combining local-specificity strength work with coordinative training, which no study in the review tests directly.
athleteDev: Treat deceleration as a performance quality with its own profile covering braking force control, braking force attenuation, eccentric strength and reactive strength. The review notes that normative deceleration data are not yet available, so it cannot supply benchmarks for judging an individual athlete.
rtp: The review does not test return-to-sport criteria. It may suggest which deceleration qualities to rebuild, since the authors link braking ability to tissue tolerance, but it cannot set return-to-sport thresholds.

citation: Cheung CP, Baker RE, Coates AM, Burr JF. Cannabis containing THC impairs 20-min cycling time trial performance irrespective of the method of inhalation. J Appl Physiol. 2024;136:583-591.
abstract: This crossover study compared exercise responses after smoked THC-predominant cannabis, vaporized THC-predominant cannabis, vaporized CBD-predominant cannabis and a control condition in 14 habitual cannabis users. THC-containing cannabis altered heart rate and ventilation during exercise and reduced mean power in a 20-minute cycling time trial whether smoked or vaporized. CBD-predominant cannabis had little physiological effect and no effect on time-trial performance.
tldr: In habitual cannabis users who were trained athletes, THC-containing cannabis reduced 20-minute cycling time-trial power whether smoked or vaporized, while CBD-predominant cannabis had no measurable effect. The study is small and laboratory-based, so it is best read as evidence that THC can impair sustained hard exercise, not as a dosing guide.
methods: Semirandomized crossover study. Fourteen habitual cannabis users completed a control visit, then three inhalation conditions in randomized order: smoked THC-predominant cannabis (13.6% THC, under 1% CBD, 100 mg), vaporized THC-predominant cannabis, and vaporized CBD-predominant cannabis (14.5% CBD, under 1% THC). Each visit included 10 minutes at 100 W and a 20-minute all-out cycling time trial, with expired gases, heart rate and RPE recorded; participants and researchers were not blinded and there was no placebo.
findings: During submaximal cycling, heart rate rose by 14 beats/min after smoked THC and 18 beats/min after vaporized THC relative to control, and was significantly higher than both control and CBD (all P < 0.02); maximal-exercise heart rate did not differ. Mean 20-minute time-trial power was significantly lower after both THC conditions than after control and CBD (all P < 0.04), which the authors report as reductions of 5.1% when smoked and 7.5% when vaporized, with no difference in RPE or pacing. Vaporized CBD-predominant cannabis did not differ from control in time-trial power or RPE.
limitations: Only 14 habitual users took part. Regulators required the control visit to come first, so conditions were not fully randomized; the authors note the highest time-trial power was in the control visit and argue any learning effect would, if anything, understate the THC effect. Blood cannabinoids, intoxication and hydration were not measured, inhalation technique was self-selected so the dose was not controlled, and there was no placebo or blinding. The findings cover one cycling time trial and do not show effects in non-users or in other sports.
practicalImplications: Staff working with athletes who use cannabis should ask about THC use and timing before hard training or competition, because this study found reduced sustained output after THC even in trained habitual users. The study measured no effect of CBD-predominant cannabis on time-trial power, but with 14 participants and one product it should not be read as proof that CBD is performance-neutral.
athleteDev: THC-containing cannabis reduced mean power in a 20-minute cycling time trial by about 5 to 8 percent, a decrement the authors judge larger than typical within-athlete variability. Staff should not assume THC use is performance-neutral for hard endurance efforts in habitual users. In this study, CBD-predominant inhalation did not change time-trial power or perceived exertion compared with control.
rtp: The study measured healthy, habitual cannabis users in a single laboratory session and does not address injury, concussion or clinical recovery. Its findings cannot be used to clear, time or medicate an athlete returning from injury.

citation: Pérez-Castilla A, García-Ramos A. Changes in the Load-Velocity Profile Following Power- and Strength-Oriented Resistance-Training Programs. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020 (ahead of print).
abstract: Thirty physically active men were randomly assigned to a power-oriented or a strength-oriented 4-week program of 8 sessions, and their individualized load-velocity profiles for squat and bench press were measured before and after. The authors report that the power group moderately increased velocity across the load spectrum, while the strength group changed little. They conclude that load-velocity profiles can be modified by a 4-week program and tend to be training specific.
tldr: A short power-oriented program shifted the squat load-velocity profile upward in physically active men, while a strength-oriented program did little. Group-by-time interactions were not significant, so the training-specific claim is suggestive rather than settled.
methods: Thirty physically active men (mean age 23 years, about 2.8 years of resistance training) were randomly assigned to two groups of 15 and trained twice weekly for 4 weeks. Velocity at 30, 60 and 90% 1RM was recorded with a linear transducer during an incremental Smith-machine test and modeled by linear regression, and the squat 1RM was estimated from the individual profile.
findings: In the power group, squat velocity rose at all three loads (effect sizes 0.70 to 0.93; +5.3%, +4.6% and +2.7% at 30, 60 and 90% 1RM), while the strength group showed effect sizes of 0.00 to 0.35; the time main effect was significant only at 60% and 90% 1RM for the squat. Bench-press time effects were not significant at any load; the power group's largest change was at 30% 1RM (effect size 0.67, 95% CI -0.05 to 1.39) and the strength group ranged from -0.33 to -0.06. Between-group effect sizes favored the power group (squat 0.54 to 0.63; bench press 0.25 to 0.53), but no group-by-time interaction was significant (squat P at least .07; bench press P at least .12).
limitations: No untrained control group, a single 4-week block, and squat 1RM estimated from a fixed velocity at 1RM of 0.33 m/s, which the authors say may have confounded results. The sample was physically active men rather than trained athletes, and the between-group effect sizes are not backed by significant interactions.
practicalImplications: Re-test the individual load-velocity profile periodically when prescribing loads by velocity, especially after a block of power-oriented or ballistic work, because the profile shifted in the power group. After a strength-focused block the profile changed little, but this was a single 4-week program.
athleteDev: Re-check the individual load-velocity profile during training blocks when prescribing by velocity, because in this study the squat profile shifted after 8 power-oriented sessions. The bench-press shift was small and uncertain, and strength-oriented work changed the profile little.
rtp: Not applicable: the study used physically active men with no injuries and measured no return-to-sport outcome, so it cannot inform return-to-sport loading.

citation: Wilk M, Krzysztofik M, Drozd M, Zajac A. Changes of Power Output and Velocity During Successive Sets of the Bench Press with Different Duration of Eccentric Movement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
abstract: Thirty-three strength-trained men performed three sets of one bench-press repetition at 70% 1RM with either a 2-second or a 6-second eccentric tempo, with 5 minutes between sets. Peak and mean power and bar velocity were compared across sets. The authors report that power rose across sets with the 2-second tempo and that peak power rose from set 1 to set 2 with the 6-second tempo, which they interpret as a post-activation potentiation effect.
tldr: Power rose over three bench-press sets at 70% 1RM when the eccentric phase lasted 2 seconds, while with a 6-second eccentric only peak power rose, and only on the second set. Without a control condition, the potentiation explanation remains a hypothesis.
methods: Randomized crossover laboratory study in which 33 men with at least one year of strength training completed sessions with a 2-second or 6-second eccentric tempo, one week apart. Each session had three sets of one repetition at 70% 1RM with 5 minutes of rest, and power and velocity were recorded with a linear position transducer and compared across sets by repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: With the 2-second eccentric tempo, peak power was 671.6 W in set 1, 702.3 W in set 2 and 713.1 W in set 3, and mean power rose from 467.7 to 480.1 to 492.2 W, with each later set reported higher than the earlier ones (P=.03 to .04, d=0.83 to 0.88). With the 6-second tempo, only peak power differed, with set 2 (587.9 W) higher than set 1 (565.7 W) and set 3 (563.1 W), and mean power did not change. The text reports no significant set-to-set difference in mean or peak bar velocity for either tempo.
limitations: No control or non-potentiating condition, a single 5-minute rest, one-repetition sets, and 1RM measured only at the 2-second tempo, as the authors acknowledge; the authors also say they cannot separate potentiation from stretch-shortening effects. The manuscript is internally inconsistent: Table 1 marks set 3 mean velocity as significant while the text says velocities did not differ, and the Discussion quotes peak velocities for the 2-second tempo (0.69, 0.70, 0.68 m/s) that match the 6-second tempo table (Table 1 shows 0.79, 0.82, 0.81). This is the accepted, uncopyedited manuscript.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend checking power in each set when stacking sets, because power changed across sets here. In this study the 2-second eccentric kept power rising across three sets at 70% 1RM, while the 6-second eccentric did not; the authors' conclusion that slow tempo may suit maximal strength and strength endurance was not tested.
athleteDev: For power-focused bench sessions at 70% 1RM, a 2-second eccentric kept power rising across three sets in this study, while a 6-second eccentric did not. Staff should check set-by-set power rather than assume a gain in one set carries into the next.
rtp: Not applicable: the study used healthy, strength-trained men performing single repetitions, with no injury or return-to-sport measures.

citation: Pradhan S, Parganiha A, Agashe CD, Pati AK. Circadian rhythm in sportspersons and athletic performance: A mini review. Chronobiol Int. 2024;41(2):137-181.
abstract: This mini review examines how circadian rhythms, chronotype, sleep, body temperature, hormones, light exposure and jet lag relate to peak athletic performance. The authors argue that training should be scheduled around each athlete's chronotype and peak time, while noting that some reports do not support this. The review is aimed at sport managers and policymakers.
tldr: Peak performance in athletes appears to vary with time of day and chronotype, and sleep loss, naps and jet lag also affect it. Treat the evidence as suggestive: the reviewed studies are small and some contradict one another.
methods: A narrative review of studies found by keyword searches of PubMed, Google Scholar and Scopus, covering roughly the last two decades. Original studies are tabulated with sample, method and outcome (Table 1), and reviews are listed with their main issues (Table 2). No inclusion criteria, screening steps or quality appraisal are described.
findings: The review reports that morning-type athletes often perform better in the morning and evening types in the evening, with one swimming study showing chronotype shifted peak performance time but not peak ability. Sleep deprivation is described as impairing reaction time, accuracy, submaximal strength, endurance, cognition and mood, and studies of roughly 30-minute naps after lunch or before training are cited as improving alertness and performance after sleep loss. Several cited studies place anaerobic power and jump performance highest between about 13:00 and 20:00, while the authors also cite studies that found no time-of-day effect.
limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected or appraised, and it reports some results from very small samples (for example 6 to 12 participants). The authors acknowledge that a few reports are inconsistent with their conclusions, but they do not resolve these disagreements, and several of the studies cited are not sports-specific.
practicalImplications: Ask athletes about chronotype and habitual sleep timing before setting session times, especially for skill-based work. Protect sleep before competition and consider a short nap after sleep loss, but do not assume a single best training time for all athletes or sports.
athleteDev: Chronotype and time-of-day effects may be worth considering when scheduling skill-based and high-intensity sessions. The evidence is mixed, so treat these as hypotheses to check against the athlete's own data rather than fixed training rules.
rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport timing. Its sleep and recovery material may be useful for general recovery planning, but it should not set return-to-play criteria.

citation: Shamji R, James SLJ, Botchu R, Khurniawan KA, Bhogal G, Rushton A. Association of the British Athletic Muscle Injury Classification and anatomic location with return to full training and reinjury following hamstring injury in elite football. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2021;7:e001010.
abstract: A retrospective cohort of 36 elite male footballers with 61 hamstring muscle injuries over eight seasons at one English club (Premier League, then Championship). Injuries extending into the intramuscular tendon (BAMIC c) were associated with a longer time to return to full training and a higher reinjury rate, and most biceps femoris reinjuries involved the distal musculotendinous junction.
tldr: In one elite football club, hamstring injuries that reached the intramuscular tendon on MRI took longer to return to full training and were reinjured more often. The study is small and retrospective, so it supports closer monitoring of these injuries rather than a fixed return timeline.
methods: Retrospective observational cohort using club medical records and MRI from all first-team male players with acute hamstring injuries. Two musculoskeletal radiologists graded injuries with the BAMIC and recorded location; time to return to full training (TRFT) and recurrence were compared using Kruskal-Wallis and Fisher's exact tests, with descriptive analysis of location.
findings: Of 61 injuries, 13 (21.3%) involved the intramuscular tendon (BAMIC c). These had a longer TRFT (mean rank 36 vs 24 days, p = 0.013) and higher reinjury (5 of 13, 38.5%, vs 12.5% without tendon involvement, p = 0.031). Overall reinjury was 16.4% (10 of 61, including 4 exacerbations), and the BAMIC-reinjury association across all grades was not significant (p = 0.083). Of the nine reinjuries to biceps femoris, five were at the distal third and distal tendon, involving both heads.
limitations: Single club, retrospective design and small subgroup numbers, with only three grade 3c injuries. Repeated injuries in 12 players breaks the independence assumption. Clinicians were not blinded to MRI findings. The text reports Kruskal-Wallis mean ranks as days, while the tables give medians (for example 2c median 37 days, range 8-103); the table values are the ones reported here. Only 1.5T MRI was used and the location pattern was not tested statistically.
practicalImplications: Where MRI shows intramuscular tendon involvement (BAMIC c), staff should expect a longer path to full training and plan closer reinjury monitoring. The distal biceps femoris pattern is worth noting in reinjury review but is not yet a validated decision rule.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance outcomes. Its only development relevance is for planning a player's return to training after hamstring injury, not for performance programming.
rtp: The findings can inform expectations for a player with tendon involvement on MRI, but they do not set a return date: the 2c group had a median of 37 days (range 8-103) to full training, while the three 3c injuries had a median of 15 days (range 9-63). Injuries not involving the tendon also reinjured in this cohort, and the study does not validate a return-to-play criterion.

citation: Bertozzi F, Fischer PD, Hutchison KA, Zago M, Sforza C, Monfort SM. Associations Between Cognitive Function and ACL Injury-Related Biomechanics: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2023;15(6):855-866.
abstract: A systematic review of six cross-sectional studies asking whether lower baseline cognitive function is associated with ACL injury-related knee and lower-limb biomechanics during cognitively challenging sport movements. Five studies found that worse cognitive performance was associated with higher-risk biomechanics (one of these also reported an opposite direction for one variable), and one found no interaction.
tldr: Across six small cross-sectional studies, athletes with weaker cognitive performance tended to show riskier knee and landing mechanics when a movement had an unexpected or dual-task demand. The evidence is associative and cannot yet be used to identify who will be injured.
methods: PRISMA-P-guided systematic review of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and SciELO (1990 to June 2021), with two reviewers screening independently. Six studies were included and scored with a modified Downs and Black checklist and ROBINS-I for risk of bias. Data were synthesised narratively by cognitive domain, task and biomechanical outcome.
findings: Six studies with 15 to 40 participants each (145 in total) were included. Five found worse cognitive performance associated with riskier biomechanics during cognitively challenging movements, although one of these (Giesche et al.) also found that more standing errors correlated with better working and short-term memory; the sixth (Fischer et al.) found no interaction. Herman and Barth's low-performing group had 31% higher peak vertical ground-reaction force and 4.8 degrees greater knee abduction angle than the high-performing group. Downs and Black scores were 10 to 15 of 17 and three studies had low risk of bias.
limitations: The studies are cross-sectional, so no injuries were tracked and causality cannot be inferred. Sample sizes are small, 22 different cognitive tests were used, and task designs varied widely. The authors note that publication bias may inflate effects and that cognitive measures were entered together in some models, which may have reduced their individual associations. Participants with recent injury or concussion were excluded.
practicalImplications: When assessing landing or cutting mechanics, consider testing with an unanticipated cue or a dual-task demand, because the review found movement patterns can change under cognitive load. Cognitive testing should not be used alone to decide who is at ACL risk on the basis of this review.
athleteDev: The review does not measure performance. It suggests that adding unanticipated or dual-task demands to cutting and landing drills is a plausible way to train athletes under the cognitive load of competition, but no training intervention was tested.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It excluded participants with recent injury or concussion and includes no return-to-play data, so cognitive or biomechanical findings from these studies should not be used to clear an athlete.

citation: Wilmes E, de Ruiter CJ, Bastiaansen BJC, Goedhart EA, Brink MS, van der Helm FCT, Savelsbergh GJP. Associations between Hamstring Fatigue and Sprint Kinematics during a Simulated Football (Soccer) Match. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021 (published ahead of print).
abstract: A within-subject study of ten amateur male footballers who completed a 90-minute simulated match protocol. Hamstring maximal voluntary torque, rate of torque development, EMG and 20 m sprint kinematics were measured before and after each 15-minute segment. Hamstring torque declined during the protocol, and the decline was associated with reduced knee angle at peak knee extension and an increase in peak combined hip-knee angle during sprinting.
tldr: After a 90-minute football simulation, amateur players lost about 14% of hamstring isometric strength and ran slower sprints, with changes in late-swing sprint kinematics that were linked to the loss of strength. Inertial sensors could capture these changes, but the link to injury risk is untested.
methods: Ten healthy amateur male footballers completed a familiarisation and an experimental session with the SAFT90 running protocol in six 15-minute segments. Before and after each segment, participants completed a 20 m sprint with five inertial sensors, then hamstring MVT and RTD tests on a dynamometer with EMG. Linear mixed models assessed time and half effects, and repeated-measures correlation assessed within-person associations between torque and kinematics.
findings: Hamstring MVT fell from 105.0 to 90.3 Nm across the protocol (about 14%, Table 1), and sprint time rose from 3.58 to 3.85 s (about 7.5%, Table 2). Knee angle at peak knee extension decreased between halves (mean -2.7 degrees, p < 0.001), and hip angle at peak hip flexion decreased within and between halves. MVT loss correlated with reduced knee angle at peak knee extension (R = 0.342) and with increased peak combined angle (R = -0.251). RTD showed no consistent fatigue effect on short time intervals.
limitations: Ten amateur players only, and the protocol included extra maximal sprints and strength tests that may have added fatigue. The within-half change in knee angle and the change in peak combined angle were not significant in the mixed models, so the conclusion about combined angle rests on the repeated-measures correlation. The abstract gives MVT reduction as 7.5% and sprint decline as 14.3%, which conflicts with the results and discussion (MVT about 14%, sprint time up 7.5%); the table values are reported here. About 150 of 480 RTD attempts were discarded for pre-tension or countermovement, and one or two participants showed within-person associations that contradicted the group result. No injury outcomes were collected.
practicalImplications: Inertial sensors on sprinting players can detect fatigue-related changes in hamstring-relevant kinematics, so they may be worth trialling for monitoring training load. The study does not establish thresholds for action, so these measures should not be used to make substitution or injury-risk decisions yet.
athleteDev: In these players, a football-specific 90-minute protocol reduced sprint performance and hamstring strength, which supports tracking sprint time and kinematics as fatigue markers during training. The sample is amateur, so the size of the effect in trained professional players may be smaller.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. Players with a hamstring injury in the previous 12 months were excluded, and the study has no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes, so these fatigue measures should not be used to clear an injured player.

citation: Bullard, L.E., Coffman, C.A., Kay, J.J.M., Holloway, J.P., Moore, R.D., Pontifex, M.B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder-Related Self-Reported Symptoms Are Associated With Elevated Concussion Symptomatology. Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology. 2022;44(2):116-126.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of 99 youths assessed during the subacute phase of concussion recovery. Inattentive ADHD symptoms, but not an ADHD diagnosis, were associated with more concussion symptoms and greater symptom severity on the SCAT5. The association was not explained by overlap between the two questionnaires or by a global executive function deficit.
tldr: In youths with concussion, parent-rated inattentive ADHD symptoms were linked to higher SCAT5 symptom reports, while an ADHD diagnosis alone was not. The link did not appear to be explained by item overlap or executive function.
methods: 99 participants (mean age 13.6 years; 45 female) were assessed 4 to 44 days after a physician-confirmed concussion at a pediatric sports medicine clinic. Parents or guardians, in consultation with participants, completed the ADHD-IV rating scale, the SCAT5 symptom inventory and the BRIEF executive function questionnaire. Hierarchical regression, cluster and factor analyses, and mediation analysis were used, adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, learning disorder, days since injury, loss of consciousness, prior concussions and ADHD medication.
findings: Inattentive ADHD-IV percentile was associated with more SCAT5 symptoms endorsed (B = 0.06, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]; R2 change = .073; p = .004) and greater symptom severity (B = 0.24, 95% CI [0.08, 0.40]; p = .003). ADHD diagnosis was not associated with symptom count (B = -1.62, p = .5) or severity (B = -4.90, p = .6), and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were not associated with either outcome. Cluster and factor analyses separated SCAT5 items from ADHD-IV items, and the BRIEF executive function composite did not significantly mediate either association.
limitations: The cross-sectional design had no preinjury baseline, and the authors note that ADHD-related comorbidities such as depression and anxiety may account for the association. Despite the 'self-reported' title, parents completed all three questionnaires in consultation with participants, and the mediation analyses were underpowered by the authors' own estimate. The results prose repeats the diagnosis coefficient (B = -1.62) for the inattentive symptom-count model, while Table 2 gives B = 0.06; the table value is reported here.
practicalImplications: When a clinician records a history of attention problems after concussion, parent-rated inattentive symptoms may add more information than a yes or no ADHD diagnosis. The authors suggest the nine inattentive items of the ADHD-IV could be used as a short subset, but this has not been tested against recovery outcomes.
athleteDev: This study does not address performance training or athlete development. It cannot show how attention profiles relate to training response or performance.
rtp: The study can inform how attention symptoms are considered when interpreting symptom reports in the subacute period after concussion. It cannot be used to set return-to-play timing, because recovery time was not measured and the design is cross-sectional.

citation: Evangelidis PE, Massey GJ, Pain MTG, Folland JP. Biceps Femoris Aponeurosis Size: A Potential Risk Factor for Strain Injury? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2015;47(7):1383-1389.
abstract: The biceps femoris long head (BFlh) proximal aponeurosis has been proposed as a hamstring strain risk factor because a small aponeurosis may concentrate strain in the surrounding muscle. In 30 healthy young men, the authors measured aponeurosis area and muscle size on MRI and isometric and eccentric knee flexor torque, and found that aponeurosis area was highly variable and unrelated to muscle size or strength.
tldr: Proximal aponeurosis size varied more than fourfold between healthy young men, but it did not track muscle size or knee flexor strength. The authors suggest a small aponeurosis could be an injury risk factor, which this study did not test.
methods: Thirty healthy, recreationally active men had MRI of the dominant thigh to measure BFlh proximal aponeurosis area, ACSAmax, volume and BFlh/ST tendon CSA. Isometric knee flexor torque was measured prone on a custom dynamometer at hip and knee angles of 40 and 30 degrees, and eccentric torque on an isokinetic dynamometer (hip at 60 degrees) at 50 and 350 degrees per second. Relationships were tested with Pearson correlations.
findings: Aponeurosis area ranged from 7.5 to 33.5 cm2 (mean 20.4 cm2, CV 26.6%) and was not related to BFlh ACSAmax (r = 0.04, P = 0.83). The aponeurosis/muscle area ratio ranged from 0.53 to 3.09. Aponeurosis area was not related to isometric (r = 0.28, P = 0.13) or eccentric torque (r = 0.24 at both velocities, P of 0.20 or greater). By contrast, BFlh ACSAmax was related to isometric torque (r = 0.42, P less than 0.05) and to eccentric torque (r = 0.44 at 50 degrees per second and r = 0.50 at 350 degrees per second, P less than 0.05 and 0.01).
limitations: Participants were healthy recreationally active men with no strength or power training, not athletes or injured players, and no injuries were recorded, so the proposed injury-risk link is untested. The knee axis was located by surface anatomy, and the authors assumed that in vivo knee flexor torque reflects BFlh force capacity. Eccentric data are from 29 participants.
practicalImplications: Coaches and clinicians should not yet screen athletes using aponeurosis size, because the study did not link it to hamstring injury. The finding that aponeurosis size varies widely between men of similar muscle size supports that the aponeurosis is a separate anatomical characteristic to consider in future prospective research.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not show that aponeurosis size changes with training or improves strength. Its relationship with knee flexor torque was absent, so it should not be used to set training loads or to predict strength gains.
rtp: Not applicable for return-to-sport decisions. The study used healthy participants without injury and did not assess rehabilitation, re-injury or post-injury aponeurosis size. Do not use the proposed injury-risk interpretation to clear or restrict an athlete.

citation: Lazarczuk SL, Collings TJ, Hams AH, Timmins RG, Opar DA, Edwards S, et al. Biceps femoris long head muscle and aponeurosis geometry in males with and without a history of hamstring strain injury. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34:e14619.
abstract: Narrow proximal biceps femoris long head (BFlh) aponeuroses and large muscle-to-aponeurosis width ratios are proposed to raise tissue strain and hamstring strain injury risk. In 26 recreationally active males with and without a recent unilateral hamstring strain injury, the authors compared BFlh muscle and aponeurosis geometry on MRI. Previously injured limbs had larger proximal aponeurosis volumes and smaller muscle-to-aponeurosis volume ratios than control limbs, but no differences from their uninjured contralateral limbs.
tldr: Recreational male athletes with a recent hamstring strain had a larger proximal BFlh aponeurosis volume and a smaller muscle-to-aponeurosis volume ratio than controls with no injury history. The difference was not seen against their own uninjured leg, and the cross-sectional design cannot show whether it preceded injury.
methods: Cross-sectional retrospective analysis of 3 T MRI from both thighs of 13 males with a unilateral hamstring strain in the previous 24 months (9 to the BFlh, 4 to the medial hamstrings) and 13 males without a history, pooled from three earlier data sets. Muscle and proximal aponeurosis cross-sectional area, length, volume and interface area were segmented manually by a blinded rater. Injured limbs were compared with contralateral limbs (Wilcoxon signed-rank) and control limbs (Mann-Whitney U), with statistical parametric mapping for regional differences along the tissue length.
findings: Previously injured limbs had larger proximal aponeurosis volumes than control limbs (P = .019, effect size 0.46, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.75) and smaller muscle-to-aponeurosis volume ratios (P = .029, effect size 0.43, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.73). No significant differences from uninjured contralateral limbs were found for these variables, and muscle volume, length and interface area did not differ between groups (P = .081 to 1.000 for the other comparisons). Aponeurosis and muscle volume were correlated in injured limbs (rho = 0.64, P = .022) but not in contralateral or control limbs. Regional SPM analysis found no group-by-limb interactions along the tissue length.
limitations: The retrospective design cannot show whether geometric differences preceded or followed injury. Participants came from three earlier studies with different MRI parameters and slice thickness, time from injury to MRI ranged from 2 to 24 months, rehabilitation length ranged from 1 to 24 weeks, the precise injury site was unknown, and 4 of 13 injuries were not to the BFlh (results were unchanged when only the 9 BFlh injuries were analysed). The sample was powered at 0.7 to detect d = 1.0, and only proximal aponeurosis geometry was analysed.
practicalImplications: Practitioners who measure hamstring structure should consider the whole muscle-tendon unit, not the aponeurosis alone. The finding should not yet be used to screen athletes for injury risk, because the authors note that prospective data are lacking and that the geometry may be a result of injury.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not measure strength, sprint performance or training response. It shows only a difference in tissue geometry between injured and uninjured limbs, so it should not be used to set training prescriptions.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: All injured participants had returned to pre-injury activity, and the study compared structure only, with no functional outcomes. It can inform the interpretation of imaging after hamstring injury but cannot establish whether the geometry predicts re-injury or should guide return-to-sport decisions.

citation: Miyamoto N, Yamazaki K, Iwasaki T, Mujika I, Yamashita D, Hirata K. Biceps femoris long head stiffens after 2 weeks of training cessation in highly trained sprinters. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2024.
abstract: Passive muscle stiffness has been proposed as a sprint-type hamstring strain risk factor, but the effect of short-term training cessation on it is unknown. In 28 male sprinters, the authors measured passive biceps femoris long head shear-wave speed by ultrasound elastography before and after 2 weeks of either training cessation or continued coach-prescribed training. Shear-wave speed increased after cessation and was unchanged with continued training.
tldr: Two weeks without training increased passive biceps femoris long head stiffness in sprinters, while continued training left it unchanged. The study does not show whether this change raises injury risk or affects performance.
methods: Twenty-eight male track-and-field sprinters were allocated (not randomised) to a training-cessation group (n = 14) or a training-continuation group (n = 14), matched on physical characteristics, event and performance level. The 2-week period began immediately after the last competition of the season. Passive BFlh shear-wave speed of the dominant leg was measured with ultrasound elastography with the hip at 70 degrees and knee fully extended, one day before and just after the 2 weeks, and analysed with a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t tests and an ANCOVA on post-intervention values.
findings: Pre-intervention values did not differ between groups (P = 0.606). In the cessation group, shear-wave speed increased from 4.75 +/- 0.77 to 5.00 +/- 0.88 m/s (P less than 0.001, Cohen d 0.305). In the continuation group it changed from 4.90 +/- 0.85 to 4.93 +/- 0.85 m/s (P = 0.521). The group-by-time interaction was significant (P less than 0.001, partial eta squared 0.399), and ANCOVA showed a higher post-intervention value in the cessation group (P less than 0.001).
limitations: Only males and only the dominant leg were studied, so the results may not apply to women or to the other leg. Intramuscular water content and glycogen were not controlled or measured, and only one 2-week period was tested. The authors note that the study did not assess the link between stiffness and injury incidence or sprint performance.
practicalImplications: Coaches managing a planned break or a return from illness or injury may consider that passive hamstring stiffness rose after 2 weeks of no training in this group. The authors suggest that the return to training should include work to restore muscle stiffness, but this study did not test a specific intervention.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Passive BFlh stiffness rose during 2 weeks off training in these sprinters. The authors suggest that explosive performance is likely to improve after short-term cessation, but they did not measure any performance outcome, so use this as a reason to monitor the return to training rather than as a measured effect.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study concerns athletes without injury and does not evaluate injured athletes, rehabilitation or return-to-sport testing. The stiffness change is not a validated criterion for clearance, and it cannot be used to judge hamstring readiness after injury.

citation: Astrella A, Iordanov D, De Caro D, Jiménez-Reyes P, Mendiguchia J. Biceps femoris muscle-tendon strain during an entire overground sprint acceleration: a biomechanical explanation for hamstring injuries in the acceleration phase. Sports Biomech. 2024.
abstract: Hamstring injuries are common in sprinting, and most occur during acceleration. The authors estimated peak muscle-tendon strain in the hamstring muscles across the first 16 steps of a 40 m overground sprint in 21 male semi-professional soccer players, using inertial motion capture and musculoskeletal modelling. Biceps femoris long head showed the largest peak strain, which decreased as speed increased and was linked to pelvic and hip angles.
tldr: In a 40 m sprint, the model-estimated peak strain in the biceps femoris long head was highest at the start and fell as speed increased, and it was linked to anterior pelvic tilt. The authors use this to propose a biomechanical reason for acceleration-phase hamstring injuries, but injuries were not measured.
methods: Twenty-one male semi-professional soccer players performed two maximal 40 m sprints on natural grass. Kinematics were recorded with 17 inertial sensors at 240 Hz (Xsens MVN), and the fastest trial per player was processed in OpenSim with a scaled 37-degree-of-freedom model driven by 80 Hill-type muscle-tendon units. Peak strain of the biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus was identified for each step up to step 16. Repeated-measures ANOVA, linear mixed-effects models and simple linear regression were used.
findings: Peak strain was 9.03 +/- 1.42% for the biceps femoris long head, 6.09 +/- 1.62% for the semitendinosus and 6.10 +/- 1.43% for the semimembranosus; the biceps femoris long head differed from both (P less than 0.001), and the other two did not differ (P = 0.974). Peak biceps femoris strain fell with step number (estimate -0.05 per step, P less than 0.001), and hip flexion (estimate 0.21) and knee flexion (estimate -0.11) predicted it (P less than 0.001). In the segment model only pelvis orientation was a significant predictor (estimate -0.05, P less than 0.001; femur P = 0.45), and a simple regression of the 16 step means gave r = -0.86 between anterior pelvic tilt and peak strain.
limitations: Muscle activation and force were not measured, so strain values are model estimates of whole muscle-tendon length change, and the authors note that fascicle behaviour would be more appropriate. The study was a single session in semi-professional players with no injury data, players with a past hamstring strain were not excluded, and the pelvic tilt correlation uses 16 step means rather than individual data. The reported negative sign for anterior pelvic tilt is not reconciled in the text with the authors' interpretation that greater anterior tilt raises strain.
practicalImplications: Coaches and clinicians designing acceleration drills or hamstring prevention work could consider how pelvic tilt and hip angle change the modelled strain demand in the biceps femoris long head during early steps. These are model-based relationships in healthy players, so they suggest topics to test rather than established rules for training prescription.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings describe how the modelled hamstring strain demand changes across acceleration steps, which may inform acceleration technique discussions. Speed or performance outcomes were not measured, so the study does not show that changing pelvic tilt improves sprinting.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study tested uninjured players and did not assess rehabilitation, hamstring capacity or re-injury. The modelled strain values cannot be used to clear an athlete for sprinting or to set return-to-sprint loads.

citation: Kibria F, Bragina OA, Trofimov AO, Bragin D. Bidirectional Interplay Between Traumatic Brain Injury and Cardiovascular Dysfunction in Athletes. J Clin Med. 2025;14:7712.
abstract: Sports-related traumatic brain injury may drive acute and chronic cardiovascular disease. The authors review epidemiological, clinical and mechanistic evidence on how brain injury affects cardiac structure and function and how cardiac disease affects brain outcomes, and they propose screening, rehabilitation and research priorities for athletes.
tldr: Concussion and other sport-related brain injuries are linked to autonomic imbalance, neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy and later cardiovascular risk, and cardiac disease can in turn affect the brain. The authors propose adding neuro-cardiac checks to athlete screening, but these proposals are not yet validated in trials.
methods: Narrative literature review. PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for brain injury or concussion combined with sport or athlete and cardiovascular terms. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and included studies were synthesised narratively across epidemiology, acute neurocardiac complications, chronic cardiovascular sequelae and reverse brain-heart interactions. Randomised, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and case series (3 or more participants) studies and animal models were eligible.
findings: The authors report that moderate-to-severe TBI carried up to a two-fold excess risk of hypertension, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction and stroke that persisted for at least a decade in larger population studies, and that higher lifetime concussion burden in former professional American-style football players was associated with a more atherogenic cardiometabolic profile and greater long-term stroke risk. They describe reduced heart rate variability and impaired baroreflex sensitivity weeks to months after concussion, and cite general (not athlete-specific) human cohorts in which 25 to 35% of patients with moderate-to-severe TBI developed QT prolongation, arrhythmia, wall motion abnormalities, troponin elevation or myocardial stunning.
limitations: The review does not include a formal limitations section, and it does not apply a risk-of-bias tool or PRISMA reporting. The authors note that the scarcity of robust clinical evidence precludes definitive conclusions. Human evidence is drawn partly from non-athlete TBI cohorts and animal models, and the review was limited to English-language studies found through two databases and reference lists.
practicalImplications: Staff managing athletes after concussion may consider cardiovascular symptoms and autonomic function alongside neurological recovery, since the review links brain injury to later cardiovascular risk. The proposed neuro-cardiac screening markers and HRV-guided return-to-play decisions are research proposals and are not yet validated in athletes.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The review links athletic brain injury to changes in cardiac and autonomic function, which could affect exercise capacity, but it does not measure or prescribe training load. Use it to inform monitoring after injury rather than as a basis for training prescriptions.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review supports assessing cardiovascular and autonomic status alongside neurological recovery after concussion. It proposes HRV-guided return-to-play decisions and graded aerobic exercise, but these are not validated. It should not be used alone to clear an athlete for return to play.

citation: Oberlohr V, Lengel H, Hambright WS, Whitney KE, Evans TA, Huard J. Biologics for Skeletal Muscle Healing: The Role of Senescence and Platelet-Based Treatment Modalities. Oper Tech Sports Med. 2020;00:150754.
abstract: This narrative review covers skeletal muscle repair, the role of cellular senescence in weaker regeneration with aging, and the current evidence for platelet-rich plasma and platelet-poor plasma in muscle healing. It concludes that clinical data on platelet-poor plasma are very limited and that the role of senescence in biologic treatment needs targeted study.
tldr: Muscle repair slows with age as satellite cells fail and senescent cells add pro-inflammatory and fibrotic signals. PRP has short-term clinical signals, but PPP has almost no in vivo or clinical testing, so neither is ready to guide routine muscle-injury care.
methods: Narrative review. The authors summarise 9 registered clinical trials (results posted for 4), 5 in vitro studies and 10 preclinical in vivo studies of PRP or PPP. The literature search is described only in general terms, with no databases, dates or screening criteria reported.
findings: Aging reduces satellite cell number and function, and senescent cells add inflammatory and fibrotic signals; the review also notes a possible protective role for early fibro-adipogenic progenitor senescence. In clinical trials, PRP was linked to short-term pain improvement where pain was reported (one of these was a temporomandibular disorder trial), and one trial in athletes with acute hamstring strain found faster return to play with PRP than PPP. In vitro, all 5 PRP studies reported increased myogenic proliferation, and none of the 10 preclinical studies used PPP as the investigational treatment.
limitations: The review is narrative, with no stated appraisal of study quality and no pooled analysis. Results were posted for only 4 of 9 registered trials, and most mechanistic evidence comes from cell and animal models that may not transfer to human muscle injury. The authors state that the studies used different treatments and outcomes, so no concise conclusion on PRP in skeletal muscle could be drawn.
practicalImplications: When discussing PRP for a muscle strain, tell athletes that most of the evidence comes from laboratory and animal work and from a few clinical trials of mixed design. Do not plan around PPP for muscle injury: none of the 10 preclinical studies used it as the investigational treatment, and only 2 registered clinical trials included it (one as the comparator to PRP). Treat the senescence-targeting and customized PRP ideas as future research rather than current practice.
athleteDev: The review does not address performance enhancement. Its athlete-relevant material is limited to injury recovery, so it cannot support using PRP or PPP to improve strength or training capacity in healthy athletes.
rtp: Use with caution. One trial in athletes with acute hamstring strain reported faster return to play with PRP than PPP, and a randomized trial in acute muscle tears reported faster return to play with PRP than no injection, although the review notes the difference was not significant at 2-year follow-up. These trials are few and varied, so they cannot set return-to-sport criteria or a PRP-based timeline.

citation: Wang D, Sun D, Gu Y. Biomechanical impact of soccer shoe outsole design on knee joint during cutting movements. Footwear Science. 2025;17(S1):S264-S265.
abstract: This conference abstract compares two soccer shoe outsole designs with 8 and 9 forefoot studs during sidestep cutting in 17 healthy male players. The 9-stud shoe gave more traction and higher knee valgus and internal rotation moments, while peak vertical ground reaction force did not differ.
tldr: In a small lab study, a soccer shoe with nine forefoot studs gave more traction and higher knee valgus and internal rotation moments during sidestep cutting than one with eight. The study is a short abstract that did not measure injury, so it cannot say whether this changes injury risk.
methods: Seventeen healthy male soccer players performed 45-degree dribbling sidestep cuts in two shoe conditions, presented in random order: 8 studs and 9 studs in the forefoot, with other shoe features reported as similar. Motion was captured with 12 Vicon cameras at 250 Hz, ground reaction forces with a Kistler force plate at 1000 Hz, and knee moments were modelled in Visual3D. Paired t-tests (alpha 0.05) compared the conditions.
findings: The 9-stud shoe (ATM2) had a higher dynamic traction coefficient than the 8-stud shoe (0.34 vs 0.27, p<0.05). Its knee valgus moment (0.98 vs 0.83 N·m·BW-1) and knee internal rotation moment (1.16 vs 0.79 N·m·BW-1) were also higher (both p<0.05). Peak vertical ground reaction force, knee varus, external rotation, flexion and extension moments did not differ significantly (Table 1).
limitations: The text is a two-page abstract, so effect sizes, participant characteristics, trial numbers and full methods are not reported. The abstract does not state outright which condition is ATM1 or ATM2; this record assumes ATM1 is the 8-stud shoe and ATM2 the 9-stud shoe, following the order the conditions are listed. The discussion says the 9-stud shoe had a larger effect on knee valgus, varus and rotation angles, but no angle values appear in the results or Table 1, and its claim that more studs improve stability was not measured.
practicalImplications: More forefoot studs appear to add traction, but in this sample they also raised knee valgus and internal rotation moments during sidestep cuts. Staff choosing stud layouts should weigh the traction gain against the knee load increase, and the authors advise players to consider their own needs and use scenarios. The study did not include injured players, so it does not show that either layout is safer for a player with a knee history.
athleteDev: A forefoot stud layout that adds traction may also raise knee loads during sidestep cuts. Judge stud configuration against the cutting demands of the player and surface, and check the trade-off on the player's own movement rather than by traction alone.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study tested healthy players only and did not measure injured knees or return-to-play outcomes, so it cannot inform footwear decisions after a knee injury.

citation: Windmueller RA, Gbayisomore OO, Mead RL, Desai MJ, Bowman EN. Brachial plexus injuries in the contact athlete: a narrative review. Annals of Joint. 2025;10:18.
abstract: Narrative review of brachial plexus injuries (BPIs) in contact athletes, from transient neuropraxia ('burners' or 'stingers') to neurotmesis. The review covers epidemiology, injury mechanisms, diagnosis, treatment and return to sport, based on an English-language literature search from inception to October 2024.
tldr: Most contact-athlete brachial plexus injuries are transient neuropraxias that resolve within minutes to hours. Symptoms lasting beyond 2 to 3 weeks warrant further evaluation for axonal injury.
methods: Narrative literature review, not systematic. Searches of PubMed, Cochrane Review and Google Scholar covered English-language sources from inception to October 2024, using key terms; three co-authors selected sources by consensus and reference lists were checked.
findings: Neuropraxia is common, with a 49% to 65% prevalence among career football players in cross-sectional studies. In a 2015 to 2019 NFL epidemiological study, the average single-season stinger risk was about 3.74%, and 76% of affected players missed no time. Repeated burners have been linked to a smaller Torg ratio, but no prospective or retrospective study shows that repeated burners increase the risk of axonal injury.
limitations: The review is narrative and has no reported quality appraisal, and the literature it draws on is weighted toward football and rugby in English-speaking countries. Severe injuries are covered mainly by small case series, and there are no randomized trials on rehabilitation, return to sport or prevention.
practicalImplications: For a contact athlete with a burner or stinger, the review supports concussion screening and checking for full return to neurologic baseline and pain-free neck and shoulder motion before return. Symptoms beyond about 2 weeks or recurrent burners call for further evaluation (EMG or nerve conduction, MRI or CT myelogram), and inability to hold the shoulder protracted or scapular winging should raise suspicion of root avulsion. Neck rolls and collars are empirically recommended in the absence of harm; lab studies show they reduce hyperextension but not passive lateral flexion.
athleteDev: The review gives no performance or training guidance. Its use for performance staff is in referral: arm weakness, burning pain or symptoms that persist beyond the expected window should go to medical staff, not be trained through.
rtp: Supports same-game or same-week return for typical neuropraxic burners once neurologic baseline and pain-free neck and shoulder motion are restored, after concussion evaluation. It cannot be used to set return dates for axonotmesis or neurotmesis, where timelines depend on injury grade and nerve regeneration of about 1 mm per day, and the review says return-to-sport outcomes need further study.

citation: Baumgarten KM, Sandhurst ES, Sun H. Can human growth hormone accelerate tendon and ligament injury recovery? Sports Health. 2024.
abstract: Basic science study of human tendon and ligament fibroblasts from 24 patients exposed to human growth hormone (HGH) in single-dose and sustained-dose models. HGH did not improve cell proliferation or collagen production in most conditions, and several doses reduced proliferation, so the authors do not support HGH for accelerating injury recovery.
tldr: In a cell culture study of human tendon and ligament fibroblasts, growth hormone did not increase cell growth or collagen production and reduced growth at several doses. This is laboratory evidence only and cannot show what happens to an injured athlete.
methods: Ligament fibroblasts were harvested from the ACL during knee arthroplasty (13 patients) and tendon fibroblasts from hamstring autograft excess during ACL reconstruction (11 patients). Cells were treated with HGH in a single-dose model and a sustained-dose model (re-dosed on days 2, 4 and 6), with MTS proliferation assays at days 4 and 7 and Picrosirius Red collagen staining at day 14. One-way ANOVA compared each dose with untreated controls, and the 100 ng/mL dose was re-tested with 18 treated wells against 6 controls.
findings: Single-dose HGH reduced day-7 ligament fibroblast proliferation at 100 pg/mL (90.9%, p<0.01), 1 ng/mL (89.7%), 1 µg/mL (90.4%) and 10 µg/mL (90.7%), and tendon fibroblast proliferation at 100 pg/mL (94.5%), 1 ng/mL (93.7%) and 10 ng/mL (96.7%, p=0.03). In the sustained model, ligament cells grew more at day 4 at 100 ng/mL (107.7%, p=0.03) and 10 µg/mL (104.6%, p<0.01), tendon cells grew less at day 4 at 1 µg/mL and 100 µg/mL, and no dose improved proliferation at day 7. When 100 ng/mL was re-tested with 18 treated wells, single-dose proliferation was not improved (ligament 96.1%, p=0.33; tendon 99.5%, p=0.63), sustained-dose proliferation was lower (ligament day 7, 95.1%, p<0.01; tendon day 4, 95.6%, p=0.03), and collagen production was similar or lower than controls, significantly so in ligament cells at 1 ng/mL (93.5%, p=0.05).
limitations: Cell culture cannot reproduce pulsatile pituitary release or systemic HGH effects, and the study tested only paracrine exposure. Donor cells came from patients of different ages and from two tissue sources, which the authors note as a confounder, and there was no tissue mechanical or in vivo outcome. The Methods give a dose range to 100 µg/mL while the Abstract gives 10 µg/mL, and the Abstract names 100 ng/mL as the only sustained-dose ligament concentration that was similar or better, although the Results also report a day-4 increase at 10 µg/mL (104.6%). Pfizer donated the HGH, and the sponsors had no stated role in design or reporting.
practicalImplications: Do not use this study to justify HGH for tendon or ligament injury recovery, and do not treat it as evidence that HGH slows healing either. The paper notes HGH is not FDA-approved for injury recovery, so staff should not plan rehabilitation or return timelines around it.
athleteDev: This in vitro work gives no basis for using HGH to improve tendon or ligament capacity or performance in athletes. Staff should base any recovery or performance plan on tested interventions rather than this cell study.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It used fibroblasts from non-athlete surgical patients in culture and measured no clinical healing, strength, or return-to-play outcomes.

citation: Malone S, Hughes B, Doran DA, Collins K, Gabbett TJ. Can the workload-injury relationship be moderated by improved strength, speed and repeated-sprint qualities? J Sci Med Sport. 2018.
abstract: Observational cohort study of 40 male amateur hurling players over two seasons, linking session-RPE workload, time-loss injuries and physical qualities (relative strength, 5- to 20-m sprint speed and repeated-sprint ability). Moderate weekly loads were linked to lower injury odds, large week-to-week load changes to higher odds, and stronger, faster and better repeated-sprint players to lower odds of injury at higher loads.
tldr: In 40 amateur hurling players over two seasons, moderate weekly loads carried lower injury odds, and players with greater strength, faster sprint times and better repeated-sprint ability tolerated higher loads with lower odds of injury. These are observational associations from one team, not tested causes.
methods: Observational cohort of 40 male amateur hurling players from one team over two seasons. Weekly training load was session-RPE multiplied by duration, with time-loss injuries (missed day or more) recorded. Relative lower-body strength was tested by 3RM trap-bar deadlift, sprint speed over 5, 10 and 20 m, and repeated-sprint ability (6 x 35 m, total time). Weekly load, ACWR, week-to-week change, and physical qualities were modelled against injury with polynomial regression, with odds ratios against quartile reference groups and VIF checks for multicollinearity.
findings: Moderate weekly loads of 1400 to 1900 AU had lower injury odds than loads of 1200 AU or less in the pre-season (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.66) and in-season (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.82). Large absolute week-to-week changes of 1000 AU or more had higher odds (pre-season OR 5.58, in-season OR 4.98). At weekly loads of 1750 AU or more, slower 5-m (OR 3.11), 10-m (OR 3.45) and 20-m (OR 3.12) times were linked to higher injury odds. For repeated-sprint total time at the same loads, the authors report an OR of 5.55 (95% CI 3.98 to 7.94) and describe better repeated-sprint players as at reduced risk. An ACWR of 0.90 to 1.30 was described as protective, and ACWR explained 60% of the variance in injury.
limitations: Single team, 40 players and 93 injuries, with no interaction test and no adjustment for previous injury, age, soreness, sleep or other factors the authors name. The Abstract gives height 184.2 cm and mass 82.6 ± 4.7 kg, while the Methods give 182.2 cm and 81.3 ± 3.7 kg; the Abstract's 5-m and 10-m confidence intervals differ from Table 2 (5-m 2.23 to 3.87, 10-m 2.71 to 4.12); and in Table 1 some odds ratios have confidence intervals that exclude 1 but p values above 0.4 (for example OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.29, p = 0.459). The repeated-sprint OR of 5.55 is reported beside a 'reduced risk' statement without a clearly stated reference group.
