practicalImplications: In this amateur squad, absolute week-to-week changes of 1000 AU or more and very low weekly loads (1200 AU or less) carried higher injury odds than moderate weekly loads of 1400 to 1900 AU, so these session-RPE bands are a starting point for flags only in similar squads. Strength, 5- to 20-m sprint and repeated-sprint testing can help identify players who had higher injury odds at high loads, but the study did not test whether improving these qualities lowers injury risk.
athleteDev: Use strength, sprint and repeated-sprint results to identify players who may tolerate high weekly loads or large load changes less well, and track weekly load changes alongside them. The authors' claim that improving these qualities will reduce injury risk was not tested, and the cut-offs are cohort-specific; the authors recommend testing the model in other teams and sports.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It models the risk of injury occurring in training and matches, not recovery from injury or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Thompson ES, Alcorn J, Neary JP. Cannabinoid Therapy in Athletics: A Review of Current Cannabis Research to Evaluate Potential Real-World Cannabinoid Applications in Sport. Sports Medicine. 2024.
abstract: This narrative review evaluates published cannabis research for its possible uses in athletes. It covers the endocannabinoid system, inflammation, pain and opioid-sparing effects, concussion, mental health, performance, product forms and administration routes, and regulation. The authors note that elite athletes are under-represented in cannabis research and that sport policies are inconsistent.
tldr: Athletes are turning to cannabinoids for inflammation, pain, sleep, concussion and mood, but the human athlete evidence is thin and inconsistent. Use this review to frame questions about product, dose and route, not as a case for use.
methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Medline, EMBASE, EBSCOhost, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar using keywords and subject headings, and also checked reference lists, meta-analyses and clinical trial registries. No inclusion criteria, screening process or quality appraisal are reported.
findings: Human results are mixed. In trained people, one 60 mg oral CBD study found lower myoglobin than placebo only in more advanced athletes, with no effect on creatine kinase, strength, power or endurance; another 150 mg CBD study found no effect on muscle damage markers, as the review reports them. A 10 mg THC edible had no ergogenic or ergolytic effect in habitually active adults, while inhaled THC impaired vigorous exercise performance in another trial and inhaled CBD without THC did not.
limitations: The narrative design gives no reproducible search strategy or quality appraisal, so the weight given to each study cannot be checked. Most of the mechanistic and anti-concussion evidence is preclinical or drawn from non-athlete populations, and the review describes the same 60 mg CBD trial inconsistently (the inflammation section says it reduced creatine kinase and myoglobin; the recovery section says only myoglobin fell, in advanced athletes, with no change in creatine kinase). The glossary has errors (for example, IL-2 is defined as interleukin-6 and GABA as G-protein coupled receptors).
practicalImplications: Staff should ask what product, cannabinoid content and dose an athlete uses, and whether it has third-party testing, because the review documents CBD products that contain THC or are mislabelled. Because the athlete evidence does not show a recovery or performance benefit, CBD should not be presented as a proven recovery aid, and athletes should check their league or testing body's rules first (WADA still bans THC but not CBD).
athleteDev: The review does not show a performance gain from cannabinoids. THC trials range from no effect to impaired vigorous exercise performance, and CBD trials show no clear change in strength, power or endurance. The review also notes, without testing it for CBD, that anti-inflammatory agents taken close to resistance training may blunt adaptation, so timing should be considered.
rtp: The review does not show that cannabinoids speed return to sport after injury or concussion. Its concussion and pain sections rest mainly on rodent, in vitro and mechanistic work, and the one cited human concussion study reported lower symptom burden in weeks 3 and 4 with no change in recovery time. It should not guide clearance, medication or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Singh J, Ellingson CJ, Ellingson CA, Scott P, Neary JP. Cardiac cycle timing and contractility following acute sport-related concussion. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Twelve varsity athletes were assessed within 5 days of a diagnosed sport-related concussion and compared with their own pre-season baseline. A non-invasive sternal sensor recorded one minute of supine cardiac cycle data. Systolic time decreased and atrial contractile force increased during the acute phase, while the other timing and contractility measures did not change significantly.
tldr: In 12 varsity athletes tested within 5 days of concussion, a one-minute resting sensor recording showed a shorter systolic time and higher atrial contractile force than their own baseline. The sample is small and uncontrolled, so this is a signal to watch, not a diagnostic marker.
methods: Within-subject comparison of 12 concussed athletes with their own pre-season baseline, using follow-up at 3 ± 1 days post-injury. A sensor placed over the sternum on a single adhesive ECG electrode recorded one minute of supine data, from which cardiac timing intervals and twist and atrial contractile force were derived. Paired changes were tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
findings: Median systolic time fell from 298 ms (IQR 42) at baseline to 276 ms (IQR 32) during the acute phase (p = 0.034). Median atrial systole force rose from 10 mG (IQR 6) to 13 mG (IQR 5) (p = 0.013). Heart rate, isovolumic times, diastole, twist force and the performance indices did not change significantly.
limitations: The study has no control group and only 12 athletes (3 female, 9 male). Thirteen variables were compared with no stated correction for multiple testing. The discussion proposes reduced stroke volume and cerebral perfusion changes, but neither was measured. The methods describe repeated follow-up visits, yet only acute-phase results are reported. The sensor maker, LLA Technologies, funded the work through a Mitacs grant and its proprietary algorithm extracted the cardiac features.
practicalImplications: This study alone does not show that a resting sensor recording can screen for cardiac problems after concussion, or that it would change return-to-play decisions. The authors argue for baseline cardiac testing in competitive athletes. Any change in an athlete should be read against that athlete's own baseline.
athleteDev: No performance outcomes were measured. The study can inform only how to read resting cardiac sensor data in an athlete who has had a concussion: compare the athlete with their own baseline.
rtp: The study cannot be used to set return-to-sport timing or clearance. It reports only the acute phase (within 5 days) and does not show whether the cardiac changes resolve, persist, or relate to symptoms.

citation: Adami PE, Koutlianos N, Baggish A, Bermon S, Cavarretta E, Deligiannis A, et al. Cardiovascular effects of doping substances, commonly prescribed medications and ergogenic aids in relation to sports: a position statement of the sport cardiology and exercise nucleus of the European Association of Preventive Cardiology. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 2022;29(3):559-575.
abstract: The use of substances and medications with potential cardiovascular effects among people practising sport and physical activity has increased in recent years. This position paper reviews recent literature and updates a 2006 statement on the adverse cardiovascular effects of doping substances, commonly prescribed medications and ergogenic aids in sport and exercise. The cardiovascular effect depends on the type of substance, the amount, the duration of use and the individual response.
tldr: A European cardiology position statement that reviews heart risks from doping agents, prescribed medicines and sports supplements. It documents the most serious heart harms for anabolic steroids, while for many legal supplements it lists the cardiovascular effects as unknown.
methods: Expert position statement by the EAPC sport cardiology and exercise section. The authors undertook a comprehensive review of published evidence and assessed pharmacology, cardiovascular mechanisms, effects on exercise performance and benefit-risk for each substance group. The text does not describe a search strategy or an evidence-grading system.
findings: Anabolic steroid users show increased cardiomyopathy and left ventricular dysfunction, and the statement estimates mortality 6 to 20 times higher than in clean athletes, with around 30% of these deaths attributed to cardiovascular causes. Stimulants, beta-2 agonists and clenbuterol are linked to arrhythmias, hypertension and tachycardia, and caffeine intakes above about 9 mg/kg raise side-effect risk. Energy drinks, ephedra-contaminated products and nicotine are linked to arrhythmias, vasoconstriction and hypertension, while creatine has no well-established cardiovascular effects but has case reports of thrombosis, atrial fibrillation and sudden death.
limitations: This is a narrative expert statement, not a systematic review, and its search and evidence-grading methods are not described. Many anabolic steroid studies are small, rely on self-reported dose and duration, and involve several substances at once, so effects cannot be attributed to a single agent. Several agents discussed, including SARMs, peptides, cobalt and gene doping, have little or no human cardiovascular data.
practicalImplications: The statement advises physicians to discuss substance and supplement risks openly with athletes, to recommend supplements only for a demonstrated need such as a deficiency, and to favour products from established manufacturers because contamination rates of 12% to 58% are reported. Athletes with established heart disease should consult a physician before using any supplement or ergogenic aid. Before prescribing beta-blockers or antiarrhythmics to an athlete, it advises maximal exercise testing before prescription and during up-titration, and a TUE may be needed in some sports.
athleteDev: The statement reports little or no performance evidence for growth hormone, inhaled beta-2 agonists and PDE5 inhibitors in normoxia, while anabolic steroids, blood doping and rhEPO show gains in small controlled trials alongside serious cardiovascular risk. Among legal supplements it lists caffeine, creatine, carbohydrate, beta-alanine, bicarbonate, nitrate and protein as having reliable performance evidence, and notes that caffeine side effects become more common above about 9 mg/kg.
rtp: The statement does not set return-to-sport criteria. For returning athletes, its relevant points are that anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs raise bleeding risk in contact and collision sports, and that athletes with established heart disease should consult a physician before resuming supplements or ergogenic aids.

citation: Hakkaku T, Nakazato K, Koyama K, Kouzaki K, Hiranuma K. Cervical Intervertebral Disc Degeneration and Low Cervical Extension Independently Associated With a History of Stinger Syndrome. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;5(11):2325967117735830.
abstract: This cross-sectional study examined whether cervical intervertebral disc degeneration (CIDD) and neck function are related to a history of stinger syndrome in Japanese collegiate football players. Forty-nine players were divided into stinger and control groups, and CIDD was assessed by T2-weighted MRI, with range of motion and isometric strength also measured. CIDD was more common in the stinger group, and cervical extension range of motion was lower, and both were independently associated with stinger history in logistic regression.
tldr: In 49 collegiate football players, a stinger in the past year was linked to disc degeneration on MRI and to reduced neck extension range. The design is cross-sectional, so these are associations and not predictors of future stingers.
methods: Cross-sectional study of 49 male first-division collegiate football players. Stinger syndrome was identified by questionnaire, interview and health record review, and players were grouped into stinger (n=19) and control (n=30). Five cervical discs (C2/C3 to C6/C7) were scored on T2-weighted MRI by two blinded spine surgeons, and neck range of motion (goniometer) and handheld dynamometer strength were measured after the season. Group differences were tested with t tests and chi-square, and logistic regression was used for adjusted associations.
findings: CIDD was seen in 13 of 19 players with stinger history (68%) and 9 of 30 controls (30%), P < .01, and 14 of 23 defensive players versus 5 of 26 offensive players had stingers. Cervical extension range was lower in the stinger group (50.9 vs 60.2 degrees, P < .01, d = 0.83), and neck isometric strength did not differ. In logistic regression, CIDD (adjusted OR 5.58, 95% CI 1.43 to 21.76) and extension range (adjusted OR 0.93 per degree, 95% CI 0.87 to 0.99) were independently associated with stinger history.
limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot show causality, and only 49 players (19 with stinger history) were studied. Stinger history depends on questionnaire, interview and records, and neck function was measured after the season, not before the stingers occurred. Table 7 gives the crude OR for CIDD as 5.06 with a 95% CI of 1.46 to 5.06, where the upper limit equals the estimate, so this entry looks wrong. The methods say 'lumbar disc degeneration was graded' with the Pfirrmann scale, which appears to be a labelling slip since the discussion states the lumbar scale was applied to cervical discs, and MRI used a low-field 0.3-T unit.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that pre-season checks include neck extension range and MRI or physical examination, since both features were linked to stinger history. If reduced extension range or disc degeneration is found, the authors suggest coaching a head-up tackling technique, but this study does not show that doing so prevents stingers. Neck strength testing alone did not separate the groups, so it should not be relied on for screening.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance. Its findings concern neck injury history and neck function, so it cannot be used to judge playing ability.
rtp: The study does not address return to play. It is cross-sectional, so it cannot show whether low extension range or disc degeneration predicts recurrent stingers or affects the timing of a return to play.

citation: Wiacek M, Trąbka B, Tomasiuk R, Zubrzycki IZ. Changes in Health-Related Parameters Associated with Sports Performance Enhancement Drugs. Int J Sports Med. 2022.
abstract: Eight male bodybuilders were measured monthly over a six-month competition preparation that included self-administered anabolic steroids, growth hormone, fat-burning drugs and other agents. Lipids, liver enzymes, bilirubin, urea and body composition were compared with a NHANES-based reference sample. The authors conclude that the drugs had no immediate detrimental impact on the parameters studied, while acknowledging the small sample and unverified drug quality.
tldr: In eight drug-using bodybuilders, AST, ALT, bilirubin and BUN were higher and HDL-C lower than in the reference sample during a six-month preparation, although the authors judge most values physiologically acceptable. The study is too small and uncontrolled to show long-term safety.
methods: Analysis of competitor medical notes and monthly fasting blood tests and DXA body composition in eight male bodybuilders (age 30 to 35, 97 to 110 kg) who self-administered drugs during 6 months of preparation. Values were compared with 100 NHANES men aged 30 to 35 using Welch ANOVA over time and Games-Howell post hoc tests.
findings: Body mass rose from about 105 to 109 kg and body fat fell over the preparation. Table 2 (column labeled Month 1) marks total cholesterol (4.15 vs 5.17 mmol/L), HDL-C (0.52 vs 1.18 mmol/L), AST (1.60 vs 0.45 µkat/L), ALT (1.99 vs 0.53 µkat/L), bilirubin (6.83 vs 4.63 µmol/L), BUN (8.29 vs 4.8 mmol/L) and body fat (7.62% vs 26.56%) as different from the reference sample, while TG and LDL-C were not marked. The authors describe AST and ALT as in the high range throughout, BUN moving between desirable and high, and mean BMD of 1.34 vs 1.44 g/cm2 in the first and sixth months without a statistical test.
limitations: Eight men, no untreated control, unverified drug quality, dosing given as ranges, and a general-population NHANES reference rather than matched athletes. The text is internally inconsistent: the Results say all parameters except LDL-C were in normal ranges while later sections place AST and ALT in the high range and BUN in the high range, the TG section states no significant TC difference although Table 2 and the TC section report one, and Table 2 is labeled Month 1 while presented as the overall comparison. The BMD change rests on two time points with no test.
practicalImplications: In this group the markers that sat furthest from reference values were AST, ALT, HDL-C and BUN, so these are the ones the data flag for athletes known to use these drugs. The study does not show the drugs are safe, and the authors state long-term effects are not established, so it should not be used to reassure athletes about risk.
athleteDev: The study has no direct training application because it describes health markers during drug-assisted preparation rather than training effects. Performance staff should not read the body mass or body fat changes as a training response, since drug use, diet and training were not separated.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport or clearance decisions: there were no injured athletes and no function or return outcomes. The conclusion of no immediate harm should not be used as a clearance standard for athletes with a drug-use history.

citation: Alonso-Fernandez D, Docampo-Blanco P, Martinez-Fernandez J. Changes in muscle architecture of biceps femoris induced by eccentric strength training with nordic hamstring exercise. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2017;1-7.
abstract: This single-group study followed 23 recreational men through 8 weeks of nordic hamstring exercise and 4 weeks of detraining, measuring biceps femoris long head architecture by 2D ultrasound at three time points. Fascicle length increased and pennation angle decreased after training, and both moved back toward baseline after detraining. The authors conclude that NHE changes this muscle's architecture in ways that may matter for injury prevention and rehabilitation.
tldr: Eight weeks of nordic hamstring exercise lengthened biceps femoris fascicles and lowered pennation angle in recreational men, and four weeks off partly reversed these changes. Architecture is a structural marker, so the study does not show fewer injuries.
methods: Twenty-three men with no lower-limb injury in the prior 12 months completed baseline testing, 8 weeks of progressive NHE (2 to 3 sessions per week, 10 to 20 minutes each), and 4 weeks of detraining. Fascicle length, relative fascicle length, muscle thickness and pennation angle were measured at rest by 2D B-mode ultrasound and compared across time with one-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.
findings: Fascicle length rose from 8.17 to 10.12 cm by week 9 (+23.9%, d=2.28, P<.001) and fell to 8.90 cm by week 13 (P<.001 vs week 9). Pennation angle fell from 14.74 to 12.55 degrees (-14.8%, P<.001) and rose to 13.71 degrees after detraining, while muscle thickness rose from 2.09 to 2.25 cm (+7.7%, P<.001) and returned to 2.10 cm (P<.05 vs week 9).
limitations: No control group, so changes could partly reflect repeated testing or time, and fascicle length depends on an estimation equation whose reliability was tested in 12 people. The Table 3 caption labels the values as mean±SEM, but the spread (for example 8.17±1.83 cm) looks like SD for n=23, so check dispersion before quoting.
practicalImplications: Partner-assisted NHE, needing no equipment beyond a partner holding the heels, changed fascicle length and pennation angle in recreational men within 8 weeks. Because these changes partly reversed within 4 weeks off eccentric work, the authors suggest continued exposure is needed to keep them.
athleteDev: NHE is an accessible eccentric hamstring stimulus, and this protocol used 2 to 3 sessions per week of 10 to 20 minutes. The study did not measure strength, speed or sprint performance, so it shows no performance benefit.
rtp: The study cannot serve as a return-to-sport standard because it had no injured athletes and no function or reinjury measures. The authors' suggestion that architectural change may help rehabilitation is untested in this sample.

citation: Nielsen LB, Svensson RB, Fredskild NU, Mertz KH, Magnusson SP, Kjaer M, et al. Chronic changes in muscle architecture and aponeurosis structure following calf muscle strain injuries. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;1-13.
abstract: Ten people with a previous chronic calf strain had their medial gastrocnemius studied with dynamic ultrasound and EMG, comparing the injured and uninjured calf. The injured distal muscle showed a larger pennation angle increase during contraction, shorter fascicles, a curved fascicle shape, a thicker aponeurosis and higher relative soleus activity. The authors conclude that some distal fibers may not be actively engaged after a strain injury and that the aponeurosis changes are long-lasting.
tldr: Long after a calf strain, the injured medial gastrocnemius showed steeper, curved fascicles during contraction and a thicker aponeurosis than the uninjured side. The study is small and cross-sectional, so it describes the injured calf rather than proving permanent change.
methods: Ten participants with chronic calf strain injuries (3 women, 7 men) had 2D ultrasound of the medial gastrocnemius at three ankle angles and during unilateral heel rise, with fascicle length and pennation angle measured by an automated tracking macro, plus EMG of the gastrocnemius and soleus. Injured and uninjured sides were compared with repeated-measures mixed models and paired t-tests.
findings: At the most distal fascicle, pennation angle rose 18.9 degrees from relaxed to peak contraction on the injured side and 6.6 degrees on the uninjured side (difference 12.4 degrees, P=.01), with a similar pattern at the next fascicle (difference 12.1 degrees, P=.005). Fascicles were shorter on the injured side at the central distal site on still images (11.0 mm, P=.004) and at the most distal fascicle on video (11.9 mm, P=.009), and the aponeurosis was thicker on the injured side distally (5.9 mm, P=.0003) and at mid-belly sites in six participants (3.1 to 3.5 mm, P=.04). Soleus EMG during heel rise was higher on the injured side (P=.02) and the soleus-to-gastrocnemius ratio was higher (P=.04), while gastrocnemius EMG and MVC strength did not differ.
limitations: No healthy control group, only 10 participants (six for mid-belly video), and time since injury that varied widely (mean 47 months, SD 25). The Discussion calls the changes possibly permanent, but one cross-sectional visit cannot show that, the linear fascicle estimate underestimates the curved injured fascicles, and EMG electrodes sat at mid-belly rather than the injured distal site.
practicalImplications: Long-standing calf strains may leave altered muscle and aponeurosis structure, so rehabilitation planning should not assume full structural recovery once the injury has settled. This is a hypothesis from one cross-sectional study and has not been tested in a trial.
athleteDev: This study has no training application: it measured calf structure and muscle activity in people with long-standing strains and tested no training intervention. The authors note it is unknown whether eccentric training would lengthen the distal fascicles of the injured muscle.
rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions: no function, strength or reinjury outcome was measured, and the injuries were years old. The proposed link between altered fascicles and reinjury risk is the authors' hypothesis.

citation: Fontanier V, Bruchard A, Tremblay M, Mohammed R, da Silva-Oolup S, Suri-Chilana M, et al. Classification of myo-connective tissue injuries for severity grading and return to play prediction: a scoping review. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
abstract: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review searched Medline and SPORTDiscus from 2010 to April 2022 for classifications of acute non-contact muscle injuries in sporting adults. From 13,426 records, 37 studies were included, identifying 24 classifications, most developed for hamstring or lower-limb injuries. Time to return to play was the most reported outcome, and the authors conclude that the evidence is inconsistent and that classifications are not sufficient to predict return to play.
tldr: Muscle injury grading systems such as BAMIC, modified Peetrons, Munich and Cohen are widely used, but evidence that their grades predict return-to-play time is weak and inconsistent. Use them to describe injuries and to communicate with the medical team, not to set an individual return date.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR. Medline (PubMed) and SPORTDiscus were searched from 1 January 2010 to 19 April 2022 using MeSH and free-text terms for muscle injury and classification. Included studies were English-language, peer-reviewed, in sporting adults aged 18 or older with acute non-contact muscle or tendon injury, and reported a severity grading applicable to prognosis. Pairs of reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts, one reviewer extracted data and a second verified it, and findings were synthesized qualitatively.
findings: Of 37 included studies, 24 classifications with reported outcomes were identified, and the six most cited (BAMIC, modified Peetrons, Munich, Cohen, Chan and MLG-R) accounted for 70% of reports. Time to return to play was reported in 86% of studies; higher grades were linked to longer return times in reports for BAMIC (n = 12), modified Peetrons (n = 6), Munich (n = 6) and Cohen (n = 5), but the authors' Table 4 rates the evidence as conflicting for modified Peetrons and Cohen, and correlations appeared driven by extreme grades with limited value for intermediate grades. Good interrater reliability was reported for four classifications (kappa 0.80 to 1.00 for BAMIC, modified Peetrons and Chan; 0.82 to 1.00 for Munich), and validity was not reported for any classification.
limitations: As a scoping review it did not critically appraise included studies, and the evidence is mostly low level. Only classifications with prognostic or return-to-play outcomes were included, so findings cannot be generalized to other muscle classifications. This copy is an accepted pre-proof without volume or page numbers, so the citation should be checked against the version of record.
practicalImplications: Use a classification grade as one piece of information, since the authors conclude that classifications may help decision-making but are not accurate enough to predict time to return to play. When recording a muscle injury, state the classification and the return-to-play definition used (daily activity, training or competition), because the review shows these definitions vary widely.
athleteDev: Performance staff who track injury severity should use the same grading system and return-to-play definition across seasons so that data are comparable. The paper does not study performance outcomes, so its relevance here is limited to injury data quality.
rtp: This review is directly relevant to return to play, but it does not set return dates or criteria. It supports using BAMIC, modified Peetrons, Munich and Cohen grades as descriptive tools with an inconsistent link to return time, notes that intermediate grades have limited prognostic value, and shows that validity was not reported for any classification. The authors call for a systematic review of evidence-based return-to-play criteria.

citation: Tampere T, Victor J, Luyckx T, Vermue H, Arnout N, Witvrouw E, et al. Biceps Femoris Compensates for Semitendinosus After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction With a Hamstring Autograft: A Muscle Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study in Male Soccer Players. Am J Sports Med. 2021.
abstract: After ACL reconstruction (ACLR) with a semitendinosus (ST) autograft, male soccer players may have altered hamstring activation. The authors compared exercise-induced T2 shifts on muscle functional MRI between ACLR players and healthy controls, and between operated and contralateral legs, after a prone leg-curl. The biceps femoris long head (BF) showed greater relative activity and the ST less activity in the ACLR group.
tldr: After ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft, cleared male soccer players used more biceps femoris and less semitendinosus during a prone leg-curl than healthy controls. The authors interpret this as BF partly compensating for ST, a pattern that needs confirmation with running or kicking tasks.
methods: Male soccer players aged 18 to 35 years, cleared for return to play after ST-autograft ACLR (RTP at a mean of 10 months), were compared with healthy controls. Muscle functional MRI (3.0 T, CPMG T2 mapping) was taken before and after a standardized prone leg-curl with 5 kg ankle weights to a Borg score of 20 or loss of motor control. Relative T2 shifts were compared between groups and between operated and contralateral legs, with proportional values normalised to total posterior thigh activity.
findings: Analysed sample: 23 ACLR players and 29 controls. The BF T2 shift was higher in the ACLR group (13.92% vs 8.48%, mean difference 5.44%, P = .003, Cohen d 1.0), and the ST was lower (19.97% vs 25.32%, P = .049). Within the ACLR group, the operated leg showed higher BF (14.54% vs 11.63%, P less than .001) and SM (15.64% vs 13.54%, P = .014) shifts and lower ST shifts (17.31% vs 22.37%, P less than .001) than the contralateral leg. No group differences were found for the gracilis, the SM between groups, total posterior thigh activity or number of leg curls.
limitations: The abstract states that 30 ACLR players and 30 controls were allocated, but results are reported for 23 ACLR players and 29 controls (52 of 60) after scan irregularities and participant exclusions. The authors list multiple surgeons (trained by one senior surgeon, standardized harvest), a limited sample despite an a priori power analysis, male players only at regional and national level, a prone leg-curl that differs from high-speed running, an exercise endpoint based on subjective exertion, and imaging of the long head of biceps only. Many ACLR players also had additional procedures (lateral extra-articular tenodesis in 18, meniscal surgery in 8).
practicalImplications: Clinicians treating ACLR players with a hamstring graft may consider muscle-belly-specific assessment of hamstring activation under eccentric load, as the authors suggest, rather than relying on isokinetic strength alone. The study does not establish that training the ST or BF changes outcomes, so any such programme should be justified by its own evidence.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The findings are limited to hamstring activation during a single prone leg-curl in male soccer players after ACLR. They do not test sprinting, kicking or performance outcomes, so they should not be used to set training prescriptions for performance.
rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study includes players cleared for return to play, about 10 months after surgery, and it supports examining hamstring activation patterns before clearance. It does not show that the pattern predicts re-injury or return to pre-injury performance, so it cannot be used alone as a clearance criterion.

citation: Fontanet R, Donat R, Carballeira E. Blood Flow Restriction Training Prior to and After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Scoping Review. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10:450.
abstract: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review of 15 randomized and quasi-randomized trials (417 patients) examines blood flow restriction resistance training before and after ACL reconstruction. Across the included studies, BFR-RT was generally at least as effective as comparison training for strength, muscle size, function and knee pain, and no endurance BFR studies were found.
tldr: Blood flow restriction resistance training before and after ACL reconstruction was at least as effective as comparison training in most of the trials reviewed. The trials are small with mixed quality and no standard BFR protocol, so the authors present it as an interim step rather than a settled standard.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, registered on OSF in April 2024. Six databases (Web of Science, PEDro, Scopus, PubMed, SportDiscus, Cochrane) were searched to 24 September 2025, with citation chasing and grey literature. Eligible studies were RCTs or quasi-RCTs of BFR combined with resistance or endurance exercise in ACL reconstruction patients with autografts. Quality was rated with PEDro, and exercise reporting with CERT; quantitative synthesis was judged not feasible.
findings: Fifteen studies were included, with 417 patients. 2 of 5 preoperative and 5 of 9 postoperative studies reported superior BFR-RT outcomes, and the rest reported comparable outcomes. Reported BFR-RT benefits included muscle size, strength, endurance, knee pain, self-report scores and lower serum Atrogin-1 and MuRF1 in one study, and one trial found return to sport 1.4 months sooner with low-load BFR than low-load training alone. Low-load BFR gave a faster reduction in knee pain than heavy-load training in three trials, but caused more pain during training in one.
limitations: The review is a scoping map with no pooled effect size, and data could not be extracted from several studies. PEDro scores were modest (median 6.87, IQR 6-8), and most studies did not blind participants or therapists. The conclusions state that preoperative BFR-RT significantly increased strength and endurance compared with low-load training, while the discussion reports superior outcomes in only 2 of 5 preoperative studies, so the conclusions read more strongly than the study-level results; the pain-during-training finding is also described as knee pain in the discussion but muscle pain in the results.
practicalImplications: BFR resistance training is a reasonable option for limiting quadriceps loss or managing knee pain before and after ACL reconstruction, particularly when heavy loads are poorly tolerated or weight bearing is limited. Set cuff pressure relative to measured limb occlusion pressure and prefer supervised sessions, since unsupervised home-based protocols generally showed less significant improvements. Expect results comparable to heavy-load training in most trials rather than clear superiority, and screen for thromboembolism risk, as the included trials largely excluded high-risk patients.
athleteDev: BFR resistance training may help maintain or rebuild lower-limb strength and muscle size with lighter loads in athletes rehabilitating an ACL. The evidence comes from ACL reconstruction patients rather than athletes training for performance, so it does not show a performance gain.
rtp: The review supports BFR resistance training as an add-on in early ACL rehabilitation, including when weight bearing is limited. Return-to-activity time was reported in only two trials: one found return to sport 1.4 months sooner with low-load BFR than low-load training, and the other found no difference between BFR with heavy loads and heavy-load training alone. Reinjury and long-term function were not studied, so it cannot set return-to-sport criteria or timelines.

citation: Pagan-Rosado R, Troyer W, Rosario-Concepcion R, Feaster B, Encalada S, Kindle B, et al. Calf strains in athletes: a narrative review of management, injury grading, and return to sport. Sports Med Open. 2025;11:158.
abstract: Narrative review of imaging and injury grading as predictors of return to sport after calf strains in athletes. Eleven included studies, mainly retrospective, suggest that ultrasound and MRI give useful information on injury severity and recovery time, that different grading systems correlate with outcomes, and that no single modality or grading system is clearly superior.
tldr: Ultrasound and MRI help grade calf strains and give a rough sense of recovery time, but no imaging grade reliably decides return to play. Clinical assessment remains the basis of return-to-play decisions, with imaging as a supplement.
methods: Self-described narrative review following the SANRA guideline, with selected PRISMA 2020 elements and a librarian-designed Boolean search of PubMed and Scopus. Thirty-one articles were retrieved and 11 met the inclusion criteria (human calf muscle injuries, MRI or ultrasound grading, and return-to-play outcomes). Screening was done by four investigators, and no risk-of-bias or certainty-of-evidence grading was performed.
findings: The review text gives an overall return-to-play range of 2 to 102 days with a mean of 39 ± 18 days, but Table 2 attributes the 2 to 102 day range to Green et al. (index injuries, Australian football) and the 39 ± 18 day mean to Pedret et al. (medial gastrocnemius tears). In Australian football players, injuries with no, mild and severe aponeurotic disruption took a mean of 19.4, 26.7 and 31.3 days to return to play, and in Premiership rugby players myofascial-interface injuries returned to full training in a mean of 20.1 days versus 46.8 days for tendon or aponeurosis injuries (p = 0.02). The authors state that no specific imaging factor has been linked to return to play, and that the classifications studied correlated with return-to-play time without one being clearly superior.
limitations: Most included studies were retrospective, study sizes ranged from 10 to 184 injuries, and seven of eleven studies had fewer than 50 injuries with complete imaging data. Imaging protocols and return-to-play definitions varied, and only two studies assessed interobserver reliability, which was fair to moderate. The text has internal conflicts: the search date (June 2024 in the Abstract, 10 October 2025 in the Methods), the number of MRI studies (eight in the Discussion, nine in the Limitations), the source of the 2 to 102 day and 39 day figures, and the Key Points' return-to-play range of 2 to 12 weeks.
practicalImplications: Use MRI or ultrasound to grade a calf strain and to flag features such as aponeurotic disruption or asynchronous gastrocnemius-soleus movement, which were linked to longer recovery in the included studies. Do not set a return date from the imaging grade alone, since the authors conclude that imaging should supplement the clinical examination.
athleteDev: Use imaging grade and location as context for expected time loss when planning a calf-strain return, and avoid treating a single grade as a fixed return date. The studies come mainly from professional football and rugby, so the timelines may not transfer to other sports or to recreational athletes.
rtp: This review is directly about return to sport, but it cannot support a clearance decision by itself. The authors state that clinical examination (absence of palpation pain, calf strength and sport-specific activity without symptoms) remains the gold standard, with imaging used to support those decisions.

citation: McAllister TW, Broglio SP, Katz BP, Perkins SM, LaPradd M, Zhou W, et al. Characteristics and Outcomes of Athletes With Slow Recovery From Sports-Related Concussion: A CARE Consortium Study. Neurology. 2023;100(14):e1510-e1519.
abstract: This prospective multisite study followed 1,751 concussed collegiate athletes and defined slow recovery as taking at least 14 days to become asymptomatic or 24 days to return to play, slower than about 80% of peers. Slow recovery applied to 399 athletes (22.8%), who were more often female and had higher early symptom burden than typical recoverers. The authors conclude that most slow recoverers returned to play within months, which they present as a reassuring prognosis.
tldr: About one in five concussed collegiate athletes recovered slowly, and most of those returned to play within about two months. Sex and early symptom scores did not predict return among slow recoverers, and about 1 in 10 had not returned by 6 months.
methods: Prospective observational cohort at 26 civilian universities and four service academies, with baseline testing, daily symptom reports for 14 days, and assessments at five postinjury points through 6 months. Slow recovery was defined by time to the asymptomatic point and to return to play, analyzed with Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models.
findings: Slow-recovery athletes were more often female (41.1% vs 35.6%, P=.05), reported more prior concussions (0.72 vs 0.59, P=.03), had higher postinjury SCAT symptom scores (36.6 vs 25.4, P<.001), worse postinjury SAC and BESS scores, lower compliance with daily symptom checks in the first 14 days (48.8% vs 67.9%), and were more often injured in practice (70.7% vs 65.1%, P=.04). In the slow group, median return to play was 34.7 days, with 77.6% returned by 60 days and 83.4% by 88 days, and 10.6% (2.4% of the whole cohort) had not returned by 180 days. Within the slow group no candidate predictor reached P<.05; prior concussion history was borderline (HR 0.90, P=.05) and all C-statistics were 0.49 to 0.53.
limitations: The slow group is defined by cut-offs taken from the cohort's own timing distribution, 73 athletes were censored, and missing dates were imputed for 292 athletes. Nearly half the slow group's postinjury BSI values were missing (46%), and results apply only to collegiate varsity athletes and cadets. The text has internal inconsistencies: the abstract gives 83.4% returning within 90 days as n = 349, which is 87.5% of 399, and the Discussion says slow recoverers were more often injured in noncontact or limited-contact sport although the sport-category difference was not significant (P=.12).
practicalImplications: Use these figures to set expectations with slow recoverers (athletes taking at least 14 days to become asymptomatic or 24 days to return to play): most returned within about two months, but about 10% had not returned by six months. Do not use sex or early symptom scores to predict an individual athlete's timeline, because they did not predict return within the slow group.
athleteDev: This study concerns concussion recovery timelines rather than training or performance, so it has no direct performance application. It should not be used to plan training loads for athletes returning from concussion, since it reports no load or performance outcome.
rtp: Useful for setting expectations: 77.6% of slow recoverers returned to play within 60 days and 10.6% had not returned by six months, and the return curve flattened after about 60 days. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or predict an individual's course, and clearance in the study rested on the treating clinician's examination.

citation: King E, Franklyn-Miller A, Richter C, O'Reilly E, Doolan M, Moran K, et al. Clinical and biomechanical outcomes of rehabilitation targeting intersegmental control in athletic groin pain: prospective cohort of 205 patients. Br J Sports Med. 2018;52:1054-1062.
abstract: This prospective, uncontrolled study followed 205 male patients with athletic groin pain through a three-level rehabilitation programme targeting intersegmental control. HAGOS scores improved on all subscales, 73% returned to play pain-free at a mean of 9.9 weeks, and cutting biomechanics changed, including greater pelvic rotation towards the direction of travel. The authors suggest the approach is an alternative to anatomically specific rehabilitation and warrants randomised comparison.
tldr: In 205 male athletes with groin pain, a programme that trained coordination between the trunk, pelvis and legs was followed by 73% pain-free return to play in about 10 weeks. With no control group, treat this as a promising programme to test against standard care, not as proof that it works better.
methods: Prospective uncontrolled series of consecutive male patients seen at one Dublin sports clinic from January 2013 to May 2015; 205 of 322 assessed patients were eligible. Patients had a clinical examination, including squeeze and crossover tests, a 110-degree cutting task with 3D analysis, and a three-level rehabilitation programme covering intersegmental control and strength, linear running, and multidirectional drills. The primary outcome was HAGOS, with pain-free return to play, squeeze test and 3D cutting biomechanics as secondary outcomes, analysed with paired t tests and statistical parametric mapping.
findings: Of 150 patients with repeat HAGOS scores, all six subscales improved, for example pain from 72.9 to 88.0 and sport from 50.7 to 86.3 (effect sizes 0.59 to 1.78, p < 0.001). Pain-free squeeze at 0, 45 and 90 degrees was achieved by 94% (105 of 112) at discharge, and pain-free return to play occurred in 73% (150 of 205) after a mean of 9.9 weeks, with no difference by anatomical diagnosis (p = 0.56). In the cutting analysis (n = 112), the largest within-group changes were greater thorax side flexion (effect size 0.79) and pelvic rotation (0.76) towards the direction of travel, with ankle work increasing and hip work decreasing.
limitations: The study has no control group and was not randomised, with 27% lost before the repeat HAGOS and a further 14% returning to play without the final 3D test, and re-injury is not reported. The abstract gives squeeze effect sizes of 0.49 to 0.68 while Table 3 gives 0.46 to 0.68, and return time SD is 3.5 weeks in the abstract and 3.4 in the Discussion; table values are used here. The comparisons with faster return than earlier randomised trials are across studies, and the clinic declares it operates an athletic groin pain programme.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest that rehabilitation for groin pain can target coordination between body segments rather than one anatomical structure, and that 3D cutting analysis can identify specific targets. Because there is no control group, use the programme as a structured option with clear progression goals, not as a proven superior approach.
athleteDev: The authors link cutting strategy to cutting performance and to groin pain risk, and suggest movement strategy may be part of the injury mechanism. The study does not measure performance outcomes directly, so treat movement-pattern findings as a reason to monitor cutting mechanics, not as a training target on their own.
rtp: This study is directly relevant to return to sport: 73% of field-sport athletes returned pain-free after a mean of 9.9 weeks. Clearance was based on completing all three rehabilitation levels with symptom-free linear and multidirectional drills; squeeze testing and repeat 3D analysis guided further follow-up, and 7 patients returned with residual squeeze symptoms. It cannot show that the programme beats standard care because there is no control group, and re-injury after return is not reported.

citation: Lytle C, Krishnan P, Saraf SM, Mulcahey MK. Association between sports injuries and sleep as measured by sleep actigraphy: a scoping review. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2026. Accepted author version, online 31 January 2026.
abstract: This scoping review mapped studies that used wrist actigraphy to examine sleep in relation to sports injuries and athletic performance. Among 17 studies with 455 athletes, injury findings were mixed, while all eight performance studies linked poorer sleep metrics to worse performance, with aerobic and reaction-time measures most consistently affected.
tldr: Wrist actigraphy studies in athletes link poorer sleep to worse performance, most consistently aerobic and reaction-time measures. The evidence that poor sleep raises injury risk is inconclusive, and the small, varied sample limits firm conclusions.
methods: Scoping review following the PRISMA-ScR checklist. PubMed, Medline, Embase and SPORTDiscus were searched in January 2024 and updated in January 2025 for peer-reviewed English-language studies, published within 24 years, that used sleep actigraphy and reported injury or athletic performance outcomes. Concussion studies, reviews and studies using questionnaires or other sleep measures were excluded; two authors screened abstracts and full texts, and no formal risk-of-bias appraisal was performed.
findings: Of seven injury studies, four (57%) found poorer sleep metrics (longer sleep onset latency, more wake after sleep onset, lower sleep efficiency) associated with more injuries, in Paralympic, adolescent track and field and elite soccer athletes, while three (43%) found no association with sleep duration or efficiency. All eight performance studies (47% of the 17 included) found poorer sleep associated with worse performance, including aerobic capacity, race or time-trial times and reaction time; sprint and sport-specific accuracy findings were mixed.
limitations: The conclusion states that no significant relationship was found between sleep and injury rates in adult athletes, but the results report significant associations in adult elite soccer players (two studies, one a single-athlete case study) and Paralympic athletes; the abstract's 'no consensus' wording fits the results better. The review did not appraise study quality, included only seven injury studies with small samples (1 to 94 athletes), and had 23% female participants; its statement that actigraphy is reliable was not tested by the review.
practicalImplications: Staff can use wrist actigraphy to track sleep duration, latency and efficiency alongside performance testing, since the included studies connect those metrics to aerobic and reaction-time results. Staff should not treat poor sleep as a proven injury risk factor for adult athletes, and should record recent sleep when interpreting a weak aerobic or reaction-time result.
athleteDev: In the included studies, poorer sleep metrics were associated with worse aerobic performance, reaction time and some anaerobic tests, so sleep monitoring can sit alongside performance testing. The review cannot show that improving sleep causes better performance, and the anaerobic and sprint findings are mixed.
rtp: Not designed for return to sport. The review does not study injured athletes or recovery after injury, and it describes the injury link as inconclusive, so it cannot be used to set sleep criteria for return to training or competition.

citation: Goldman JT, Donohoe B, Hatamiya N, Boland NF, Vail J, Holmes KE, et al. Baseline Sleep Characteristics in NCAA Division I Collegiate Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
abstract: This prospective study measured baseline sleep in 82 Division I collegiate athletes using a wearable sleep device worn for at least 14 nights, plus two validated sleep questionnaires. Total sleep time averaged about 6.8 hours with no sex difference, and men had longer wake time after sleep onset than women. Sleep architecture, sleep consistency and questionnaire scores did not differ by sex.
tldr: Division I athletes at one university averaged about 6.8 hours of wearable-measured sleep, with no sex difference in total sleep, sleep stages or consistency. Men had about 11 more minutes of wake time after sleep onset than women.
methods: Prospective study of varsity athletes from nine teams at one Division I university, who wore a WHOOP 4.0 band for at least 14 nights (average 67.7 days of data) and completed the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale. Men and women were compared with t tests or Wilcoxon rank sum tests at a significance level of 0.05, with no multiple-comparison correction reported.
findings: Mean total sleep time was 409.2 +/- 36.3 minutes, with no sex difference (403.8 vs 416.5 minutes, P = 0.215). Average wake time after sleep onset was 50.2 +/- 16.2 minutes and was longer in men (55.0 vs 43.7 minutes, P = 0.020). Sleep stages (REM 25.6%, slow-wave 19.9%, light 54.4%), sleep consistency (61.6 +/- 8.9%), Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale scores (6.48 +/- 1.71) and Epworth scores (7.57 +/- 3.82) did not differ significantly by sex.
limitations: The study was supported by grant funding from WHOOP, Inc., and three authors are WHOOP employees, although the article states the authors report no conflicts of interest. Data were collected at varying times of the year without accounting for competition or academic schedules, the sport groups are small and unequal, and the wake-time result was not corrected for multiple comparisons. The questionnaires were validated in the general population, not in athletes, and the authors' conclusion that many athletes sleep less than 6 hours and that sleep optimization improves performance goes beyond the data reported.
practicalImplications: Staff can use about 6.8 hours of total sleep and about 50 minutes of wake time after sleep onset as a reference for this group of athletes. The study does not show whether these values are a problem or how they relate to performance, injury or illness, so an individual's own trend matters more than the group average.
athleteDev: Wearable sleep data gave this group a baseline for sleep duration, stages and consistency that staff can compare with an individual athlete's own trend. The study did not link sleep to performance, so it cannot justify a performance-based sleep target.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes baseline sleep in varsity athletes and does not measure sleep after injury or any link between sleep and recovery from injury.

citation: Cintron HE, Heyburn JJ, Sterner RL, Dankel SJ. Blood Flow Restricted Electrical Stimulations to Prevent or Attenuate Symptoms of Muscle Damage. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
abstract: Eighteen participants completed a damaging eccentric exercise bout with both arms, followed by electrical stimulation with or without blood flow restriction on each arm, repeated 24 hours later. Discomfort, muscle thickness and strength changed over time after the damaging exercise, but the two treatment conditions did not differ.
tldr: Adding blood flow restriction to low-frequency electrical stimulation did not reduce soreness, strength loss or swelling after an eccentric arm exercise bout. The study had no control arm and used one muscle group, so it cannot show that either treatment works.
methods: Within-subject design. Eighteen participants (9 female, 9 male; 21 years, 170 cm, 78 kg) performed eccentric elbow flexion to failure at 80% of concentric 1RM with both arms. One arm then received 20 minutes of 5 Hz electrical stimulation alone, and the other the same stimulation with the cuff inflated to 100% of arterial occlusion pressure in 2-minute bouts with 1-minute rests, with conditions counterbalanced for limb dominance. Treatments were given immediately and 24 hours after the exercise; discomfort (Borg CR10), isometric strength and ultrasound muscle thickness were analysed with Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVA.
findings: Eccentric exercise produced clear time effects: discomfort rose from 0 to 4.2 au at 48 h, muscle thickness from 3.5 to 3.8 cm, and isometric strength fell from 278 N to 232 N, with strength lower at both 24 h and 48 h. There was no condition by time interaction on any outcome (BF10 0.154 to 0.279). Condition main effects were absent for strength (BF10 0.208, moderate support for no difference) and muscle thickness (BF10 0.388, inconclusive by the authors' thresholds).
limitations: There was no control condition and no BFR-only condition, so the design cannot separate treatment effects from the natural course of muscle damage. The abstract states all Bayes factors were below 0.28, but the results report BF10 0.388 for the muscle thickness condition effect. The authors also note that the results may depend on the specific stimulation and BFR protocols and on timing, since both were applied at 0 and 24 h only.
practicalImplications: On this evidence, do not add blood flow restriction to low-frequency electrical stimulation expecting less soreness or strength loss after heavy eccentric arm work. The study also cannot show that either treatment beats doing nothing, so it does not support using either one for recovery planning.
athleteDev: The study gives no support for using blood flow restriction with electrical stimulation to speed recovery of strength or readiness after heavy eccentric work. Athletic status was not reported, so any performance use would need separate testing in trained athletes.
rtp: Not applicable. The participants were uninjured and the study measured no injured muscle or return-to-sport outcome.

citation: Daab W, Bouzid MA, Lajri M, Bouchiba M, Rebai H. Brief cycles of lower-limb occlusion accelerate recovery kinetics in soccer players. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2020.
abstract: Twelve male semiprofessional soccer players completed a simulated match (Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test) in a placebo-controlled crossover design, with intermittent lower-limb occlusion (IVO) or low-pressure placebo applied afterwards. Compared with placebo, IVO was associated with better maintained MVC and 20 m sprint over 48 hours, lower soreness, and lower CK at 0 and 24 h; jump results did not differ significantly between conditions.
tldr: In semiprofessional soccer players, brief intermittent occlusion after a simulated match was followed by less soreness, lower CK at 0 and 24 h, and better maintained MVC and sprint than placebo, but not significantly different jump recovery. The sample was small and players were not blinded, so this is an early signal rather than settled evidence.
methods: Single-blind, placebo-randomized crossover with two sessions a week apart. Players did the Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test; then IVO (three 5-minute occlusions with 5-minute reperfusion, cuff on the proximal thigh at 50 mmHg above systolic) or placebo (20 mmHg) was applied. MVC, squat jump, countermovement jump, 20 m sprint, CK, LDH, CRP and soreness were measured before, immediately after, and at 24, 48 and 72 h.
findings: Compared with placebo, IVO gave higher MVC at 0, 24 and 48 h and faster 20 m sprints at 24 and 48 h (significant condition by time interactions). For squat jump and countermovement jump there was no significant condition by time interaction (p = 0.06 and p = 0.15), although jumps fell only in the placebo condition on within-condition tests. CK was lower with IVO at 0 and 24 h, LDH at 0 h only, and soreness at 0 and 24 h; CRP did not differ between conditions.
limitations: Only 12 players from one team, with no non-cuff control, and participants could not be blinded because of the obvious cuff pressure difference. Sprint (ICC 0.69, CV 11.2%) and CK (ICC 0.70) reliability were low. The abstract states that IVO attenuated jump decrements and lowered LDH over recovery, but the results show no significant interaction for jumps and an LDH difference only at 0 h.
practicalImplications: For squads playing frequent matches, IVO after a match-like session may be a practical recovery option at the pressures used here (three 5-minute cycles, 50 mmHg above systolic). The benefit was limited to some time points and was tested once in a small group. Monitor CK, soreness and jump or sprint tests to see whether it helps your own players.
athleteDev: Performance staff can note that IVO after a simulated match was associated with less soreness and with MVC and 20 m sprint closer to baseline over 48 hours, while jump recovery did not differ significantly from placebo. If repeating the approach, use a similar test battery and note that sprint and CK reliability were low in this study.
rtp: Not applicable. Players were healthy and no injury or return-to-play outcomes were measured. The study covers short-term recovery of function after a simulated match in uninjured athletes and cannot inform return to sport after injury.

citation: Vitale J, McCall A, Cina A, Athlete Travel and Sleep Interest Group (ATSIG), Janse van Rensburg DC, Halson S. "Can we trust them?" An expert evaluation of large language models to provide sleep and jet lag recommendations for athletes. Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: Expert evaluation of sleep and jet lag advice from three large language models (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard) for athletes, using 10 frequently asked questions per topic and 20 experts rating answers at two time points. Sleep answers were largely rated valid with no significant differences between models, while jet lag answers were valid only for ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard was rated lowest, and inter-rater reliability was low while intra-rater agreement was high.
tldr: Experts judged most large language model sleep answers for athletes to be appropriate, but jet lag answers were mostly not, and only ChatGPT-4's jet lag answers passed the content validity threshold overall. Experts disagreed substantially on what counted as appropriate, so model output needs expert review before use.
methods: Ten sleep and ten jet lag FAQs were chosen by three investigators, with ChatGPT-4 also suggesting questions. The three models answered each question on 25 January 2024 with a 150-word instruction, and 20 experts, blinded to model, rated each answer on a 6-point scale with reasons for inappropriate answers, at two time points 8 weeks apart. Lawshe's content validity ratio treated scores of 4 to 6 as appropriate, with Fleiss' kappa for inter-rater reliability, the Jaccard index for intra-rater agreement, and Friedman, ANOVA and chi-square tests for model differences.
findings: Sleep: CVR was 0.5 or higher for 70%, 60% and 90% of answers from ChatGPT-3.5, Google Bard and ChatGPT-4, with no significant differences between models in sleep CVR. Jet lag: ChatGPT-4 answers were all valid (CVI 0.68), ChatGPT-3.5 reached validity on 10% and Google Bard on none, with Google Bard lower than ChatGPT-3.5 (p = 0.0073) and ChatGPT-4 (p < 0.0001) and ChatGPT-4 higher than ChatGPT-3.5 (p = 0.0017). Inter-rater reliability was low (Fleiss' kappa 0.17 to 0.26), while at least 52.6% of experts reached a Jaccard index of 0.76 or more for each model; for jet lag, 'too few information' was the most common criticism (Google Bard 39%), and Google Bard drew the most 'clear mistakes' ratings (21%).
limitations: Small expert panel of 20 with low inter-rater agreement, no athlete or coach raters, and models tested in one period, so results may not hold for current versions. The abstract's Fleiss' kappa range (0.21 to 0.39) does not match Table 3 (0.17 to 0.26). The authors could not calculate an ICC, and the study did not test whether the advice changed athlete outcomes. The Key Points and Conclusion say ChatGPT-4 was consistently better on sleep, but sleep CVR did not differ significantly between models.
practicalImplications: Use language models only as a starting point for athlete sleep and jet lag advice, and have a qualified staff member check the content before passing it on. Expect weaker answers on jet lag than on sleep, and check sleep answers for generic content, since experts' open comments on sleep answers flagged generic wording and missing sport-specific context.
athleteDev: Staff who use a language model to draft sleep or travel guidance should check each answer against their own sport-specific evidence before it goes to athletes or coaches. The models gave different advice on jet lag, and experts disagreed among themselves, so a single model answer should not set a travel plan.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It assessed general sleep and jet lag advice for athletes and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Pinzone AG, Erb EK, Humm SM, Kearney SG, Kingsley JD. Cannabis use for exercise recovery in trained individuals: a survey study. Journal of Cannabis Research. 2023;5:32.
abstract: This survey asked 111 regular cannabis users who also exercised whether they used CBD or THC to recover from aerobic or resistance exercise, and what other recovery methods they used. Most respondents trained aerobically or with resistance and most felt that cannabis helped their recovery. The authors conclude that the role of cannabis in exercise recovery needs more data.
tldr: Regular cannabis users who exercise widely believe CBD or THC helps their recovery, but this was a self-report survey with no objective recovery measures or control group. It shows how exercisers use cannabis, not whether it works.
methods: Voluntary, anonymous online questionnaire ('Cannabis and Exercise') advertised on social media, by word of mouth and by flyer, collected June to November 2022. Eligible respondents were at least 18, currently using cannabis and exercising regularly; items covered cannabis use, exercise habits, recovery methods and demographics. Analysis used Kruskal-Wallis tests, chi-square tests and Pearson correlations.
findings: Of 111 respondents, 85% reported aerobic training, 85% resistance training and 72% both. Respondents reported using THC after aerobic exercise (68 people, 61%) or resistance exercise (67 people, 60%) for recovery, and 22 (20%) and 25 (23%) used CBD for each. The authors report that 93% felt CBD and 87% felt THC aided recovery, and found no significant correlation between motives for use and reported recovery.
limitations: The survey is anonymous, voluntary and self-reported, so it measures belief and use rather than recovery, and it has no control group; the authors call it exploratory with a small, mostly Midwest US sample. Reported counts do not reconcile (85% of 111 trained aerobically, yet n = 72 is used; 22 used CBD for recovery but only 20 are CBD users), and the Discussion says women CBD users had higher aerobic intensity while the Results and Table 2 show the difference for resistance exercise. The study asked whether respondents exercised with a team but does not report competition level, so it cannot be read as an athlete sample.
practicalImplications: Staff should expect athletes who train regularly to raise cannabis as a recovery aid and should ask about the product, form and timing they use; respondents reported both CBD and THC use after training, and some reported negative effects such as feeling too high, too sleepy or a racing heart. Because the evidence here is perceived benefit only, staff should not present cannabis as a proven recovery aid.
athleteDev: The survey shows that regular exercisers use CBD and THC as a recovery aid, and men CBD users reported higher aerobic and resistance training intensity, and women CBD users higher resistance intensity, than THC users. It does not measure performance or recovery, so it cannot show that cannabis improves training output.
rtp: The survey does not measure injury, pain, return to sport or clinical recovery, although pain relief was one of the stated motives. It should not be used to guide return-to-play, medication or clearance decisions for an injured athlete.

citation: Pradzynska M, Rylands LP, Canham DC. Causes of sleep deprivation in competative athletes: A scoping review. Science & Sports. 2023.
abstract: This scoping review aimed to identify themes in peer-reviewed studies related to possible causes of sleep deprivation in competitive athletes. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance and searches of PubMed, MEDLINE and EBSCO, 16 studies were included. Five themes were identified, covering travel, night performance, the period before, during and after competition, and concussion, with short-term and long-term causes separated.
tldr: A review of 16 studies found that travel, late-night training or matches, and competition periods were linked to shorter or poorer sleep in athletes, and that concussion history was linked to insomnia. The included studies show associations, so the causes are not proven.
methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, using three databases searched for 2015 to 2022 with keywords on athletes, sleep and sport. Titles and abstracts were screened, and full texts were checked for eligibility, which required English-language, peer-reviewed, primary studies in athletes that addressed causes of sleep disturbance. Qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method studies were eligible, and reviews were excluded.
findings: Short-term causes: five studies linked long-haul travel, sleeping on the bus or unfamiliar environments to poorer sleep or more fatigue, although one triathlon study reported no change in sleep quality and an increase in sleep duration after long-haul travel; all four night-performance studies showed at least one significant change in sleep quality or quantity after night training or matches. Around competition, one study of professional rugby players reported a 68% sleep efficiency on the night of competition, and 64% of athletes in another study reported worse sleep on at least one night before an important competition, while a cricket study found no change in pre-competition sleep. Long-term causes: a history of concussion was associated with a higher risk of moderate to severe insomnia (P = 0.006) and with short sleep and sleep disturbance across three studies.
limitations: The review did not assess the quality or risk of bias of the included studies, and it covers only English-language studies from 2015 to 2022 in three databases. Most included designs are observational, and the review's own conclusion is that it is a starting point rather than a definitive summary of causes. The suggested interventions (napping, relaxation, sleep hygiene and a climatisation period) are not tested in the included studies, and the abstract states they 'could aid' performance without measuring performance.
practicalImplications: The authors suggest timing travel to allow a settling period before competition, giving athletes psychological strategies for pre-competition nerves, and scheduling heavy training earlier in the day rather than late at night. These are suggestions drawn from associations, not tested interventions. Athletes with a concussion history reported more insomnia and short sleep, so sleep is worth asking about in that group.
athleteDev: The review's introduction cites sleep loss linked to lower sprint performance and tennis accuracy, but the 16 included studies measured sleep rather than performance. Any performance effect of the travel, night-training and competition-night findings is therefore inferred from sleep outcomes alone.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport. One included study linked insufficient sleep during recovery from sport-related concussion to more migraine, cognitive and neuropsychological symptoms, but the review gives no recovery timelines and cannot be used to decide when an athlete returns to play or training.

citation: Borghi S, Bizzozero S, Vitale JA, Tallini E, Corazza F, La Torre A, et al. Chronotype, sleep hygiene, and sleep characteristics among athletes of different disciplines. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
abstract: This cross-sectional survey of 280 Italian athletes compared chronotype, sleep quality and sleep hygiene by sex, sport discipline (team or individual) and competition level (elite or non-elite). Nearly half the sample were poor sleepers by PSQI, and sleep hygiene correlated with both sleep quality and chronotype. The authors conclude that recovery and sleep deserve more attention from coaches.
tldr: Many athletes in this Italian sample had weak sleep habits: 44.6% were poor sleepers by PSQI. Because the data are self-reported and cross-sectional, use the findings to flag athletes for sleep-habit screening rather than to set sport-specific sleep targets.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey, reported to STROBE guidance, of athletes aged 18 to 40 who trained at least three times weekly during the 2022/2023 season. Participants completed the MEQ, the Italian PSQI, the Italian SHI and questions on training and ideal sleep. Non-normal data were compared with Mann-Whitney tests and correlated with Spearman tests.
findings: Of 280 athletes, 66.4% were intermediate-type, 21.8% morning-type and 11.8% evening-type, and 44.6% were poor sleepers by PSQI. Females reported 14 minutes more total sleep than males (p = 0.022). Individual-sport athletes had lower PSQI (p = 0.006) and SHI (p < 0.001) scores, higher MEQ scores (p = 0.001) and a 36-minute earlier bedtime (p < 0.001) than team-sport athletes, and elite athletes reported higher sleep efficiency (+2.8%, p = 0.009), 2.1 minutes shorter latency (p = 0.018) and 11.3 minutes less WASO (p = 0.043) than non-elite athletes; all group effect sizes were small (about 0.25 to 0.51). PSQI correlated with SHI (r = 0.43) and MEQ with SHI (r = -0.35), both p < 0.001.
limitations: Sleep was measured only by retrospective self-report, with possible recall bias, and naps, sleeping arrangements and second jobs were not controlled. The Discussion says team and individual athletes did not differ in quantitative or qualitative sleep parameters, but Table 2 shows PSQI, bedtime and wake-up time differed (total sleep time, efficiency, latency and WASO did not); the Results values are used here. The Discussion also says PSQI and MEQ were not correlated, while Figure 3 prints r = -0.23, p < 0.001, below the authors' r > 0.3 threshold.
practicalImplications: Screening athletes with the PSQI and SHI may help staff identify who needs individual sleep-hygiene education, since poor sleep quality and poor sleep hygiene were linked in this sample. The study does not show that changing sleep hygiene improves sleep, so any intervention should be checked against the athlete's own sleep data.
athleteDev: Team-sport athletes in this sample leaned later in chronotype and bedtime, which may be useful context when scheduling early sessions. The study does not measure performance, so it cannot show that any training time improves performance.
rtp: This study does not include injured athletes or any return-to-sport outcome, so it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It is relevant only to general sleep-hygiene education for athletes who are not injured.

citation: Larson-Meyer DE, Woolf K, Burke L. Assessment of Nutrient Status in Athletes and the Need for Supplementation. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018 (ahead of print).
abstract: This scholarly review sets out how to assess an athlete's nutrient status before deciding on dietary supplementation, using the anthropometric, biochemical, clinical, dietary and environmental (A-E) framework. The authors conclude that supplements cannot compensate for an inadequate diet and that reference norms specific to well-trained athletes are still needed.
tldr: Before recommending a supplement, review the athlete's diet, body composition, biomarkers, clinical signs, medications and environment together, because each method has known error. Supplements cannot make up for poor food choices.
methods: Narrative scholarly review organised around the A-E framework. It summarises the advantages and errors of dietary assessment methods, body composition techniques, biochemical markers (with cut-offs and sources), clinical and nutrition-focused examination, food-drug interactions and environmental factors. The paper does not describe a systematic literature search.
findings: Dietary methods all carry error: food records and recalls tend to under-report energy, with athlete under-reporting estimated at 10 to 45% of total energy expenditure, and coding with nutrient databases adds further error. Body composition methods carry standard errors of estimate of about 2 to 3% for DXA and 1.8% for BOD POD, and skinfold-based body fat depends on population-specific equations. Many biomarkers are affected by exercise, hydration or inflammation (for example, ferritin may be artificially raised after a strenuous session), cut-offs are not available for all nutrients, and overt deficiencies are described as rare in healthy athletes, so physical examinations are often unremarkable.
limitations: This is a narrative review, so source selection and evidence strength are not reported. The authors note that the number of diet-record days needed to estimate usual intake in athletes is not known, and that many reference standards were derived from non-athlete populations.
practicalImplications: Before supplementing an athlete, review intake over several days (the authors suggest a 5 to 8 day average as a reasonable reference point against the EAR, AI and UL), check relevant biomarkers under standardised collection conditions, and screen for medication and supplement interactions. Treat supplements as an addition to a well-chosen diet, not a replacement, and interpret markers such as ferritin and zinc in light of recent exercise and hydration because general-population cut-offs may not suit well-trained athletes.
athleteDev: Use this assessment to find out whether diet, rather than a supplement, is the main gap before aligning any supplement with performance goals. The review gives no supplement-specific effect sizes, so it cannot show that a given supplement improves performance.
rtp: Not designed for return to sport. The review does not address injury or rehabilitation and sets no return-to-play nutrition criteria.

citation: Wilson PB. Associations of Urine Specific Gravity With Body Mass Index and Lean Body Mass at the Population Level: Implications for Hydration Monitoring. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2021 (ahead of print).
abstract: A cross-sectional analysis of 3,634 adults from the 2007-2008 US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey examined whether body mass index and estimated lean body mass were associated with elevated urine specific gravity (USG of 1.020 or more and 1.025 or more), after accounting for dietary moisture and sodium. Adults in the highest quintiles of BMI or lean mass had roughly two to nearly four times the odds of elevated USG compared with the lowest quintile, which raises questions about fixed USG thresholds for people with large body size.
tldr: In a large US adult sample, people with more body mass or lean mass were more likely to exceed the common USG cutoffs of 1.020 and 1.025, independent of food and fluid moisture and sodium intake. The author suggests fixed USG cutoffs may over-flag large individuals, such as football or rugby players, but this was not tested in athletes.
methods: Secondary analysis of NHANES 2007-2008 data, excluding people under 20, pregnant women, and those with kidney disease, major cardiovascular conditions or diabetes. USG was measured by refractometer on random spot urine samples, LBM was estimated from validated anthropometric equations, and dietary moisture and sodium came from a 24-hour recall. Survey-weighted logistic regression compared BMI and LBM quintiles 2 to 5 against quintile 1, separately for men and women.
findings: Prevalence of USG of 1.020 or more was 46.8% in men and 27.6% in women, and 16.7% and 11.5% for USG of 1.025 or more.
