Fifth-quintile BMI or LBM carried higher odds of elevated USG (for example LBM Q5: men OR 2.61 and 2.18, women OR 3.16 and 3.68 for the 1.020 and 1.025 cutoffs), except BMI with USG of 1.025 or more in men (OR 1.40, not significant); quintiles 2 and 3 were mostly not significant. LBM explained slightly more USG variance than fat mass (R2 0.026 vs 0.016 in men, 0.060 vs 0.043 in women).
limitations: Participants were general US adults, not athletes, and no reference measure of hydration status was used, so whether elevated USG in larger people reflects true hypohydration was not tested. LBM was predicted from equations rather than measured, USG came from a single spot sample at varying times of day, and the associations with body size were modest in size (R2 values of 0.06 or less).
practicalImplications: When USG is used to screen hydration, readings in the 1.020 to 1.025 range in very large or muscular individuals may partly reflect body size rather than fluid status, so a single fixed cutoff should be interpreted with caution in those athletes. The study does not provide alternative cutoffs, so it supports cautious interpretation rather than a new threshold.
athleteDev: The study does not measure performance. The author notes that athletes in sports with large body size and lean mass, such as American football, rugby and throwing events, are the ones most likely to be affected, which matters when USG is used for hydration or weight-certification decisions.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It reports no injury or athlete data and should not be used to clear an athlete or to judge heat-illness readiness.

citation: Tomczyk M, Heileson JL, Babiarz M, Calder PC. Athletes Can Benefit from Increased Intake of EPA and DHA: Evaluating the Evidence. Nutrients. 2023;15:4925.
abstract: A narrative review of the effects of EPA and DHA relevant to athletes. The authors report that athletes commonly have low Omega-3 Index values and summarise evidence on inflammation, brain health, muscle recovery after injury, soreness, training adaptation and safety. They conclude that EPA and DHA supplementation is reasonable for athletes to consider, while calling for more research on dose and duration.
tldr: Many athletes have low omega-3 status, and supplemental EPA and DHA show some benefits for soreness, strength and training adaptation in small studies. The review supports considering supplements, but the evidence for athletes is still limited on dose, duration and performance outcomes.
methods: Narrative review of the literature on EPA and DHA in athletes and related physiology. The text does not describe a systematic search, screening or quality rating, and the review draws on cited trials in healthy, recreational, collegiate and professional samples.
findings: Omega-3 Index values in professional athletes averaged 4.29% to 5.02% and in amateur athletes 4.58% to 5.70%, all below the 8% optimal level cited by the review. Doses of about 1,000 to 1,500 mg EPA plus DHA per day for at least 12 weeks were needed to reach an Omega-3 Index of 8% in a scoping review of 58 studies. Trials reported less muscle soreness with 0.54 to 4.20 g per day of EPA plus DHA, and one 10-week resistance-training study in recreational exercisers found greater 1RM bench press and squat gains with EPA plus DHA than with placebo. Two American football studies found that DHA or EPA plus DHA attenuated serum neurofilament light, but a third did not.
limitations: The review is narrative, uses no systematic search, and cites several studies by its own authors (for example refs 22, 26 and 79). Many cited athlete studies are small, short or in recreational samples, and several outcomes (such as muscle mass after injury) rest on rodent studies or a single small trial in young women. The authors state that dose, duration and athlete-specific outcomes remain uncertain, and note that EPA and DHA effects on oxygen kinetics, cycling efficiency or peak oxygen uptake do not translate into improved physical performance as such.
practicalImplications: Athletes with low fish intake may have low Omega-3 Index values, so staff can consider assessing intake or status. If supplementing, the review advises choosing products with a high EPA and/or DHA content and taking them with or around a meal, notes the IOC-cited dose of about 2 g per day, and lists fishy taste and burps as common side effects. Effects are not certain for individuals, and any supplement decision should be reviewed against the athlete's diet and context.
athleteDev: Small trials in recreational and amateur athletes report improvements in running economy, strength and soreness with EPA and DHA. Staff could test supplementation with clear outcome measures in their own athletes, but the review gives no proven performance benefit for elite athletes.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It cites one pilot randomised trial of DHA after diagnosed mild traumatic brain injury that reported faster return-to-play clearance, but a single trial and biomarker studies cannot set a return protocol or clear an athlete.

citation: Gurton WH, Greally J, Chudzikiewicz K, Gough LA, Lynn A, Ranchordas MK. Beneficial effects of oral and topical sodium bicarbonate during a battery of team sport-specific exercise tests in recreationally trained male athletes. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. 2023;20(1):2216678.
abstract: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 14 recreationally trained male team sport athletes compared oral sodium bicarbonate, a topical bicarbonate lotion (PR Lotion) and placebo before countermovement jumps, 8 x 25 m repeated sprints and the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Level 2 test. Oral bicarbonate increased Yo-Yo distance and improved repeated sprint times, and the topical lotion improved repeated sprint times only. Blood buffering changed with oral bicarbonate but not with the lotion.
tldr: In 14 recreational team sport athletes, oral sodium bicarbonate increased Yo-Yo IR2 distance by 21% and cut repeated sprint times by about 2% versus placebo. A topical bicarbonate lotion improved repeated sprints by about 2% but not Yo-Yo distance, and its effect is not explained by blood buffering.
methods: Block-randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design with three test days separated by 5 to 7 days. Athletes received oral sodium bicarbonate (0.3 g/kg body mass in capsules with placebo lotion), topical PR Lotion (0.9036 g/kg with placebo capsules) or placebo, with capsules given from 135 minutes and the lotion 120 minutes before testing. Outcomes were countermovement jump height, total and average 8 x 25 m sprint times, Yo-Yo IR2 distance, blood acid-base balance, electrolytes, plasma volume, urine measures and ratings of perceived exertion; analysis used repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests.
findings: Yo-Yo IR2 distance was 94 m greater with oral bicarbonate than placebo (P = 0.009, d = 0.64) and 31 m greater with the topical lotion (P = 0.084). Total repeated sprint time was 0.61 s faster with oral bicarbonate (1.8%, P = 0.020, d = 0.38) and 0.64 s faster with the lotion (2.0%, P = 0.036, d = 0.34), with no significant difference between the two bicarbonate conditions. Countermovement jump results did not differ. Oral bicarbonate raised pre-exercise blood bicarbonate by 5.3 to 6.5 mmol/L versus placebo and increased plasma volume, while the lotion did not change blood acid-base balance. The lotion lowered perceived exertion after the fifth, sixth and eighth sprints.
limitations: Only 14 of 18 recruited athletes completed the study, from five sports, against a sample size target of 15. Half of participants identified the lotion and expectations were higher for it than for the other conditions, and the authors offer an untested menthol-cooling explanation for its effect. The abstract reports a 1.9% total sprint improvement with oral bicarbonate, but the results report 1.8%. Momentous, the lotion maker, supplied the products and funds a PhD studentship linked to this work.
practicalImplications: In this single-dose study, oral sodium bicarbonate improved Yo-Yo IR2 distance and repeated sprint times, and gastrointestinal discomfort did not differ significantly between conditions. The topical lotion improved repeated sprints but not Yo-Yo distance or blood buffering, so it rests on one small study that the authors say needs replication.
athleteDev: The study tested supplements taken before one test session, so it speaks only to acute effects on repeated sprint and Yo-Yo performance. Oral bicarbonate was the condition that improved both tests, while the topical lotion's benefit was limited to a roughly 2% change in repeated sprints.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tested recreationally trained athletes after one supplement dose, enrolled no injured athletes, and does not address rehabilitation or recovery from injury.

citation: Shaw KA, Zello GA, Rodgers CD, Warkentin TD, Baerwald AR, Chilibeck PD. Benefits of a plant-based diet and considerations for the athlete. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2022.
abstract: This invited narrative review summarizes research on plant-based diets for health and exercise performance. It covers nutrient bioavailability, sources of nutrients that are hard to obtain without animal products, and sport supplements relevant to plant-based athletes. The authors conclude that such diets must be carefully planned to meet energy and nutrient needs.
tldr: A well-planned, whole-food plant-based diet can support health and neither hinders nor aids exercise performance, according to this review. Athletes on these diets need deliberate planning for protein quality, energy, iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin B12 and creatine.
methods: Narrative review with no described search strategy or appraisal method. The authors summarize epidemiological, clinical and performance studies by nutrient, including protein quality, creatine, iron, zinc, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin B12, beta-alanine, taurine, carbohydrate, body composition and antioxidants.
findings: Plant-based diets are associated with health benefits, but these are likely linked to more fruit, vegetables and whole grains, and cause and effect cannot be inferred from the epidemiological evidence. Plant proteins are often lower in leucine, and vegetarians and vegans have lower muscle creatine, but the authors report that a varied plant diet with adequate energy can meet amino acid needs. Iron, zinc and calcium absorption is lower from plant sources, and vitamin B12 is found only in animal products. The authors conclude that neither a plant-based nor an omnivorous diet is clearly superior for aerobic performance, and that evidence for strength and power performance is limited.
limitations: The review uses no described systematic search, so the selection of studies cannot be verified. Much of the health evidence is epidemiological, the authors state that evidence on strength and power performance is limited, and the antioxidant section relies largely on supplement studies rather than whole foods.
practicalImplications: Athletes on plant-based diets should plan energy and protein intake carefully, with variety in protein sources, and monitor body weight to avoid low energy availability. The review recommends that supplementation of nutrients such as iron, vitamin D, calcium and vitamin B12 be informed by a registered dietitian, and suggests creatine supplementation may be considered for short, high-intensity performance, with 5 g per day associated with optimal tissue saturation.
athleteDev: The review's conclusion is that a well-planned plant-based diet neither helps nor harms performance, so the main issue is adequate planning. Protein quantity and variety, energy availability and creatine status are the nutrition points it highlights for plant-based athletes.
rtp: The review does not assess injury rehabilitation or return to sport. Its only concussion comment suggests creatine may help recovery as a precaution, which is not evidence that should guide return-to-play decisions.

citation: Huang B, Zhao L, Campbell SC. Bidirectional link between exercise and the gut microbiota. Exerc Sport Sci Rev. 2024;52(4):132-144.
abstract: Exercise alters the gut microbiota, and an emerging question is whether the gut microbiota in turn regulates exercise tolerance. This review summarises how exercise changes gut microbial communities and how disrupting or depleting an intact gut microbiota affects exercise tolerance, with a table of the animal and human studies reviewed.
tldr: Exercise is linked to gut microbial changes in animals, general adults and athletes, and in mouse models removing or depleting the microbiota reduced endurance. Human evidence that the microbiota drives performance is lacking, and the one human probiotic trial cited showed no benefit.
methods: Narrative review of animal and human studies of exercise and the gut microbiota, including germ-free, gnotobiotic and antibiotic-treated mouse models, summarised in a table giving the population, exercise stimulus, diet, groups, main outcomes and microbial findings. The review does not describe a formal search or risk-of-bias appraisal.
findings: Several studies report that exercise increases alpha diversity and Bacillota and reduces Bacteroidota, with SCFA-producing taxa such as Akkermansia often rising; athlete cohorts (rugby, rowing, cycling, martial arts, triathlon) differed in composition or metabolic pathways from controls or lower-level athletes. In mice, germ-free or antibiotic-treated animals mostly had shorter swim or treadmill times, and one study found antibiotics reversed training gains in run distance, but another found antibiotics did not hinder endurance training improvements. A randomized crossover trial of 14 days of V. atypica supplementation in 7 active adults found no difference in exhaustion time or anaerobic capacity.
limitations: The review does not describe its literature search or quality appraisal, so study selection cannot be checked. Much of the mechanistic and performance evidence is from rodents, often males, and the authors state that research must translate animal findings to humans and include both sexes. The authors also note that the taxonomic resolution of many studies is too low to identify specific microbes.
practicalImplications: Athletes and practitioners should not yet use the gut microbiota as a performance target, since the performance evidence comes mainly from animal studies. The authors call for clarity on how antibiotic use in humans affects exercise performance, which they describe as a paramount question given how often antibiotics are prescribed.
athleteDev: Performance Application: The review links gut microbial composition with endurance mainly in mice, and athlete data are associative. The one human supplementation trial cited found no performance benefit, so the review does not support probiotic or microbiota-targeted interventions for performance.
rtp: Not applicable. The review covers exercise and microbiota in healthy animals and general human cohorts, and it does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

citation: Pokrywka A, Surała O, Grabowska K, et al. „Brain doping” substances: prohibited or not in sports? Biology of Sport. 2025;42(4):189-202.
abstract: Systematic review of PubMed studies on substances marketed as 'brain doping', combined with a scan of Polish dietary supplement retailers. Nine studies (seven randomized crossover trials, two case reports) were included, and 120 synthetic supplement ingredients were classified by anti-doping status. The authors conclude that 'brain doping' is largely a marketing term, and that many marketed substances are prohibited or of unclear status.
tldr: Few studies show that substances sold as 'brain doping' improve cognition in sport, and none of the four trials that tested physical performance found an improvement. Many supplements sold for brain performance are prohibited or have unclear anti-doping status, so athletes face a risk of unintentional doping.
methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, using PubMed searches (March 2023, updated April 2024) with eight brain-doping term categories combined with sport and athlete terms. Two reviewers screened 455 titles and abstracts down to nine included studies. Separately, 32 Polish online stores were reviewed in 2023, and synthetic ingredients were classified against WADA lists and certifier databases.
findings: Of seven randomized crossover trials, three reported a benefit in at least one cognitive domain (tramadol, inositol-stabilized arginine silicate, a polyphenol drink), three showed no effect, and one (snus) showed a negative effect. Four trials tested physical performance and none found an improvement in exercise capacity. Of 120 synthetic market ingredients, 22% were prohibited, 41% non-prohibited and 37% unclear, with 16% presumed to meet WADA criteria.
limitations: Only nine studies from one database (PubMed) were included, mostly small, and only two trials included women. The authors note they reviewed only one side of the evidence (substances with proven benefit), and their classification of trained versus recreational samples is inconsistent (one 'trained' sample was experienced gamers). The market scan is a single 2023 snapshot of Polish retailers, and 'unclear' status rests on the authors' judgment of chemical or biological similarity.
practicalImplications: Staff who receive supplement questions should not assume that products marketed as brain or cognitive boosters are proven or permitted. Check each ingredient against the current WADA list and certified-supplement databases, because status changes, and treat unclear ingredients as a risk until confirmed. The authors also note that 'not forbidden' does not mean 'allowed'.
athleteDev: Performance staff should not promote 'brain doping' or cognitive supplements as performance aids, because the review finds little evidence of benefit in athletes and no improvement in exercise capacity. Check any supplement request for prohibited or unclear ingredients first.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. Safety data are thin: adverse reactions were reported in only four of the trials, and the two case reports describe excessive use.

citation: Murugappan KR, Cocchi MN, Bose S, Neves SE, Cook CH, Sarge T, et al. Case Study: Fatal Exertional Rhabdomyolysis Possibly Related to Drastic Weight Cutting. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2018. (Ahead of Print)
abstract: Rapid weight loss, or weight cutting, is common in combat sports but underrepresented in the medical literature. The authors describe exertional rhabdomyolysis in a mixed martial artist with sickle cell trait who collapsed during a bout after a 5 kg weight cut and later died of multiorgan failure. They argue for sickle cell trait screening in combat sports and for safer weight-control practices among all combat athletes.
tldr: A fatal case in an amateur mixed martial artist with sickle cell trait, who had lost 26% of his body mass over three months before fighting. The authors believe dehydration from weight cutting set the stage for the event, a risk for any combat athlete and not only those with sickle cell trait.
methods: Single-case clinical report from one tertiary hospital, based on the patient's hospital course, with written consent from the patient's health care proxy. The authors also discuss three earlier combat sports deaths linked to exertional sickling and cite published weight-cutting data.
findings: Before his first bout the patient lost 26.1% of his body mass over three months, most of it in the week before weigh-in, using fluid and food restriction and sauna sessions, and afterwards had difficulty rehydrating. For his second bout he cut 5 kg in a sauna within 24 hours of weigh-in, then presented after collapse with hyperkalemia, hypernatremia, acidemia and acute kidney injury, and developed rhabdomyolysis (CK peaked at 223,100 IU/L), compartment syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, ARDS, and asystolic cardiac arrest, and died. The authors also describe three earlier combat sports deaths linked to exertional sickling.
limitations: This is one case, with no autopsy result reported for this patient, no sickle cell testing details, and no measured hydration status before the bout. The authors infer dehydration from the weight cut, but the case cannot separate its effect from the restricted diet, the sauna use and the sickle cell trait. The screening and weight-cut recommendations are the authors' opinion and were not tested here.
practicalImplications: The authors advise that staff working with athletes cutting weight regularly assess weight and hydration status and encourage long-term weight-loss methods that avoid extreme hypohydration. They cite a review recommending weight loss no greater than 8% of body mass, or 5% with shorter recovery before competition. They suggest a potential role for sickle cell trait screening in combat sports, while noting that the NCAA screening policy has faced scrutiny over stigmatisation and low absolute risk.
athleteDev: The case does not measure performance. The only performance-related guidance is the cited review's limit of 8% body mass loss, or 5% with short recovery, set for safety and to preserve performance.
rtp: The case cannot inform return to sport, because the athlete died. Its useful point for clinicians is post-collapse care after a weight cut: monitor kidney function, electrolytes and telemetry, and consider genetic causes of exertional rhabdomyolysis, which the authors list in the differential diagnosis.

citation: Syrydiuk RA, Boltz AJ, Lempke LB, van Pelt K, Balendran V, Scott K, et al. Association between magnetic resonance imaging use and recovery time following concussion: a CARE consortium study. Research in Sports Medicine. 2025.
abstract: This study compared concussion recovery in collegiate athletes who had a research MRI within 72 hours of injury with propensity-matched athletes who did not have one. Time to return-to-play initiation and unrestricted return to play did not differ significantly after adjustment for symptom severity, although the MRI group reported higher symptom burden after injury.
tldr: In a small matched sample of collegiate athletes with concussion, a research MRI was not associated with a statistically significant change in return-to-play timelines. The confidence intervals are wide, so a meaningful delay cannot be excluded.
methods: Matched cohort analysis of the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium data, using the first concussion of athletes at four Advanced Research Core sites (Fall 2014 to Spring 2020). Nearest-neighbour propensity matching on sex, prior concussion, injury situation and site produced 45 MRI and 45 non-MRI athletes, and symptoms were measured with SCAT total symptom severity and BSI-18. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models estimated MRI status effects on days to return-to-play initiation and unrestricted return to play, adjusted for SCAT total symptom severity.
findings: Median days to return-to-play initiation were 10 (IQR 7 to 15) with MRI and 7 (IQR 4 to 9) without (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.28 to 1.21; p = 0.23). Median days to unrestricted return were 17 (IQR 11 to 60) and 12 (IQR 8 to 24) (HR 0.77; 95% CI 0.29 to 1.26; p = 0.30). Post-injury, the MRI group had higher SCAT total symptom severity (median 38 vs 21; p = 0.01) and higher SCAT nervous/anxious ratings (p = 0.04), but BSI-18 anxiety and global severity did not differ significantly.
limitations: The Table 3 confidence intervals are symmetric around the hazard ratios on the linear scale (0.75 plus or minus 0.47; 0.77 plus or minus 0.48) rather than on the log scale, which suggests they were computed on the HR scale; the exact bounds should be treated with caution. The order of MRI and symptom assessment was not recorded, so higher post-injury symptoms cannot be attributed to the scan or the injury, and post-injury scores are described as collected under 24 h in the tables but as over 24 h in the discussion. The matched sample was small (45 pairs from 2,072 eligible), 82% male and limited to NCAA high-contact sports.
practicalImplications: Staff planning a research MRI after concussion can note that this matched study found no statistically significant change in return-to-play timelines, but the intervals do not exclude a large delay. The authors suggest measuring anxiety at the time of the scan in future work, since the MRI group had higher post-injury symptom scores and the study could not show whether the scan or the injury caused them.
athleteDev: Not a performance study. It addresses concussion recovery in collegiate athletes and does not measure training, performance or load outcomes.
rtp: Relevant to return-to-play timing, but limited: it found no statistically significant difference in days to return-to-play initiation or unrestricted return between MRI and matched non-MRI athletes, with wide confidence intervals. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play criterion, to judge whether MRI findings should change clearance, or to show that MRI is clinically necessary, and the authors do not recommend mandating MRI.

citation: Han, D.H., McDuff, D., Thompson, D., Hitchcock, M.E., Reardon, C.L., Hainline, B. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in elite athletes: a narrative review. Br J Sports Med. 2019.
abstract: Narrative review of ADHD in elite athletes covering symptoms, comorbidities, effects on performance and management. The authors estimate ADHD prevalence in student and elite athletes at about 7% to 8%. They conclude that psychosocial treatment should form the foundation of management, with medication used when needed, and that prescribers must manage cardiovascular, heat and anti-doping issues.
tldr: ADHD may be more common in elite athletes than in the general population, but the evidence is narrative and mostly from non-athlete samples. The authors recommend psychosocial treatment as the base of care, with careful medication management and anti-doping compliance where stimulants are used.
methods: Narrative review. One author searched PubMed, SportDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus and Cochrane in November 2018, combined ADHD, sport participation and elite-level terms, and checked reference lists. Other literature was used where athlete-specific evidence was missing. Elite athletes were defined as professional, Olympic or collegiate competitors.
findings: The authors estimate ADHD prevalence in student and elite athletes at about 7% to 8%, and report that 101 Major League Baseball players (about 8.4%) received therapeutic use exemptions for ADHD stimulants in the 2017 to 2018 cycle, which they note probably underestimates true prevalence. They describe possible performance effects in both directions, including impulsivity and hyperfocus that may help some athletes and attention, emotional and comorbidity problems that may impair performance. They report that stimulant side effects, including heat intolerance and cardiac risk, need monitoring in athletes, and that psychosocial interventions are recommended with or without medication.
limitations: The review does not use a systematic method or a formal appraisal of study quality, and the sources are mostly general-population, child or non-athlete studies. The authors state that positive effects of ADHD on athletic performance have not been systematically studied. The link between ADHD and prolonged concussion recovery is cited to other reviews and was not assessed by the authors.
practicalImplications: Team physicians, athletic trainers and prescribers should coordinate when an athlete with ADHD takes stimulant medication, including blood pressure, hydration and heat monitoring. Staff should check the athlete's anti-doping status, since stimulants require a therapeutic use exemption where prescribed. Psychosocial support can be considered alongside or instead of medication, as the authors recommend.
athleteDev: The review notes that ADHD traits may help some athletes, for example through impulsivity or hyperfocus, while attention and emotional problems may hinder others. The authors state that these performance effects have not been systematically studied, so the review cannot guide training design or talent selection.
rtp: The review does not address return to sport after injury. It may inform medication safety checks, such as heat and cardiovascular risk for an athlete taking stimulants, but it does not provide evidence on concussion recovery or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Vander Vegt CB, Register-Mihalik JK, Ford CB, Rodrigo CJ, Guskiewicz KM, Mihalik JP. Baseline Concussion Clinical Measures Are Related to Sensory Organization and Balance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(2):264-270.
abstract: This cross-sectional analysis of baseline concussion assessments in 207 NCAA Division I varsity athletes tested whether symptom severity, concussion history, sex and CNS Vital Signs neurocognitive domains were associated with Sensory Organization Test (SOT) balance scores. Reaction time and executive function were associated with the composite and vestibular ratio scores, and reaction time was associated with the visual ratio score. Symptom severity, concussion history and sex were not significant contributors.
tldr: At baseline, athletes with faster reaction times and better executive function had better SOT balance, but these cognitive measures explained only a modest share of balance differences. Symptom severity, concussion history and sex did not add to the models.
methods: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of pre-season baseline symptom checklists, CNS Vital Signs and SOT results from varsity athletes at one NCAA Division I institution, 2014 to 2016. Symptom severity was split at the 75th percentile (high group at a score of 5 or more). Stepwise linear regression models entered sex and concussion history first, then symptom level and the CNS Vital Signs domains representing processing speed, attention and memory, with Bonferroni alpha set at 0.017.
findings: After sex, concussion history and symptom level were entered, reaction time added 11% of the variance in the composite score and executive function added a further 6% (final model R2 = 0.18). Reaction time and executive function were both significant in the vestibular model (R2 = 0.14). Reaction time alone was significantly associated with the visual ratio (R2 = 0.09; final model R2 = 0.10), and no predictor was significant for the somatosensory ratio. Sex, concussion history and symptom level were not significant in any model.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional and uses baseline data only, so the findings do not show how these relationships change after concussion or predict injury. The sample came from one university, was mostly male and mostly played contact or collision sports, and the authors state that clinical application may be limited by the small explained variance.
practicalImplications: Baseline reaction time and executive function from CNS Vital Signs can be reviewed alongside SOT balance results when building an athlete's baseline profile. The associations are modest and cross-sectional, so they should not be used alone to label an athlete as impaired or to make a training or return-to-play decision.
athleteDev: Reaction time and executive function explain part of the balance differences between athletes, so cognitive and balance measures can be reviewed together. The authors point to balance work that challenges sensory input, such as visual occlusion, perturbations, unstable surfaces and single leg stance, but the study did not test any training intervention.
rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It examined baseline measures only, and the authors state that post-injury inferences are limited, so it does not show that balance or cognitive scores change after concussion or predict re-injury.

citation: Currie A, Gorczynski P, Rice SM, Purcell R, McAllister-Williams RH, Hitchcock ME, et al. Bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes: a narrative review. Br J Sports Med. 2019;0:1-9.
abstract: This narrative review covers bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes, including diagnosis, prevalence, impact on performance and management. The authors found little athlete-specific research, and they report that recommendations depend mainly on expert opinion and extrapolation from general population guidance.
tldr: Bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes are under-studied, and training, exercise and substance use can mask or mimic symptoms. Medication choice relies on expert opinion, with side effects such as sedation, weight gain and QTc prolongation weighed against sporting demands.
methods: Narrative review. One author searched PubMed, SportDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus and Cochrane (repeated in November 2018) for studies conducted only in current elite athletes that reported bipolar or psychotic disorders. Of 420 potential references, 12 met the criteria, and related references were added. Elite athletes were defined as competing at professional, Olympic or collegiate/university level.
findings: No reliable prevalence data exist for bipolar or psychotic disorders in elite athletes, and schizophrenia appears under-represented. Exercise can mask or normalise overactivity in mania, and anabolic steroid and stimulant use can cause or confuse hypomanic or psychotic symptoms. Case reports indicate that high-profile athletes with bipolar disorder can still succeed, and the authors note a possible role for continued recreational exercise. Lithium needs careful monitoring, since sweat loss can lower levels and dehydration can raise them.
limitations: The review rests on 12 eligible references, none of them athlete-specific trials, and the authors state that recommendations are largely expert opinion extrapolated from general population guidance. Performance effects are described from case reports and small studies, and no sports-specific psychosis screening tool exists; the 16-item Prodromal Questionnaire is a general tool that the authors suggest may help.
practicalImplications: Consider a mood or psychotic disorder when an athlete shows marked changes in sleep, energy, mood or training behaviour, and do not assume extra training is only commitment, since overactivity can be hidden by training. Ask about anabolic steroid and stimulant use, and refer suspected first-episode psychosis to a specialist mental health service promptly. Medication decisions need specialist input that weighs sedation, weight gain, QTc prolongation and lithium monitoring against the athlete's sport.
athleteDev: Training can hide or normalise the overactivity of mania, and the authors note vigorous exercise may precipitate or perpetuate mania, so an athlete with bipolar disorder may be limited in how much they can safely train. The authors suggest continued recreational exercise can help, and where symptoms impair elite participation, a supported exit to a lower level of sport.
rtp: The review does not study return to sport after a bipolar or psychotic episode. It suggests a supported step down to lower-level sport when symptoms impair elite participation, and notes that some medications (such as aripiprazole with akathisia, or sedating agents) could affect motor function, so return decisions should rest on specialist mental health assessment.

citation: Iverson GL. Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Neuropathologic Change Is Not Associated With Suicide in Former Athletes. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2025;35:e70086.
abstract: This review responds to a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis that concluded suicide is a potential outcome of CTE neuropathologic change, and it re-examines the four postmortem studies that assessed suicide as a manner of death. The author argues that these studies, together with other postmortem and cohort studies, show no consistent association between CTE neuropathologic change and suicide. The author concludes that the best available evidence suggests CTE neuropathologic change is not associated with depression, suicidality or suicide.
tldr: A narrative critique argues that available postmortem and cohort studies show no link between CTE neuropathologic change and suicide in former athletes. The cited samples are small brain-donor series with mixed results, so the conclusion is a reading of limited evidence.
methods: Narrative review that re-examines the four postmortem studies used by a 2025 meta-analysis, adds other postmortem and cohort studies, and summarizes suicide outcomes in a comparison table. It is not a systematic search, and conclusions are drawn from the reported counts and percentages.
findings: The author reports that the largest included study (Daneshvar, 631 football-playing donors) found suicide less often in donors with CTE-NC (13.7% vs 26.3%, P<0.001), that McKee (2023, 152 donors under 30) found no difference (52.4% vs 60.7%), and that two small series (Suter, Taskina) showed higher rates with CTE-NC. Across the eight postmortem comparisons in Table 1, the CTE-NC group had a higher suicide rate in three, a lower rate in four and an equal rate in one; in a 336-donor study suicidality during life was 29.5% with and 33.7% without CTE-NC. The author reports that five cohort studies of former professional football or soccer players found lower or no different suicide risk than general-population men.
limitations: This is a single-author narrative critique without a systematic search, and the author discloses forensic consulting on mild TBI and suicide and NFL research funding. Some numbers do not reconcile: the Iverson (2023) row of Table 1 lists 10 CTE-NC cases although the text says that study had no definitive CTE-NC and these 10 had only 'features', the Bieniek row likewise pools CTE-NC with features, and the reported odds ratio for Daneshvar (0.64, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.71) does not match the raw counts. Brain-donor series cannot estimate risk in living athletes.
practicalImplications: When athletes raise concern about CTE and suicide, the author advises conveying the Concussion in Sport Group position that it is not known whether CTE-NC causes specific psychiatric problems, and instilling hope that depression and suicidality improve with treatment. The reviewed evidence does not support presenting suicide as a known outcome of CTE-NC.
athleteDev: No direct performance application: the review concerns mental health and neuropathology in former athletes, not training or performance.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport, since the review does not study concussion recovery or return to play. Its relevance is to former athletes with repeated head impacts who raise concern about CTE, where the author advises conveying the knowledge gap rather than a firm answer.

citation: Wolfson DI, Kuhn AW, Kerr ZY, Brett BL, Yengo-Kahn AM, Solomon GS, et al. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy research viewed in the public domain: What makes headlines? Brain Injury. 2020;34(4):528-534.
abstract: This systematic PubMed review identified 270 CTE-in-sport publications and coded their impact factor, publication type, football discussion and conclusion. Most publications (60%) had no primary data collection. Higher Altmetric scores were linked to primary data, CTE in the title, football discussion and, among papers concluding a contact sport-CTE association, higher impact factor.
tldr: Most CTE-in-sport papers are reviews or commentaries rather than new data, and papers that link contact sport to CTE drew more online attention. Use this to understand how CTE evidence is publicized, not as evidence of CTE risk.
methods: PubMed was searched on 15 October 2018 for CTE with sport terms in the title or abstract, with no exclusions. Four authors coded publication year, impact factor, data type, sample size, CTE in title, football mention and conclusion, and Altmetric scores were collected. Analyses used Wilcoxon, chi-square and multivariable ordinal logistic regression.
findings: Of 270 publications, 60% had no primary data collection and 67% discussed American football; of the 268 with coded conclusions, 39% concluded a contact sport-CTE association. The median Altmetric score was 12 (range 0 to 3745). Adjusted odds ratios for a higher Altmetric level were 2.29 for primary data (95% CI 1.35 to 3.89), 2.35 for CTE in the title (1.41 to 3.92), 2.11 for football discussion (1.24 to 3.59) and, only among association-concluding papers, 2.11 per 3-point JIF increase (1.24 to 3.59).
limitations: Only PubMed was searched, the paper measures attention rather than scientific quality, Altmetric scores rise over time, and the authors note that coding of football mention and conclusion involved judgment. The football and JIF odds ratios are printed identically (2.11, 1.24 to 3.59) in the abstract, results and Table 2, which may be a reporting error. The text gives 19% no association and 41% neutral, but the Table 1 footnote lists 110 no-association and 51 neutral papers, the reverse.
practicalImplications: Before relying on a CTE headline, check whether the paper collects primary data or is a review or commentary. Public attention in this literature tracks positive findings and is not a measure of evidence strength.
athleteDev: This paper does not measure athlete performance or training outcomes. Its relevance to performance staff is limited to understanding how CTE claims reach athletes and coaches in the media.
rtp: This paper cannot inform return to sport decisions because it contains no athlete recovery, concussion or symptom data. It is relevant only to how staff weigh CTE media claims when discussing long-term brain health.

citation: Pichler EM, Ewers S, Ajdacic-Gross V, et al. Athletes are not at greater risk for death by suicide: A review. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023;00:1-17.
abstract: A review of the literature on suicide and suicidality in elite athletes. Many studies report lower suicide rates among professional and high-performance athletes than in the general population, and similar rates of depression and anxiety. Athletes remain exposed to specific risks, including traumatic brain injury, misuse of performance-enhancing drugs, sport-related stressors, serious injury, and the period after retirement.
tldr: Elite athletes generally have lower or similar suicide rates to the general population, but specific risks such as concussion, anabolic steroid misuse, serious injury and retirement mean they should be screened. The authors recommend a multidisciplinary approach focused on reducing suicide-related harm.
methods: Narrative review of PubMed and Embase literature to March 2022, including original studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and selected practice guidelines and consensus statements. Study selection was by consensus of two authors based on conceptual relevance, practical applicability, novelty and methodological strength, and the findings are organised by epidemiology, risk factors, specific conditions and screening recommendations.
findings: Former NFL players with five or more seasons had lower suicide mortality than the US population (SMR 0.47, 95% CI 0.24-0.82), and NCAA data showed lower suicide rates in collegiate athletes than in non-athlete students, although American football athletes had a higher suicide incidence than athletes in several other collegiate sports (RR 3.27, 95% CI 1.65-6.5). A Finnish cohort found similar suicide rates between former elite athletes and non-athletes but higher rates among power sports athletes. In a meta-analysis of 17 studies (over 7 million people, not athlete-specific), concussion or mild TBI was associated with about twice the suicide risk (RR 2.03, 95% CI 1.47-2.80), with absolute risk under 1%, and anabolic-androgenic steroid use was linked to suicide and psychiatric disorders.
limitations: The review is narrative and does not give a formal quality assessment or pooled estimate. It searched two databases and was limited to English and German publications, and narrative reviews and commentaries were used only to check references. Many included studies are cross-sectional, self-reported or not adjusted for confounders, and the evidence on chronic traumatic encephalopathy and suicide rests on case reports and small series. The title states that athletes are not at greater risk, but the body reports that some studies find higher rates in particular groups, including female athletes in one study and power sports athletes in another.
practicalImplications: Staff should screen athletes for suicide risk factors, particularly previous traumatic brain injury, anabolic steroid misuse, serious injury, chronic pain, life stressors and retirement. Coaches and staff can help by limiting unnecessary stressors, supporting connection within the team and encouraging help-seeking.
athleteDev: The review links poor performance, overtraining, toxic team environments and sport-specific stressors with mental health and suicide risk. Staff planning training loads and team culture should treat these as wellbeing risks, not only performance variables.
rtp: This review cannot set return to sport criteria, because it reports no return outcomes. It does note that serious injury, long rehabilitation, loss of competence and being replaced can increase suicide risk, so injured athletes returning to sport should also be screened for mental health.

citation: Kataveni S, Gourishetty RP, Mundada SM, Avvaru MP, Kollipara VS, Gottimukkala SP. Clenbuterol abuse in bodybuilding and athletics: unsupervised use, psychological motivations, and health consequences. Cureus. 2025;17(5):e84904.
abstract: This narrative review describes clenbuterol, a beta2-agonist developed as an asthma treatment, and its unsupervised use in bodybuilding and athletics. It covers pharmacology, animal and case-report evidence of cardiovascular and muscle harm, psychological drivers, food contamination and anti-doping rules. The authors conclude that misuse carries significant risk and call for greater public awareness, better food monitoring and safer alternatives.
tldr: Athletes and bodybuilders use clenbuterol off-label for fat loss and muscle gain, and case reports link it to myocardial infarction and myocarditis, including one case at 40 micrograms per day for a week. Treat suspected use as both a medical and an anti-doping concern, and remember that contaminated meat can cause a positive test.
methods: Narrative review. The paper does not describe a search strategy, databases, date range or inclusion criteria. It draws on pharmacology and pharmacokinetic studies, animal studies in horses, rats and other species, human trials and case reports, FDA and WADA material, and news reports of doping cases.
findings: In young healthy men, clenbuterol raised resting metabolic rate by 21% and fat oxidation by 39% (Jessen et al., 2020, as summarized). The review notes that anabolic effects are unlikely to be sustained with chronic use because of beta2-receptor desensitization. Adverse effects range from palpitations, tremor and hypokalemia to myocardial infarction, pulmonary edema and rhabdomyolysis. Anti-doping rules treat urine concentrations below 5 ng/mL as atypical findings and 5 ng/mL or above as violations. Food-contamination outbreaks are described, including about 300 cases in Spain from 1989 to 1992.
limitations: No search or selection method is reported, and much of the cited evidence comes from animals, case reports and older pharmacokinetic work. The review states that no human studies have been done in non-asthmatic adults yet cites a trial in healthy young men (reference 1, Jessen et al. 2020); it also calls clenbuterol initially created for veterinary use after describing it as developed for asthma, and gives the half-life as about 35 hours in one place and 25 to 35 hours in another. A China case total 'by the year 2025' is attributed to a 2015 reference, so that figure lacks a clear source.
practicalImplications: Ask athletes about clenbuterol and other 'fat burner' or thermogenic products, since the review reports clenbuterol in products sold for weight loss. Because the review states that athletes must prove unintentional ingestion, a positive or atypical test should trigger a documented investigation, including the possibility of contaminated meat or supplements.
athleteDev: Staff should recognize that athletes may use clenbuterol to lose fat or hold muscle, often around competition and sometimes after steroids. The review's account of psychological drivers suggests that clean-sport education should address body image and peer norms, not only the rules.
rtp: The review includes no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes and cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its relevance is limited to recognizing the cardiac harm from misuse that it describes through case reports.

citation: Thomas RJ, Timmins RG, Tofari PJ, Williams MD, Opar DA. Assessing isometric kicking force and post-match responses using the Kicker test. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
abstract: This study examined the inter-session reliability of a novel isometric Kicker test of combined hip flexion and knee extension force, and whether it could monitor force for 72 h after soccer matches. Reliability was high across sessions, and in academy soccer players Kicker force remained below baseline at 24, 48 and 72 h after matches in both limbs.
tldr: A field-based isometric test of combined hip flexion and knee extension showed good reliability, and force stayed suppressed for 72 h after matches in academy soccer players. The authors propose it as a monitoring tool once athletes are familiarised, but it was not tested against injury or return-to-play outcomes.
methods: Part A: 20 participants (13 male, 7 female; recreational or higher) completed the Kicker in three sessions across consecutive weeks, with the best of three maximal efforts per limb used; reliability was summarised with ICC, typical error, %CV and MDC95. Part B: 17 male academy soccer players were tested at baseline and at +24, +48 and +72 h after matches over three weeks, after a familiarisation week, and analysed with a linear mixed model (player as random intercept) and effect sizes.
findings: Inter-session ICC was 0.91 to 0.98 and %CV was 3.7 to 10.3 (Table 1); typical error fell from 17.6 N to 9.5 N for the preferred limb after initial exposure. After matches, Kicker force was below baseline at every time point in both limbs (preferred -10.7% at +24 h, -12.5% at +48 h, -5.8% at +72 h; non-preferred -9.2%, -9.8%, -7.8%; all p < 0.01), with effect sizes of d -0.26 to -0.43, which the authors' scale rates as small.
limitations: The abstract's post-familiarisation reliability figures (ICC above 0.95, typical error below 14 N, CV below 6%, MDC below 40 N) match the session 2 to 3 rows of Table 1; session 1 to 2 error was larger (typical error about 18 N, CV up to 10.3%, MDC95 49 N). The post-match group was a convenience sample of 17 academy players with no external load data, no testing beyond 72 h, unexplained outliers, and reliability measured in a different, older recreational cohort; the device was supplied free of charge by its manufacturer.
practicalImplications: The Kicker takes under 5 minutes per athlete, and a familiarisation session is needed because error fell after the first session. The authors suggest that after familiarisation, changes beyond the 5.3% CV, or beyond the MDC95 of 26 to 38 N, can be treated as real, and that post-match deviations could guide shooting or sprinting volume for 72 h after a match; this use was not tested.
athleteDev: Use the Kicker after a familiarisation block to track force against an individual baseline, treating changes beyond the MDC95 (26 to 38 N for sessions 2 to 3) as meaningful. The evidence is from healthy recreational and academy soccer players, and does not show that the test predicts injury or sets training thresholds.
rtp: Not validated for return to sport. Only healthy players were tested, so the study cannot set return-to-kicking or return-to-play criteria; the authors suggest a possible future role in kicking progressions after rectus femoris injury, which was not studied.

citation: Lin YC, Price K, Carmichael D, Maniar N, Hickey J, Timmins RG, et al. Assessing the Validity of Wearable Inertial Sensors in Evaluating Joint Kinetics and Hamstring Musculotendon Mechanics at Various Running Speeds. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025 (published ahead of print).
abstract: This validation study compared inertial measurement unit (IMU) and optical motion capture (OMC) estimates of sagittal-plane joint moments and hamstring musculotendon mechanics in 18 healthy adults running on a treadmill at 70% to 100% of maximal speed. The authors report close waveform agreement overall, with better agreement for knee than hip moments, and an IMU overestimate of peak hip extension moment at higher speeds.
tldr: Wearable IMUs combined with musculoskeletal modelling reproduced optical-capture knee moments and hamstring strain and velocity waveforms well during treadmill running in healthy adults. Peak hip extension moment was overestimated more as speed rose, and peak hamstring force limits of agreement were wide for BFLH and SM, so the method needs checking before field use.
methods: Eighteen healthy, recreationally active adults ran on an instrumented treadmill at six speeds from 70% to 100% of their maximal speed, with simultaneous Vicon and Xsens data and hamstring EMG. Two participant-specific OpenSim models (one per system) were used for inverse dynamics and muscle force estimation, and agreement was assessed with RMSE, NRMSE, CMC, Bland-Altman analysis and linear mixed models of RMSE against speed. Joint moments and muscle forces were compared over the swing phase only.
findings: Median CMC was above 0.96 for hip and knee moments in swing, and 0.88 to 0.98 for hamstring muscle forces; hamstring strain and velocity CMC were above 0.98 at all speeds. The IMU system overestimated peak hip extension moment, with bias rising from 0.12 Nm/kg at 80% speed to 0.47 Nm/kg at maximal speed, and overestimated peak knee flexion moment by 0.07 to 0.15 Nm/kg. Limits of agreement for peak hamstring force were wider for BFLH and SM (above 0.57 BW) than for BFSH and ST (above 0.16 BW).
limitations: Only one IMU system (Xsens) and one optical system (Vicon) were tested, using the manufacturer's own Kalman filter for IMU joint angles, and separate musculoskeletal models were built for each system. Comparisons were restricted to swing phase on a treadmill, in recreationally active adults with a mean maximal speed of 7.44 m/s. The abstract gives the RMSE increase per 1 m/s for joint moments in N/m, but the results report it in Nm/kg (0.23 for hip, 0.04 for knee); the results values are used here, and the peak hip moment bias is given as 0.47 Nm/kg at maximal speed in the results but 0.49 Nm/kg at 95% speed in the discussion.
practicalImplications: The results support using this IMU approach for knee flexion moment and hamstring strain waveforms during running, where agreement was excellent. Peak hip extension moment bias grew with speed (above 10% of the optical value from 85% speed), and peak lengthening velocity was systematically overestimated for BFLH, SM and ST, so staff should validate these outputs in their own set-up before comparing athletes or setting loading targets.
athleteDev: IMU-based estimates of hamstring strain and knee moment tracked optical capture well across running speeds in healthy adults, which supports their use as a trend measure of sprint mechanics. Peak hip moment and peak BFLH and SM force carry wide limits of agreement (hip up to about 1.5 Nm/kg; BFLH and SM force 0.57 to 1.2 BW), so they should not be used for absolute load comparisons between athletes without local validation.
rtp: Not designed for return to sport. The sample was healthy and recreationally active, with no injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes. The hamstring late-swing focus relates to injury risk, but the study does not test whether these estimates track injury, healing or readiness to return to running.

citation: Bache-Mathiesen LK, Andersen TE, Dalen-Lorentsen T, Clarsen B, Fagerland MW. Assessing the cumulative effect of long-term training load on the risk of injury in team sports. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2022;8:e001342.
abstract: This study set out to determine how to assess the cumulative effect of training load on injury or health problem risk in team sports. A simulation based on a football dataset compared seven modelling methods, and the best-performing method, a distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM), was then illustrated on a youth handball cohort.
tldr: In simulated team-sport data, a distributed lag non-linear model recovered cumulative training-load effects more accurately than rolling averages, EWMA, REDI, ACWR or week-to-week change. The handball demonstration found no statistically significant effects, so the method is not yet a basis for load decisions.
methods: Simulated players were given sRPE values sampled from a 36-player Norwegian Premier League football dataset, with 250 players followed for 300 days. Seven time-dependent relationships were simulated for absolute and relative (daily %change) load, and seven methods were compared on RMSE, AIC and 95% CI coverage over 1900 simulations. The DLNM was then fitted to 205 Norwegian elite youth handball players (471 self-reported health problems; 64% of sRPE values missing and imputed) using Cox regression adjusted for sex and age, with a frailty term for recurrent events.
findings: For absolute load, DLNM had the lowest external RMSE in every scenario (1.44 vs 4.77 to 5.53 under the constant scenario; 0.76 vs 1.88 to 2.13 under exponential decay) and the lowest AIC in almost all simulations. EWMA outperformed rolling average under decay scenarios, and no method recovered the direct-then-inverse relationship. In the handball data, high sRPE (above 4000 AU) was associated with a hazard ratio of about 1.2 or more on the current day, with high uncertainty; none of the effects were significant (p >= 0.8).
limitations: The simulated relationships were chosen by the authors, and the simulation assumed day-to-day differences matter, which favoured DLNM for relative load. The handball analysis had poor data quality, few covariates and no causal design, and the authors caution that the effects may be spurious. Only seven methods and a limited set of ACWR variants were compared.
practicalImplications: When analysing cumulative training load and injury or illness in team sports, a distributed lag model can show how load magnitude and time since exposure interact, which rolling averages and single ratios cannot. For absolute load, the authors describe EWMA as a simpler alternative when the aim is to adjust for training load rather than estimate its effect. The handball output should not be read as a load threshold because none of its effects were significant.
athleteDev: For analysts modelling load and injury data, the simulation favours DLNM, and EWMA over rolling averages or REDI, for absolute load; ACWR and week-to-week change failed to detect the simulated relationship in some scenarios. It is a statistical methods comparison, not evidence for specific training load thresholds, and the handball example did not show a significant link between load and health problems.
rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study models self-reported health problems in team-sport squads and does not use rehabilitation or return-to-play data, so it cannot set return-to-play load criteria.

citation: Timmerman WP, Abbiss CR, Lawler NG, Stanley M, Raynor AJ. Athlete monitoring perspectives of sports coaches and support staff: A scoping review. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024:1-20.
abstract: A scoping review of 42 studies that explored the perspectives of sports coaches and support staff on athlete monitoring. Most studies were from the Anglosphere and involved national or international level teams. Coaches and staff most often monitored to reduce injury and illness, inform training and maintain performance, and they valued monitoring while emphasising communication and the limits of quantification.
tldr: Coaches and support staff generally see athlete monitoring as useful for managing injury, training and performance, but they say no single scientific approach is perfect and that conversation with athletes remains essential. The evidence is largely self-reported perspectives from a narrow set of countries and levels.
methods: Scoping review following the JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR, searching SPORTDiscus, MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo and Embase up to 6 September 2022. Two reviewers screened records and full texts, one author charted data, and frequency analysis was combined with topic summaries of qualitative findings. No formal quality appraisal was done.
findings: Of 4,381 records, 42 studies met the criteria, and 55% (23 of 42) were published since 2020. Training load was the most studied focus (11 of 42 studies). Of the 23 studies reporting purposes, the most common were reducing injury and illness (12), informing training (8) and improving or maintaining performance (8). Expected effectiveness was significantly higher than perceived effectiveness in one football study (Akenhead and Nassis, 2016), and sex or gender was reported in only 18 of 42 studies, with women averaging 16% of samples.
limitations: Most studies were in English-speaking countries and at national or international level, and few reported participant characteristics clearly. Terms such as elite were not defined, and the review did not separate perspectives by role or athlete level. The search omitted some terms (for example medical staff and assess or evaluate), and data were charted by one reviewer.
practicalImplications: Staff who plan monitoring should expect coaches and support staff to value subjective information and regular conversation with athletes alongside objective data, and to cite time, expertise, resources and buy-in as the main barriers. Where expected and perceived effectiveness were compared (football staff, and gymnastics coaches and medical staff), perceived effectiveness of training load monitoring was lower than expected, which supports checking how monitoring data are actually used rather than assuming value.
athleteDev: Coaches in the included studies reported using athlete self-report measures as a conversation starter and early alert, and combining load data with athlete feedback and coach observation when adjusting training. The review describes these practices but does not test whether any monitoring approach improves performance.
rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. It summarises coach and staff perceptions of monitoring and does not report injured athletes, return timelines or return outcomes.

citation: Snegireva, N., Derman, W., Patricios, J., Welman, K.E. Awareness and Perceived Value of Eye Tracking Technology for Concussion Assessment among Sports Medicine Clinicians: A Multinational Study. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2020;48(2):165-172.
abstract: Cross-sectional online survey of 171 sports medicine clinicians from 32 countries on their awareness and use of eye tracking for concussion assessment and their views on its value. Few clinicians had used eye tracking, most relied on their own clinical assessment, and about half saw potential benefit in the technology. The authors call for more education and practical experience with concussion assessment tools.
tldr: Few sports medicine clinicians had used eye tracking for concussion, and most relied on standard clinical assessment. About half saw potential benefit, mainly for its objectivity and ease of use.
methods: Cross-sectional online survey (18 questions, Google Forms) distributed by email to sports medicine associations and through LinkedIn, Twitter and conference channels from January to December 2017. Responses came from 171 clinicians in 32 countries, most often sport physicians (46%), with therapists, general practitioners, neuropsychologists and other medical practitioners. Analyses were descriptive, with chi-squared tests for associations between profession and familiarity, and between eye tracking experience and perceived benefit.
findings: Eleven percent of respondents had experience working with eye tracking, 66% had heard of it but never used it, and 88% did not use it in practice. Seventy-seven percent used no eye movement assessment tool beyond their own clinical assessment, and 20% did not check for any eye movement deficit; those who did check reported at least one deficit in 29.9% of concussed patients on average. Profession was associated with familiarity (chi-squared p = 0.004), and eye tracking experience was associated with perceived benefit (chi-squared p = 0.015).
limitations: The response rate could not be determined, so non-response and selection bias cannot be ruled out, and self-report may be affected by social desirability. The abstract reports eye tracking use by 12% (consistent with 88% non-use), but only 5% (n = 8) named an eye tracking device or saccadometer as a tool they use to diagnose concussion, so use figures depend on which question is read. The sample was small and mostly from South Africa, Europe and North America, so the authors could not compare regions.
practicalImplications: Clinicians should note that the survey shows low awareness of eye movement deficits after concussion and a lack of access to eye tracking equipment. Education and hands-on exposure to eye tracking may be needed before clinicians can judge its value. The paper does not show that eye tracking improves diagnosis, so it should not be used to justify changes to concussion protocols.
athleteDev: This survey addresses concussion assessment among clinicians and does not measure athletic performance or training. It cannot inform athlete development.
rtp: The study does not test eye tracking as a return-to-play tool and reports no diagnostic accuracy data. It can show how clinicians currently assess concussion and which tool limitations they report, but it cannot support an eye tracking return-to-play protocol.

citation: Glazer AK, Parast L, Hooten MB. Beyond the Yard Line: Accommodating Rounded Sports Data in Statistical Models. The American Statistician. 2025.
abstract: Recorded American football yardage is a whole number produced by a floor-based rounding of line-of-scrimmage and downed-spot positions, and it can be negative and strongly right-skewed. The authors build parametric models that treat the true yardage as unrounded, derive the discrete probability mass function for the recorded data, and compare rounded-normal and rounded asymmetric Laplace models using 2023 NFL running back data.
tldr: Recorded rushing yards are rounded, can be negative, and are right-skewed, so standard continuous models can mislead. In 2023 NFL running back data, a rounded asymmetric Laplace model fit better than a rounded normal model and changed which players and covariates looked important.
methods: Bayesian models with a discrete likelihood derived from a floor-rounding transformation were fitted by MCMC. A single-player model (Bijan Robinson, 193 carries) and a hierarchical model with a player random intercept (133 running backs, 10,223 carries) were compared using posterior predictive checks and DIC. Covariates included down, yards to go, line of scrimmage, score differential, game seconds remaining, rest, opponent rushing EPA, home-field status and travel distance.
findings: The rounded normal model failed posterior predictive checks for skewness and kurtosis (p of 0.001 or less), while the rounded asymmetric Laplace model did not (p of 0.06 and 0.09), and it had lower DIC in both analyses. In the hierarchical model the authors report 8 of 12 fixed effects with credible intervals not overlapping zero under the asymmetric Laplace model (one, down squared, only nearly so) versus 5 of 12 under the normal model, and C. McCaffrey fell from 2nd to 17th in the player random-intercept ranking.
limitations: The authors assume yardlines are always rounded down, but NFL record-keeping sometimes differs, and some 1-yard-to-go plays (4.7% of 2023 plays are recorded as 1 yard to go) can erase physical gains. Only rushing was modeled, true unrounded yardage was not observed because ball-tracking data were unavailable, and the analysis covers one season with no external validation.
practicalImplications: Analysts who build player-evaluation or yardage models from recorded NFL yardage can use the rounded models described here to avoid treating whole-number, skewed yardage as continuous normal data. Model choice changed some player rankings and covariate conclusions in this sample, so sensitivity checks against a skewed base distribution are worth running.
athleteDev: Performance Application: Applicable to analysis of running back rushing performance data. The paper supports choosing a skewed, discrete model for recorded yards per carry. Its covariate findings (for example, game seconds remaining or yards to go) are model associations from one NFL season and are not coaching prescriptions.
rtp: Not applicable. The paper models recorded rushing yardage in healthy professional players and does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport.

citation: Murray NB, Gabbett TJ, Townshend AD, Blanch P. Calculating acute:chronic workload ratios using exponentially weighted moving averages provides a more sensitive indicator of injury likelihood than rolling averages. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(9):749-754.
abstract: Compared rolling-average and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) models and their link to non-contact time-loss injury in 59 elite AFL players over two seasons using GPS data. EWMA ACWR values were significantly lower than rolling-average values at moderate, high and very high ranges, and ACWR above 2.0 was associated with higher injury risk under both models, with EWMA explaining more of the injury variance.
tldr: In elite AFL players, the EWMA ACWR gave lower values than rolling averages at moderate to very high ranges and explained more injury variance. Both models linked very high ACWR spikes (above 2.0) to higher injury risk, so the spike signal is the more solid finding.
methods: Two-season cohort of 59 AFL players from one club (92 individual seasons), with 10 Hz GPS workloads for six variables and non-contact time-loss injuries recorded by club medical staff. ACWR was calculated with rolling 7-day and 28-day averages and with EWMA, and binary logistic regression modelled injury against ACWR range.
findings: ACWR above 2.0 was associated with higher injury risk under both models for several variables, for example in-season total distance (rolling average RR 6.52, 95% CI 4.83 to 8.80; EWMA RR 21.28, 95% CI 20.02 to 22.62), each compared with an ACWR of 1.0 to 1.49. The EWMA model gave significantly lower ACWR values than rolling averages at moderate (1.07 vs 1.19), high (1.27 vs 1.64) and very high (1.51 vs 2.29) ranges, and explained more of the variance in injury for total distance (preseason R2 0.87 vs 0.21; in-season 0.78 vs 0.40).
limitations: One club, 59 players and 40 injuries limit generalisation, and the authors note possible type I error from multiple models and small samples above 2.0. The abstract gives a high-speed distance RR range of 5.87 to 13.43, but the Results give 4.66 for rolling-average high-speed distance and 5.87 and 13.43 for player load, so the Results values are used here. The Methods name the 2.0 or above group as reference, while the Results compare against 1.0 to 1.49.
practicalImplications: Treat an ACWR above 2.0 on total distance as a spike to review, since it was the one variable linked to higher non-contact injury risk under both models in both preseason and in-season; under EWMA the same held for moderate-speed distance and player load. Confirm which calculation method a monitoring system uses, because the rolling-average and EWMA values differed for the same day and could place a player in a different risk band.
athleteDev: Use acute:chronic ratios on total distance (and, with EWMA, player load and moderate-speed distance) to flag large workload spikes. The authors also advise building chronic load so acute increases stay moderate, but this study did not test that strategy, and the EWMA method should not replace the rolling-average method as a club standard on the strength of one squad.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It tracked non-contact time-loss injuries in squad training and matches and did not assess rehabilitation, readiness or return-to-play decisions.

citation: Harper DJ, Cohen DD, Carling C, Kiely J. Can countermovement jump neuromuscular performance qualities differentiate maximal horizontal deceleration ability in team sport athletes? Sports. 2020;8:76.
abstract: Cross-sectional study of 27 male university team-sport athletes who performed a 20 m sprint followed by a maximal horizontal deceleration, measured by radar, and a countermovement jump on force plates. Athletes split at the median on average deceleration (HDEC) or horizontal braking impulse (HBI) differed in several CMJ eccentric and concentric variables, with force variables standing out for HDEC and velocity variables for HBI. Only concentric mean power differed for both measures.
tldr: Concentric force and power from a countermovement jump separated university team-sport athletes with higher from lower horizontal deceleration ability. Average deceleration and braking impulse pointed to different jump profiles, so both should be reported when profiling deceleration.
methods: Cross-sectional design in which 27 male university athletes completed a 20 m sprint and a maximal horizontal deceleration test measured by radar (47 Hz), and five CMJs on dual portable force plates (1000 Hz). Athletes were median-split into high and low HDEC and separately into high and low HBI groups, and CMJ variables were compared with independent-samples t-tests and Cohen's ds with 90% CIs. Test-retest CV was 4.3% for HDEC and 3.7% for HBI.
findings: The high HDEC group had higher concentric peak force (25.87 vs 23.53 N/kg, p=0.02, ds=0.95), concentric mean force (20.07 vs 18.86 N/kg, p=0.03) and concentric mean power (28.72 vs 25.92 W/kg, p=0.04, ds=0.85). Eccentric peak force was higher but not significant (24.66 vs 22.89 N/kg, p=0.07, ds=0.72). For HBI, the high group had higher concentric peak velocity (2.76 vs 2.52 m/s, p=0.01, ds=1.15), concentric peak power (52.39 vs 45.98 W/kg, p=0.01), concentric mean power (28.76 vs 25.67 W/kg, p=0.02) and CMJ height (36.8 vs 29.9 cm, p=0.01), and a faster (more negative) eccentric peak velocity (-1.30 vs -1.10 m/s, p=0.02). High HBI athletes were heavier (85.2 vs 68.1 kg).
limitations: Cross-sectional design, 27 young male university athletes with 13 to 14 per group, and no test of whether training changes deceleration. The Results text gives concentric peak power as -52.39 W/kg, while Table 4 gives 52.39, and the Discussion gives concentric peak velocity as 2.72 m/s and eccentric peak force as 22.69 N/kg, while Tables 3 and 4 give 2.76 and 22.89. The Figure 3 text gives a concentric peak force effect size of 0.52 (Table 3: 0.95), and the group body masses in Table 2 do not average to the 73.0 kg reported for the whole sample; table values are used here. Many comparisons were run without correction, and the authors note the sample is not representative of female athletes or other sports.
practicalImplications: When profiling horizontal deceleration, record both average deceleration and braking impulse, since in this sample they separated athletes on different CMJ variables and braking impulse depends on body mass. Concentric mean power was the one CMJ variable that differed between groups on both measures, so it may be a useful snapshot of neuromuscular capacity for deceleration.
athleteDev: Use the CMJ as a monitoring snapshot alongside sprint-to-deceleration testing, and record body mass, since heavier athletes carry more approach momentum. The paper's suggested training changes, such as accentuated eccentric loading or fast eccentric squats, were not tested here and should be treated as hypotheses.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. Participants were university athletes with no musculoskeletal injury in the previous three months, and the study did not assess injured athletes or readiness after injury.

citation: Oxendale CL, Highton J, Smith G, Twist C. Can player tracking devices monitor changes in internal response during multidirectional running? Res Q Exerc Sport. 2023;94(4):975-981.
abstract: Compared movement, physiological and muscle function responses to linear and multidirectional running in 12 team-sport athletes. Multidirectional running gave more accelerations, more time at high metabolic power, higher summated heart rate and higher bout 8 blood lactate, while linear running gave more high-speed distance. Ratios using time at high metabolic power did not differ significantly between trials, whereas high-speed ratios did, and the authors conclude that time at high metabolic power better reflects the internal response to multidirectional running.
tldr: In 12 team-sport athletes, multidirectional running raised summated heart rate and late blood lactate despite less high-speed distance than linear running. Ratios of time at high metabolic power to internal load did not differ significantly between trials while high-speed ratios did, which the authors read as high metabolic power better reflecting the internal response; this is a small, single-session comparison.
methods: Repeated-measures study with two trials (linear, 3 x 35 m sprints with jogs; and multidirectional, with accelerations, decelerations, sprinting, backward and lateral running) of eight 60 s bouts with 120 s rest, on an outdoor track, in random order. An OptimEye S5 GPS unit (10 Hz) recorded external load; heart rate, VO2 and blood lactate were recorded as internal responses, with isometric knee peak torque before and after each trial. External:internal ratios were compared with paired t-tests and effect sizes.
findings: Multidirectional running produced more accelerations (48.3 vs 7.2) and decelerations (38.8 vs 3.8) than linear running (p<0.001), and more time at high metabolic power (118.4 vs 111.5 s, p=0.046). Summated heart rate (78.1 vs 69.1 AU, p=0.003) and bout 8 blood lactate (10.2 vs 8.2 mmol/L, p=0.002) were higher in the multidirectional trial, while high-speed distance was higher in the linear trial (677.2 vs 416.5 m, p<0.001). Total VO2 did not differ significantly (46.9 vs 44.2 L, p=0.087). Ratios for high-speed running against summated heart rate and total VO2 differed between trials (p<=0.001), while ratios for high metabolic power against these internal measures were similar (p>=0.246). Peak knee extensor and flexor torque fell after both trials (p=0.004 and p=0.003, small effects), with similar falls between trials.
limitations: Twelve athletes, pooled across sexes and sports, with the same participants and data collection as an earlier report by the same group, although these variables were not previously reported.
