Only one trial per condition was run, running technique was not controlled, the multidirectional trial lasted longer (1428 vs 1382 s), and GPS repeatability for acceleration and deceleration counts is less certain than for distance. The ratio results are non-significant differences, not evidence of equivalence, and no metric was compared against a criterion measure.
practicalImplications: When monitoring multidirectional sessions, do not rely on high-speed distance alone, since it was much lower in the multidirectional trial even though heart rate and blood lactate were higher. Time at high metabolic power can be used alongside high-speed distance, with the caution that this study gives only a small, single-session comparison.
athleteDev: Use time at high metabolic power, together with heart rate or blood lactate where available, to judge the internal demand of multidirectional drills and games, rather than high-speed distance alone. Treat the threshold choice as a practical convention, since the study did not test whether the 20 W/kg cut-off predicts individual responses better than other settings.
rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It recruited university athletes and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play decisions. The authors suggest the metric might help when moving from linear to multidirectional work after injury, but this was not tested.

citation: Sugisaki N, Tsuchie H, Takai Y, Kobayashi K, Yoshimoto T, Kanehisa H. Causes of Different Force-Velocity Relationships in Sprint Running Depending on Horizontal Loads and Profiling Methods. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025;57(5):1032-1042.
abstract: This study clarified how the horizontal force-velocity relationship in overground sprint running differs with horizontal resistance loads and with profiling methods (multiple-trial and single-trial). Twelve males sprinted unresisted and with five resistance loads while ground reaction forces were recorded on a 50-m force plate system. Force-velocity plots overlapped during acceleration but deviated to lower forces near maximal velocity, the single-trial linear parameters depended on load, and the multiple-trial linear relationship was biased toward lower forces with less negative slopes. Curvilinear models fitted the pooled data better, while the unresisted linear relationship was almost linear.
tldr: Using a 50-m force plate, the sprint force-velocity profile changed with resistance load and with profiling method. The authors recommend the single-trial method with a linear fit to unresisted sprinting over the multiple-trial method for over-ground sprint profiling.
methods: Twelve males each completed six sprints: one unresisted and five resisted at 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 kg, pulled by a motorized loading device, in ascending load order with at least 5 minutes of rest between trials. Horizontal and vertical ground reaction forces were sampled at 1000 Hz, and step-averaged force-velocity profiles were built with single-trial and multiple-trial methods and fitted with linear, Hill's equation and second-order polynomial models.
findings: Force-velocity plots overlapped across loads during acceleration, but horizontal force dropped near maximal velocity. With the single-trial method, F0 rose and the slope became more negative with heavier loads (unresisted F0 7.26 N/kg, 12 kg 8.67 N/kg), while Pmax did not differ significantly. The multiple-trial method gave lower F0 (6.08 N/kg), lower Pmax and a less negative slope (-0.60 vs -0.71 N/kg per m/s) than the unresisted single-trial method, and curvilinear models fitted the pooled data better (adjusted R2 0.986 to 0.987) than a linear fit to the pooled data (0.977) or the unresisted linear profile (0.964).
limitations: This study used 12 men (nine sprinters and three soccer players) and a fixed ascending load order, and the authors could not measure fatigue, so they cannot exclude a fatigue effect on the force drop near maximal velocity. Only step-averaged values were analysed, and intra-step and stance-averaged analyses were not done. The curvilinear models have more parameters, so part of their better fit reflects extra degrees of freedom, and some participants had very high F0 values (up to 12.3 N/kg).
practicalImplications: For over-ground sprint profiling with force plates, follow the authors' recommendation to use the unresisted single-trial method with a linear fit, rather than fitting loaded trials at maximal velocity. Force-velocity values from different profiling methods are not interchangeable, so F0 and slope values should not be compared across studies that used different methods. Loaded sprints should not be assumed to reproduce the profile of unresisted sprints, particularly at very low velocities.
athleteDev: The authors suggest the unresisted single-trial linear profile is the more practical choice for profiling sprint force-velocity, because its fit is close to the curvilinear fits. The paper does not measure performance, and its performance links (v0 and Pmax, not F0) come from earlier studies it cites.
rtp: This study does not address injury or return to sport, and its participants were male sprinters and soccer players. It cannot be used to judge rehabilitation or return-to-play readiness from loaded sprint force data.

citation: Ellens S, Carey D, Gastin P, Varley MC. Changing the criteria applied to acceleration and deceleration efforts changes the types of player actions detected. Science and Medicine in Football. 2022.
abstract: Acceleration and deceleration efforts of 22 elite Australian football players across two matches were labeled with the player action at the time, using synchronized video and 10-Hz GNSS data. Linear movement and jumps were most common in high accelerations, and stops and tackles in high decelerations. The authors report that higher commencing speed was linked to longer durations above the deceleration threshold.
tldr: In elite Australian football, high accelerations were mostly linear running and high decelerations mostly stops and contact actions, and the actions captured shift with the minimum duration above threshold. The authors suggest a dwell time of at least 0.5 s if the goal is to count linear accelerations.
methods: Efforts above plus or minus 3 m/s2 were detected from filtered 10-Hz GNSS data for 22 players, and each effort was labeled with one of 15 player actions by manual video coding in Hudl Sportscode. Linear mixed models with player and game random effects tested commencing speed by action and commencing speed against effort duration.
findings: High accelerations were mostly linear movement (about 5 per player per match) and jumps, and high decelerations were mostly stops (about 10 per player per match), being tackled (6) and tackling (4). Commencing speed differed by action only for decelerations, with jumps (+14%, P=.022) and tackles (+17%, P=.003) starting faster than stops, and each 1 m/s higher commencing speed added 0.14 s above the deceleration threshold (95% CI 0.12 to 0.16). Most high accelerations exceeded the threshold for 0.3 s or less (228 of 268 by the reported counts), while about half of decelerations did.
limitations: Two matches from one elite team, a single absolute 3 m/s2 threshold, and device validity taken from manufacturer testing only. Reported numbers do not fully reconcile: 46 efforts per player per match across 22 players and two matches does not match the 1,178 total, the duration counts sum to 1,172, and the Discussion states that most deceleration efforts lasted 0.3 s or less although the counts put about half there. The 0.5 s recommendation for linear movement is read from a histogram, not tested, and only about 30 acceleration efforts lasted 0.5 s or more.
practicalImplications: Choose the minimum duration above threshold to match the actions of interest, because the mix of detected actions changes with it. The authors also recommend training accelerations and decelerations across a range of commencing speeds; this follows from the speed spread observed but was not tested as a training intervention.
athleteDev: If the aim is to count linear accelerations, a longer minimum duration (the authors suggest 0.5 s) helps exclude jumps and other actions. Set the minimum duration to match the action of interest rather than accepting the software default.
rtp: Not applicable: this is match profiling in healthy elite players with no injury or return-to-play outcome. The link between high decelerations and muscle damage that the authors cite comes from other work and was not tested here.

citation: Geneau MC, Gastin PB, Robertson S, James LP. Classification of lower body strength qualities: A data-driven approach. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2025:1-24.
abstract: This systematic review grouped lower-body extensor strength metrics from multi-joint, weight-bearing tests by how much variance they share. The authors propose five domains of lower-body strength: reactive dynamic, unloaded dynamic, loaded dynamic, early isometric and maximal isometric. They call for more empirical work to test these domains before they are used in practice.
tldr: Lower-body strength metrics appear to fall into five groups that measure different things, which may help choose a smaller test battery. Treat the grouping as a proposal: the relationships depend on how each metric is calculated, and no single study has tested the full classification.
methods: Systematic search (September 2024) of Google Scholar, MEDLINE, SportDiscus, Cochrane and CINAHL, English language, no date limit, with reference-list checks. Included studies assessed multi-joint, vertical, dynamic or isometric lower-body tests in athletes or resistance-trained people and compared metrics statistically. Metrics were classified by muscle action, external load and time constraint, then compared within and across categories, with 49% or more shared variance (r of 0.70 or more) treated as similar. No meta-analysis was performed.
findings: Within most task categories, metrics shared more than 50% of variance, except timing and outcome metrics in unloaded ballistic tasks, which shared about 1 to 10%. Drop and rebound jump metrics shared only about 50% of variance with other dynamic and isometric tests, and drop-jump RSI correlated with 1 to 3RM at r = 0.07 to 0.33 in absolute and r = 0.52 to 0.69 in relative values. CMJ height and peak power shared R2 from 0.07 to 0.94 across studies depending on calculation method, and the authors propose five domains while grouping unloaded ballistic timing and outcome metrics into one domain because evidence for separating them was insufficient.
limitations: The authors state that variable methods and populations limit consolidation, the 49% threshold is a simplification, most studies were cross-sectional, and highly correlated metrics can reflect different physiology. The authors say it is unclear where loaded ballistic tasks belong, yet loaded dynamic is listed as a domain, and the five domains need direct testing. The acknowledgements state the work is part of a PhD project partially funded by VALD Performance, while the funding statement reports no financial support.
practicalImplications: The authors recommend a parsimonious test battery, so choosing one test per proposed domain is a reasonable starting point to test. For drop-jump tasks, check that contact time stays under 0.25 s, and confirm how each metric is calculated before comparing values across tools or studies.
athleteDev: The domains can help decide which strength qualities a test battery covers, so that staff do not run several tests that measure the same quality. Because the domains are a proposal, confirm them with each sport's athletes before using them to set training priorities.
rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport criteria, so it cannot set return-to-play thresholds. It can only help choose lower-body strength tests, and the reactive and maximal isometric domains would need checking in injured groups before use in return-to-sport testing.
